text:
$CABO Q3 2026 earnings: Cable One loses fewer customers, but it warns of bankruptcy

Cable One, the rural internet provider behind Sparklight, is losing fewer customers while its debt problems grow more urgent. Chief executive Jim Holanda said it lost only about 7,500 home internet customers, its best result in seven quarters. But lower prices pushed revenue down 12% from a year ago. The company also wrote that it may need bankruptcy protection if it cannot refinance.

• Revenue: $𝟑𝟑𝟐.𝟐𝐌 (−11.7% from a year ago)
• Average monthly home internet bill: $𝟕𝟖.𝟒𝟖 ($82.17 a year ago)
• Ebitda, excluding one-offs: $𝟏𝟓𝟗.𝟖𝐌 (−20.8% from a year ago)
• Full-year capital spending plan: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (high-$200 millions, close to 2025)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse, because Cable One now says its cash cannot repay the debts due in 2027 and 2028. A court has also blocked its purchase of MBI, a smaller cable company. The good news: new sales channels cut customer losses by more than half. But each new customer pays less, so revenue and cash profit kept falling.

The question now is how Cable One refinances its debt. Either lenders extend the loans because the business still earns steady cash, or they set the terms in a restructuring. The November 13 court hearing and any refinancing deal will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐂𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐅𝐚𝐫 𝐅𝐞𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬
Cable One sells home internet under the Sparklight brand and has lost internet customers every quarter for two years. In the third quarter it lost about 7,500, against 17,100 in the second, which chief executive Jim Holanda called its "best residential data subscriber results in seven quarters".

Holanda credited new sales channels: door-to-door sales nearly doubled from the second quarter. Those visits plus online orders brought in 44% of new connections, against 27% a year ago. But the customer base still shrank 5% from a year ago, because each quarter more people still leave than join.

What to watch: net customer losses in the fourth quarter, reported early next year. A second quarter of smaller losses would show that the new channels, not a single good season, explain the gain.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Several newer products and sales efforts could help Cable One keep customers and lift what each one pays, but the quarter gave no figures that show their effect on revenue yet.

• Mobile phone service for Sparklight internet customers: Holanda said results are "in line with our expectations" but gave no line count; a published count would show whether bundles cut cancellations.
• Business sales: Holanda said "sold revenue increased 17% in the third quarter", meaning contracts signed but not yet billed; business revenue over the next two quarters will show how much turns into sales.
• Faster home internet: the cable operator offers multi-gigabit speeds in over half of its markets, according to its quarterly filing; a wider rollout would give it a speed edge over wireless rivals.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐌𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐫𝐮𝐩𝐭𝐜𝐲 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞
Cable One owes $3.55 billion, and most of it falls due by mid-2028. The cable operator wrote in its results release that its cash and operating cash flow will be "insufficient to repay the debt described above on the applicable maturity dates". Without a financing deal, it may need to "seek relief under Chapter 11 of the U. S. Bankruptcy Code", the release said.

• Cash on September 30: $675 million
• Bank credit line: fully drawn after a final $200 million on October 8
• Costs written off on abandoned financing deals: $7.0 million
• 2030 bonds: fair value of $122 million in its own filing, against $503 million owed

Finance chief Todd Koetje put net debt at 4.1 times Ebitda, meaning earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and one-offs, over the last four quarters. Last quarter he quoted the latest quarter times four instead. On that measure the ratio climbed to about 4.5 times by our math, from 4.2, because Ebitda keeps falling.

What to watch: a signed refinancing, which the Sparklight owner says it is still negotiating, before its 2028 loans and the MBI loans come due. Until lenders agree to extend those loans, bankruptcy remains a real possibility for the business.

🔴🔴 𝐀 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭 𝐁𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐁𝐈 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞
MBI is a regional cable company in which Cable One owns about 45%. Its other owners, led by investment firm GTCR, used an option in January that obliges the Sparklight owner to buy the rest for about $480 million. On October 9 a federal court, acting on a suit by CoBank, one of Cable One's own lenders, barred the purchase for now.

CoBank argues that paying the price would be a "constructive fraudulent transfer", a payment that harms existing creditors. GTCR now says Cable One "failed to use their reasonable best efforts to contest and resist the CoBank Action". The cable operator calls those claims without merit.

• MBI revenue: down 9.2% from a year ago
• MBI internet customers: down 7.1%, against 4.9% at Cable One
• Purchase obligation on Cable One's books: $479 million, up $53 million in the quarter
• MBI loans due in November 2027: $916 million

What to watch: the court hearing set for November 13. If the deal closes, Cable One spends cash it needs for its own debts and adds a business that loses internet customers faster than it does, with loans due within about a year.

🔴🔴 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞
Home internet brings in 61% of Cable One's revenue. Fiber networks overlap mid-to-high 50s percent of its homes, Koetje said, and wireless rivals reach nearly every market. Holanda said rival offers held down ARPU, the average monthly bill per customer: "Competitive pricing and promotional activity remained elevated and put pressure on ARPU and revenue."

The average monthly internet bill fell to $78.48 from $80.56 in the second quarter. Koetje said new customers sign up at lower prices than existing ones pay. So internet revenue dropped 10.3% from a year ago, about twice the pace at which the customer base shrank.

Koetje said of the write-downs: "These accounting charges do not impact our cash flow, liquidity, operating strategy or long-term growth initiatives." But the quarterly filing tied a $159 million cut in the value of its local cable licences to "reduced estimated future cash flows due to increased competition in certain of our markets".

What to watch: the average internet bill in the fourth quarter. Holanda expects it to settle $2 to $5 below its peak. A bill under about $77 would mean price cuts have gone past his range.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞
Holanda cited "the meaningful cash flow that continues to be generated by the business". The quarter cuts against that claim. Ebitda, meaning earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and one-offs, fell 21% from a year ago, while revenue declined 12%.

Two cost lines moved in opposite directions. Operating costs, which cover the network, software and TV programming, went from 25.5% of revenue to 29.7%, on higher software and contract labour bills. Lower pay cut overhead and sales costs by 2.0 percentage points of revenue. So the Ebitda margin lost 5.6 percentage points.

Capital spending rose 9%, mostly on modems and installation for new customers. It took 49% of Ebitda, against 36% a year ago. That leaves less cash for debt. Ebitda minus capital spending, the measure Koetje calls free cash flow, came to $81.9 million, down 37%.

What to watch: the Ebitda margin in the fourth quarter, the first after an early retirement offer to staff. If it keeps falling, cost cuts are not keeping pace with the lower prices.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐑𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Holanda described rivals whose prices change month to month. He agreed that providers raised prices at the start of the fourth quarter, but said the increase "lasted all of 30 days near as I can tell". He also pointed to "surge pricing" at Starlink, the satellite service. His answer is to sell gigabit speeds at a steady price, because wireless and satellite rivals cannot match them.

𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐦
On July 1 Cable One handed its advertising sales to an outside company. It now books that revenue after the agency's fee, so advertising revenue fell about $2.8 million from a year ago, Koetje said. Its costs fell in step, "largely offset by lower costs" in his words. Part of the revenue drop therefore reflects bookkeeping, not lost customers.

𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐞𝐟 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫
Cable One hired Heather McCallion as chief operating officer, plus three senior vice presidents for operations and customer service. Holanda also announced "an early retirement offering launched this quarter" to match costs to lower revenue. The cable operator has not said how many staff accepted or what it saves, so its effect on profit will show only in later quarters.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟑.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Internet sales to businesses fell 6.7% from a year ago, about the same drop as in the second quarter. Most of the gap comes from tower contracts sold in March; without them, the decline was about 3% by our math. Koetje said business data "has actually been effectively flat to growing" on that basis, which our figure does not support.

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟔.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Deferred revenue, meaning fees customers paid in advance for service and installation, dropped 29% from a year ago to $16.4 million. The balance has shrunk in each of the last four quarters, from $23.1 million. The company notes that most customers pay month to month, so the balance says little about future sales.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟒.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Interest costs climbed 8.2% from a year ago, because the Sparklight owner carried more debt at a higher average rate. Its weighted average cost of debt reached 4.8%, against 3.9% a year earlier. The fully drawn credit line charges about 6.7%, so interest costs will keep rising while that borrowing stays in place.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡-$𝟐𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from Consistent with 2025 capital spending of $285.3 million
Unchanged. The plan still has capital spending close to last year's $285 million. By our math, that leaves about $65 million for the fourth quarter, 12% below a year ago. Koetje tied the third quarter's higher spending to more new connections and in-home Wi-Fi equipment, and said the company still aims to cut debt.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐲 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭𝐬?
The company says its cash cannot cover these maturities and that talks with lenders continue. Investors need the structure under discussion, and whether it covers the MBI loans, before the November 2027 deadline arrives.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐭 𝐝𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐬𝐞𝐭?
The company says it meets its loan terms and expects to for a year. Ebitda keeps falling, so readers need the maximum ratio to judge how much room is left.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐰?
Last quarter Koetje gave net debt against the latest quarter's Ebitda times four. On that measure the ratio rose to about 4.5 times by our math, against 4.1 on the new basis.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐥 𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡?
New connections improved, but Holanda called retention the remaining opportunity. A monthly cancellation rate would show whether the new retention tools work, or whether lower prices alone explain the smaller losses.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐌𝐁𝐈 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐧𝐞'𝐬 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞?
Cable One may have to buy MBI and carry its debt. MBI's revenue minus operating costs fell to about 51% of revenue from 54% by our math, but the company gives no Ebitda figure.

monad mainnet turns 1 on nov 24. same day as the unlock everyone's been dreading

so i went back through the whole year, month by month. here's my honest report card

tech: A
blocks went from 400ms to 300ms in july, finality down to 600ms. 10k tps, full evm, around 200 validators. and cadence is already proposing 100ms blocks

defi: A-
@aave  went live in july and passed $250m tvl in under a month. @ethena , maple  and @pendle_fi  came too. @perpltrade  crossed $1b in volume. tvl passed $1b by the end of august, and august set a new monthly dex volume record at $3.6b+

real world: A
@Visa  settlement. @MetaMask  money account built only on monad. cbbtc came in through chainlink ccip back in march. 1,100+ tokenized stocks from @xStocksFi , spacex and nvidia trading on uniswap v4. by the foundation's own numbers, monad is the third biggest chain for rwas in defi, after ethereum and solana

access: A-
mon on @RobinhoodApp  and interactive brokers. staking on kraken and ledger. the monad foundation got a seat on the x402 foundation board next to stripe, visa, mastercard and google

users: C+
4.3m wallets, 860m+ transactions, 170+ apps. but the chain still needs more reasons for normal people to come and stay

token price: D
we don't talk about it

tokenomics: C
the unlock is real. investors get their one year cliff, about 4.9b mon, then monthly unlocks after. category labs gets about 1b. and per the foundation, released team tokens hit ~10.7% of initial supply on the same day
but when the foundation offered some early investors up to $60m to exit early at a discount, almost all of them said no. unlocked doesn't mean sold

homework for year two:
ship private settlement, get cadence live, and give people a reason to use monad beyond yield

final grade: B
passed. still holding. year two is where it gets interesting

text:
14 August 1985. 

Kampala. 

The dust from the coup had barely settled when General Tito Okello began staging a massive act of political theater. 

He invited scattered rebel groups into a new Military Council, attempting to project national unity. 

But the big monkey on his back was gathering in the bush.

The Theater of Unity.

Okello's Fragile Peace.

Okello attempted a delicate balancing act to legitimize his rule. 

He co-opted the Democratic Party (DP) and tapped into the powerful Buganda political sphere. 

Bringing in figures like Dr. Andrew Kayiira of the Uganda Freedom Movement was meant to project the illusion that old guerrilla enemies could suddenly govern together. 

Yet, the council was a fragile coalition of convenience, a patchwork of former Obote loyalists and old Idi Amin-era figures united only by their shared desire to see Obote gone. 

The central contradiction was embodied by Kayiira himself, who accepted his seat but told CBC’s Ann Medina that he "did not give up his arms." 

It was a stark warning of deep-seated mistrust as the national army, the UNLA, continued its brutal atrocities.

While Okello tried to manage these fragile political factions in the council chamber, the real threat was gathering in the bush. 

Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army (NRA), a disciplined force of roughly 4,000 fighters, pointedly refused to join the Military Council or observe the ceasefire. 

As the politicians talked, NRA columns marched. Reports from western Uganda indicated the rebels had seized control of key towns like Fort Portal, Kabale, and Mbarara, and were advancing toward Masaka, a major town just 129 kilometers from the capital.

The NRA's price for peace was steep. 

It demanded that Okello negotiate not as head of state, but merely as an army officer, a humiliating condition that exposed the regime's fundamental military weakness and its isolation from the real power on the ground. 

The tragedy of July 1985 was that the "calm" was never a true peace, only a brief interlude before the inevitable reckoning. 

For ordinary Ugandans, the release of prisoners and the rhetoric of change offered only a "little breather of freedom," not a solution to the cycle of violence.

Okello’s government was a house built on sand, paralyzed by the very factions he had invited to the table while the real military threat gathered in the west. 

Unable to control its own brutal army or bring the NRA in from the cold, the regime was fundamentally doomed. 

Within six months, this fragile patchwork of DP politicians, Buganda loyalists, and armed guests would be swept away by the very forces it had failed to accommodate, proving the storm had only paused to gather its strength.

What does it mean when a government tries to build a house of peace out of the shattered pieces of old rivalries, while the real architects of the future are marching toward the capital? 

The council chamber was filled with handshakes and promises. 

The bush was filled with armed men who refused to compromise. 

Okello tried to stage a play of national unity, but the NRA was already writing the final act. 

The calm was just a pause. 

The storm was already on its way.

🚨UPDATE: GAF CLARIFIES SUPPORT TO KUMASI STAMPEDE VICTIM, FAMILY RECEIVES OVER GH¢93,000 HEALTH SUPPORT

The Ghana Armed Forces (GAF) has refuted suggestions that it abandoned Sandra, a victim of the November 12, 2025, military recruitment stampede, outlining the financial, medical and other support it says has provided to her and her family.

According to the military, Sandra initially received treatment at the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH), where her medical bills reportedly amounted to approximately GH¢85,000.

On February 26, 2026, she was airlifted to the 37 Military Hospital in Accra for specialist medical care, where she received treatment for eight months at a reported cost of GH¢28,800.

The GAF says her treatment will continue at the 4th Military Hospital in Kumasi.

The military further disclosed that Sandra's mother received GH¢30,000 in cash, alongside an air bed, during a presentation ceremony at the General Headquarters in Accra on October 28, 2026, the same day Sandra was discharged.

As part of its support to the family, the GAF says Sandra's sister, Mercy Bioh, has been admitted into training at the Army Recruit Training School at Shai Hills under an arrangement that provides enlistment opportunities for relatives of victims.

On her return journey to Kumasi, the military says it offered a military ambulance to transport Sandra and her family. However, her mother reportedly requested air transportation instead. After an airlift could not be arranged, the family travelled with the National Ambulance Service.

Meanwhile, in March 2026, Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh told Parliament that the government was covering Sandra's medical expenses and remained open to sending her abroad for further treatment if recommended by her doctors.

The Ghana Armed Forces maintains that it has continued to support Sandra and her family since the tragic recruitment stampede.

text:
The M1916 (M16) Stahlhelm worn by German soldier, lieutenant, and author Ernst Jünger (1895–1998) during WWI...

Before he was a writer, Jünger was a soldier. He fought on the Western Front for almost the entire war and was one of the most wounded men in the German army, hit at least 14 times by bullets, shrapnel and grenade fragments and decorated with Germany's highest military honor for bravery, the Pour le Mérite, becoming its youngest recipient.

During the Battle of Cambrai in 1917, a bullet struck the side of Jünger's steel helmet while he was leading troops. The heavy steel dented and tore open on impact, absorbing and deflecting enough kinetic energy to prevent a fatal head wound, though he was wounded multiple times elsewhere during the war. Jünger survived the war and later wrote Storm of Steel (In Stahlgewittern), a landmark and stark memoir detailing his front-line experiences in the trenches.

The original damaged helmet (alongside allied artifacts) has been preserved at his former residence in Wilflingen, Germany.

. . . 

The helmet he wore, the M1916 Stahlhelm, German for “steel helmet,” was introduced in 1916 to replace the famous spiked leather helmet, which offered almost no protection. Its deep shape covered more of the head, neck and ears.

He chronicled his brutal, dispassionate experiences in his 1920 self-published memoir, Storm of Steel. Rather than a traditional anti-war lament, the book portrayed trench warfare with a chilling, hyper-realistic intensity that turned him into a literary and nationalist figure.

During the Weimar Republic, Jünger wrote provocative works viewing war as a transformative, mystical experience. While he was a radical conservative nationalist who opposed the democratic Weimar government, he notably refused Adolf Hitler's overtures and personal invitations to join the Nazi Party.

During World War II, Jünger served as an army staff officer in Paris. His wartime diaries (A German Officer in Occupied Paris) captured his quiet disillusionment and alienation from Nazi totalitarianism. He published this allegorical novel depicting two brothers who retreat from a brutal warlord (the Chief Ranger) to study flowers and butterflies—an indirect, philosophical critique of tyranny and the choice to preserve inner freedom rather than validate violence.

Outside of literature, Jünger was an avid entomologist who amassed a collection of tens of thousands of insect specimens, experimented with psychoactive substances, and wrote extensively on modern technology, metaphysics, and individual resistance (such as in his essay Der Waldgang).

He lived to be 103 years old, converting to Roman Catholicism shortly before his death in 1998.

✅ Curated product showcases and sampling sessions

text:
One of the most fascinating things about Fremen culture is how completely Arrakis changes the meaning of ordinary human gestures.

On a planet where water determines whether you live or die, even saliva has enormous value. When Stilgar spits on Duke Leto’s table, he isn’t trying to insult him. He’s offering a part of his own body’s precious moisture as a sign of respect.

What’s even more interesting is Leto’s reaction. He understands that this isn’t an act of disrespect and stops his servant from wiping it away.

That small moment tells us a lot about Duke Leto’s character. He doesn’t dismiss a custom simply because it seems strange to him. He recognises the value behind it.

On Arrakis, respect isn’t always expressed through words or expensive gifts. Sometimes, giving someone your water is the greatest honour you can offer.

text:
While mainstream travellers often rush to crowded Arctic hubs, #Abisko in #SwedishLapland quietly stands out as the most underrated destination on Earth for witnessing the Northern Lights.

Tucked 250 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle, this remote national park sits directly beneath the auroral oval, ensuring frequent geomagnetic activity overhead. 

Yet, unlike more commercialised alternatives, Abisko offers an intimate, unhurried wilderness experience where pristine landscapes and near-zero light pollution allow the  #AuroraBorealis  to take centre stage.

The true secret behind Abisko’s astronomical success rate is a rare meteorological phenomenon known locally as the  #AbiskoBlueHole 

As moist prevailing winds sweep eastward from the Atlantic Ocean, they collide with the towering Scandinavian mountain range along the Norwegian border. 

Forced upward, the air dumps its moisture before descending into the Lake Torneträsk basin as dry, cloud-dissolving air. 

This rain-shadow effect creates a persistent 10-to-20-square-kilometre patch of clear sky directly above Abisko, allowing visitors to marvel at dancing green and violet ribbons even when surrounding Arctic regions are completely blanketed in cloud.

Beyond its famous microclimate, Abisko holds several distinct advantages over major rivals like Tromsø, Reykjavik, and Rovaniemi. 

While coastal Norwegian and Icelandic destinations frequently suffer from unpredictable maritime cloud cover that forces travellers onto exhausting, hours-long bus chases, Abisko is one of the driest places in Scandinavia, allowing you to simply step outside your lodge and look up. 

Furthermore, whereas popular Finnish hubs sit on the southern edge of the aurora zone and contend with heavy resort crowds, Abisko offers superior geomagnetic positioning, direct rail connectivity, and elevated viewing at the renowned  #AuroraSkyStation —making it the smartest, highest-odds choice for serious aurora seekers.

#HiddenGems

text:
🎒 MARSAXLOKK FISHING HARBOUR | BEFORE YOU GO
☀️ Personal Preparation

Wear comfortable, non-slip shoes for walking along the waterfront. Bring sun protection and drinking water, especially during warmer weather, as exposed sections of the harbour offer limited shade.

⚓ Working Harbour Etiquette

Marsaxlokk is an active fishing community, not simply a tourist attraction. Keep working areas, mooring ropes, and fishing equipment unobstructed. Admire the colourful luzzu boats without boarding or touching them. Ask permission before photographing fishermen at work.

⛪ Local Courtesy

The village's Church of Our Lady of Pompeii remains an active place of worship. Dress respectfully if entering, and avoid disturbing religious services.

🌊 Coastal Safety

If exploring nearby St Peter's Pool, expect uneven limestone, slippery surfaces, and deep water. Check sea conditions before swimming, never dive into unfamiliar water, and avoid cliff jumping.
Rockfall concerns have led to access restrictions around parts of St Peter's Pool. Respect all current barriers and warning signs.

🌿 Leave No Trace

Keep the waterfront clean, take rubbish away, and respect the boats, equipment, and daily routines that sustain this fishing village.

text:
🧭 MARSAXLOKK FISHING HARBOUR | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Located on Malta’s southeastern coast, Marsaxlokk is an easy day trip from Valletta. Take public bus 81 or 85 (approximately 30–50 minutes). The faster TD10 service operates on Sundays, while bus 119 connects the village with Malta International Airport.

🗺️ What to Explore

Walk along the colourful harbour, browse the Sunday fish market, and enjoy seafood at the waterfront restaurants. For a different coastal experience, continue to St Peter’s Pool, a natural rocky swimming spot approximately 30–40 minutes away on foot.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow 2–3 hours for the harbour, market, and a relaxed meal. Plan most of a day if combining Marsaxlokk with St Peter’s Pool.

🌤️ When to Visit

Sunday mornings offer the liveliest market atmosphere. Weekdays are generally quieter, while warmer months are better suited to coastal swimming.

💰 Costs & Planning

Harbour access and market entry are free. As of November 2026, standard winter bus tickets cost €2, while TD10 costs €3. Check updated schedules before travelling.

💡 Local Insight

Visit early on Sunday for the fish market, or choose a weekday if photographing the boats and enjoying a slower waterfront atmosphere matter more.

Nestled among the peaceful rice fields of Konan City, Kochi Prefecture,
this temple offers a calm and welcoming atmosphere.

Passing through the wooden temple gate,
visitors are greeted by the Main Hall, rebuilt using traditional wooden joinery without a single nail.

One of the highlights is the "Nail-Carved Yakushi" enshrined in the inner sanctuary.
According to legend, Kobo Daishi carved the image of Yakushi Buddha into a camphor tree using only his fingernails.

It is believed to bring blessings for ailments affecting the head and neck.
Nearby, the sacred spring known as "Daishi's Blessed Water"
offers a peaceful place for tired pilgrims to refresh themselves.

text:
When 63-year-old Margaret lost her husband, she had nowhere permanent to live.

Her daughter, Jessica, offered her a room in her three-bedroom house in Atlanta, Georgia.

At first, everything seemed fine.

But after three months, Jessica sat her mother down.

“Mom, things are expensive. I can’t keep paying for everything. You’ll have to contribute $900 every month.”

Margaret looked surprised.

“Sweetheart, I’m retired. My monthly Social Security payment is only $1,200.”

Jessica shrugged.

“Then you’ll have to figure something out. I’m not running a charity.”

Margaret began paying.

She stopped buying new clothes, reduced her medication expenses, and barely had money left for groceries.

One evening, she asked Jessica if she could pay $500 instead.

Jessica became furious.

“This is my house. If you can’t afford to live here, you can find somewhere else.”

Margaret quietly nodded.

Two weeks later, she packed her belongings and left without arguing.

Jessica thought her mother had moved into a cheap retirement facility.

Then, one Monday morning, a lawyer arrived at her house.

He handed Jessica an envelope.

Inside was a property deed.

Margaret had inherited a small apartment building from her late husband, worth approximately $780,000.

But that wasn’t the biggest surprise.

The lawyer explained that Margaret had secretly been using the rental income to pay off Jessica’s mortgage for the past four years.

She had contributed more than $96,000.

Jessica immediately called her mother.

“Mom, why didn’t you tell me you owned all that property?”

Margaret calmly replied:

“You never asked me how I was doing. You only asked when I was going to pay you.”

Jessica started crying.

“Can we please talk? I want you to come home.”

Her mother answered:

“I spent years making sure you had a comfortable home. I thought I could finally feel at home with my own daughter.”

Then she hung up.

The question is: Was Jessica right to charge her retired mother rent in her own home, or did she cross a line by treating her mother like a stranger?

text:
$CLNE Q3 2026 earnings: Tax credits lift Clean Energy, but its fuel profits fall

Clean Energy, which fuels truck fleets with natural gas, profited from a tax credit while its fuel business weakened. A September federal rule raised that credit for manure-based gas, adding $8 million for gas made in the first half. Sales before a non-cash Amazon discount hardly moved. Chief executive Clay Corbus lifted the yearly profit outlook by $5 million.

• Sales before the non-cash Amazon discount: $𝟏𝟐𝟐.𝟖𝐌 ($122.9M a year ago)
• Profit before interest, tax and depreciation, excluding one-offs: $𝟐𝟕.𝟐𝐌 ($17.3M a year ago)
• Same profit without the first-half credit catch-up: $𝟏𝟖.𝟗𝐌 (+9% from a year ago)
• Full-year profit outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟓𝐌 (middle of the range: $77.5M)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the tax credit the yearly plan relied on arrived, at a value Corbus said beat the company's assumption. One caution: without credits owed by its gas suppliers, the fuel-selling business earned about $10 million, by our math. Clean Energy also cut that unit's yearly outlook.

The question now is whether the fuel-selling business has stopped losing profit per gallon. Either the sharper focus on fleets where gas costs less than diesel wins customers, or renewed contracts keep pushing prices down. Fourth-quarter results and the 2027 outlook, due in February, will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 concern eased — 𝐀 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐅𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐮𝐥𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐮𝐫𝐞-𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭
Section 45Z is a federal tax credit for makers of low-carbon fuel, such as renewable natural gas (RNG) made from cow manure. Chief executive Clay Corbus said the earlier yearly plan already counted on some gain from a pending update to the credit's value.

In September the Energy Department published that update, and the IRS issued matching rules for manure-based gas. Corbus said "the value came in above what we assumed". Clean Energy then booked an $8.3 million catch-up for gas its dairy plants made in the first half.

This settles the largest standing doubt about the yearly plan, because the credit now has a published value. Corbus expects the credit to keep contributing "through at least 2029", and he raised the profit outlook on that basis. But the catch-up will not repeat, so this quarter overstates what the credit adds in a normal quarter.

What to watch: the 2027 outlook, which Corbus plans to give in February, and how much of it rests on the credit. A large share would leave yearly profit dependent on a single federal program.

🟢 𝐃𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐲 𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐮𝐭 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐅𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐝
Clean Energy co-owns plants that turn cow manure into renewable natural gas (RNG), mostly in ventures with bp and TotalEnergies. The standing worry is execution, because one partner farm, Ash Grove Dairy, went bankrupt and still awaits court approval of its plan.

Finance chief JJ Armstrong said the plants made 2.2 million gallons in the quarter, nearly five times last year's output. He credited better operations and two more large projects, in Texas and Idaho. This matters because the producer keeps the full credit and fuel value on its own gas.

• Production unit's core profit, before interest, tax, depreciation and the first-half credit catch-up: about $2.7 million, by our math
• Same measure last quarter: a $0.6 million loss
• Own output: about 3% of the RNG Clean Energy sold
• Maas Energy Works plants: one starting up, one due in December, one in mid-2027

What to watch: fourth-quarter production, once the Maas plants begin delivering gas. Output growth there would show the dairy business can earn money without one-time credit gains.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚 𝐇𝐲𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐞𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐖𝐢𝐧
Clean Energy also builds fueling stations for transit agencies and fleets. The worry was that construction sales would shrink as old orders ran out, and they fell in the quarter to $6.2 million from $9.9 million.

But new orders arrived. The Orange County Transportation Authority hired the station builder "to design and build a new hydrogen fueling station" at its Garden Grove bus base. The $27.5 million contract includes fuel supply.

• Work ordered but not yet done: $71.4 million, against $33.4 million in June
• Sales in Canada: up 17%, as new freight and refuse fleets signed up

The backlog matters because Clean Energy plans to complete that work over the next one to two years. But station building earns thin margins, so the gain will show in sales more than in profit.

What to watch: construction sales in the fourth quarter. A rebound toward the second quarter's level would show the new orders turning into work.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐅𝐮𝐞𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐬' 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐬
Fuel distribution, the business of selling natural gas to fleets at Clean Energy's stations, earns most of its profit. We track its core profit: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and one-off items. "In our fuel distribution business, volumes are steady and results were solid," chief executive Clay Corbus told analysts.

The unit's core profit fell 21% from a year ago. That total includes $5.8 million, its share of suppliers' tax credits on last year's gas. Without it, by our math, the unit earned about $10.4 million, against $16.6 million last quarter.

• Gallons sold: up 11% from a year ago
• Fuel sales per gallon, before a non-cash discount tied to Amazon: down 16%, by our math
• Station operating costs and overhead: up 1.8 and 1.7 percentage points of revenue

So the fuel seller moved more gas at lower prices, after contract renewals it flagged early this year. Finance chief JJ Armstrong said "our third quarter SG&A expense is not indicative of a go-forward run rate". But the price drop alone exceeds the overhead rise, and Clean Energy trimmed the unit's yearly outlook.

What to watch: the unit's fourth-quarter core profit, which the new yearly outlook puts near $14 million by our math. A figure under that would mean price resets still outweigh volume gains.

🔴 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐤 𝐅𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐋𝐚𝐠
Clean Energy's growth case rests on heavy trucks adopting the Cummins X15N, a large natural gas engine. Chief executive Clay Corbus said "the truck is working extremely well now", and high diesel prices make gas cheaper to run.

Corbus said large fleets now seek bids for stations. Penske, a truck-leasing firm, will offer fleets "a discounted price on RNG", meaning renewable natural gas. But the engine's extra cost has not fallen "because you haven't seen volume go up", he added.

Interest has not yet turned into gallons: renewable gas volume grew 9% from a year ago. Corbus warned that new fleets will not be on the road in the first quarter, because sales and station building take time.

What to watch: a count of X15N trucks fueling on the network, which Clean Energy does not publish. A count climbing through 2027 would show the interest has become fuel sales.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing concerns got no decisive reading this quarter. Each needs a specific disclosure before it can move the case in either direction.

• Amazon's share warrant: Amazon earns rights to buy stock as it buys fuel, and Clean Energy books them as a sales discount; the terms of the station-use deal behind part of the charge remain undisclosed.
• Stonepeak loan: the 9.5% loan still falls due in a single payment in December 2029; a refinancing plan would settle the question.
• Credit prices: sales of federal and state clean-fuel credits rose 39% from a year ago, helped by higher prices; a price drop would reverse the gain.
• California low-carbon credits: the dairy plants still sell them under temporary approvals; final approvals would remove the doubt.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬
Chief executive Clay Corbus hired a consulting firm to study trucking demand and other markets for Clean Energy's gas. He named JJ Armstrong finance chief and Sean Wine chief revenue officer. Corbus said: "This is not a change in strategy." Yet the company will now target only fleets where gas clearly costs less than diesel, and Corbus warned of "onetime charges in the fourth quarter".

𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬
Chief executive Clay Corbus plans to sell more natural gas outside vehicle fueling. He said warehouses and food plants waiting for grid power could use trucked gas as "bridge energy solutions", supplied with spare trailers and compressors. He also named fuel for ships that burn liquefied gas near Houston and Los Angeles. Clean Energy has disclosed no revenue for these lines yet.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏𝟑.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money customers owe Clean Energy rose 17.5% from a year ago, about three times the pace of sales. Receivables equalled about 101% of quarterly revenue, against 86% in June. The quarterly filing points to the timing of billings and collections, which also held back operating cash this year.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟕𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Debt minus cash fell to about $77 million from $92 million in June, by our math. The fuel supplier sold $30.7 million of tax credits and used part of the money to repay $15 million of its loan. That early repayment cost a $1.4 million premium.

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟔.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Operating cash flow reached $36.2 million in the quarter, finance chief JJ Armstrong said. Tax credit sales supplied $23.3 million, so the business itself produced about $12.9 million, by our math. Over nine months, operating cash flow trails last year's by 22%.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟐𝟐𝟎.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
The share count barely moved, up 0.5% from a year ago, and Clean Energy bought back no stock this year. Its lender caps buybacks at $15 million. Warrants held by Amazon and lender Stonepeak cover about 79 million extra shares, over a third of today's count.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟕𝟓–𝟖𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $70–75 million
Raised. The plan now has core profit (before interest, tax, depreciation and one-offs) rising about 15% this year. By our math, that leaves about $17.8 million for the fourth quarter, 13% above last year but well below this quarter. It is the first change to the outlook this year, and the company has beaten its yearly outlook in recent years.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲: $(𝟓𝟓)–(𝟓𝟎) 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $(71)–(66) million
Raised. The plan now has a much smaller loss under standard accounting rules, mainly because of the tax credit and lower Amazon charges. By our math, it leaves a fourth-quarter loss of about $19.5 million, against $43.0 million a year earlier. That earlier quarter carried a large write-off of loan costs.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐅𝐮𝐞𝐥 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟔𝟓.𝟎–𝟔𝟖.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $67.0–69.9 million
Cut. Clean Energy trimmed the fuel-selling unit's yearly core profit by about $2 million at the middle of the range. By our math, that leaves about $14.2 million for the fourth quarter, 19% below a year ago. The unit has trailed the prior year in every quarter of 2026.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐍𝐆 𝐮𝐩𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟏𝟎.𝟎–𝟏𝟐.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $3.0–5.1 million
Raised. The dairy gas unit's yearly core profit target more than doubled after the new credit rule. By our math, the plan leaves about $3.5 million for the fourth quarter, against $11.0 million in the third. The third quarter carried the first-half credit catch-up, which will not repeat.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐦𝐚𝐳𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬: 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟒𝟒.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from about $47.0 million
Lowered. The estimate covers non-cash charges for Amazon's warrant, a right to buy stock that vests as Amazon buys fuel; Clean Energy books them as a sales discount. By our math, the estimate leaves $13.7 million for the fourth quarter, above this quarter's $10.6 million.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟒𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from $49.0 million
Lowered. Depreciation, the yearly write-down of stations and plants, now sits $4 million under the earlier plan. By our math, about $12.8 million remains for the fourth quarter, above this quarter's $10.6 million.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞: $𝟐𝟒.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $24.5 million
Raised slightly. The rise likely reflects the $2.6 million loss the group booked on repaying part of its loan early. By our math, about $5.7 million remains for the fourth quarter, under this quarter's $7.9 million, because the loan is smaller.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤-𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟗.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from $11.0 million
Lowered. The plan now puts share-based pay at $9.5 million for the year. By our math, about $2.9 million remains for the fourth quarter, near this quarter's $2.4 million.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐠𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐧?
Corbus said the new value beat the company's assumption but gave no figure. Without it, readers cannot tell how much of 2027 profit will rest on one federal program.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭?
Corbus warned of charges from the operating review but gave no range. The size will show how deep the reorganisation goes.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐟𝐮𝐞𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐠𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐨 𝐟𝐚𝐫?
Gallons rose 11%, yet fuel sales before the Amazon discount fell. Investors need to know how much came from renewed contracts and how much from cheaper conventional gas.

text:
The US has a major problem with education inequality. Children from low-income families are less likely to receive high-quality education, partly because poorer districts struggle to retain experienced teachers. 

Artificial intelligence could help, by improving the one-on-one tutoring sometimes used to supplement class instruction in these schools. With help from an AI tool, tutors could tap into more experienced teachers’ expertise during virtual tutoring sessions. 

Researchers from Stanford University developed an AI system calledTutor CoPilot on top of OpenAI’s GPT-4 and integrated it into a platform called FEV Tutor, which connects students with tutors virtually. Tutors and students type messages to one another through a chat interface, and a tutor who needs help explaining how and why a student went wrong can press a button to generate suggestions from Tutor CoPilot. 

The researchers created the model by training GPT-4 on a database of 700 real tutoring sessions in which experienced teachers worked on on one with first- to fifth-grade students on math lessons, identifying the students’ errors and then working with them to correct the errors in such a way that they learned to understand the broader concepts being taught. From this, the model generates responses that tutors can customize to help their online students.

“I’m really excited about the future of human-AI collaboration systems,” says Rose Wang, a PhD student at Stanford University who worked on the project, which was published on arXiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed “I think this technology is a huge enabler, but only if it’s designed well.”

The tool isn’t designed to actually teach the students math—instead, it offers tutors helpful advice on how to nudge students toward correct answers while encouraging deeper learning. 

For example, it can suggest that the tutor ask how the student came up with an answer, or propose questions that could point to a different way to solve a problem. 

To test its efficacy, the team examined the interactions of 900 tutors virtually teaching math to 1,787 students between five and 13 years old from historically underserved communities in the US South. Half the tutors had the option to activate Tutor CoPilot, while the other half did not. 

The students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass their exit ticket—an assessment of whether a student has mastered a subject—than those whose tutors did not have access to it. (Pass rates were 66% and 62%, respectively.)

The tool works as well as it does because it’s being used to teach relatively basic mathematics, says Simon Frieder, a machine-learning researcher at the University of Oxford, who did not work on the project. “You couldn’t really do a study with much more advanced mathematics at this current point in time,” he says.

The team estimates that the tool could improve student learning at a cost of around $20 per tutor annually to the tutoring provider, which is significantly cheaper than the thousands of dollars it usually takes to train educators in person. 

It has the potential to improve the relationship between novice tutors and their students by training them to approach problems the way experienced teachers do, says Mina Lee, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Chicago, who was not involved in the project.

“This work demonstrates that the tool actually does work in real settings,” she says. “We want to facilitate human connection, and this really highlights how AI can augment human-to-human interaction.”

As a next step, Wang and her colleagues are interested in exploring how well novice tutors remember the teaching methods imparted by Tutor CoPilot. This could help them gain a sense of how long the effects of these kinds of AI interventions might last. They also plan to try to work out which other school subjects or age groups could benefit from such an approach.

“There’s a lot of substantial ways in which the underlying technology can get better,” Wang says. “But we’re not deploying an AI technology willy-nilly without pre-validating it—we want to be sure we’re able to rigorously evaluate it before we actually send it out into the wild. For me, the worst fear is that we’re wasting the students’ time.”

text:
In 212 BCE, the Romans captured Syracuse, and the great mathematician Archimedes was killed. 

But centuries later, Czech writer Karel Čapek imagined a very different version of his final encounter. In Čapek's story, the Roman soldier who visits Archimedes is not an ordinary plunderer. He is an educated centurion named Lucius.

He knows that Archimedes' ingenious war machines helped Syracuse resist Roman attacks for nearly two years. And he has an extraordinary proposal.

Why not work for Rome?

With Archimedes' mathematical genius, the Romans could build even more powerful machines and conquer the world. Archimedes is not impressed.

He asks why Rome needs to conquer everything.

Lucius explains that Rome must become stronger than every other power to maintain its supremacy. But Archimedes points out an uncomfortable consequence. The larger an empire becomes, the more territory it must defend. Its growing strength brings growing difficulties.

Then Archimedes offers a mathematical comparison. A large circle is still only a circle. Its size does not make it more perfect than a small one.

Lucius continues talking about world domination.

Archimedes returns to his calculations.

He wants to complete his geometrical work, something he considers more enduring than military conquest.

Finally, he warns the soldier not to spoil his circles.

The story ends with the announcement that Archimedes died in an accident.

This is Karel Čapek's fictional retelling, not a transcript of a historical conversation.

The actual death of Archimedes during the Roman capture of Syracuse is recorded by ancient historians, including Plutarch, who preserves several conflicting versions.

Čapek transformed that historical incident into a memorable story about mathematics, intellectual freedom, and the ambitions of military power.

Source: Karel Čapek, The Death of Archimedes, reproduced in Clifton Fadiman's Fantasia Mathematica.

text:
In 2021, 20 years after the death of her older sister, Vauhini Vara was still unable to tell the story of her loss. “I wondered,” she writes in Searches, her new collection of essays on AI technology, “if Sam Altman’s machine could do it for me.” So she tried GPT-3. But as it expanded on Vara’s prompts in sentences ranging from the stilted to the unsettling to the sublime, the thing she’d enlisted as a tool stopped seeming so mechanical. 

“Once upon a time, she taught me to exist,” the AI model wrote of the young woman Vara had idolized. Vara, a journalist and novelist, called the resulting essay “Ghosts,” and in her opinion, the best lines didn’t come from her: “I found myself irresistibly attracted to GPT-3—to the way it offered, without judgment, to deliver words to a writer who has found herself at a loss for them … as I tried to write more honestly, the AI seemed to be doing the same.”

The rapid proliferation of AI in our lives introduces new challenges around authorship, authenticity, and ethics in work and art. But it also offers a particularly human problem in narrative: How can we make sense of these machines, not just use them? And how do the words we choose and stories we tell about technology affect the role we allow it to take on (or even take over) in our creative lives? Both Vara’s book and The Uncanny Muse, a collection of essays on the history of art and automation by the music critic David Hajdu, explore how humans have historically and personally wrestled with the ways in which machines relate to our own bodies, brains, and creativity. At the same time, The Mind Electric, a new book by a neurologist, Pria Anand, reminds us that our own inner workings may not be so easy to replicate.

Searches is a strange artifact. Part memoir, part critical analysis, and part AI-assisted creative experimentation, Vara’s essays trace her time as a tech reporter and then novelist in the San Francisco Bay Area alongside the history of the industry she watched grow up. Tech was always close enough to touch: One college friend was an early Google employee, and when Vara started reporting on Facebook (now Meta), she and Mark Zuckerberg became “friends” on his platform. In 2007, she published a scoop that the company was planning to introduce ad targeting based on users’ personal information—the first shot fired in the long, gnarly data war to come. In her essay “Stealing Great Ideas,” she talks about turning down a job reporting on Apple to go to graduate school for fiction. There, she wrote a novel about a tech founder, which was later published as The Immortal King Rao. Vara points out that in some ways at the time, her art was “inextricable from the resources [she] used to create it”—products like Google Docs, a MacBook, an iPhone. But these pre-AI resources were tools, plain and simple. What came next was different.

Interspersed with Vara’s essays are chapters of back-and-forths between the author and ChatGPT about the book itself, where the bot serves as editor at Vara’s prompting. ChatGPT obligingly summarizes and critiques her writing in a corporate-­shaded tone that’s now familiar to any knowledge worker. “If there’s a place for disagreement,” it offers about the first few chapters on tech companies, “it might be in the balance of these narratives. Some might argue that the ­benefits—such as job creation, innovation in various sectors like AI and logistics, and contributions to the global economy—can outweigh the negatives.” 

Vara notices that ChatGPT writes “we” and “our” in these responses, pulling it into the human story, not the tech one: “Earlier you mentioned ‘our access to information’ and ‘our collective experiences and understandings.’” When she asks what the rhetorical purpose of that choice is, ChatGPT responds with a numbered list of benefits including “inclusivity and solidarity” and “neutrality and objectivity.” It adds that “using the first-person plural helps to frame the discussion in terms of shared human experiences and collective challenges.” Does the bot believe it’s human? Or at least, do the humans who made it want other humans to believe it does? “Can corporations use these [rhetorical] tools in their products too, to subtly make people identify with, and not in opposition to, them?” Vara asks. ChatGPT replies, “Absolutely.”

Vara has concerns about the words she’s used as well. In “Thank You for Your Important Work,” she worries about the impact of “Ghosts,” which went viral after it was first published. Had her writing helped corporations hide the reality of AI behind a velvet curtain? She’d meant to offer a nuanced “provocation,” exploring how uncanny generative AI can be. But instead, she’d produced something beautiful enough to resonate as an ad for its creative potential. Even Vara herself felt fooled. She particularly loved one passage the bot wrote, about Vara and her sister as kids holding hands on a long drive. But she couldn’t imagine either of them being so sentimental. What Vara had elicited from the machine, she realized, was “wish fulfillment,” not a haunting. 

The rapid proliferation of AI in our lives introduces new challenges around authorship, authenticity, and ethics in work and art. How can we make sense of these machines, not just use them? 

The machine wasn’t the only thing crouching behind that too-good-to-be-true curtain. The GPT models and others are trained through human labor, in sometimes exploitative conditions. And much of the training data was the creative work of human writers before her. “I’d conjured artificial language about grief through the extraction of real human beings’ language about grief,” she writes. The creative ghosts in the model were made of code, yes, but also, ultimately, made of people. Maybe Vara’s essay helped cover up that truth too.

In the book’s final essay, Vara offers a mirror image of those AI call-and-­response exchanges as an antidote. After sending out an anonymous survey to women of various ages, she presents the replies to each question, one after the other. “Describe something that doesn’t exist,” she prompts, and the women respond: “God.” “God.” “God.” “Perfection.” “My job. (Lost it.)” Real people contradict each other, joke, yell, mourn, and reminisce. Instead of a single authoritative voice—an editor, or a company’s limited style guide—Vara gives us the full gasping crowd of human creativity. “What’s it like to be alive?” Vara asks the group. “It depends,” one woman answers.    

David Hajdu, now music editor at The Nation and previously a music critic for The New Republic, goes back much further than the early years of Facebook to tell the history of how humans have made and used machines to express ourselves. Player pianos, microphones, synthesizers, and electrical instruments were all assistive technologies that faced skepticism before acceptance and, sometimes, elevation in music and popular culture. They even influenced the kind of art people were able to and wanted to make. Electrical amplification, for instance, allowed singers to use a wider vocal range and still reach an audience. The synthesizer introduced a new lexicon of sound to rock music. “What’s so bad about being mechanical, anyway?” Hajdu asks in The Uncanny Muse. And “what’s so great about being human?” 

But Hajdu is also interested in how intertwined the history of man and machine can be, and how often we’ve used one as a metaphor for the other. Descartes saw the body as empty machinery for consciousness, he reminds us. Hobbes wrote that “life is but a motion of limbs.” Freud described the mind as a steam engine. Andy Warhol told an interviewer that “everybody should be a machine.” And when computers entered the scene, humans used them as metaphors for themselves too. “Where the machine model had once helped us understand the human body … a new category of machines led us to imagine the brain (how we think, what we know, even how we feel or how we think about what we feel) in terms of the computer,” Hajdu writes. 

But what is lost with these one-to-one mappings? What happens when we imagine that the complexity of the brain—an organ we do not even come close to fully understanding—can be replicated in 1s and 0s? Maybe what happens is we get a world full of chatbots and agents, computer-­generated artworks and AI DJs, that companies claim are singular creative voices rather than remixes of a million human inputs. And perhaps we also get projects like the painfully named Painting Fool—an AI that paints, developed by Simon Colton, a scholar at Queen Mary University of London. He told Hajdu that he wanted to “demonstrate the potential of a computer program to be taken seriously as a creative artist in its own right.” What Colton means is not just a machine that makes art but one that expresses its own worldview: “Art that communicates what it’s like to be a machine.”  

What happens when we imagine that the complexity of the brain—an organ we do not even come close to fully understanding—can be replicated in 1s and 0s?

Hajdu seems to be curious and optimistic about this line of inquiry. “Machines of many kinds have been communicating things for ages, playing invaluable roles in our communication through art,” he says. “Growing in intelligence, machines may still have more to communicate, if we let them.” But the question that The Uncanny Muse raises at the end is: Why should we art-­making humans be so quick to hand over the paint to the paintbrush? Why do we care how the paintbrush sees the world? Are we truly finished telling our own stories ourselves?

Pria Anand might say no. In The Mind Electric, she writes: “Narrative is universally, spectacularly human; it is as unconscious as breathing, as essential as sleep, as comforting as familiarity. It has the capacity to bind us, but also to other, to lay bare, but also obscure.” The electricity in The Mind Electric belongs entirely to the human brain—no metaphor necessary. Instead, the book explores a number of neurological afflictions and the stories patients and doctors tell to better understand them. “The truth of our bodies and minds is as strange as fiction,” Anand writes—and the language she uses throughout the book is as evocative as that in any novel. 

In personal and deeply researched vignettes in the tradition of Oliver Sacks, Anand shows that any comparison between brains and machines will inevitably fall flat. She tells of patients who see clear images when they’re functionally blind, invent entire backstories when they’ve lost a memory, break along seams that few can find, and—yes—see and hear ghosts. In fact, Anand cites one study of 375 college students in which researchers found that nearly three-quarters “had heard a voice that no one else could hear.” These were not diagnosed schizophrenics or sufferers of brain tumors—just people listening to their own uncanny muses. Many heard their name, others heard God, and some could make out the voice of a loved one who’d passed on. Anand suggests that writers throughout history have harnessed organic exchanges with these internal apparitions to make art. “I see myself taking the breath of these voices in my sails,” Virginia Woolf wrote of her own experiences with ghostly sounds. “I am a porous vessel afloat on sensation.” The mind in The Mind Electric is vast, mysterious, and populated. The narratives people construct to traverse it are just as full of wonder. 

Humans are not going to stop using technology to help us create anytime soon—and there’s no reason we should. Machines make for wonderful tools, as they always have. But when we turn the tools themselves into artists and storytellers, brains and bodies, magicians and ghosts, we bypass truth for wish fulfillment. Maybe what’s worse, we rob ourselves of the opportunity to contribute our own voices to the lively and loud chorus of human experience. And we keep others from the human pleasure of hearing them too. 

Rebecca Ackermann is a writer, designer, and artist based in San Francisco.

The easiest way to make an AI offer harder to sell is to focus on the technology instead of the problem.

A business owner doesn't wake up wanting an AI chatbot.

They want fewer missed leads.

They don't want an automation workflow.

They want their team to stop wasting hours on repetitive admin.

They don't want a fancy AI receptionist.

They want every enquiry answered, qualified, and followed up with without someone having to constantly monitor it.

The technology is just how you deliver the result.

When you're looking for opportunities, pay attention to what businesses complain about.

Where are they losing time?

Where are they losing money?

What tasks are taking up hours every week?

What happens when someone forgets to follow up?

Those are the problems worth solving.

Because when your offer is connected to something expensive, the conversation changes.

You're no longer trying to convince someone that AI is interesting.

You're showing them how fixing a real problem can make their business better.

" Beauseant at Montgisard 1177 "
by Artist Michael Rucker
copyright ©

Description
This painting places a Templar knight at the heart of one of the most improbable victories of the Crusades. On 25 November 1177, sixteen-year-old King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem already marked by leprosy rode out with a few hundred knights to stop Saladins Ayyubid army from reaching the Holy City. With him came Grand Master Eudes de Saint-Amand and roughly eighty Knights Templar from Gaza.

Contemporary estimates give the Christians perhaps 375450 knights and several thousand infantry against a far larger Muslim host that had been allowed to scatter while raiding. Saladin, confident the leper king would stay behind walls, was caught crossing broken ground near Montgisard (Tell Gezer / Mons Gisardi), between Ramla and Yibna. Baldwin knelt before a fragment of the True Cross, then ordered the charge. The Templars formed the spearhead. Their war banner, the Beauseant black above white, black to enemies, white to friends was the signal that no brother might quit the field while it still flew.

The shock of heavy cavalry smashed the unready Ayyubid line. Saladin himself barely escaped; most of his army did not.The scene you see is not a portrait of one named man but an emblem of that hour: white mantle and red cross pattee of the Temple, kite shield, the Beauseant replacing later anachronisms, stone churches of the Latin East rising behind the dust. It is offered so visitors may remember that history is not only catastrophe. Sometimes a small, disciplined force, a young king who would not hide, and a banner that meant we do not leave changed the map for a season.

Baldwins victory bought the Kingdom of Jerusalem nearly a decade. Saladin would return; Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem still lay ahead. Yet Montgisard remains the day the Temples black-and-white standard flew over a field that should have been lost.Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam.

" The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat "
by Artist Michael rucker
copyright ©

Description
The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat -
In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, verses 26-38 (KJV), the angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a young virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David in Nazareth. Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee, the angel declares. He announces that she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest. Mary, troubled yet reverent, asks how this can be since she knows not a man. Gabriel explains the Holy Spirit will come upon her; for with God nothing shall be impossible.

Mary's response is one of the most profound moments in Scripture the only recorded instance where she speaks words of total surrender: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38). This Latin phrase, Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Let it be done to me according to your word), is universally known as Mary's Fiat. In that single sentence she offers her entire being body, will, and future to Gods plan of salvation. The angel then departs, and the Incarnation begins.This humble virgin from an obscure village becomes the mother of the Messiah. She travels to visit her cousin Elizabeth (pregnant with John the Baptist), where she sings the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), a soaring hymn of praise that magnifies the Lord for lifting up the lowly.

She gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, wraps Him in swaddling clothes, and lays Him in a manger. She ponders the shepherds and Magis words in her heart (Luke 2:19, 51). At the Presentation in the Temple, Simeon foretells a sword will pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). She is present at the wedding in Cana, prompting Jesus first miracle (John 2:1-11), and stands at the foot of the cross, where the dying Savior entrusts her to the beloved disciple (John 19:25-27).

After the Ascension, she is seen praying with the apostles in the upper room, awaiting the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:14).Scripture portrays Mary not as a distant saint but as a real woman of extraordinary faith, courage, and obedience. Though the Bible does not record many of her words, her fiat echoes through salvation history as the perfect model of human cooperation with divine grace. She exemplifies what it means to say yes to God when the cost is everything.Your striking black-and-white artwork beautifully captures this very moment: Mary veiled, head bowed, hands clasped in prayerful surrender, her flowing hair and garments stirred by the unseen wind of the Spirit.

The dramatic lighting and ethereal atmosphere evoke the solemn hush of the Annunciation the instant heaven touched earth through a virgins willing heart. It is a powerful visual meditation on Luke 1:38, inviting viewers to contemplate the same radical trust Mary offered.
