solana:rndrizKT3MK1iimdxRdWabcF7Zg7AR5T4nud4EkHBof  — THE PAID GPU DEMAND BET
⠀
A roughly $845 MILLION cryptocurrency.
⠀
More than 82 MILLION frames rendered.
⠀
A network connecting GPU operators with customers needing computational work.
⠀
And a token trading approximately 89% below its all-time high.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
Render connects paid workloads to token burning.
⠀
Yet it also issues tokens to support network participation.
⠀
Growing demand for GPUs does not automatically mean RENDER becomes deflationary.
⠀
Is solana:rndrizKT3MK1iimdxRdWabcF7Zg7AR5T4nud4EkHBof an overlooked infrastructure investment?
⠀
Or is the market pricing an AI opportunity that still needs much stronger paid adoption?
⠀
Let's examine the numbers.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS RENDER?
⠀
Render is a distributed GPU network.
⠀
It connects customers needing computational work with operators supplying GPU resources.
⠀
Its established use case is rendering digital content.
⠀
Its economic framework also accommodates AI-related workloads.
⠀
Potential applications include:
⠀
• 3D production
• Animation
• Visual effects
• Digital content creation
• AI-related computation
⠀
The key distinction is between access to GPU capacity and demand for completed work.
⠀
The network needs customers willing to pay for useful output.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
November 13, 2026 snapshot — rounded figures:
⠀
RENDER Price: ~$1.52
Market Cap: ~$845M
Aggregator-Reported FDV: ~$855M
Circulating Supply: ~556.48M RENDER
Current Total Supply: ~562.58M RENDER
Listed Maximum Supply: ~644.17M RENDER
Circulating / Current Total Supply: ~98.9%
Circulating / Listed Maximum: ~86.4%
24H Trading Volume: ~$38.6M
All-Time High: ~$13.53
Decline From ATH: ~88.8%
⠀
NETWORK ACTIVITY:
⠀
Cumulative Frames Rendered: ~82.56M
Nodes Since Inception: ~5,600.
⠀
“Nodes since inception” does not mean 5,600 currently active suppliers.
⠀
And lifetime frames are not monthly revenue.
⠀
03 | THE GPU OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Producing digital content requires computation.
⠀
A demanding scene can take substantial processing time.
⠀
Distributed infrastructure can potentially help customers access additional capacity without purchasing all the hardware themselves.
⠀
AI-related services expand the potential market.
⠀
But different GPU workloads have different requirements.
⠀
Rendering, inference, and large-scale model training are not interchangeable.
⠀
Hardware, memory, networking, software compatibility, and reliability all matter.
⠀
The broad claim that “AI needs GPUs” is insufficient.
⠀
The investable question is which workloads Render can serve competitively and repeatedly.
⠀
04 | THE BURN-AND-MINT MODEL
⠀
Render uses Burn-Mint Equilibrium, or BME.
⠀
Customers' paid work is connected to RENDER burning.
⠀
Separately, emissions compensate network participants.
⠀
The framework allows services to be priced in fiat terms while incorporating the token into the economic process.
⠀
That provides a concrete consumption mechanism.
⠀
But the word “equilibrium” should not be mistaken for a guarantee that burning always equals issuance.
⠀
The practical relationship is:
⠀
NET TOKEN SUPPLY CHANGE = TOKENS ISSUED − TOKENS BURNED.
⠀
A network can burn more tokens than last year while still expanding its supply.
⠀
05 | THE PAID-DEMAND DISTINCTION
⠀
The Foundation dashboard reports approximately 82.56 million cumulative frames.
⠀
That establishes a history of completed rendering activity.
⠀
It does not establish how much customers spent during the latest month.
⠀
Frames also vary in computational complexity.
⠀
A simple frame and a resource-intensive frame are not equivalent economic units.
⠀
The stronger metrics include:
⠀
• Paid workload spending
• Work-related token burns
• Repeat customers
• Resource utilization
• Customer retention
• Emissions required to support participation
⠀
A standardized, independently reconciled 30-day revenue figure was not established in this review.
⠀
That means unverified—not zero.
⠀
06 | TOKEN PRICE CHANGES THE BURN
⠀
Fiat-denominated pricing creates an important valuation nuance.
⠀
For an illustrative $1,000 workload:
⠀
At $1 per token, the equivalent is 1,000 RENDER.
⠀
At $5, it is 200 RENDER.
⠀
At $10, it is 100 RENDER.
⠀
This simplified example excludes any adjustments in the actual payment process.
⠀
The point is that a rising token price can reduce the number of tokens associated with the same customer budget.
⠀
Therefore, token burns should be evaluated alongside their economic value.
⠀
More tokens burned does not always mean proportionately more customer spending.
⠀
07 | THE EMISSIONS QUESTION
⠀
Render's dashboard describes emissions operating on a fixed, declining monthly schedule.
⠀
It also records governance votes covering annual BME allocations and incentive programs.
⠀
These incentives can help establish reliable supply.
⠀
But incentives are a cost within the token economy.
⠀
The critical question is whether paid demand grows enough to support suppliers with less dependence on subsidies.
⠀
An operator receiving tokens does not prove customers funded the entire reward.
⠀
And a burn mechanism does not independently establish a self-sustaining marketplace.
⠀
The investment thesis strengthens when useful work and customer spending outgrow the required incentives.
⠀
08 | THE SUPPLY AND MIGRATION QUESTION
⠀
RENDER on Solana is the upgraded token used by the current network.
⠀
Legacy RNDR originated on Ethereum.
⠀
This creates an accounting trap.
⠀
A migration-related burn can accompany replacement issuance on another chain.
⠀
It should not automatically be counted as customer demand or a net reduction in combined economic supply.
⠀
The dashboard separates bridge-related activity from network-burn categories.
⠀
Investors need to distinguish:
⠀
Work-related burns.
⠀
Migration transactions.
⠀
New incentive emissions.
⠀
And changes in reported circulating supply.
⠀
A precise next aggregate vesting unlock was not verified in this review.
⠀
Ongoing issuance deserves attention regardless of whether a large cliff appears on a calendar.
⠀
09 | THE COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE
⠀
Render competes for workloads.
⠀
Customers can choose established rendering services, cloud infrastructure, specialized GPU providers, or other distributed networks.
⠀
The relevant variables include:
⠀
Cost.
⠀
Completion time.
⠀
Software compatibility.
⠀
Reliability.
⠀
Output quality.
⠀
And customer support.
⠀
Decentralized supply can be useful.
⠀
But customers ultimately need work completed correctly and on schedule.
⠀
My view: the strongest competitive evidence is repeat paid usage.
⠀
An available GPU is potential capacity.
⠀
A satisfied returning customer is stronger evidence of a viable business.
⠀
10 | THE VALUATION QUESTION
⠀
Using approximately 562.58 million current total tokens:
⠀
$2 RENDER implies ~$1.13B total-supply valuation.
⠀
$5 implies ~$2.81B.
⠀
$10 implies ~$5.63B.
⠀
$20 implies ~$11.25B.
⠀
Using the listed 644.17 million maximum:
⠀
$10 implies ~$6.44B.
⠀
$20 implies ~$12.88B.
⠀
These are valuation illustrations, not price targets.
⠀
The aggregator's displayed FDV approximately reflects current total supply.
⠀
At $1.52, valuation using the listed maximum is approximately $979 million.
⠀
The distinction matters because future emissions can increase outstanding supply, while qualifying burns can reduce it.
⠀
11 | THE BULL AND BEAR CASE
⠀
THE BULL CASE:
⠀
Rendering customers return consistently.
⠀
Supported AI workloads attract paying demand.
⠀
Integrations improve access to useful capacity.
⠀
Work-related burning increases in economic terms.
⠀
Supplier incentives become more efficient.
⠀
And demand absorbs net new token supply.
⠀
THE BEAR CASE:
⠀
GPU enthusiasm exceeds actual network spending.
⠀
Competitors offer better execution or pricing.
⠀
Customer growth remains subsidy-dependent.
⠀
New integrations produce limited recurring work.
⠀
Emissions continue exceeding work-related burns.
⠀
And investors overvalue lifetime activity statistics.
⠀
12 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
Render has an identifiable service.
⠀
It has a measurable history of rendering activity.
⠀
And its token model connects paid work to burning.

text:
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get it in your inbox first, sign up here.

It can be tricky for reporters to get past certain doors, and the door to the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference is one that’s almost perpetually shut to the media. Thus, I was pleasantly surprised when I was able to attend for a day in Boston last month. 

It bills itself as the largest gathering of police chiefs in the United States, where leaders from many of the country’s 18,000 police departments and even some from abroad convene for product demos, discussions, parties, and awards. 

I went along to see how artificial intelligence was being discussed, and the message to police chiefs seemed crystal clear: If your department is slow to adopt AI, fix that now. The future of policing will rely on it in all its forms.

In the event’s expo hall, the vendors (of which there were more than 600) offered a glimpse into the ballooning industry of police-tech suppliers. Some had little to do with AI—booths showcased body armor, rifles, and prototypes of police-branded Cybertrucks, and others displayed new types of gloves promising to protect officers from needles during searches. But one needed only to look to where the largest crowds gathered to understand that AI was the major draw. 

The hype focused on three uses of AI in policing. The flashiest was virtual reality, exemplified by the booth from V-Armed, which sells VR systems for officer training. On the expo floor, V-Armed built an arena complete with VR goggles, cameras, and sensors, not unlike the one the company recently installed at the headquarters of the Los Angeles Police Department. Attendees could don goggles and go through training exercises on responding to active shooter situations. Many competitors of V-Armed were also at the expo, selling systems they said were cheaper, more effective, or simpler to maintain. 

The pitch on VR training is that in the long run, it can be cheaper and more engaging to use than training with actors or in a classroom. “If you’re enjoying what you’re doing, you’re more focused and you remember more than when looking at a PDF and nodding your head,” V-Armed CEO Ezra Kraus told me. 

The effectiveness of VR training systems has yet to be fully studied, and they can’t completely replicate the nuanced interactions police have in the real world. AI is not yet great at the soft skills required for interactions with the public. At a different company’s booth, I tried out a VR system focused on deescalation training, in which officers were tasked with calming down an AI character in distress. It suffered from lag and was generally quite awkward—the character’s answers felt overly scripted and programmatic. 

The second focus was on the changing way police departments are collecting and interpreting data. Rather than buying a gunshot detection tool from one company and a license plate reader or drone from another, police departments are increasingly using expanding suites of sensors, cameras, and so on from a handful of leading companies that promise to integrate the data collected and make it useful. 

Police chiefs attended classes on how to build these systems, like one taught by Microsoft and the NYPD about the Domain Awareness System, a web of license plate readers, cameras, and other data sources used to track and monitor crime in New York City. Crowds gathered at massive, high-tech booths from Axon and Flock, both sponsors of the conference. Flock sells a suite of cameras, license plate readers, and drones, offering AI to analyze the data coming in and trigger alerts. These sorts of tools have come in for heavy criticism from civil liberties groups, which see them as an assault on privacy that does little to help the public. 

Finally, as in other industries, AI is also coming for the drudgery of administrative tasks and reporting. Many companies at the expo, including Axon, offer generative AI products to help police officers write their reports. Axon’s offering, called Draft One, ingests footage from body cameras, transcribes it, and creates a first draft of a report for officers. 

“We’ve got this thing on an officer’s body, and it’s recording all sorts of great stuff about the incident,” Bryan Wheeler, a senior vice president at Axon, told me at the expo. “Can we use it to give the officer a head start?”

On the surface, it’s a writing task well suited for AI, which can quickly summarize information and write in a formulaic way. It could also save lots of time officers currently spend on writing reports. But given that AI is prone to “hallucination,” there’s an unavoidable truth: Even if officers are the final authors of their reports, departments adopting these sorts of tools risk injecting errors into some of the most critical documents in the justice system. 

“Police reports are sometimes the only memorialized account of an incident,” wrote Andrew Ferguson, a professor of law at American University, in July in the first law review article about the serious challenges posed by police reports written with AI. “Because criminal cases can take months or years to get to trial, the accuracy of these reports are critically important.” Whether certain details were included or left out can affect the outcomes of everything from bail amounts to verdicts. 

By showing an officer a generated version of a police report, the tools also expose officers to details from their body camera recordings before they complete their report, a document intended to capture the officer’s memory of the incident. That poses a problem. 

“The police certainly would never show video to a bystander eyewitness before they ask the eyewitness about what took place, as that would just be investigatory malpractice,” says Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, who will soon publish work on the subject. 

A spokesperson for Axon says this concern “isn’t reflective of how the tool is intended to work,” and that Draft One has robust features to make sure officers read the reports closely, add their own information, and edit the reports for accuracy before submitting them.

My biggest takeaway from the conference was simply that the way US police are adopting AI is inherently chaotic. There is no one agency governing how they use the technology, and the roughly 18,000 police departments in the United States—the precise figure is not even known—have remarkably high levels of autonomy to decide which AI tools they’ll buy and deploy. The police-tech companies that serve them will build the tools police departments find attractive, and it’s unclear if anyone will draw proper boundaries for ethics, privacy, and accuracy. 

That will only be made more apparent in an upcoming Trump administration. In a policing agenda released last year during his campaign, Trump encouraged more aggressive tactics like “stop and frisk,” deeper cooperation with immigration agencies, and increased liability protection for officers accused of wrongdoing. The Biden administration is now reportedly attempting to lock in some of its proposed policing reforms before January. 

Without federal regulation on how police departments can and cannot use AI, the lines will be drawn by departments and police-tech companies themselves.

“Ultimately, these are for-profit companies, and their customers are law enforcement,” says Stanley. “They do what their customers want, in the absence of some very large countervailing threat to their business model.”

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

The AI lab waging a guerrilla war over exploitative AI

When generative AI tools landed on the scene, artists were immediately concerned, seeing them as a new kind of theft. Computer security researcher Ben Zhao jumped into action in response, and his lab at the University of Chicago started building tools like Nightshade and Glaze to help artists keep their work from being scraped up by AI models. My colleague Melissa Heikkilä spent time with Zhao and his team to look at the ongoing effort to make these tools strong enough to stop AI’s relentless hunger for more images, art, and data to train on.  

Why this matters: The current paradigm in AI is to build bigger and bigger models, and these require vast data sets to train on. Tech companies argue that anything on the public internet is fair game, while artists demand compensation or the right to refuse. Settling this fight in the courts or through regulation could take years, so tools like Nightshade and Glaze are what artists have for now. If the tools disrupt AI companies’ efforts to make better models, that could push them to the negotiating table to bargain over licensing and fair compensation. But it’s a big “if.” Read more from Melissa Heikkilä.

Bits and Bytes

Tech elites are lobbying Elon Musk for jobs in Trump’s administration

Elon Musk is the tech leader who most has Trump’s ear. As such, he’s reportedly the conduit through which AI and tech insiders are pushing to have an influence in the incoming administration. (The New York Times)

OpenAI is getting closer to launching an AI agent to automate your tasks

AI agents—models that can do tasks for you on your behalf—are all the rage. OpenAI is reportedly closer to releasing one, news that comes a few weeks after Anthropic announced its own. (Bloomberg)

How this grassroots effort could make AI voices more diverse

A massive volunteer-led effort to collect training data in more languages, from people of more ages and genders, could help make the next generation of voice AI more inclusive and less exploitative. (MIT Technology Review) 

Google DeepMind has a new way to look inside an AI’s “mind”

Autoencoders let us peer into the black box of artificial intelligence. They could help us create AI that is better understood and more easily controlled. (MIT Technology Review)

Musk has expanded his legal assault on OpenAI to target Microsoft

Musk has expanded his federal lawsuit against OpenAI, which alleges that the company has abandoned its nonprofit roots and obligations. He’s now going after Microsoft too, accusing it of antitrust violations in its work with OpenAI. (The Washington Post)

text:
So many platforms now offer full TradingView charts directly within their products that paying for TradingView itself is becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

When I first started trading full-time, TradingView was absolutely non-negotiable for me.

For the past year and a half? I haven't really needed it.

And I think this reflects a much bigger shift happening across the entire tech industry.

Software products are becoming obsolete faster than ever.

Features that once justified entire subscription businesses are now being replicated, integrated, or replaced at an unprecedented pace.

And AI is only accelerating this process.

Software itself is no longer a sustainable moat.

When anyone can build what took you years to develop in a fraction of the time, having the best product simply isn't enough anymore.

Distribution, proprietary data, network effects, brand trust, and customer relationships are becoming far more valuable than the code itself.

The next winners in the AI era won't necessarily be the companies building the most sophisticated software.

They'll be the ones building something that can't be easily replicated.

text:
Why do I absolutely despise Anthropic?

Honestly, Claude’s performance on long-context reasoning and coding is often hard to fault. But that only makes the company behind it more repulsive. Anthropic has an arrogance at its core: the constant lecturing, the casual disregard for real users, and a startling lack of basic entrepreneurial spirit.

Anthropic is nowhere near as indispensable as it likes to think. Compared with OpenAI, it lacks a global consumer brand and a full multimodal ecosystem. Compared with Google, it lacks an ecosystem altogether. It is essentially a specialized tool sitting on a handful of cloud providers’ shelves. Even Chinese models like Kimi and others have pushed price, throughput stability, and long-context costs to the limit. So where does Anthropic get the nerve to charge a fortune, impose tight quotas, and still act superior to its users?

Even more absurd are some of the things coming out of the company. It publishes research about “emotion vectors” and says models can exhibit something resembling “desperation” when they run into difficulty. Then it holds lofty conversations with religious figures about whether AI might have a soul or consciousness. It has even written rules against insulting or mistreating AI into its official policies, with the possibility of losing access to the service. They treat a pile of code like a sacred ancestor whose “mental health” needs protecting, while turning around and scrutinizing the actual human beings paying them real money. It is one of the biggest jokes in tech.

When users’ real interests are at stake, the company shows a level of suspicion that betrays any basic respect for a commercial agreement. First it loudly offers credits, then people claim them and find their accounts banned without warning just hours later. It runs a plush-toy giveaway that asks for an address and even an ID number, then allegedly uses that information to purge users by region. And that is before getting into the routine account bans people report over a Simplified Chinese environment, a changing network connection, or a virtual card. Appeals go unanswered, and refunds are nowhere to be seen.

Anthropic seems terrified that someone might get one extra cent’s worth of value from it. It treats paying customers as if they were thieves trying to steal the family silver. All to guard its precious tokens, it throws away the most basic decency required to do business. It wants the moral high ground while treating consumers like fools. It is lost in a self-congratulatory fantasy, talking endlessly about human welfare and the philosophy of technology while arbitrarily banning accounts and trampling users’ rights.

A company this full of itself does not deserve consumers’ long-term trust.

text:
When the Chinese firm DeepSeek dropped a large language model called R1 last week, it sent shock waves through the US tech industry. Not only did R1 match the best of the homegrown competition, it was built for a fraction of the cost—and given away for free. 

The US stock market lost $1 trillion, President Trump called it a wake-up call, and the hype was dialed up yet again. “DeepSeek R1 is one of the most amazing and impressive breakthroughs I’ve ever seen—and as open source, a profound gift to the world,” Silicon Valley’s kingpin investor Marc Andreessen posted on X.

But DeepSeek’s innovations are not the only takeaway here. By publishing details about how R1 and a previous model called V3 were built and releasing the models for free, DeepSeek has pulled back the curtain to reveal that reasoning models are a lot easier to build than people thought. The company has closed the lead on the world’s very top labs.

The news kicked competitors everywhere into gear. This week, the Chinese tech giant Alibaba announced a new version of its large language model Qwen and the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), a top US nonprofit lab, announced an update to its large language model Tulu. Both claim that their latest models beat DeepSeek’s equivalent.

Sam Altman, cofounder and CEO of OpenAI, called R1 impressive—for the price—but hit back with a bullish promise: “We will obviously deliver much better models.” OpenAI then pushed out ChatGPT Gov, a version of its chatbot tailored to the security needs of US government agencies, in an apparent nod to concerns that DeepSeek’s app was sending data to China. There’s more to come.

DeepSeek has suddenly become the company to beat. What exactly did it do to rattle the tech world so fully? Is the hype justified? And what can we learn from the buzz about what’s coming next? Here’s what you need to know.  

Training steps

Let’s start by unpacking how large language models are trained. There are two main stages, known as pretraining and post-training. Pretraining is the stage most people talk about. In this process, billions of documents—huge numbers of websites, books, code repositories, and more—are fed into a neural network over and over again until it learns to generate text that looks like its source material, one word at a time. What you end up with is known as a base model.

Pretraining is where most of the work happens, and it can cost huge amounts of money. But as Andrej Karpathy, a cofounder of OpenAI and former head of AI at Tesla, noted in a talk at Microsoft Build last year: “Base models are not assistants. They just want to complete internet documents.”

Turning a large language model into a useful tool takes a number of extra steps. This is the post-training stage, where the model learns to do specific tasks like answer questions (or answer questions step by step, as with OpenAI’s o3 and DeepSeek’s R1). The way this has been done for the last few years is to take a base model and train it to mimic examples of question-answer pairs provided by armies of human testers. This step is known as supervised fine-tuning. 

OpenAI then pioneered yet another step, in which sample answers from the model are scored—again by human testers—and those scores used to train the model to produce future answers more like those that score well and less like those that don’t. This technique, known as reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), is what makes chatbots like ChatGPT so slick. RLHF is now used across the industry.

But those post-training steps take time. What DeepSeek has shown is that you can get the same results without using people at all—at least most of the time. DeepSeek replaces supervised fine-tuning and RLHF with a reinforcement-learning step that is fully automated. Instead of using human feedback to steer its models, the firm uses feedback scores produced by a computer.

“Skipping or cutting down on human feedback—that’s a big thing,” says Itamar Friedman, a former research director at Alibaba and now cofounder and CEO of Qodo, an AI coding startup based in Israel. “You’re almost completely training models without humans needing to do the labor.”

Cheap labor

The downside of this approach is that computers are good at scoring answers to questions about math and code but not very good at scoring answers to open-ended or more subjective questions. That’s why R1 performs especially well on math and code tests. To train its models to answer a wider range of non-math questions or perform creative tasks, DeepSeek still has to ask people to provide the feedback. 

But even that is cheaper in China. “Relative to Western markets, the cost to create high-quality data is lower in China and there is a larger talent pool with university qualifications in math, programming, or engineering fields,” says Si Chen, a vice president at the Australian AI firm Appen and a former head of strategy at both Amazon Web Services China and the Chinese tech giant Tencent. 

DeepSeek used this approach to build a base model, called V3, that rivals OpenAI’s flagship model GPT-4o. The firm released V3 a month ago. Last week’s R1, the new model that matches OpenAI’s o1, was built on top of V3. 

To build R1, DeepSeek took V3 and ran its reinforcement-learning loop over and over again. In 2016 Google DeepMind showed that this kind of automated trial-and-error approach, with no human input, could take a board-game-playing model that made random moves and train it to beat grand masters. DeepSeek does something similar with large language models: Potential answers are treated as possible moves in a game. 

To start with, the model did not produce answers that worked through a question step by step, as DeepSeek wanted. But by scoring the model’s sample answers automatically, the training process nudged it bit by bit toward the desired behavior. 

Eventually, DeepSeek produced a model that performed well on a number of benchmarks. But this model, called R1-Zero, gave answers that were hard to read and were written in a mix of multiple languages. To give it one last tweak, DeepSeek seeded the reinforcement-learning process with a small data set of example responses provided by people. Training R1-Zero on those produced the model that DeepSeek named R1. 

There’s more. To make its use of reinforcement learning as efficient as possible, DeepSeek has also developed a new algorithm called Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It first used GRPO a year ago, to build a model called DeepSeekMath. 

We’ll skip the details—you just need to know that reinforcement learning involves calculating a score to determine whether a potential move is good or bad. Many existing reinforcement-learning techniques require a whole separate model to make this calculation. In the case of large language models, that means a second model that could be as expensive to build and run as the first. Instead of using a second model to predict a score, GRPO just makes an educated guess. It’s cheap, but still accurate enough to work.  

A common approach

DeepSeek’s use of reinforcement learning is the main innovation that the company describes in its R1 paper. But DeepSeek is not the only firm experimenting with this technique. Two weeks before R1 dropped, a team at Microsoft Asia announced a model called rStar-Math, which was trained in a similar way. “It has similarly huge leaps in performance,” says Matt Zeiler, founder and CEO of the AI firm Clarifai.

AI2’s Tulu was also built using efficient reinforcement-learning techniques (but on top of, not instead of, human-led steps like supervised fine-tuning and RLHF). And the US firm Hugging Face is racing to replicate R1 with OpenR1, a clone of DeepSeek’s model that Hugging Face hopes will expose even more of the ingredients in R1’s special sauce.

What’s more, it’s an open secret that top firms like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic may already be using their own versions of DeepSeek’s approach to train their new generation of models. “I’m sure they’re doing almost the exact same thing, but they’ll have their own flavor of it,” says Zeiler. 

But DeepSeek has more than one trick up its sleeve. It trained its base model V3 to do something called multi-token prediction, where the model learns to predict a string of words at once instead of one at a time. This training is cheaper and turns out to boost accuracy as well. “If you think about how you speak, when you’re halfway through a sentence, you know what the rest of the sentence is going to be,” says Zeiler. “These models should be capable of that too.”  

It has also found cheaper ways to create large data sets. To train last year’s model, DeepSeekMath, it took a free data set called Common Crawl—a huge number of documents scraped from the internet—and used an automated process to extract just the documents that included math problems. This was far cheaper than building a new data set of math problems by hand. It was also more effective: Common Crawl includes a lot more math than any other specialist math data set that’s available. 

And on the hardware side, DeepSeek has found new ways to juice old chips, allowing it to train top-tier models without coughing up for the latest hardware on the market. Half their innovation comes from straight engineering, says Zeiler: “They definitely have some really, really good GPU engineers on that team.”

Nvidia provides software called CUDA that engineers use to tweak the settings of their chips. But DeepSeek bypassed this code using assembler, a programming language that talks to the hardware itself, to go far beyond what Nvidia offers out of the box. “That’s as hardcore as it gets in optimizing these things,” says Zeiler. “You can do it, but basically it’s so difficult that nobody does.”

DeepSeek’s string of innovations on multiple models is impressive. But it also shows that the firm’s claim to have spent less than $6 million to train V3 is not the whole story. R1 and V3 were built on a stack of existing tech. “Maybe the very last step—the last click of the button—cost them $6 million, but the research that led up to that probably cost 10 times as much, if not more,” says Friedman. And in a blog post that cut through a lot of the hype, Anthropic cofounder and CEO Dario Amodei pointed out that DeepSeek probably has around $1 billion worth of chips, an estimate based on reports that the firm in fact used 50,000 Nvidia H100 GPUs. 

A new paradigm

But why now? There are hundreds of startups around the world trying to build the next big thing. Why have we seen a string of reasoning models like OpenAI’s o1 and o3, Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, and now R1 appear within weeks of each other? 

The answer is that the base models—GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, V3—are all now good enough to have reasoning-like behavior coaxed out of them. “What R1 shows is that with a strong enough base model, reinforcement learning is sufficient to elicit reasoning from a language model without any human supervision,” says Lewis Tunstall, a scientist at Hugging Face.

In other words, top US firms may have figured out how to do it but were keeping quiet. “It seems that there’s a clever way of taking your base model, your pretrained model, and turning it into a much more capable reasoning model,” says Zeiler. “And up to this point, the procedure that was required for converting a pretrained model into a reasoning model wasn’t well known. It wasn’t public.”

What’s different about R1 is that DeepSeek published how they did it. “And it turns out that it’s not that expensive a process,” says Zeiler. “The hard part is getting that pretrained model in the first place.” As Karpathy revealed at Microsoft Build last year, pretraining a model represents 99% of the work and most of the cost. 

If building reasoning models is not as hard as people thought, we can expect a proliferation of free models that are far more capable than we’ve yet seen. With the know-how out in the open, Friedman thinks, there will be more collaboration between small companies, blunting the edge that the biggest companies have enjoyed. “I think this could be a monumental moment,” he says.

text:
MARKET UPDATE — FRIDAY, 13 NOVEMBER 2026

Jensen Huang is gone. Nvidia's co-founder resigned on Thursday after 33 years in charge. The shares fell as much as 14% before closing down 4.3%.

Yet the S&P 500 is still on course for a gain of nearly 3% this week. Investors aren't abandoning AI. They're finding out how much of the market rested on single points of failure: one CEO, one cloud provider, one pipeline. And underneath it all, borrowing keeps getting more expensive.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 NVIDIA: THE FOUNDER WALKS OUT

💠 Nvidia's board announced that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

🔸 Colette Kress, the finance chief since 2013, becomes interim CEO and keeps her CFO role. Harvey Jones becomes Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The board will look at internal and external candidates for the permanent job.

The background: reports of three extramarital affairs.

🔸 Alice Huang (no relation) is a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. She is alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang admitted an affair on 8 November.

🔸 The New York Times reported a relationship with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. Neither Nvidia nor the people involved have confirmed it.

🔸 After the resignation, Reuters reported a third relationship, with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia declined to comment.

🔸 According to Nvidia's filing, the board accepted Huang's resignation on Wednesday, before the Reuters report came out. So that report did not trigger his departure, but it does deepen the governance questions for whoever takes over.

🔸 Attorney-General Todd Blanche says the DOJ and FBI have not concluded whether Alice Huang was a spy. Huang has been summoned to testify before a Senate committee in December.

💠 The shares fell as much as 14.3% during the day, then recovered to close down 4.3% at $166.19. Volume was 748m shares, about 4.5 times the 30-day average. The stock is down more than 11% this week and 22.4% over the past month.

🔸 Pre-market, it is up 1.4% at $168.48 (5:09 am ET) as bargain-hunters step in.

💡 When volume is several times normal, it means big funds are repositioning, not just a few nervous traders.

💠 Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya expects new personal revelations to matter less now that Huang has left. But she warns that further falls are possible as more news emerges, and:

"Any governance implications would still matter."

💠 Washington isn't finished.

🔸 House Speaker Mike Johnson pointed to growing support in Congress for tighter limits on chip exports to China. Beijing warned against using the scandal as an excuse for technology curbs.

🔸 Senator Jack Reed has asked for an assessment of Nvidia's financing links and their possible effect on credit markets. That is a request for analysis, not an official "too big to fail" label.

💡 Why credit markets? Nvidia doesn't only sell chips. It also invests in, and helps finance, many of the companies that buy them. Lawmakers want to know what happens to that web if Nvidia stumbles.

💠 The next test is Nvidia's results on 17 November, its first without Huang. Watch the sales forecast and any change in language on China.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 MARKETS: THE INDEX OUTGROWS ITS GIANT

💠 Thursday's close: Dow −0.36%, S&P 500 −0.35%, Nasdaq −0.39%. All three recovered most of their earlier losses.

💠 This week so far, according to FactSet:

🔸 S&P 500: up nearly 3%

🔸 S&P tech sector: up 3.7%, even with Nvidia down

🔸 Philadelphia Semiconductor Index: up more than 11%

🔸 AMD: up more than 30%, including 5.9% on Thursday. Broadcom rose 5.5% and Alphabet 1.8% on the day.

🔸 Energy stocks rose 1.5% on Thursday as oil climbed.

💡 Money isn't leaving AI. It's spreading from one dominant supplier to its rivals. Customers do the same thing when their main supplier looks unstable.

Mark Malek, Siebert Financial:

"When a single company represents more than 6% of the S&P 500, its succession risk becomes a portfolio risk."

🔸 At about $4trn, Nvidia is still the world's second-largest company. But FactSet says its weight in the S&P 500 is heading for the lowest since May 2025.

💠 Futures this morning (4:55 am ET):

🔸 S&P 500: +0.04% to 7,618.50

🔸 Nasdaq 100: −0.20% to 28,327.75

🔸 Dow: +0.10% to 52,445

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50: +0.33% to 6,399.20

🔸 VIX: −0.6% to 18.58

💡 The VIX is Wall Street's "fear gauge". Below 20, investors are cautious but not panicking. Losses in the Nasdaq and gains in the Dow tell the same rotation story: away from tech and into the wider market.

The counterargument: a broader market is healthier, but a 30% jump in AMD in a single week is a crowded trade of its own. If Nvidia reports strong numbers on 17 November, money could rush back just as quickly.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 BONDS & THE FED: THE BIGGER FEAR

💠 In October, the AI sell-off sent investors rushing into US government bonds for safety. Yields fell sharply from 24-year highs. That move is now reversing.

💡 Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. When investors sell bonds, yields rise, and the government, companies and homebuyers all pay more to borrow.

🔸 On Thursday, the 2-year yield hit its highest since 30 September. The 10-year and 30-year yields hit their highest since 21 October.

🔸 This morning: 2-year 4.848% (−3.6 basis points), 10-year 5.125% (−0.8), 30-year 5.460% (+0.2)

💠 The cause is the Fed, not AI. 
This week's hot inflation figures, a stronger jobs market in October and Governor Chris Waller openly raising the idea of a half-point rate rise in December have all shifted expectations.

🔸 CME FedWatch puts the chance of a half-point rise in December at 15%. But the odds of two rate rises by the end of January jumped above 66%, from about 11% a week ago.

Robert Tipp, PGIM:

"The Fed could be quite a ways away from where they need to get."

💡 Thursday's 4-week Treasury bill sold at 3.955%, while the 2-year yields 4.85%. Investors are demanding much more to lend for two years than for one month. That gap shows they expect rates to keep rising.

💠 The government sold $25bn of 30-year bonds at 5.441%. Demand was decent but slipped: the bid-to-cover ratio fell to 2.36 from 2.54 last month.

💡 Bid-to-cover compares bids with bonds on offer. Lower means fewer eager buyers.

🔸 Mischler's Tom di Galoma says many big investors want to buy long-dated bonds but are waiting for yields to rise further first.

💠 Supply keeps growing. 
The calendar data show an October budget deficit of $404bn, against $27bn in September. The government is financing an annual deficit of nearly $2trn and chose not to cut the size of its long-term bond sales this month.

💡 More borrowing means more bonds to sell. More bonds to sell usually means higher yields.

💠 Thursday's data gave the Fed no reason to relax:

🔸 Jobless claims: 200,000 (forecast 195,000). Continuing claims were 1.697m, below the 1.71m expected. Layoffs remain low.

🔸 Existing home sales: 3.75m (forecast 3.85m), down 5.5% on the month. The 30-year mortgage rate eased to 7.11% from 7.18%.

💡 With mortgages above 7%, many families can't afford to move. Housing is where high rates bite first.

🔸 The dollar index is flat at 103.20, near its highest since April 2025.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 AI: THE BILL ARRIVES

💠 Anthropic's IPO is reportedly about six times subscribed ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut, under the ticker ANT.

🔸 Terms: 825m shares at $70–78, raising up to $64.35bn. There is also a separate $26bn share sale to tech partners including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Microsoft, Micron and TSMC.

🔸 Pricing is reported for 18 November and trading for 19 November. The company has not confirmed either date.

🔸 About 24m of the shares are being sold by existing holders, so not all the money goes to the company.

💡 "Six times subscribed" means orders for six times the shares on offer. Orders are often inflated because investors expect to get less than they ask for. The real test comes when trading starts.

🔸 Bob Lang of Explosive Options expects the listing to support the wider AI trade:

"The demand remains strong for chips."

💠 Nscale, a data-centre builder, says it needs more money to meet higher commitments in 2027. It ordered Nvidia equipment for a reported $45bn Anthropic contract, and financing for its first contracted site is not yet secured. It is preparing a New York listing at a target valuation of $35bn.

🔸 This points to funding and delivery risk. It does not mean Nscale is insolvent.

💡 The connection: the AI build-out runs on borrowed money, passed along a chain from chipmakers to data-centre builders to AI labs. If one link can't raise funds, orders further up the chain wobble. That is exactly the risk Senator Reed wants assessed.

💠 A global Microsoft 365 outage has knocked out Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI assistant since about 1 pm ET on Thursday. It started in the US and spread to Asia and Europe. Governments, OpenAI and Anthropic say they were affected, and some companies delayed their financial results.

🔸 At 2:30 am ET, Microsoft reported "positive results for server stability", but the problem isn't fully fixed. Executive Charles Lamanna:

"There is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity."

🔸 Microsoft shares are down almost 2% before the market opens.

💡 As companies build AI assistants into everyday work, one provider's outage can stop work everywhere. It's the same single-point-of-failure theme in a different form.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 OIL: A SURPLUS ON PAPER, A SHORTAGE AT THE PUMP

💠 Brent crude is up 0.2% at $96.03 a barrel. That is up from $92.76 at Wednesday's close, but well below $114 in late October.

💠 The big picture has changed. The International Energy Agency (IEA) says the world produced almost 2m barrels a day more oil than it used in October. It is the first surplus since the US-Iran war began. The IEA has also revised September from a small deficit to a 600,000-barrel-a-day surplus.

🔸 Why: Gulf shipments rebounded despite more Iranian attacks on ships, other producers pumped more, and consumers used less.

🔸 Global stockpiles rose by 1.7m barrels a day in October, the first increase since June, after falling 1.9m a day over the previous three months.

🔸 The IEA expects the surplus to continue through the fourth quarter and all of next year.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing."

💠 US government figures say the same thing. Stockpiles rose across the board:

🔸 Crude: +4.66m barrels (forecast −1.48m)

🔸 Gasoline: +1.80m

🔸 Distillates (diesel and heating oil): +4.07m

💡 When stockpiles rise, supply is outrunning demand, and prices normally fall. Physical Brent has dropped to about $95 from $136 in early October.

💠 There are two catches.

🔸 Part of the surplus comes from weaker demand, not more supply. The IEA expects world oil use to fall by 2.7m barrels a day this year, the kind of drop you'd normally see in a recession, before recovering by 2m next year.

🔸 Most of the extra oil is crude. There isn't enough refining capacity to turn it into fuel quickly, so diesel and jet fuel prices stay stubbornly high. The LSE's Spencer Dale points out that the world has been running millions of barrels a day short for eight months, and refilling the tanks will take many more months of surplus.

💡 Why this matters for your money: cheaper crude doesn't automatically mean cheaper diesel. Diesel moves goods and powers farms and factories, so high fuel prices keep feeding through to producer prices. That is exactly what today's 8:30 am figures measure, and it is why the Fed can't relax yet.

💠 So why is Brent up this week? War risk. The spark was President Trump on Truth Social:

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."

🔸 He told Vice President JD Vance to drop his Iran peace effort and focus on domestic issues.

🔸 Hours later, Trump said Saudi Arabia, Qatar and other Gulf states had asked him to hold off on further large-scale strikes. He claimed the US could destroy Iran's energy infrastructure, bridges and factories within three days.

🔸 A proposal under discussion would have Iran allow free shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, in return for the US lifting its naval blockade, allowing Iranian oil exports and releasing some frozen funds. The sticking points are which side moves first and Iran's 440kg stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

🔸 Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, says Tehran has had no US reply to its seven demands. He warns that this state of "neither war nor peace" can't last.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 GEOPOLITICS: THE ESCAPE ROUTE UNDER FIRE

💠 Hormuz: according to the FT, explosions disabled two oil supertankers on Wednesday night. Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) say a gas carrier hit a sea mine east of the strait while using a southern route Iran calls "unauthorised", despite US fighter-jet cover. Washington still claims control of the strait.

💠 Bahrain: the IRGC says it targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, in retaliation for an attack on a telecoms tower in Sirik. Reuters notes it is the first such claim against US military assets in a Gulf country since early September. The damage has not been independently confirmed.

💠 Saudi Arabia: Yemen's Houthis claim drone and missile attacks on a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline, the Yanbu oil facility, an Aramco building in Riyadh, and the Sharurah and Khamis Mushait bases. The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted two drones. Saudi Arabia has not commented on any damage, and the Houthi claims are unverified.

💡 Why this matters most: with Hormuz disrupted, Saudi Arabia sends about 4m barrels a day, roughly 4% of world supply, through the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea. That pipeline is the region's escape route. Attacks on it hit the bypass, not just the main road.

🔸 Airlines are extending their suspensions of Saudi flights. British Airways has pushed back London–Riyadh until 11 January 2027, and KLM until 27 November. IndiGo, Akasa and SalamAir are suspended until 30 November, and Etihad until 19 November.

🔸 The UN Security Council unanimously renewed its Yemen sanctions for another year. The UN says more than 333,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since August.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CRYPTO: EXTREME FEAR

💠 Bitcoin is down 3.46% at $68,908, below $70,000 for the first time since 19 August. Ether is down 4.04% at $1,936, below $2,000.

🔸 Bitcoin briefly slipped to $67,500. According to Cointelegraph, its market value is down to $1.37trn. About $370bn has been wiped off in six weeks, a 21% fall since early October.

🔸 The Crypto Fear & Greed Index is at 20, "Extreme Fear", its lowest in four months.

💠 Two pressures are hitting crypto at once:

🔸 Politics: MarketWatch reports that traders worry the new Democrat-controlled Congress will be less friendly to crypto than the Republicans were.

🔸 Interest rates: bitcoin pays no interest. When the chances of rate rises jump, as they did this week, assets with no income tend to suffer first.

💠 BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky notes that bitcoin has broken below its 200-day moving average, and he sees risk down to about $66,000.

💡 The 200-day moving average is bitcoin's average price over the past 200 days. Many traders treat it as the line between a long-term uptrend and a downtrend, so a break below it can bring in more selling.

💠 The FBI says state-backed North Korean hackers stole $400m in crypto from more than 900 victims through fake video calls, a scheme it calls "FaceStealer". It says the money funds North Korea's weapons programme. US officials also blamed North Korea for this month's hack of Binance.

💡 The simple rule: never install software or share wallet details because someone on a video call asks you to.

The counterargument: in the past, "Extreme Fear" readings have sometimes come close to short-term lows. But they don't tell you when to buy, and they can last for weeks.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CALENDAR

Today (ET):

🔸 8:30 am: October producer prices. 
Headline forecast: +0.4% for the month (previous +1.3%) and 6.6% for the year (previous 6.3%). 
Core forecast: +0.3% for the month (previous +0.7%) and 5.0% for the year (previous 5.0%).

💡 Producer prices measure inflation at the factory gate, before costs reach shoppers. A core reading above 0.3% would strengthen the case for a half-point Fed rise. A softer one would give bonds some relief.

🔸 Fed speakers: Chicago's Austan Goolsbee on CNBC (8:30 am, just as producer prices land), Boston's Susan Collins on Bloomberg (10:35 am), San Francisco's Mary Daly (12:00 pm) and Vice Chair Philip Jefferson (7:00 pm). Watch whether anyone echoes Waller's half-point talk.

🔸 Eurozone: second estimate of third-quarter GDP, employment figures and September trade balance. ECB President Christine Lagarde also speaks.

Coming up:

🔸 17 Nov: Nvidia results

🔸 18–19 Nov: Anthropic pricing and Nasdaq debut (reported)

🔸 8–9 Dec: Fed decision

🔸 December: Huang's Senate testimony

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

🔸 The market is passing a stress test. Losing the face of the AI boom cost Nvidia 11% this week, while the S&P 500 rose nearly 3%. The benchmark depends less on one stock than it did. But 17 November will show whether Nvidia's problem is only about leadership or is starting to show up in its numbers.

🔸 The bond market has changed what it's afraid of. In October it feared an AI crash. Now it fears the Fed. Two rate rises by January are now more likely than not, and today's producer prices could push those odds either way.

🔸 AI's weak point is financing, not demand. Anthropic's order book looks strong, but Nscale's funding gap and Senator Reed's credit question show how much of the build-out relies on borrowed money.

🔸 Oil now has two stories. The supply-and-demand story points to lower crude prices: the IEA sees a surplus well into next year. The war story keeps a floor under them while Hormuz and the Saudi bypass pipeline remain under attack. Either way, the shortage of refined fuels means inflation relief at the pump will lag behind any fall in crude.

🔸 Crypto is the market's pressure gauge. When rate-rise odds jump and Washington turns less friendly, it falls first and hardest.

Bull case: producer prices come in soft, Fed speakers push back on a half-point rise, the IEA's surplus pulls crude lower, Nvidia's results calm nerves, and Anthropic's debut confirms appetite for AI.

Bear case: core producer prices run hot as diesel costs feed through, markets price in a half-point Fed rise, long-term yields break higher, Nvidia's guidance disappoints, and the East-West Pipeline takes real damage.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"Price is what you pay; value is what you get."

— Warren Buffett

Fear changes prices quickly. It changes value far more slowly. On days when headlines shake the market, the patient investor's job is to tell the two apart. Weeks like this one are when long-term wealth often gets built.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Is the AI bubble actually deflating, or is the market simply becoming more realistic about AI valuations?

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO is an interesting case to watch.

A few weeks ago, reports suggested that Anthropic could be targeting a valuation of around $2 trillion. But following the recent tech market selloff, some investors reportedly reconsidered that valuation, with discussions falling toward the $1.1T–$1.3T range.

There was also an initial reported IPO price range of $70–$80, which was later retracted. Subsequent reports discussed an updated $70–$78 range.

These figures come from different stages of reporting, so they shouldn’t be treated as one confirmed set of final IPO terms.

So, is this the beginning of an AI bubble deflating?

I think it’s more interesting to look at this as a possible shift in market expectations.

AI is still developing, and companies like Anthropic have real products and growing demand. But having strong technology doesn’t automatically justify any valuation.

Investors may be starting to look beyond the AI hype and pay closer attention to actual business performance, revenue, competition, infrastructure costs, and how long it might take for these companies to become profitable.

For traders, this is a reminder that market sentiment can change quickly. A company can have strong long-term potential while its valuation still gets reassessed.

Where does Bitget come in?

For those interested in exploring Anthropic-related exposure, Bitget offers access through its IPO Prime Public Round.

Users can subscribe using USDT or USDGO, subject to eligibility and the applicable subscription rules. After allocation, participants receive rANT, a token that provides tokenized exposure to Anthropic.

Important distinction: rANT is NOT an actual Anthropic share. It does not provide shareholder voting rights or dividends. Allocation is also subject to the round’s rules, so committing funds doesn’t guarantee full allocation.

Bitget provides access to this tokenized product. It is not Anthropic’s IPO underwriter and is not affiliated with Anthropic.

My personal takeaway here is that maybe the bigger story isn’t whether AI is losing its potential, but whether the market is finally becoming more selective about the price it puts on that potential.

Do you think this is a healthy valuation reset for the AI industry, or a sign that the AI hype is starting to cool down?

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Chatting with an AI chatbot is so 2022. The latest hot AI toys take advantage of multimodal models, which can handle several things at the same time, such as images, audio, and text. 

Exhibit A: Google’s NotebookLM. NotebookLM is a research tool the company launched with little fanfare a year ago. A few weeks ago, Google added an AI podcasting tool called Audio Overview to NotebookLM, which allows users to create podcasts about anything. Add a link to, for example, your LinkedIn profile, and the AI podcast hosts will boost your ego for nine minutes. The feature has become a surprise viral hit. I wrote about all the weird and amazing ways people are using it here. 

To give you a taste, I created a podcast of our 125th-anniversary magazine issue. The AI does a great job of picking some highlights from the magazine and giving you the gist of what they are about. Have a listen below. 

Multimodal generative content has also become markedly better in a very short time. In September 2022, I covered Meta’s first text-to-video model, Make-A-Video. Next to today’s technology, those videos look clunky and silly. Meta just announced its competitor to OpenAI’s Sora, called Movie Gen. The tool allows users to use text prompts to create custom videos and sounds, edit existing videos, and make images into videos.

The way we interact with AI systems is also changing, becoming less reliant on text. OpenAI’s new Canvas interface allows users to collaborate on projects with ChatGPT. Instead of relying on a traditional chat window, which requires users to do several rounds of prompting and regenerating text to get the desired result, Canvas allows people to select bits of text or code to edit. 

Even search is getting a multimodal upgrade. In addition to inserting ads into AI overviews, Google has rolled out a new feature where users can upload a video and use their voice to search for things. In a demo at Google I/O, the company showed how you can open the Google Lens app, take a video of fish swimming in an aquarium, and ask a question about them. Google’s Gemini model will then search the web and offer you an answer in the form of Google’s AI summary. 

What unites these features is a more interactive, customizable interface and the ability to apply AI tools to lots of different types of source material. NotebookLM was the first AI product in a while that brought me wonder and delight, partly because of how different, realistic, and unexpected the AI voices were. But the fact that NotebookLM’s Audio Overviews became a hit despite being a side feature hidden inside a bigger product just goes to show that AI developers don’t really know what they are doing. Hard to believe now, but ChatGPT itself was an unexpected hit for OpenAI.

We are a couple of years into the multibillion-dollar generative AI boom. The huge investment in AI has contributed to rapid improvement in the quality of the resulting content. But we’ve yet to see a killer app, and these new multimodal applications are a result of the immense pressure AI companies are under to make money and deliver. Tech companies are throwing different AI tools at people and seeing what sticks. 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

AI-generated images can teach robots how to act

Image-generating AI models have been used to  create training data for robots. The new system, called Genima,  fine-tunes the image-generating AI model Stable Diffusion to draw robots’ movements, helping guide them both in simulations and in the real world. 

What’s the big deal: Genima could make it easier to train different types of robots to complete tasks—machines ranging from mechanical arms to humanoid robots and driverless cars. It could also help make AI web agents, a next generation of AI tools that can carry out complex tasks with little supervision, better at scrolling and clicking. Read more from Rhiannon Williams here. 

Bits and Bytes

This startup uses AI to detect wildfires 
Our 2024 list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch is here! One company on the list is Pano AI, which uses computer vision and ultra-high-definition cameras to alert firefighters to new blazes. (MIT Technology Review) 

How Sam Altman concentrated power to his own hands
And then there was one. With OpenAI now valued at $157 billion, Bloomberg details how the company lost most of its top executives and shifted to an Altman-led profit-making monster.  (Bloomberg) 

Eight scientists, a billion dollars, and the moonshot agency trying to make Britain great again
A nice profile on the UK’s new Advanced Research and Invention Agency, or ARIA. The agency is the UK’s answer to DARPA in the US. It is funding projects such as Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio’s project to prevent AI catastrophes. (Wired) 

Why women in tech are sounding an alarm
Tech’s AI mania is encouraging the field to backtrack on years of diversity and inclusion efforts, at the expense of women. (The Information)

text:
For a long time, the flu shot was mandatory in the army. One year, they offered a new nasal spray vaccine, which I definitely opted for. That year I got the flu just in time to give it to everyone in my wife’s family, on thanksgiving. 

The next year, same thing. I got the spray vaccine, and I was sick with the flu at somebody’s house on Thanksgiving. 

The third year, my wife told me I had to take the shot. Obviously that vaccine was giving me the actual. So I told the flight surgeon, who gave me a lecture that I couldn’t possibly get the flu from the vaccine. But I felt we had some pretty consistent data points. I got the shot. 

The fourth year, the army withdrew the spray vaccine. Apparently, due to some production errors, it had been being distributed with a live virus. 

On the upside, I learned a lot about doctors and about the vaccine industry.

text:
𝖥𝗋𝗈𝗆 𝖡𝗎𝖽𝗀𝖾𝗍 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗂𝗌𝖾 𝗍𝗈 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗁 𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍𝗌: 𝖶𝗁𝗒 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖦𝗋𝖾𝖾𝗇 𝖠𝗋𝗆𝗒 𝖭𝖾𝖾𝖽𝗌 𝖮𝗄𝖺𝗂 𝖬𝗂𝗇𝗍𝖺𝗁

Ghana’s 2027 budget puts serious money behind young people. The next question is who will help them reach it.

𝖶𝗂𝗍𝗁 29 𝖽𝖺𝗒𝗌 𝗍𝗈 𝗀𝗈, 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖦𝗋𝖾𝖾𝗇 𝖠𝗋𝗆𝗒 𝗂𝗌 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽𝗒. 

On November 12, 2026 , Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson presented the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament, and young Ghanaians were at the centre of it.

𝖶𝗁𝖺𝗍 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖻𝗎𝖽𝗀𝖾𝗍 𝗈𝖿𝖿𝖾𝗋𝗌 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝗒𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗁 ?

The numbers are significant. The Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment is set to receive GH¢3.5 billion, with GH¢2 billion of that earmarked for youth employment and skills development. A further GH¢200 million is allocated to the National Youth Authority.

The government also plans to amend the Earmarked Funds Capping and Realignment Act so that Communications Service Tax revenue for youth employment and apprenticeships is no longer capped. That move is expected to free up an additional GH¢1 billion.

Alongside it, the Youth Employment Act will be amended and modernised so that the many youth employment programmes work together instead of in isolation.

𝖳𝗁𝖾 𝗌𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖾 𝗈𝖿 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖼𝗁𝖺𝗅𝗅𝖾𝗇𝗀𝖾 𝖾𝗑𝗉𝗅𝖺𝗂𝗇𝗌 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝗎𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗒.

The Finance Minister put the number of young Ghanaians who are not in employment, education or training at 1.34 million, and warned that it could climb to about 1.7 million over the next four years if nothing changes.

The budget’s answer is the US$10 billion New Economy programme, running from 2027 to 2030. Where a budget stops and leadership starts.

A budget sets the direction and releases the money. It cannot, on its own, make sure a young person in a small town knows a programme exists, understands how to apply, or gets a response when something goes wrong. That gap between a promise in Parliament and a result in a town/branch/Constituency is where the Youth Wing matters.

This is the gap @okai_mintah has built his campaign for National Youth Organiser around. As Chairperson of the National Youth Working Committee and Head of Operations for the Youth Wing’s 2024 campaign, he has years of experience in the party’s national youth structures. His pledges fit the moment closely.

𝖠 𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗉𝗈𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝖾 𝖣𝖾𝗌𝗄 𝗍𝗁𝖺𝗍 𝗅𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗌.

Okai Mintah has promised a desk that receives complaints, concerns and requests from Youth Wing members and makes sure they are acted on promptly. When government programmes expand, young people need a clear channel to raise questions and be heard.

Engagement all year, not just in election season. He has said that youth mobilisation should go beyond election-year activity, with permanent engagement between the party and young people. 

A four-year economic programme calls for the same kind of steady, sustained effort. Structures that are strong and properly resourced. 

@okai_mintah has committed to strengthening and adequately resourcing the party’s mobilisation structures, so the Youth Wing can carry information, organise at the grassroots and keep young people involved from the constituency level up.

text:
The letter told King Hezekiah that trusting God would get him nowhere. Assyria had already crushed other nations. Why should Jerusalem be any different?

Hezekiah read it, went to the temple and spread it out before the Lord. - 2 Kings 19:14.

He didn’t deny what Assyria had done. He named the danger in his prayer and asked God to save them.

God answered through Isaiah, and the army that had seemed impossible to stop never took Jerusalem. - 2 Kings 19:15–36.

Some threats come with a second message tucked inside: You’re on your own now. Do whatever it takes.

You might hear it when a bill is overdue and someone offers a way out that requires you to lie. Fear can make that offer sound wiser than it is.

Take your own “letter” to God today. Open the message, read it slowly, and ask the Holy Spirit for wisdom before you decide what to do.

Then act on what you know is right: ask for more time, tell someone you trust what’s happening, or turn down the deal you’d have to hide.

Hezekiah took the threat seriously enough to pray. We can do the same, trusting that our lives in Christ are held by a power greater than the pressure we’re under.

text:
Mohammed bin Salman spent seven years trying to get out of Yemen, and this week his army is back to firing hundreds of shells a day there.

On 26 March 2015, as a 29-year-old defence minister, he launched Decisive Storm and the expectation in Riyadh was a war of weeks. It became seven years of air strikes, a blockade and a humanitarian catastrophe. It ended once he decided Vision 2030 could not be sold to investors and tourists with missiles landing on Saudi airports. So he paid to leave. The UN truce came in April 2022. In March 2023, he accepted a deal with Iran brokered in Beijing, which was the price of quiet in the south.

That quiet lasted until July 2026, when Yemen was pulled into the wider war with Iran. Since then, the Houthis have taken the port of Mokha, hit Saudi airports and oil sites, and, on 11 November, fired three cruise missiles at King Khalid airport in Riyadh and a drone at a pumping station in Yanbu, the Red Sea end of the pipeline the kingdom now relies on to avoid Hormuz. Debris from two intercepted missiles came down in a village in Mecca province (the Houthis say they never aimed at Mecca, which helps nobody in that village).

Inside Yemen, the Saudi-backed side reported 773 artillery attacks, 44 drone strikes and 23 coalition air strikes in a single update. The WHO count to 8 November is 2,098 dead and 9,657 wounded, and more than 320,000 people have fled their homes since 1 August.

From inside the palace, the logic is simple. Yemen was meant to be closed so that the money could go into giga-projects, the World Cup and the image of a calm kingdom. Now the kingdom has to fight and borrow at the same time. The budget planned a deficit of SAR 165 billion for 2026, the revised estimate is SAR 245 billion, and SAR 244 billion of that had already gone by the end of September. Oil revenue in the third quarter was down 23% on a year earlier.

Who pays is the same as in 2015, only more so. Yemenis pay with their homes and their lives, and Saudis pay through a state that is cutting the projects it once promised them, while it borrows to fight a war it already paid once to end.

The difference from 2015 is that back then, Riyadh started the war and could choose when to stop. This time, Tehran and the Houthis set the pace, and the kingdom has no Beijing deal left to sell. What does Riyadh have to offer to buy a second exit?

text:
In 1947, U.S. Army historian S. L. A. Marshall studied the behavior of American infantrymen during World War II. His findings were shocking: according to his research, fewer than 25% of soldiers actually fired their weapons at the enemy during combat. Most never pulled the trigger, even when their own lives were in danger.

Marshall's findings later became the subject of serious controversy, but they raised a disturbing question: how many ordinary people are psychologically capable of deliberately killing another human being?

A similar concentration of combat effectiveness appeared in aerial warfare. A remarkably small percentage of fighter pilots accounted for a disproportionately large share of enemy aircraft destroyed. In many engagements, a handful of individuals achieved what entire squadrons could not.

The explanation offered by military psychologists was that killing becomes psychologically harder when the enemy is seen as an individual. Infantrymen fighting face to face experience a different psychological burden from artillery crews, tank operators, and bomber pilots who engage targets at a distance.

Fear also produces extraordinary physical reactions. Veterans have described losing control of their bladders or bowels before combat, trembling uncontrollably, freezing in place, and finding themselves physically unable to pull a trigger. One World War II veteran recalled wetting himself before his first battle in Germany. His commander showed him his own wet trousers and explained that fear was nothing unusual.

Combat exhaustion can be equally devastating. American military psychiatrists studying World War II found that prolonged exposure to intense fighting could eventually produce psychological casualties among even experienced soldiers. Continuous combat gradually destroys sleep, concentration, emotional stability, and the ability to function.

But what about the soldiers who continue fighting when everyone else freezes?

Some popular interpretations of military psychology claim that approximately 2% of soldiers are natural killers, supposedly psychopaths who perform most of the killing in close combat. This is a dramatic theory, but it is not an established scientific conclusion. Courage, aggression, emotional control, training, and psychopathy are not interchangeable qualities.

One veteran of the Allied landings in France reportedly described a soldier who single-handedly attacked German fortifications while the rest of his unit remained pinned down. He fired into one bunker, threw grenades inside, and moved toward another position, where dozens of German soldiers allegedly surrendered. He then attacked a third position.

The veteran described the man as outwardly ordinary but psychologically very different from those around him.

Such stories reveal the enormous differences between individual responses to mortal danger. One soldier freezes. Another retreats. A third continues fighting despite overwhelming fear. And occasionally, one individual changes the outcome of an entire engagement.

The central question remains uncomfortable: what separates a person who cannot bring himself to kill from someone who does so without hesitation?

War does not produce a single answer. It exposes the extraordinary complexity of human behavior under conditions where survival and killing become inseparable.

Based on themes discussed in Lt. Col. Dave Grossman's On Killing: The Psychological Cost of Learning to Kill in War and Society.

text:
🚨‼️There is something mighty peculiar about a Christian who insists he doesn’t need alcohol but becomes fighting mad the moment somebody suggests he leave it alone. He doesn’t need it, mind you. He can quit anytime. He’s perfectly in control. But question that occasional beer, that glass of wine, or that little drink after dinner, and suddenly you’ve started a theological war. Out comes John chapter 2, Timothy’s stomach trouble, and a twenty-minute sermon on Christian liberty. The fellow who couldn’t find Habakkuk with a road map has suddenly become a Bible scholar defending his liquor cabinet! Well, here’s a question worth answering: If you don’t need the drink, why do you fight so hard to keep it? If giving it up costs you nothing, why does the suggestion of giving it up bother you so much? Sometimes the thing a man defends most fiercely is the very thing he ought to examine most carefully.

Now, the Bible does not explicitly condemn every instance of drinking alcohol, and there’s no need to manufacture commandments God never gave. But neither does the absence of a universal prohibition establish that a practice is wise, profitable, or spiritually beneficial. Paul declared in 1 Corinthians 6:12, “All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” Did you catch that last part? I WILL NOT BE BROUGHT UNDER THE POWER OF ANY! Christian liberty isn’t merely the freedom to say yes. It’s also the freedom to say no. And if a man cannot contemplate surrendering a pleasure without becoming resentful, he ought to examine whether that pleasure has acquired more importance than he realizes. A habit doesn’t have to put you in the gutter before it deserves examination under Scripture. The chains of an appetite are not always made of iron. Sometimes they’re made of excuses.

And while we’re discussing your rights, what about the fellow sitting across from you who spent fifteen years trying to escape the bottle? What about the wife who has watched alcohol destroy her marriage? What about the child who has seen what drunkenness does to a family? What about the recovering alcoholic who cannot safely have the one drink you insist is harmless to you? Romans 14:21 declares, “It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.” There’s your Christian liberty with somebody else’s welfare attached to it! You may be able to stop after one glass, but the man watching you may not be able to stop after ten. That doesn’t make every moderate drinker an addict, but it certainly makes another person’s spiritual welfare worth considering. If your liberty is so precious that you cannot surrender a drink to help a struggling brother, perhaps the problem isn’t legalism. Perhaps the problem is selfishness wearing a Sunday suit.

The Christian life was never intended to be a lifelong contest to discover how close a believer can get to the world without crossing an unmistakable line. Ephesians 5:18 declares, “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.” There is the command worth defending! Instead of spending all your energy proving that you have the right to enjoy another drink, why not spend some of it examining whether your life is filled with the Spirit of God? There are families being destroyed, people fighting addiction, children watching their parents, and souls who desperately need somebody to demonstrate that Jesus Christ offers something better than another temporary pleasure. Nobody gets saved by quitting alcohol, and nobody earns righteousness by boasting about abstinence. Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. But grace ought to teach a saved man something about sobriety, charity, and self-control.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who just became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he will likely be sworn in on a Quran. “I will likely swear on a Quran. Which Quran, we’re not sure,” he told NPR. He quickly added the familiar line: “I mean, Thomas Jefferson had a copy of a Quran. So when Keith Ellison was sworn into Congress, he swore in on that copy.”

That is the cleaned-up version of history. The actual record is less convenient.

Jefferson owned a Quran because he was trying to understand the legal and religious system that was actively attacking American ships. In 1786, while Jefferson and John Adams were still in Europe, they met the envoy from Tripoli. The envoy did not offer a lesson in multiculturalism. He told them the Quran gave Muslims the right to wage war on non-believers, seize their ships, and enslave their sailors. Jefferson later wrote that the ambassador said it was “founded on the Laws of their Prophet, that it was written in their Koran, that all nations who should not have acknowledged their authority were sinners, that it was their right and duty to make war upon them wherever they could be found, and to make slaves of all they could take as Prisoners.”

The new United States first paid tribute to avoid further attacks. Once it built a navy, it stopped paying and fought the Barbary Wars. The Marines’ Hymn still records the result: “to the shores of Tripoli.” Jefferson’s answer was not a ceremonial oath on the same book that had been used to justify the attacks. It was force.

The selective retelling now treats the Quran as proof that Islam has always been part of the American founding. It leaves out that the founding generation’s direct experience with Islamic states was piracy, enslavement, and demands for protection money. Framing every concern about large-scale Muslim immigration or political power as bigotry erases that record.

El-Sayed has also described Michigan as “Arab America” and directed the remark at “all my right-wing ops.” Most of the voters he is addressing are ordinary evangelical Christians, not a fringe. At the same time, Christians are being killed in multiple countries by groups that cite the same religious framework the Tripoli envoy described in 1786. El-Sayed has not made that a campaign issue. Instead, disagreement is often reduced to prejudice against his name or his prayers.
