text:
The companies that verify your identity are now the ones losing it.

Identity verification vendors sit between you and hundreds of apps. They see your passport, your selfie, and your address. Over the last two years, that position has made them one of fintech's most attractive targets.

A few cases on the record:

• AU10TIX (2024). 404 Media reported that administrator credentials for the ID verification vendor, whose clients have included TikTok, Uber, and X, had been exposed online for more than a year.

• Coinbase (2025). Attackers bribed overseas support contractors to pull customer data, including ID images, then demanded $20 million. Coinbase refused and instead offered a $20 million reward for information on the attackers.

• Discord (October 2025). About 70,000 users’ government ID photos were exposed through a third-party customer support vendor.

• Sumsub (disclosed February 2026). An intruder entered through a third-party support ticketing platform and went unnoticed for about 18 months. Sumsub says ID images and biometrics were not accessed.

• https://t.co/zFKfM1d0WH (September 2026). A dark web marketplace claimed more than 153 million driver’s license scans attributed to the vendor. A breach filing in Texas puts the number of affected people at about 13 million.

In most cases, attackers didn’t break the verification engine itself. They came in through support staff, contractors, or exposed credentials: the human side of the operation.

And in every case, the damage depended on what the company stored. A vendor that keeps millions of document images will always be worth attacking.

text:
Nvidia lost its chief executive days before earnings while the industry committed capital it has not earned yet.

NVIDIA · RESIGNATION EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY
Nvidia said November 12 that Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. The board accepted the resignation November 11, per its Form 8-K. CFO Colette Kress is interim chief and keeps the finance role, and director Harvey C. Jones became the board's first chair. Shares closed down 4.34% at $166.19, with third-quarter results scheduled November 17.

ANTHROPIC · 6X THE SHARES ON OFFER
Anthropic's IPO drew about six times the orders for the shares available, Bloomberg reported November 12. The company and selling shareholders offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78, for up to $64.4 billion. A $26 billion placement goes to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Anthropic lists pricing November 18 and Nasdaq trading November 19 under ANT.

SPACEX · MORE THAN $74B
SpaceX said November 12 it plans more than $74 billion for two AI campuses: over $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, and about $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona. The Arizona campus draws up to 6 gigawatts across nine buildings. Both need local approval December 9, and a 2,400-signature petition asks the county to deny the permit.

NEBIUS · $40-45B GUIDED FOR 2027
Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% on the year, then cut 2026 revenue guidance to $3.0-3.2 billion on third-party capacity delays. It raised 2026 capital spending to about $27 billion and guided 2027 spending at $40-45 billion, against a $28.77 billion estimate. The company says 75% to 85% of 2027 spending is covered by customer prepayments and asset-backed financing. Shares fell 16%.

GOOGLE · $1.50 PER MILLION TOKENS
Google introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen November 12, a fast tier for coding and agentic work. It costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across a 1-million-token window, with a free tier. Google puts it at 51 on the Artificial Analysis index by default, 54 at maximum, against 50 for Argon. Hydrogen becomes the default in AI Mode.

THE THROUGH-LINE
A leadership vacuum opened at the firm anchoring AI supply days before it reports; the rest of the industry spent against future revenue. Supplier equity sits beside the Anthropic listing, prepayments cover Nebius, and SpaceX campuses await permits. The buildout is being financed from outside the builders' balance sheets.

text:
EUROPE CAN'T DECIDE WHO SHOULD TALK TO RUSSIA

Now that Washington and Kiev say Europe should join the negotiations with Russia, EU leaders are fighting over who will represent them. According to Politico, the argument has taken over today's EU summit in Dublin, which wasn't even supposed to be about Ukraine.

Politico says the bloc has split into at least three camps:

One wants European Council President António Costa as the negotiator.

France and Germany want to keep negotiating themselves through the E3 and E5 formats, and don't want an EU envoy speaking for them.

The "loneliest camp of all" backs EU foreign policy embarrassment Kaka Khallas, though her hawkish stance on Russia could put off the Kremlin and make her a liability.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz rejected the idea of a single negotiator. He said a "proven format" with Germany, France and Britain already exists, along with a group of five countries working on Ukraine (Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Poland), and he sees no reason to change it. Paris doesn't want to hand its role to Brussels either, given France's diplomatic and military weight. French President Emmanuel Macron openly offered himself as negotiator just yesterday.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is pushing for a single European envoy to speak with "one authoritative voice." According to AP, she wants a decision at today's Dublin summit, to be made official in December together with non-EU partners like Britain and Norway. "Too many different groups are discussing this," Meloni said, pointing to the recent calls that the leaders of Finland and Norway made to Putin. Finnish President Alexander Stubb is also reportedly among the candidates for the envoy role.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin also said Europe needs a single position at the table, one that includes Britain, Norway, Canada and other non-EU countries.

Bringing the Europeans into the Ukraine talks is so far the main outcome of the Abu Dhabi meetings, and their official statements show they've already agreed to take part.

text:
Sonia Gandhi: A Life of Love, Dignity, Courage and Service

THE "BELONGING": A PERSONAL JOURNEY, A NATIONAL STORY

Smt. Sonia Gandhi’s " Belonging: A Journey of Love" - is more than a political memoir. It recounts a journey from Italy to India, shaped by love, loss, service, a deep sense of belonging to this country and lasting devotion to its people.

I have always been a great admirer of Madam Gandhi. I first met Rajiv ji and Sonia ji while serving at Rashtrapati Bhavan as an Indian Air Force fighter pilot deputed to the office of the President of India. 

As I entered public life, she placed her trust in me. She gave me the opportunity to serve as a minister and later as president of the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee. I have served six terms as MLA, represented our people in Parliament and held ministerial responsibilities in undivided Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

When I look back at my political journey, I do so with gratitude: I owe everything I have achieved in public life to her faith in me. That bond makes reading "Belonging" meaningful. The book traces Sonia Gandhi’s life from her childhood in Italy and her meeting with Rajiv Gandhi in Cambridge to her arrival in India and the making of a home here.

Its pages place the private story of a wife and mother alongside the history of a nation. The deaths of Sanjay Gandhi, Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi were not only defining public events; they were devastating losses within a family. The memoir brings that human dimension into view.

I have watched Madam Gandhi withstand personal attacks that too often descended into unfairness and prejudice. Through every phase, she has remained an example of grace, dignity and decency. The restraint and composure with which she has met hostility say much about her character.
In public life, where it is easy to answer insults with anger, she has consistently shown self-command and a profound sense of responsibility.
Her decision to enter politics after years of reluctance was an act of duty.

As Congress president, she gave the party direction and renewed purpose through difficult years. Her leadership helped bring together a broad coalition, and her decision to decline the office of Prime Minister in 2004, while supporting Dr. Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister, remains an extraordinary moment of political judgment and personal conviction.

The title captures the book’s deepest theme. "Belonging" is not determined by birthplace alone; it grows through love, shared struggle and service. Sonia Gandhi made India her home, and devoted herself to its people and democratic life. Her memoir offers a rare opportunity to understand the woman behind the public role: a person shaped by affection, bereavement, courage and commitment.

For me, this book is also a reminder of a debt of gratitude. Madam Gandhi’s confidence gave me opportunities that shaped my life in the Congress and in public service. I remain profoundly thankful.

"Belonging" is a moving account of personal endurance and public duty, and a tribute to a leader whose grace under pressure has earned the admiration of countless people, including me.

N. Uttam Kumar Reddy, 
Telangana Minister for Irrigation and Civil Supplies. 

Former Indian Air Force fighter pilot.

•A second reported affair with Kimberly Powell, NVIDIA’s VP of Healthcare (a direct report). Sources described video of them being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during GTC in March 2026; security allegedly offered an NDA to a bystander. This violated company policy and was the proximate cause of the board’s decisive action.
He apologized to employees for being “unfaithful to my wife.” The board initially investigated the spy angle and had expressed some confidence, but the employee relationship prompted a late-night meeting in which he had no real choice but to resign. Reports describe him as depleted and self-critical in the final hours.
Market and company reaction
NVIDIA stock has been hit hard—down double digits around the news, with cumulative market-cap losses in the hundreds of billions (briefly under $4T). This accelerates a prior slide and is pricing out a meaningful “Huang premium”: his hands-on technical involvement, Asian supply-chain relationships (TSMC, memory makers), customer financing of the AI buildout, and Washington lobbying.
The core franchise (CUDA moat, Blackwell/Vera Rubin roadmap, hyperscaler demand, installed base) does not disappear overnight. Quarterly results were still expected to show strong growth, and Kress has stressed operational continuity. That said, the lack of a prepared succession plan, Huang’s unusually flat org structure, and the personal relationships that underpinned priority access and deal-making create real near-term friction.
Base-case outlook
•NVIDIA the company: Survives and remains the dominant AI infrastructure platform, but with more conventional governance and some erosion of the founder-driven edge in relationships and intensity. Near-term volatility and possible brain-drain or competitive opening (AMD, custom silicon) are real risks. The AI capex cycle and product lead matter more than any single person over a multi-year horizon.
•The spy/export angle: The most material overhang. No public confirmation yet that company secrets were compromised (earlier board statements said they had no reason to believe so), but the appearance of entanglement with a major customer under investigation for diversion creates regulatory, congressional, and political exposure. Expect scrutiny, possible tighter controls, and questions about past commercial decisions.
•Huang personally: Severe reputational damage. He remains a large individual shareholder but has no formal role. Personal life is in turmoil; he is expected to face congressional questions. Unlikely to return to NVIDIA leadership. (Elon Musk’s public comment that it would be an “honor” to hire him is noted but secondary.)
In short: classic key-person risk meeting personal indiscretion, magnified by the geopolitics of the AI chip race. The AI boom and NVIDIA’s technical position continue; the singular Jensen-era intensity and personal premium do not. The stock has already begun discounting that distinction.

1) 🛢️ THE WORLD MAY HAVE MORE OIL THAN IT NEEDS - AND STILL PAY A FORTUNE FOR FUEL

🌍 The International Energy Agency just delivered the biggest energy update of the day

📊 For the final three months of 2026, the agency now expects:
🛢️ 1.7 MILLION MORE BARRELS OF OIL SUPPLIED EACH DAY THAN THE WORLD CONSUMES

📉 Previously, it expected a shortage

🚨 That's a major reversal
🚢 Global production has been recovering as Gulf exporters find ways to move more oil despite the conflict with Iran

🔍 But here's the number that makes this report genuinely interesting
🇪🇺 European diesel is still roughly 77% more expensive than before the war
📉 Even after crude oil prices have fallen dramatically

🚨 WHY?
⚙️ Because crude oil and the fuel delivered to customers aren't the same product
🚢 Oil must be transported
🏭 Refineries must turn it into usable fuels
🚚 Those products must then reach the places where they're needed
💰 And every stage has its own capacity, costs and risks
🏭 The energy agency estimates that global refineries processed only 81.3 million barrels per day in October, a seasonal low

🚢 Meanwhile, oil held aboard ships has increased sharply
⚠️ But inventories stored on land remain at their lowest levels since at least 2016

🚨 THINK ABOUT WHAT THAT MEANS
🌍 Oil can be available somewhere in the world without being available in the right place, in the right form, at the right time

🏭 A tanker carrying crude doesn't solve a factory's diesel shortage until the oil is delivered, refined and distributed

💸 And that entire process costs money

🇮🇷 Now remember Iran
🇮🇷 Tehran continues insisting on its seven conditions
🇺🇸 Washington has not accepted them
⚓ Shipping through Hormuz remains exposed to attacks and restrictions
🏗️ And damaged energy facilities still require substantial repairs

⚖️ So the world can move toward an overall crude surplus while some companies continue paying exceptionally high prices for usable energy

🚨 THIS IS WHY THE NEXT STAGE OF THE ENERGY STORY ISN'T SIMPLY ABOUT BRENT GOING UP OR DOWN
🎯 It's about where the bottlenecks remain
🏭 Who controls the working refineries?
🚚 Who can deliver fuel reliably?
🚢 Which shipping routes are commercially viable?
💰 And how much must businesses pay for that reliability?

💰 Those questions determine where the next energy investments and profits may emerge

🎯 THE OIL SHORTAGE MAY BE EASING
💵THE COST OF DELIVERING ENERGY HASN'T RETURNED TO NORMAL

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
2) 🏦 THE US GOVERNMENT BORROWED $404 BILLION IN OCTOBER
💵NOW THINK ABOUT THE PRICE OF MONEY

🚨 THIS IS AN IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT THAT DESERVES MORE ATTENTION

🗓️ IN JUST ONE MONTH
🇺🇸 AMERICA SPENT $404 BILLION MORE THAN IT EARNED

💰 In October, the US government spent $404 BILLION more than it collected in taxes and other income

📈 That's 42% more than a year earlier, partly because some payments shifted between months

🤔 SO WHERE DOES THE EXTRA MONEY COME FROM?
🏦 The government borrows it
💳 But borrowing isn't free

🚨And here's where things get interesting

🚨 THE US PAID ABOUT $115 BILLION IN INTEREST ON ITS DEBT IN OCTOBER ALONE

🚨Read that again
💸 $115 BILLION

🚫Not to build new roads
🚫Not to build hospitals
🚫Not to improve infrastructure

⚠️Just the cost of borrowing money in the past

⚠️ And now the problem is getting bigger
🔥 US inflation remains high

🏦 Investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in December
💰 That could make new government borrowing even more expensive

🙉THINK ABOUT IT
🇺🇸 America needs to borrow money to cover its spending
💳 And it already spends enormous amounts paying interest on previous borrowing
📈 If borrowing stays expensive, the interest bill becomes harder to manage over time

🚨 THE GOVERNMENT ISN'T JUST PAYING FOR WHAT IT SPENDS TODAY

💵IT'S ALSO PAYING AN ENORMOUS PRICE FOR THE MONEY IT BORROWED YESTERDAY

🚨 HERE'S THE PROBLEM
- 🏛️ The government needs financing
- 🏢 Businesses need financing
- 🤖 AI companies need financing
- 🏠 Homebuyers need financing
- 🏦 And all of them are operating in a world where interest rates remain high

⚖️ They aren't borrowing from one identical pool of money, and government borrowing doesn't mechanically determine every other interest rate

💵 But high Treasury yields raise the return investors can earn from relatively safe dollar assets

🔄 That changes the alternatives available to them.

💭 Imagine a company promising enormous profits five years from now
📈 An investor must decide whether those profits justify the uncertainty when government bonds already offer substantial income

💳 And if the company itself needs billions in loans, higher interest payments make its future profits harder to achieve

🚨 THAT'S WHY THE COST OF CAPITAL MATTERS SO MUCH RIGHT NOW
📈 Not because higher interest rates automatically destroy every stock rally
🎯 But because they raise the standard that expensive investments must meet

🤖 And this brings us directly to today's biggest technology story

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
3) 🤖 NVIDIA - JENSEN HUANG IS OUT
🙉HOW MUCH OF A $4 TRILLION COMPANY WAS ACTUALLY HIM?

🚨 Jensen Huang has officially stepped down as Nvidia's CEO
🏦 Colette Kress, who previously managed the company's finances, has temporarily taken his place

And look at how this happened
👀 First, reports emerged about a relationship involving a businesswoman suspected of Chinese intelligence connections

👀 Then another relationship was reported
⚠️ And then another

🤔 INTERESTING TIMING, ISN'T IT?
📊 Just as investors were already questioning whether AI companies could justify their enormous valuations

🏦 Borrowing money remains expensive
📉 And investors are becoming less willing to pay any price for promises of future profits

👤 AND HOW MUCH WAS INVESTORS' TRUST IN JENSEN HUANG?

👨‍💻 Its engineers haven't forgotten how to design chips

🔍 Now here's where things get even more interesting
💾 Nvidia doesn't just sell chips
💰 It also invests in companies that buy those chips and helps finance parts of the AI industry

🌐 That means its influence goes far beyond its own products

🏦 If new management becomes more cautious about investing money, some businesses depending on Nvidia's support could face a much harder time financing their expansion

💸 And remember - many AI companies are already spending enormous amounts of money before they become consistently profitable

🚨 NOW ZOOM OUT
📉 If losing one CEO can shake confidence in a company worth trillions...

🤔 What does that tell us about the valuations of other AI companies built around famous founders and their promises?

💰 How much are investors paying for technology that already earns money?

👤 And how much for the belief that one particular person will deliver an extraordinary future?

🎯 NVIDIA DIDN'T LOSE ITS CHIPS
🚨 IT LOST THE MAN INVESTORS TRUSTED TO TURN THOSE CHIPS INTO TRILLIONS
💰 AND NOW WALL STREET HAS TO DECIDE HOW MUCH THAT TRUST WAS WORTH

🇩🇪 Germany's DAX also reached a record

📉 Yet American technology stocks have been suffering from concerns about AI valuations, financing and Nvidia's leadership crisis

🚨 WHY ARE THESE MARKETS BEHAVING DIFFERENTLY?

🏭 An established industrial company may already have customers, existing factories and profits

🚨 THIS ISN'T THE SAME AS ALL INVESTORS ABANDONING TECHNOLOGY
💰 It's a change in what they are willing to pay for different kinds of earnings

🔍 There's another factor
🛢️ Europe imports substantial amounts of energy

🏦 But persistent inflation and higher interest rates remain risks for Europe too

🎯 A WEAK AI TRADE DOESN'T AUTOMATICALLY MEAN A WEAK GLOBAL STOCK MARKET
💰 CAPITAL CAN LEAVE ONE GROUP OF COMPANIES AND FIND A NEW HOME IN ANOTHER

📡 Modern military operations depend heavily on communications infrastructure
🏢 And that infrastructure can be controlled by commercial companies and foreign governments
🛡️ So security guarantees aren't only about soldiers, tanks and missiles
🛰️ They also involve access to satellites, communications networks, maintenance and technology
💰 And those systems require contracts, suppliers and long-term funding

🚨 THIS IS THE BIGGER QUESTION BEHIND A FUTURE PEACE AGREEMENT

Fiscal Overstretch, Strategic Focus, and the Iran Question

The U.S. fiscal trajectory is a genuine strategic vulnerability. With annual deficits above $1 trillion and debt-service costs rising rapidly, sustained high military outlays compound the problem and limit long-term flexibility. This is not an argument against necessary defense spending; it is a recognition that unchecked growth in obligations can constrain options, as history shows when empires overextend.
Military powers have repeatedly declined more from internal overreach and misallocation than from external defeat. Rome’s later centuries and other historical cases illustrate how resource exhaustion and loss of strategic clarity can erode primacy. Today’s United States retains formidable advantages, yet perpetual high spending without corresponding fiscal discipline risks reducing the very capacity that underpins influence.
Empires and great powers more often weaken through self-inflicted problems—hubris, domestic division, and the substitution of tactical or personal priorities for coherent strategy—than through pure external pressure. When leadership attention tilts toward post-office legal or political concerns, it can dilute focus on longer-term statecraft. Effective policy requires distinguishing core national interests from shorter-term political calculations.
Zbigniew Brzezinski warned in The Grand Chessboard (1997) that a major conflict with Iran could accelerate the relative erosion of American primacy and reorder the international system in ways unfavorable to Washington. That caution remains relevant: diplomacy led by figures such as JD Vance offers a path to manage risks without defaulting to costly confrontation. Great powers decline less by accident than by choices that favor short-term motion over sustainable strategy. Prioritizing fiscal realism alongside clear-eyed negotiation can still preserve U.S. advantages.

text:
To the best of my knowledge, I am not a robot. And yet, like other humans who spend too much time on the internet, I’m routinely asked to prove this fact by clicking on crosswalks and motorcycles in photos, deciphering distorted numbers and letters, and checking little white boxes that affirm my non-robot status. These so-called captchas, or “completely automated public Turing tests to tell computers and humans apart,” are supposed to help prevent spam and data scraping, although it now appears that bots are better at solving them than humans. Go figure. 

Thankfully, the difference between humans and machines in the real world is much easier to discern, at least for now. One of the more robust differentiators involves our unique skill sets. While machines tend to excel at things adults find difficult—playing world-champion-level chess, say, or multiplying really big numbers—they find it difficult (or impossible) to accomplish the stuff a five-year-old can do with ease, such as catching a ball or walking around a room without bumping into things. 

This discrepancy between the relative ease of teaching a machine abstract thinking and the difficulty of teaching it basic sensory, social, and motor skills is what’s known as Moravec’s paradox. Named after an observation the roboticist Hans Moravec made back in the late 1980s, the paradox states that what’s hard for humans (math, logic, scientific reasoning) is easy for machines, and what’s hard for machines (tying shoelaces, reading emotions, having a conversation) is easy for humans. 

In her latest book, Robots and the People Who Love Them: Holding On to Our Humanity in an Age of Social Robots, science writer Eve Herold argues that thanks to new approaches in machine learning and continued advances in AI, we’re finally starting to unravel this paradox. As a result, a new era of personal and social robots is about to unfold, she says—one that will force us to reimagine the nature of everything from friendship and love to work, health care, and home life. 

To give readers a sense of what this brave new world of social robots will look like, Herold points us toward Pepper, a doe-eyed humanoid robot that’s made by the Japanese company SoftBank. “Robots like Pepper will soon make themselves indispensable because of their unique, highly personalized relationships with us,” Herold writes, before describing with press-release-like zeal how this chest-high companion can effortlessly read our expressions and emotional states and respond appropriately in its own childlike voice.

If Pepper sounds vaguely familiar, it may be because it was relentlessly hyped as the world’s first “emotional robot” in the years following its 2014 introduction. That abruptly stopped in 2021, however, when SoftBank pulled the plug on Pepper production because of lack of demand and—probably not unrelatedly—the $2,000 android’s general incompetence. Books can obviously take a long time to write, and a lot can change while you’re writing them. But it’s hard to reconcile this particular oversight with the fact that Pepper was canned some three years before the book’s publication.  

Positioning a defunct product that nobody seems to have liked or bought as part of some vanguard for a new social-­robot revolution doesn’t inspire confidence. Herold might respond by pointing out that her book’s focus is less on the robots themselves than on what we humans will bring to the new social relationships we forge with them. Fair enough. 

But while she dutifully unpacks our penchant for anthropomorphizing and walks readers through some rudimentary research on deep learning and the uncanny valley, Herold’s conclusions about human nature and psychology often seem either oversimplified or divorced from the evidence she provides. For someone who says that “the only way to write about the future is with a high degree of humility,” there are also an unusually large number of deeply questionable assertions (“So far, the trust we’ve placed in algorithms has been, on balance, well placed …”) and sweeping predictions (“There’s no doubt some version of a companion robot will be coming soon to homes throughout the industrialized world”).   

Early on in the book, Herold reminds readers that “science writing that attempts to envision the future often says much more about the time it was written than it says about the future world.” In this respect, Robots and the People Who Love Them is indeed quite revealing. Among other things, the book reflects the way we tend to reduce discussions of technological impacts into binary terms (“It’ll be amazing”/”It’ll be terrible”); the shrugging acquiescence with which we seem to regard undesirable outcomes; the readiness of science and technology writers to succumb to industry hype; and the disturbing extent to which the logic and values of machines (speed, efficiency) have already been adopted by humans. It’s probably not one of Herold’s intended takeaways, but if the book demonstrates anything, it’s not that robots are becoming more like us; it’s that we’re becoming more like them. 

For a more rigorous look at one of the pillars of human social expression—and, specifically, how we’ve tried to transfer it to machines—Sarah A. Bell’s Vox ex Machina: A Cultural History of Talking Machines offers a compelling and insightful history of voice synthesis during the 20th century. Bell, a writer and professor at Michigan Technological University, is interested in how we try to digitally reproduce different expressions of human embodiment, be it speech, emotions, or visual identities. As she points out early on in the book, understanding this process often means understanding the ways in which engineers (almost universally male ones) have decided to measure and quantify aspects of our bodies.

The story begins at the epicenter for many of the century’s most important technological breakthroughs: Bell Labs. By the 1930s, researchers there were already thinking about human speech as a type of signal or, as the head of the acoustics research department put it years later, “specialized acoustic code.” One of those engineers, Homer Dudley, likened the tongue to a telegraph tapper, seeing it as merely an instrument inside our mouths that “modulated the ‘carrier wave’ emanating from the glottis.” In the same way that Morse code broke down writing into parts for later reassembly, Dudley believed, speech sounds—and everything else that makes up the richness of human vocal expression—could similarly be compressed, or reduced to pulses.

According to Bell, researchers like Dudley laid the groundwork for pretty much all the voice synthesis work that has come since, “embedding their assumptions about the mechanical nature of the human voice in all the technologies that would follow.” One of the first and most famous examples of Dudley’s work was the Voder, or Voice Demonstrator. Debuting at the 1939 World’s Fair in New York, it was basically a small voice organ that was operated by “Voderettes,” women who went through a year of training to master all the speech sounds the machine could make by manipulating 10 keys, a wrist plate, and a pedal. 

The talking-machine demonstrations, although highly choreographed, were a hit with visitors and the press—so much so that people seemed willing to attribute far more understanding and autonomy to the Voder than was warranted. Even though the Voderette was in full view during the entire demonstration, the press usually mentioned the woman responsible for making the sounds only in passing, if at all. Instead, the Voder was anthropomorphized and granted a high degree of agency. “He hasn’t any mouth, lungs, or larynx—but he talks a blue streak,” wrote Popular Science. 

From the Voder and Elektro the Moto-Man to Speak & Spell and Perfect Paul to Alexa and Siri, Vox ex Machina showcases both the products of voice synthesis and the underlying technologies that made them possible. It’s a fascinating tour, particularly when Bell focuses on the ways in which the public’s reaction to these “talking machines” presaged its reaction to the “thinking” ones that would emerge decades later. While the practice of describing humans with machine metaphors and machines with human metaphors dates back centuries, the ability of machines to simulate human speech (however poorly) “gave machinic personification a new inflection,” writes Bell.   

In other words, the more machines could “speak” and “think,” the more we started to think of ourselves as machines. Indeed, one can’t help but see striking parallels to what’s happening with today’s artificial intelligence—specifically, our willingness to reduce or minimize what makes us human to better conform to whatever “intelligent” attribute a product may be demonstrating. Sam Altman’s response to the fact that LLMs are just really good word calculators? “i am a stochastic parrot, and so r u.”

“Forget about losing jobs to automation. Remarkably, the reality is that humans steal the jobs of robots.”

The Voder may have been one of the first crude attempts at speech synthesis, but the disconnect between the way it worked (with a lot of human training and labor) and the way the public and press perceived it (as a more or less autonomous machine with its own voice) foreshadowed a problem we still face today. In Waiting for Robots: The Hired Hands of Automation, Antonio A. Casilli argues that despite claims to the contrary, human input remains a crucial component of all modern automation and artificial-intelligence tools, regardless of their sophistication. The difference is that instead of this role being obvious—as was the case with the Voderettes—it’s now hidden, and usually on purpose.

Casilli is a sociology professor at the Polytechnic Institute of Paris who studies the unseen and unacknowledged “digital labor” that undergirds many of today’s social media platforms, microtask sites, and on-demand services. Rather than viewing automation and AI as destroyers of human jobs, he makes a convincing case that they merely result in the further atomization of work, fracturing it into smaller, more meaningless, more demeaning tasks for many of us. “Forget about losing jobs to automation,” he writes. “Remarkably, the reality is that humans steal the jobs of robots.”

Whether it’s Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, a service for recruiting hundreds of thousands of micro-taskers to perform video-filtering and image-tagging tasks that machines can’t do, or the perpetual human “supervision” and “reinforcement” required for automated learning and AI training, Casilli gives readers plenty of examples of how human labor (much of it coming from Asian, Latin American, and African countries) props up—or, in some cases, pretends to actually be—intelligent systems and products.

Ultimately, Casilli is less concerned that robots will replace white-collar workers, and more worried that thousands of lower-paid or unpaid digital workers will. As he points out, we are already unwittingly being recruited by companies to collectively perform millions of hours of free work every year. Take the aforementioned captchas: Google, which owns and deploys one of the most popular versions of the service (ReCAPTCHA and No CAPTCHA), has been using this digital labor for more than a decade. The results help detect house numbers to improve Google Street View, digitize texts for Google Books, and train its computer vision algorithms to detect locations and reconstruct scenes, enhancing Google Images and improving the performance of Waymo’s self-driving cars. “The irony here is that a service that is supposed to distinguish humans from robots is actually making humans work to produce more robots,” Casilli writes.

While all the hype and hyperbole surrounding today’s AI tools can feel unprecedented, Casilli reminds readers that such rhetoric isn’t really new at all. Robots, automation, and various intelligent systems have been just on the verge of taking over all aspects of our work lives and cultural output for decades now. In the end, artificial intelligence is a technological process that isn’t actually artificial, he says. Peer behind the curtains of smooth and seamless efficiency, and it’s humans all the way down.

Bryan Gardiner is a writer based in Oakland, California.

I bought a Matic robot vacuum for one simple reason: their Vision First navigation genuinely impressed me. It felt different from everything else on the market, and I wanted it badly enough that I ignored the clear warning that India is not a supported region. I was told, in no uncertain terms, that any damage, service, or issues would be entirely my responsibility. I still went ahead and used a freight forwarder at my own risk.
It took almost a month to arrive. When it finally did, it was damaged, broken, and completely dead on arrival.
What happened after that is something I still talk about with disbelief.

I reached out to Mehul on Twitter. He replied almost instantly. He didn’t just acknowledge the problem — he assembled a team and got on a video call with me so they could try to diagnose and fix it together in real time. When that didn’t fully resolve it, Matic did something I never expected: they offered to send me an entirely new robot, free of cost.
Not just shipped through some warehouse. Kripa Shankar, one of their employees, hand-carried the replacement all the way from California to Chennai while he was traveling. A single person physically brought it across the world for one customer who had purchased outside their supported region, through a method they don’t recommend, and fully at his own risk.
Throughout the entire process, Divya stayed in constant touch with me. She kept me updated, answered every question, and made sure I never felt like just another ticket in a system. The combination of Mehul’s immediate response, the team’s willingness to jump on a call, Divya’s consistent care, and Kripa actually carrying the unit by hand created a level of customer experience I have never encountered before.
I was one person, thousands of miles away, in a country they don’t officially support. They could have easily said the situation was outside their responsibility and moved on. Instead, they treated me with genuine care and urgency. That kind of human effort is rare, and it showed me that Matic doesn’t just build interesting robots — they actually stand behind the people who believe in them.

I’ll never forget it.

text:
A wet reckless is a reduced plea bargain where a driving under the influence (DUI) charge is amended to reckless driving with a special notation that alcohol or drugs were involved (under California Vehicle Code § 23103.5), whereas a standard DUI is a full conviction for driving under the influence (Vehicle Code § 23152).

Key Similarities & Cautions

• Priorable Offense: Even though a wet reckless is formally a reckless driving conviction rather than a DUI, California and many other jurisdictions count it as a "prior" if you are arrested for a second DUI within a 10-year window. 

• DMV vs. Court: A reduction in criminal court does not automatically cancel the California DMV Administrative Per Se (APS) suspension; you still have to fight or win your separate DMV hearing to keep your license completely clear. 

• Insurance Impact: Auto insurance companies often treat a wet reckless just as harshly as a DUI, which can result in spiked premiums or dropped coverage. 

• General Consensus: Commenters on legal forums like Reddit generally agree that accepting a wet reckless plea offer is significantly more advantageous than risking a full DUI trial, as it cuts down fines, jail exposure, and program lengths.

This moment has since been recognized as a pivotal point in the evolution of AI. It was not merely a demonstration of AI’s proficiency in playing Go but a revelation that machines could think outside the box and exhibit creativity. This moment fundamentally altered the perception of AI, transforming it from a tool that follows predefined rules to an entity capable of innovation. Since that fateful match, AI continues to drive profound changes across industries, from content recommendations to fraud detection. However, the game-changing power of AI became evident when ChatGPT brought generative AI to the masses.

This capability opened up new possibilities for AI applications, from customer service to content creation. The world responded to ChatGPT with a mix of awe and excitement, recognizing the potential of AI to transform how humans communicate and interact with technology to enhance our lives.

The rise of agentic AI

Today, the rise of agentic AI — systems capable of advanced reasoning and task execution — is revolutionizing the way organizations operate. Agentic AI systems are designed to pursue complex goals with autonomy and predictability. They are productivity enablers that can effectively incorporate humans in the loop via the use of multi-modality. These systems can take goal-directed actions with minimal human oversight, make contextual decisions, and dynamically adjust plans based on changing conditions.    

Deploy agentic AI today

Physical AI and beyond

Looking ahead, the next wave in AI development is physical AI, powered by AI models that can understand and engage with our world and generate their actions based on advanced sensory input. Physical AI will enable a new frontier of digitalization for heavy industries, delivering more intelligence and autonomy to the world’s warehouses and factories, and driving major advancements in autonomous transportation. The NVIDIA Omniverse development platform is available on Microsoft Azure to enable developers to build advanced physical AI, simulation, and digital twin applications that accelerate industrial digitalization.

🖊️ Market significance: The liquidation cascade amplified spot selling and accelerated the move through major support levels.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is a meaningful leverage reset, but I would not call it complete simply because the liquidation number is large. What matters next is whether funding, open interest and dip-buying leverage actually normalize.

4⃣ Stablecoin supply continued contracting

Total dollar-stablecoin supply fell toward approximately $289.1B, down around 1.5% over seven days and roughly 4.9% over 30 days.

The contraction has continued alongside falling crypto prices and ETF withdrawals.

🖊️ Market significance: Stablecoin contraction indicates that part of the weakness reflects declining crypto-native dollar liquidity rather than capital simply moving from one token to another.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This remains one of the most important signals in the market. Price can rebound temporarily without new liquidity, but a sustained recovery becomes much harder when the stablecoin base is shrinking at the same time.

5⃣ Bitcoin ETFs recorded a sixth consecutive outflow session

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost approximately $47.8M on November 12.

The six-session outflow sequence from November 5 through November 12 now totals approximately $1.49B.

Bitwise's BITB and ARKB recorded meaningful withdrawals, while Morgan Stanley's MSBT attracted a small inflow.

🖊️ Market significance: Regulated institutional demand has remained negative throughout Bitcoin's decline rather than stepping in aggressively as prices fell.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Six consecutive outflow sessions matter more than any single day's number. Until that sequence breaks, I would not assume institutional investors are treating lower prices as an attractive accumulation opportunity.

6⃣ Ethereum ETFs also recorded a sixth consecutive negative session

Ethereum ETFs lost approximately $8M on November 12.

The amount was much smaller than the previous day's roughly $145M withdrawal, but the direction remained negative.

🖊️ Market significance: Ethereum's institutional flow profile remains weak even after ETH moved materially lower.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Smaller outflows are an improvement in pace, not a reversal in demand. I would need to see sustained positive sessions before interpreting lower ETH prices as attracting meaningful regulated capital.

7⃣ Solana ETFs returned to a small inflow

Solana investment products recorded approximately $1.7M of net inflows, ending their recent sequence of withdrawals.

XRP products were approximately flat, while Zcash products experienced additional outflows.

The broader U.S. spot-crypto ETF complex remained negative overall.

🖊️ Market significance: Solana showed isolated improvement even while institutional crypto flows remained broadly weak.

🗨️ My viewpoint: One positive session is worth noting but not extrapolating. I would watch whether SOL can develop a genuine flow divergence from BTC and ETH or whether this proves to be a one-day exception.

8⃣ Treasury yields remained above 5% ahead of PPI

The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield remained around 5.12%-5.13%, while the 30-year traded around 5.45%-5.46%.

Markets continued pricing another Federal Reserve hike in December, with a smaller probability of a larger 50-basis-point move.

October PPI is due at 8:30 AM EST.

🖊️ Market significance: Elevated long-term yields increase the opportunity cost of holding risk assets and continue tightening financial conditions.

🗨️ My viewpoint: PPI is now the immediate macro trigger. A hot print would reinforce the combination already hurting crypto: restrictive policy, high real yields and weak liquidity. I would not front-run a macro reversal before seeing the data.

9⃣ Binance said all assets affected by the $6.3B hack had been replaced

Binance announced that it had fully replaced the assets affected by its recent security breach using SAFU reserves, excess futures-insurance reserves and corporate treasury resources.

The exchange published a new proof-of-reserves snapshot covering approximately 198 tokens and committed to rebuilding SAFU toward roughly $1B.

Withdrawals continued reopening in phases.

🖊️ Market significance: Full asset replacement reduces the immediate solvency concern surrounding the exchange and shifts attention toward operational recovery and transparency.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This materially improves the financial side of the Binance story, but it does not close the operational one. Restoring assets is different from proving that the authorization weakness which caused the breach has been permanently fixed.

🔟 U.S. authorities moved against more than $1.2B of stolen Binance assets

The U.S. government moved to seize or restrain more than $1.2B of assets linked to the Binance theft.

Combined public- and private-sector intervention has reportedly frozen more than $2.7B.

The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation.

🖊️ Market significance: Large-scale asset recovery reduces the economic benefit of major exchange thefts and demonstrates increasingly coordinated enforcement across blockchain networks and centralized issuers.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The important development is the recovery architecture. Crypto crime remains large, but tracing, freezing and cross-jurisdiction coordination are becoming much faster than they were several years ago.

1⃣1⃣ TRM Labs launched a dedicated crypto seizure service

TRM Labs introduced Beacon Concierge, allowing verified law-enforcement agencies to coordinate directly with exchanges and stablecoin issuers to freeze and seize digital assets.

Its underlying network reportedly includes more than 200 organizations covering around 80% of crypto trading volume.

The system has already helped freeze more than $35M across multiple investigations.

🖊️ Market significance: Blockchain surveillance and asset-freezing infrastructure are becoming institutionalized rather than handled through ad hoc cooperation.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This changes the economics of crypto crime. The ability to move stolen assets onchain remains, but converting those assets into usable value becomes harder when exchanges and issuers coordinate at network scale.

1⃣2⃣ Trezor identified malicious hardware implants in three Safe 5 wallets

Trezor discovered malicious hardware modifications in three Safe 5 devices purchased through former Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis.

The company said no customer funds were reported lost.

Firmware version 2.13.1 now blocks the implants identified so far, while Trezor has reduced its authorized reseller network substantially.

🖊️ Market significance: The incident highlights hardware supply-chain risk even when the wallet manufacturer itself has not suffered a software compromise.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Hardware wallets are only as trustworthy as the path from manufacturer to user. Supply-chain verification needs to become part of custody security, not an assumption made after the device leaves the factory.

1⃣3⃣ Osmosis stopped producing blocks

The Osmosis blockchain stalled at approximately block 74,955,152.

Upbit and Bithumb suspended OSMO deposits and withdrawals, while Coinbase reported processing disruption.

Trading remained available on affected exchanges.

🖊️ Market significance: Network halts can interrupt settlement, withdrawals and arbitrage even when exchange trading itself remains available.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is a reminder that blockchain uptime is financial infrastructure. A chain that stops producing blocks does not merely face a technical outage; it temporarily loses settlement finality.

1⃣4⃣ The White House nominated four new SEC and CFTC commissioners

Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland were nominated to the CFTC, while Kristin Johnson and Steven Levine were nominated to the SEC.

All nominations require Senate confirmation.

Several nominees have direct experience with digital-asset policy and U.S. crypto market-structure legislation.

🖊️ Market significance: The composition of the SEC and CFTC could materially influence the regulation of crypto market structure, perpetual futures, tokenization and prediction markets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Personnel matters when regulation is still being built. The next phase of U.S. crypto policy will increasingly depend on how these agencies interpret jurisdiction in practice rather than what Congress writes in principle.

1⃣5⃣ Louisiana sued ten prediction-market operators

Louisiana filed legal action against ten prediction-market companies, including Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto .com, Gemini, ForecastEx, Novig, Underdog and ProphetX.

The state argues that sports-event contracts offered by these platforms constitute illegal gambling rather than federally protected derivatives activity.

Louisiana became the 11th U.S. state to pursue legal action against prediction-market operators.

🖊️ Market significance: Prediction markets increasingly face a fragmented legal environment in which federal derivatives regulation and state gambling law are colliding.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The industry's biggest regulatory risk is becoming jurisdictional fragmentation. A platform cannot scale nationally if federal authorization still leaves it exposed to enforcement in individual states.

1⃣6⃣ The federal government and CFTC sued Arkansas over prediction markets

The U.S. government and CFTC filed a federal case seeking to prevent Arkansas from enforcing state gambling laws against Kalshi.

The case argues that federally regulated event contracts fall under CFTC jurisdiction.

🖊️ Market significance: Federal authorities are now directly challenging state attempts to regulate federally supervised prediction markets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The prediction-market battle has moved beyond individual companies. It is becoming a direct contest between federal derivatives authority and state gambling powers, and the court decisions could define the industry's U.S. structure.

1⃣7⃣ Kalshi reportedly discussed another funding round at a $65B valuation

Kalshi is reportedly exploring additional financing at a valuation near $65B, shortly after raising $1B at approximately $40B.

The discussions are partly linked to expansion into new markets such as compute futures tied to GPU and cloud-computing prices.

🖊️ Market significance: Investors increasingly view Kalshi as a broader financial exchange rather than solely a prediction-market operator.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A $65B valuation assumes Kalshi becomes much more than an event-contract platform. Compute futures are evidence of that ambition, but the valuation leaves little room for regulatory or execution mistakes.

1⃣8⃣ New York tightened advertising expectations for crypto firms

The New York Department of Financial Services issued new standards requiring regulated crypto companies to establish stronger governance and review processes around marketing.

Firms are expected to communicate fees and risks clearly and avoid misleading claims such as advertising products as free while other charges remain.

Implementation is expected by May 10, 2027.

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto regulation is increasingly extending beyond custody and AML toward the way financial products are marketed to consumers.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is another sign that crypto is being absorbed into ordinary financial regulation. The industry is moving from debating whether rules apply to debating exactly how conventional consumer-protection standards should apply.

1⃣9⃣ BTCS sold ETH below cost to defend an Aave loan

Ethereum treasury company BTCS has reportedly been selling ETH below its acquisition cost to reduce risk surrounding a $64.1M Aave loan.

Approximately 46,676 ETH worth $99.3M backed the debt as of November 9.

Secondary estimates placed its health factor near 1.24 and potential liquidation region around $1,700-$1,717 ETH.

🖊️ Market significance: Falling ETH prices are beginning to expose leverage embedded in corporate digital-asset treasury strategies.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is one of the clearest examples of why treasury yield is not free. Once a corporate ETH position is leveraged through DeFi, falling prices can force asset sales precisely when management would prefer to hold.

2⃣0⃣ Nakamoto extended part of its $165M Bitcoin-backed Kraken loan

Bitcoin treasury company Nakamoto extended a $60M loan tranche originally due in December 2026 until December 2027.

Another $105M remains due in June 2027.

The company has approximately 3,030 BTC pledged as collateral and previously sold around 600 BTC while restructuring the facility.

🖊️ Market significance: Falling Bitcoin prices are reducing the collateral cushion supporting leveraged corporate treasury strategies.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The risk in Bitcoin treasury companies is increasingly moving from asset volatility to financing structure. A company can remain bullish on Bitcoin while still being forced to restructure because its debt matures before the market recovers.

2⃣1⃣ Gemini's trading business contracted sharply in Q3

Gemini reported third-quarter revenue of approximately $40.9M, down 19% year-over-year.

Trading volume fell from $16.4B to $4.5B, a decline of around 73%.

Net loss improved to approximately $58.6M, while adjusted EBITDA remained negative.

🖊️ Market significance: Lower exchange volumes continue pressuring crypto trading businesses even as companies diversify toward services and interest income.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The important number is the 73% collapse in trading volume. Gemini's shift toward recurring services may improve resilience, but the core exchange business is clearly operating in a much weaker demand environment.

2⃣2⃣ Tether's disclosed U.S. equity exposure was estimated around $4.8B

An analysis of public filings estimated that Tether-linked entities hold approximately $4.8B across 13 U.S.-listed companies.

Large exposures include Twenty One Capital, Rumble and Adecoagro, alongside investments in mining, infrastructure and other businesses.

The filings do not establish that these equity positions back USDT reserves.

🖊️ Market significance: Tether is increasingly functioning not only as a stablecoin issuer but as a large strategic capital allocator across crypto and traditional industries.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I would keep these investments separate from USDT reserve analysis unless the company explicitly identifies them as backing assets. The more interesting story is how stablecoin economics are creating one of the largest private investment pools in crypto.

2⃣3⃣ Aave considered reserve-factor changes across 54 assets

Aave governance is considering changes affecting 54 assets across 12 V3 deployments and Ethereum V2.

At recent balances and rates, the changes would increase estimated annualized DAO revenue by approximately $3.5M and raise the blended reserve factor from roughly 12.0% to 12.7%.

🖊️ Market significance: The proposal would redirect a larger share of borrower interest toward the protocol treasury, potentially reducing supplier yields.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is a straightforward economic decision: more protocol revenue versus more attractive depositor yields. The correct balance depends on whether Aave can increase its take rate without pushing liquidity toward competitors.

2⃣4⃣ AKT went live on Solana as Akash began its migration from Cosmos

Akash's AKT token became available on Solana through a 1:1 migration portal that will remain open for two years.

The token can now trade and interact through Solana applications including Jupiter and Raydium.

The underlying Akash compute marketplace has not yet completed its own migration.

🖊️ Market significance: The move expands AKT's liquidity and distribution while demonstrating continued migration of applications and assets toward higher-activity ecosystems.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The token migration matters less than whether Akash eventually moves actual compute activity. Liquidity can migrate quickly; application demand and infrastructure are harder to move.

2⃣5⃣ Injective opened voting for its Veyra upgrade

Injective began governance voting on its v1.21.0 Veyra mainnet upgrade.

The upgrade focuses on institutional real-world-asset infrastructure and cross-chain trading.

If approved, activation is targeted around November 24.

🖊️ Market significance: Injective continues positioning its network toward institutional trading and tokenized financial assets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The RWA narrative is increasingly crowded, so infrastructure claims alone will not differentiate a network. I would judge Veyra by the assets, institutions and actual trading activity it attracts after launch.

2⃣6⃣ Lightning Labs launched Bitcoin payments for autonomous AI agents

Lightning Labs introduced pi402, an open-source system allowing AI agents to purchase model inference using Bitcoin over the Lightning Network.

The system uses HTTP-402 and Lightning's L402 architecture, allowing agents to pay without conventional accounts, payment cards or API keys.

Spending limits can be programmed directly into the agent.

🖊️ Market significance: Machine-to-machine payments represent a practical use case for programmable, low-value and automated Bitcoin settlement.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is one of the cleaner AI-plus-crypto use cases I have seen. The value is not speculation around AI tokens; it is giving autonomous software a native way to buy the computing resources it needs.

2⃣7⃣ Tokenized-stock liquidity providers are struggling to make money

Research covering 656 tokenized-equity liquidity pools across five blockchains found approximately $7.8B of trading volume and $7.3M of generated fees.

However, liquidity providers suffered approximately $9.65M of impermanent loss.

Even after roughly $1.67M in token incentives, the group remained approximately $680K underwater.

🖊️ Market significance: High tokenized-equity trading volume does not necessarily translate into sustainable economics for the liquidity providers supporting those markets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is a useful reality check for tokenized stocks. Trading volume can look impressive while the underlying liquidity economics remain broken. Markets cannot scale sustainably if LPs require constant subsidies to stay profitable.

2⃣8⃣ Tokenized Nvidia products showed major price divergence while U.S. markets were closed

Research found that one tokenized Nvidia product traded approximately 8% above four competing Nvidia tokens for around 4.5 hours during a weekend news event.

The widest short-duration discrepancy reached approximately 13%.

The gap was linked to thin liquidity and localized demand and disappeared once additional supply entered the market.

🖊️ Market significance: Twenty-four-hour tokenized-equity trading can create price discovery when traditional markets are closed, but fragmented liquidity can produce substantial deviations between products referencing the same underlying stock.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Continuous trading is only useful if continuous pricing is credible. Tokenized equities need deeper liquidity and stronger arbitrage mechanisms before a weekend token price can reliably be treated as the market price of the underlying stock.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
Bitcoin's break below $70K, roughly $1.47B of liquidations, six consecutive sessions of BTC and ETH ETF outflows and continued stablecoin contraction show that the weakness is now affecting price, leverage and liquidity simultaneously.

The more concerning development is beginning to appear on balance sheets. BTCS is selling ETH to protect leveraged debt, while Nakamoto is extending Bitcoin-backed financing as collateral values fall. These are early examples of how sustained price weakness can move from market volatility into corporate financing stress.

Meanwhile, Binance's asset replacement, law-enforcement recovery infrastructure and continued institutional development across payments, DeFi and tokenization show that the underlying financial infrastructure continues to mature.

I remain defensive. The immediate test is PPI with the 10-year above 5%, followed by ETF flows and whether Bitcoin can recover $70K. Until liquidity improves and institutional selling slows, I would treat rebounds as tactical rather than evidence of a durable bottom.

text:
From early 2027 imec's pilot line hands European designers the tools to model leading-edge chips. Parliament and the Council must keep their own mid-2027 date and pass Chips Act 2.0, so those designs are made in Europe.

This month, imec gave European chip designers the keys. At SEMICON Europa on 10 November, imec delivered the baseline flows for the silicon interposer platform of the NanoIC pilot line: through-silicon vias, stacked routing, microbump pitches down to 20 µm. A design kit built on it lands early 2027, and then universities, start-ups and fabless companies can model the packaging that makes an AI chip real, before a single wafer is cut. This is what a European toolbox looks like, and it exists because Belgium, France, Germany, Finland, Ireland and Romania put money in beside the union.

What holds it back? Time, and the people who vote on it. Chips Act 2.0 is still a proposal, file 2026/0139(COD), in the European Parliament's preparatory phase since the Commission tabled it in June, with the institutions' target for finishing negotiations at the second quarter of 2027. Meanwhile the packaging floor is filling up elsewhere. GlobalFoundries will make TSMC interposers in New York for $2 billion, about €1.8 billion at the October ECB rate, with volume production not before 2028. In September, Amkor formally announced the second phase of its Arizona campus, lifting the planned investment to about $12 billion, about €10 billion at the September ECB rate, with completion targeted by the end of 2029. Mainland China is forecast to hold about 30.5% of global effective advanced packaging capacity in 2026. Every quarter the file waits is a quarter those lines commission. The auditors found the first Chips Act short: the European Court of Auditors concluded in 2025 that Europe is on course for 11.7% of the chip value chain by 2030, far from the 20% aimed for, and counted only about €4.5 billion of an expected €86 billion as directly managed by the Commission. Fair audit, wrong lesson. The same record shows the common parts working: four advanced pilot lines designated, 30 competence centres across 28 countries, annual semiconductor investment grown five-fold to €85 billion.

The design door is open. Legislate the factory floor behind it.

Five years from now, the engineer starting on that kit has a ladder to climb inside Europe. NanoIC already offers PDKs for fine-pitch RDL interposers and die-to-wafer hybrid bonding, and its ambition runs to physical silicon demonstrators on the pilot line, aimed at chips below 2nm. Chips Act 2.0 is the step that turns demonstrators into a route: an EU-based advanced open foundry at 3nm and below, chiplet integration and 3D packaging, pilot production in the 2030 to 2033 window, a 12-month permitting cap for strategic facilities. Design at your desk, prove it on a European pilot line, then manufacture at the leading edge here, on your side of the Atlantic instead of a plane ticket out. The 2.5D and 3D market for AI accelerators is forecast to grow from about €13 billion in 2026 to about €40 billion by 2031 at ECB rates. We should be taking that market, not renting our place in it.

The demand is small against the prize: the European Parliament and the Council should finish negotiations on Chips Act 2.0 by the target they set themselves, keeping the Commission's proposal whole. The framework itself is what those governments already asked for: in September 2025 all 27 member states joined the Semicon Coalition and called for resilience, strategically important technologies and quicker approval procedures. Tie the foundry money to that framework, and a vote to delay defends the permitting queues, nothing more. Ministers: keep the file intact, keep the date. And you: the kit lands early 2027, and what you design on it deserves a European foundry to run on.

After Trump Said “Do What You Have to Do,” Bukele’s Salvadoran Troops Help Strike Gang That Kidnapped 16 American Christian Missionaries | Antonio Graceffo, The Gateway Pundit

Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador and an ally of President Trump, is the Latin American leader who locked up his country’s gangs. Since declaring a state of exception in March 2022, his government has detained more than 90,000 people accused of gang ties and built a 40,000-inmate prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT).

El Salvador’s homicide rate fell from 106 per 100,000 people in 2015 to 1.3 in 2025. At the White House in April 2025, Trump said Bukele had “done a fantastic job,” and Bukele said, “we actually turned the murder capital of the world into the safest country in the Western Hemisphere.”

Bukele has repeatedly criticized Mexico’s failure to defeat its cartels. Speaking to business leaders from more than 20 Latin American countries in February 2025, he said criminal groups “control large sectors of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil” and that “the state is stronger than any criminal organization.”

This month, he told Belizean broadcaster Love FM, “There is no government that cannot eliminate crime.” Haiti is now testing that claim.

Haitian police, backed by Salvadoran troops, struck the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang in Croix-des-Bouquets, east of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince. Bukele announced the strike on X on Nov. 10, saying it also destroyed the home of gang leader Wilson Joseph, known as “Lanmo San Jou.” A Haitian National Police drone task force carried out the attack, which may have killed as many as 20 gunmen. Joseph was away when the strike hit.

On Oct. 16, 2021, 400 Mawozo kidnapped 17 missionaries working for Christian Aid Ministries, an Ohio-based church organization. Sixteen were Americans, one was Canadian, and five were children. The gang demanded $1 million per hostage, and Joseph threatened to kill them if the gang’s demands went unmet. The last hostages regained their freedom after 61 days.

In 2022, the Justice Department charged Joseph with hostage-taking in connection with the kidnapping. Prosecutors said 400 Mawozo claimed responsibility and sought the release of another gang leader, Joly Germine, known as “Yonyon,” who directed the kidnapping from a Haitian prison. The State Department offered a $1 million reward for information leading to Joseph’s arrest. He remains on the FBI’s wanted list.

El Salvador expanded its deployment after an Oct. 18 ambush in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets. Gunmen opened fire on an armored vehicle carrying four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), the UN-backed multinational force fighting gangs in Haiti. Haitian police later found the burned vehicle in Santo. The four men remain missing.

Bukele warned the gangs, “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.” He sent more than 2,000 troops along with military hardware. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said about 200 Salvadoran troops fall under GSF command. The rest operate under El Salvador’s agreement with the Haitian government.

Bukele discussed the operation by phone with President Trump. Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Oct. 31, Trump recounted the call. “He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. They killed some of his people. I said, ‘You’re running your country. You have to do what you have to do,’” Trump said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the exchange on Nov. 8 at Homestead Air Reserve Base in Florida. “He called the President and made them aware of what he was doing, and the President understood why he was doing it,” Rubio said, according to the State Department transcript. Rubio said El Salvador undertook the operation “bilaterally in agreement with the Haitian officials, to go after the gangs that kidnapped their forces.” He added, “We don’t have troops there, but we’ve been engaged.” Rubio said Salvadoran troops and the GSF needed to coordinate to avoid mistaking each other for gang members.

Axios reported on Nov. 10 that David Howell, the U.S. chargé d’affaires in Haiti, told Haitian officials Salvadoran operations should stop “as soon as possible … until they coordinate” with the GSF. “They are going to kill [GSF] troops or civilians,” he warned.

The U.S. Embassy also filed a diplomatic protest alleging that Salvadoran gunfire struck the embassy during an Oct. 31 gang attack on a Salvadoran convoy. El Salvador’s government rejected the allegation and said its soldiers fired away from the embassy. A source who spoke with Bukele told Axios that Bukele responded, “I checked with Trump. He said do what we have to do,” and asked why “some bureaucrat is fighting this?”

Since the Salvadoran deployment expanded, Joseph has written to the UN secretary-general asking for dialogue and citing concern about civilian deaths. He proposed Nov. 18 as a start date for negotiations. Amnesty International’s Americas director, Ana Piquer, called on both governments to publish the deployment agreement. Dominican President Luis Abinader said his government is providing Bukele with logistical and intelligence support.

After the strike, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé thanked Bukele on X, writing, “Hats off to President Nayib Bukele for his support and commitment to the national effort against gangs.” He added, “Haiti, Salvador, FRG: the same fight, the same determination!” FRG is the French abbreviation for the Gang Suppression Force. Fils-Aimé also credited the Haitian National Police and the Armed Forces of Haiti and said the collaboration would continue.

Fils-Aimé is scheduled to visit El Salvador next week to discuss the future of the deployment. In a Nov. 3 post on X addressed to Haitians, Bukele wrote, “We can help you defeat them, but we are not your enemies.” He closed with “Haiti will be free.”

text:
Daily Devotional with Pastor Jon
November 13, 2026
Then said God, Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.
Hosea 1:9
Lo-ammi means “not mine.” Even as Lo-ammi was not Hosea’s, so too, the Lord says to Israel, “If you will not let Me be your God, you will not be My people.” Be it a nation or an individual, the Lord doesn’t force His love on anyone. He offers Himself to be Lord, Father, God, Redeemer, Savior - but He will not force Himself upon anyone.

“Behold I stand at the door and knock,” Jesus said. “If any man hear my voice and open the door, I will come in and sup with him and he with Me” (see Revelation 3:20). Jesus knocks persistently, but gentlemanly. If anyone chooses to open the door, He will come in and be their Lord and live in their heart - but He won’t kick in the door.

I’m always amazed by how polite the Lord is. He constantly gives every one of us the choice to give Him entry into our lives or into any part of our lives. But the choice is always ours.

text:
50/50 Group Marks 25 Years with “Still I Rise” Celebrations and Landmark Lecture

The 50/50 Group of Sierra Leone has begun a series of events to mark 25 years of advocacy for women’s participation in politics and public life, under the theme “Still I Rise.” The programme, which runs through the end of November 2026, centres on the 14th Rajiv Bendre Women in Public Life Lecture Series and includes community outreach, interfaith services, and the formal launch of accredited leadership courses.⁠

The organisation was formally launched on 30 November 2001 at the House of Parliament by then-President Alhaji Ahmad Tejan Kabbah. The occasion featured Sierra Leone’s first all-female mock parliament and a simulated State Opening, drawing attention to the fact that women then occupied only about eight percent of parliamentary seats. Founder and Global President Dr. Nemata Majeks-Walker has said the Group was inspired by a 2000 British Council training workshop facilitated by gender and politics expert Lesley Abdela. At the time, Rajiv Bendre was Director of the British Council in Sierra Leone; his support for the early training and organisational work led to the lecture series being named in his honour when it was established in 2005.⁠

Over the past 25 years the Group has trained more than 3,000 women, opened branches across all 16 districts, and helped raise women’s representation in Parliament above 30 percent. Its advocacy formed part of the broader effort that secured the Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment Act of 2022, which introduced a 30 percent minimum quota for women in leadership positions. Current President Professor Fredline M’Cormack-Hale has described the anniversary as “a milestone, not a finish line,” noting that the next phase must focus on ensuring political parties and institutions fully implement existing commitments.⁠

The anniversary schedule opens with a press conference on Monday, 16 November 2026 at 2:00 pm at the Group’s headquarters on Tower Hill. The centrepiece event is the 14th Rajiv Bendre Lecture on Friday, 20 November 2026 at 3:00 pm at the Freetown City Council Auditorium. Professor Miriam Conteh-Morgan, Vice-Chancellor and Principal of Limkokwing University of Creative Technology, will deliver a lecture titled “In Praise of the Accidental.” Professor Conteh-Morgan, who previously served as the first female Deputy Vice-Chancellor of the Institute of Public Administration and Management at the University of Sierra Leone, brings more than four decades of experience in higher education, including teaching and research roles at The Ohio State University and Harvard University. The lecture will also serve as the platform for the launch of accredited certificate and diploma programmes at the Group’s Gender Equality and Women’s Leadership Training Institute, offered in partnership with the University of Sierra Leone.⁠

Further activities include Jummah prayers at the Mende Mosque on Friday, 27 November; a Christian thanksgiving service at Jesus Is Lord Ministries on Sunday, 29 November; and a Meet & Greet Awujoh at the Group’s headquarters on Monday, 30 November at noon. The organisation is also coordinating donations to the Female Correctional Services, new mothers at Princess Christian Maternity Hospital, and Gladv Home Orphanage in Wellington.

The Group’s long-standing slogan, “More Women, Better Politics, Better Salone, A Better World!” frames both the celebrations and its unfinished agenda. As it marks the silver jubilee, the 50/50 Group continues to argue that progress achieved since 2001, while significant, remains short of the equal representation it was founded to pursue. #SierraLeone

text:
Existing chip contracts are not the risk. The next dollar of NVIDIA paper is.

**The contracts that already exist**
Take-or-pay floors and equity already wired do not automatically die because the CEO left. CoreWeave’s initially $6.3B agreement for NVIDIA to buy qualifying unused capacity through April 2032, disclosed in a 2025 SEC filing, terminates for breach or insolvency — not a CEO change. NVIDIA’s $2B CoreWeave equity from January, and the completed ~$30B OpenAI equity, are already done. Do not recycle the old $100B OpenAI letter of intent as if it were still live.

**Where the risk actually sits**
The risk is refinancing, and the next discretionary cheque, especially with a CFO now sitting as CEO.

Joe Kaiser told Fortune the practical point: if capital providers decide “that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago,” these heavy-asset neoclouds are at risk. NVIDIA has been both supplier and credit enhancer. It offered unused-capacity floors to make banks more willing to lend, and later joined a preliminary $500B financing platform of which it may backstop up to $125B. Preliminary is the key word — that is not a signed $125B cheque. Ohio / OpenAI guarantees are capped at $105B and are staged and contingent.

**Who is most exposed**
CoreWeave ended June with about $35B of debt. Nebius sits in the same conversation. Fortune had NVIDIA holding about $329M of Nebius shares at the end of June; other coverage has cited a $2B March investment. Those figures are not the same thing, so don’t flatten them. Nebius also issued weak full-year guidance the same day it sold off, so that print is not a clean Jensen move.

Watch the smaller AI cloud names that leaned on NVIDIA’s chequebook. If the new regime is more conservative about financing customers, that is where it shows up first.

**What does not break immediately**
CUDA lock-in does not vanish in a quarter. Kaiser’s own view is NVIDIA keeps its grip on training for two or three years. The tell is whether the next project still gets NVIDIA paper behind it — and whether Google or Amazon, which have real balance sheets and their own chips, step into that backstop role.

**What to watch**
- Don’t assume CoreWeave or Nebius contracts evaporate. Watch the cost of their next dollar of capital, and NVIDIA’s tone on customer financing at earnings.
- Next catalyst: NVIDIA earnings Tuesday 17 Nov, results at about 1:20 p.m. PT / 5:20 a.m. Wednesday 18 Nov HKT, call at 2 p.m. PT. Listen for backstop language, allocation, and whether Kress sounds like a closer or a rationer.

**Affected names**
- $NVDA — leadership and financing-policy risk. CUDA and the shipped backlog are still there. Earnings 17 Nov is the first official tell.
- $CRWV (CoreWeave) — about $35B of June debt and an unused-capacity floor that is still in force, but the NVIDIA guarantee may reprice for lenders.
- $NBIS (Nebius) — NVIDIA stake plus financing sensitivity. The recent drop also reflects weak full-year guidance the same day.
- $GOOGL / $AMZN — can take share in custom silicon and, in Kaiser’s framing, potentially step into backstop roles with real balance sheets.
