People should be able to access promising new treatments as quickly as possible, while still being confident that decisions are based on strong evidence and make the best use of NHS resources.

5 November 2026

NICE and NHS England are testing a new way of making some promising medicines available to NHS patients sooner. Known as the Streamlined Managed Access Route for Therapies (SMART) pilot, the approach could allow certain medicines to be used while more evidence is gathered about how well they work in practice.

Why we are testing a new approach
At the moment, medicines that enter managed access are assessed twice by NICE - once before patients can receive them and again after more evidence has been collected.

The SMART pilot will test whether some medicines can reach patients sooner by using a shorter assessment at the start, followed by a full NICE evaluation later when more evidence is available.

NICE and NHS England hope this could reduce the time it takes for suitable medicines to enter managed access from around a year to as little as six months. However, this is the aim of the pilot and is not guaranteed.

How the pilot will work
If a medicine is suggested for the pilot, NICE will carry out an initial assessment to decide whether it is suitable for managed access. Patients may then be able to receive the medicine while additional information is collected.

Once enough evidence has been gathered, NICE will carry out its full evaluation to decide whether the medicine should continue to be routinely available on the NHS.

Which medicines could be considered?
The pilot is designed for medicines that appear promising, can be introduced into the NHS relatively quickly and have clear plans for collecting additional evidence.

Any medicine considered for the pilot must also represent good value for money for the NHS.

Maintaining NICE's high standards
Speeding up access does not mean lowering standards.

Medicines accepted onto the pilot will still go through a full NICE evaluation before any decision is made on long-term NHS use. NICE's independent committees will continue to assess the evidence and consider whether treatments offer value for money for the NHS.

The pilot also includes financial safeguards to protect both the NHS and companies while additional evidence is being collected.

What we hope to learn
Through the pilot, NICE and NHS England want to understand whether suitable medicines can reach patients sooner without compromising the quality of decision-making.

The pilot will also explore whether the process can be made simpler and more efficient for everyone involved while remaining fair, transparent and evidence-based.

Gemini Analysis:

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and NHS England's rollout of the Streamlined Managed Access Route for Therapies (SMART) pilot offers a highly relevant framework for advanced, personalized therapeutic platforms like DCVax-L (Northwest Biotherapeutics), particularly given its ongoing UK regulatory review and operational integration with the NHS.
The structural synergy, commercial potential, and strategic importance of the SMART pilot for the DCVax platform encompass several key areas:
1. Bridging the Gap in Ultra-Customized Patient Access
The Traditional Bottleneck: Historically, advanced cell and gene therapies face prolonged timelines under standard Health Technology Assessment (HTA) models because traditional managed access pathways require a lengthy dual-appraisal framework (before patient access and after evidence collection), often stretching lead times to roughly a year or more.
The SMART Advantage: The SMART pilot is explicitly engineered to compress initial assessments to roughly six months by utilizing a shorter front-end review, allowing promising therapies to enter managed access sooner while real-world evidence (RWE) is concurrently gathered. For a personalized autologous dendritic cell vaccine like DCVax-L targeting glioblastoma (GBM)—where patient prognosis is exceptionally urgent—shrinking the runway to NHS availability is vital.
2. Alignment with NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) Infrastructure
Operational Synchronicity: Northwest Biotherapeutics established a formal collaboration with NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) focused on therapeutic apheresis and cellular processing infrastructure (initially scaling out via Leeds and Oxford).
Value Demonstration: A core requirement for selection into the SMART pilot is the ability to introduce a treatment rapidly and smoothly into NHS care supported by clear, robust plans for gathering real-world data. The integration of NHSBT’s nationwide apheresis network provides the exact structural framework required to meet these logistical prerequisites, proving to NICE committees that a decentralized or multi-site national delivery mechanism is already operational.
3. Re-framing the Evidence Plan and Commercial Strategy
Front-Loading Real-World Data Protocols: Under the SMART pathway, the weight of the initial hurdle shifts heavily toward the robustness of the up-front evidence collection plan. For DCVax-L—backed by its extensive 331-patient Phase III trial data published in JAMA Oncology—the platform already possesses deep clinical datasets. The SMART framework provides a structured mechanism to leverage this existing data while designing targeted RWE generation for post-initial-access tracking.
Risk-Sharing and Financial Safeguards: Because the pilot incorporates built-in commercial safeguards and managed access pricing models designed to protect both the NHS and developers during the evidence-gathering phase, it offers a predictable commercial bridge. This prevents innovative immunotherapies from stalling indefinitely over budget impact tests or interim pricing uncertainties.
Summary of Strategic Importance
For a personalized cancer vaccine platform navigating the UK regulatory landscape, pathways like the SMART pilot represent an important evolution in how the UK handles cutting-edge medical innovations. By cutting down initial appraisal friction and working hand-in-hand with national infrastructure partners like NHSBT, mechanisms like SMART help align regulatory pacing with the clinical urgency demanded by aggressive neuro-oncology indications.

$ETC. $1.06B market cap. $13 in daily chain fees. CoinGecko

NO.1 WHAT IS

Ethereum Classic is the proof-of-work chain that continued the original Ethereum ledger after the 2016 DAO fork. It runs Ethereum-compatible smart contracts. ETC pays for transactions and rewards miners for producing blocks. https://t.co/CqRoesGkY8

NO.2 WHY PEOPLE CARE

ETC gives miners a proof-of-work network that still runs the Ethereum Virtual Machine. Developers can use much of the familiar Ethereum tooling, while miners compete to secure the chain. The question is how many developers and users choose ETC when other EVM networks already offer deeper liquidity and more active apps. https://t.co/CqRoesGkY8

NO.3 NARRATIVE

The thesis is that there’s room for a proof-of-work smart contract network with predictable issuance. Olympia is the next proposed catalyst, targeting mainnet activation in 2027. It would bring newer Ethereum execution features and a base-fee market to ETC. The proposals are still drafts, and adoption will depend on what ships and what developers build with it. Ethereum Classic

NO.4 EDGE

ETC has a long operating history and gives developers a familiar execution environment on a mined chain. That’s a clear niche. The competitive gap shows up in liquidity. DefiLlama tracks roughly $71.5K in stablecoins on ETC, which limits what lending and trading apps can do at scale. https://t.co/CqRoesGkY8

NO.5 KEY METRICS | NOV 13
Price — ~$6.66
Market cap — ~$1.06B
Reported ETC trading volume — ~$23.4M
DeFi TVL / stablecoin supply — ~$103K / ~$71.5K
24H chain fees / transactions — ~$13 / ~8,100
Current base block reward — 1.6384 ETC CoinGecko

ETC trades tens of millions of dollars a day while the chain generates very little fee revenue in this snapshot. I’d track stablecoin inflows and fees over a full month to see whether on-chain demand is improving. CoinGecko
NO.6 TOKENOMICS
ETC is the gas asset and the currency miners earn. Under ECIP-1017, the base block reward falls by 20% every 5M blocks. The July 2026 reduction took it from 2.048 ETC to 1.6384 ETC per block. That slows issuance and reduces the subsidy miners receive in ETC terms. Ethereum Classic
The proposed Olympia fee market would change how base fees are handled. For now, I’d compare fees with mining rewards to see how much of the security budget users are paying for through actual network activity. Ethereum Classic
NO.7 UNLOCKS & RISKS
The main scheduled source of new supply is mining issuance. With fees this low, miners rely heavily on the block subsidy. I’d watch whether hash rate holds up after reward cuts, especially if ETC’s price weakens at the same time. Ethereum Classic

The ETC Cooperative announced on Nov 11 that it had begun winding down. Core-Geth and public infrastructure are moving to the Ethereum Classic GitHub organization. The test is whether contributors maintain reliable releases and public services through that handoff. Ethereum Classic

NO.8 BULL vs BEAR

BULL — Olympia ships, stablecoin liquidity grows, and new apps generate recurring fees while miners continue to secure the chain through lower issuance.

BEAR — ETC keeps its exchange activity while app usage stays thin, fees barely contribute to miner income, and the infrastructure handoff slows development.

NO.9 VERDICT

Project Design — B
Adoption & Ecosystem — D+
Narrative — C+
Competitive Edge — C
Market & Onchain Metrics — D+
Tokenomics & Value Capture — C
Unlocks & Protocol Risk — C
Bull vs Bear Setup — C−

Overall Grade — C

ETC has a predictable issuance schedule and a clear proof-of-work niche. At a ~$1.06B market cap, I’d need to see sustained fee growth and more stablecoin liquidity before raising the grade.

text:
Anduril says its first satellite can see adversaries maneuver in orbital night | Stephen Clark, Ars Technica

Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth’s shadow.

Funded with Anduril’s internal capital, the company’s oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit.

Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company’s satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216’s night passes allow its infrared imager to shine.

“This is a unique sensor that allows us to take imagery in long-wave [infrared],” said

Gokul Subramanian, Anduril’s senior vice president of engineering.

“What’s unique about that is it’s got a huge dynamic range. It has very low solar exclusion, so we’re blocked by the Sun very rarely, and we can see things in full dark.”

Filling a gap

The US military and a growing number of commercial data providers use a network of radars and optical sensors on the ground and in space to monitor satellite traffic. Anduril acquired one of the commercial satellite-tracking companies,

ExoAnalytic Solutions, earlier this year. But there’s a gap in optical tracking as satellites fly in Earth’s shadow, so space traffic monitors could temporarily lose track of a spacecraft if it performs a maneuver in orbital night.

The Space Force is charged with tracking satellites for two primary reasons. First, military commanders want to know if an adversary moves its satellite in a threatening manner. Second, the Space Force issues traffic alerts to global satellite operators if there’s a risk of a collision.

“Right now, we don’t have ground sensors in our adversaries’ sovereign lands, and then in the eclipse period where we are relying heavily on visible sensors, the satellites that are not illuminated by the Sun, we can’t see those,” said Adam Thurn, vice president and general manager of orbital systems at Anduril. “With the long-wave infrared space sensor, we’re looking to close that gap.”

Anduril’s long-wave infrared sensor works by detecting heat signatures from spacecraft, even in periods of eclipse. It provides a “unique capability for us to witness when an adversary or other resident space objects are maneuvering during those eclipse periods, where in the past we’ve been fairly blind,” Thurn said.

In creating the infrared space sensor, engineers applied imaging technology Anduril uses in its autonomous weapons for use in space. Anduril released a single image Tuesday from the sensor on Anduril-216 showing an infrared view of the Moon above Earth’s horizon. The Moon image offers just a taste of what the instrument can do, Thurn said.

The Moon over Earth’s horizon, as imaged by Anduril’s long-wave infrared space sensor.

Anduril Industries “The long-wave infrared capability we have on orbit can do both unresolved and resolved imagery,” Thurn said, suggesting Anduril’s sensor could be used to inspect other satellites in orbit if it flies close enough. For now, Thurn said Anduril is focusing on optimizing its tracking sensor for low-Earth orbit, but it could be used in other orbits, and eventually in cislunar space near the Moon.

Apex Space, a satellite-manufacturing startup, built the spacecraft platform for Anduril-216.

Subramanian said Anduril has no plans to start its own satellite production line. Instead, Anduril foresees buying third-party satellite platforms and integrating them with sensor and compute modules to perform a range of different missions in space.

“You’re seeing that today with Anduril-216, where we started with a simple mission, which was how do we track satellites, especially in these eclipse periods where the US currently does not have the ability to maintain custody,” Subramanian said. “And we designed a mission around that.”

The compute module on Anduril-216 is designed to fuse data from different kinds of sensors, such as infrared or visible imagers, and generate tracking solutions on its own, without intervention or analysis from the ground.

Subramanian said Anduril’s current focus is on acquiring space domain awareness data for sale to the US military, not selling entire satellites or sensors to the government. “At present, Anduril is not offering this system as a merchant supplier,” he said. “That could change in the future.”

text:
ChatGPT can now search the web for up-to-date answers to a user’s queries, OpenAI announced today. 

Until now, ChatGPT was mostly restricted to generating answers from its training data, which is current up to October 2023 for GPT-4o, and had limited web search capabilities. Searches about generalized topics will still draw on this information from the model itself, but now ChatGPT will automatically search the web in response to queries about recent information such as sports, stocks, or news of the day, and can deliver rich multi-media results. Users can also manually trigger a web search, but for the most part, the chatbot will make its own decision about when an answer would benefit from information taken from the web, says Adam Fry, OpenAI’s product lead for search.

“Our goal is to make ChatGPT the smartest assistant, and now we’re really enhancing its capabilities in terms of what it has access to from the web,” Fry tells MIT Technology Review. The feature is available today for the chatbot’s paying users. 

While ChatGPT search, as it is known, is initially available to paying customers, OpenAI intends to make it available for free later, even when people are logged out. The company also plans to combine search with its voice features and Canvas, its interactive platform for coding and writing, although these capabilities will not be available in today’s initial launch.

The company unveiled a standalone prototype of web search in July. Those capabilities are now built directly into the chatbot. OpenAI says it has “brought the best of the SearchGPT experience into ChatGPT.” 

OpenAI is the latest tech company to debut an AI-powered search assistant, challenging similar tools from competitors such as Google, Microsoft, and startup Perplexity. Meta, too, is reportedly developing its own AI search engine. As with Perplexity’s interface, users of ChatGPT search can interact with the chatbot in natural language, and it will offer an AI-generated answer with sources and links to further reading. In contrast, Google’s AI Overviews offer a short AI-generated summary at the top of the website, as well as a traditional list of indexed links. 

These new tools could eventually challenge Google’s 90% market share in online search. AI search is a very important way to draw more users, says Chirag Shah, a professor at the University of Washington, who specializes in online search. But he says it is unlikely to chip away at Google’s search dominance. Microsoft’s high-profile attempt with Bing barely made a dent in the market, Shah says. 

Instead, OpenAI is trying to create a new market for more powerful and interactive AI agents, which can take complex actions in the real world, Shah says. 

The new search function in ChatGPT is a step toward these agents. 

It can also deliver highly contextualized responses that take advantage of chat histories, allowing users to go deeper in a search. Currently, ChatGPT search is able to recall conversation histories and continue the conversation with questions on the same topic. 

ChatGPT itself can also remember things about users that it can use later —sometimes it does this automatically, or you can ask it to remember something. Those “long-term” memories affect how it responds to chats. Search doesn’t have this yet—a new web search starts from scratch— but it should get this capability in the “next couple of quarters,” says Fry. When it does, OpenAI says it will allow it to deliver far more personalized results based on what it knows.

“Those might be persistent memories, like ‘I’m a vegetarian,’ or it might be contextual, like ‘I’m going to New York in the next few days,’” says Fry. “If you say ‘I’m going to New York in four days,’ it can remember that fact and the nuance of that point,” he adds. 

To help develop ChatGPT’s web search, OpenAI says it leveraged its partnerships with news organizations such as Reuters, the Atlantic, Le Monde, the Financial Times, Axel Springer, Condé Nast, and Time. However, its results include information not only from these publishers, but any other source online that does not actively block its search crawler.   

It’s a positive development that ChatGPT will now be able to retrieve information from these reputable online sources and generate answers based on them, says Suzan Verberne, a professor of natural-language processing at Leiden University, who has studied information retrieval. It also allows users to ask follow-up questions.

But despite the enhanced ability to search the web and cross-check sources, the tool is not immune from the persistent tendency of AI language models to make things up or get it wrong. When MIT Technology Review tested the new search function and asked it for vacation destination ideas, ChatGPT suggested “luxury European destinations” such as Japan, Dubai, the Caribbean islands, Bali, the Seychelles, and Thailand. It offered as a source an article from the Times, a British newspaper, which listed these locations as well as those in Europe as luxury holiday options.

“Especially when you ask about untrue facts or events that never happened, the engine might still try to formulate a plausible response that is not necessarily correct,” says Verberne. There is also a risk that misinformation might seep into ChatGPT’s answers from the internet if the company has not filtered its sources well enough, she adds. 

Another risk is that the current push to access the web through AI search will disrupt the internet’s digital economy, argues Benjamin Brooks, a fellow at Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center, who previously led public policy for Stability AI, in an op-ed published by MIT Technology Review today.

“By shielding the web behind an all-knowing chatbot, AI search could deprive creators of the visits and ‘eyeballs’ they need to survive,” Brooks writes.

text:
Every day across Hollywood, scores of film school graduates and production assistants work as script readers. Their job is to find the diamonds in the rough from the 50,000 or so screenplays pitched each year and flag any worth pursuing further. Each script runs anywhere from 100 to 150 pages, and it can take half a day to read one and write up a “coverage,” or summary of the strengths and weaknesses. With only about 50 of these scripts selling in a given year, readers are trained to be ruthless. 

Now the film-focused tech company Cinelytic, which works with major studios like Warner Bros. and Sony Pictures to analyze film budgets and box office potential, aims to offer script feedback with generative AI. 

Today it launched a new tool called Callaia, which amateur writers and professional script readers alike can use to analyze scripts at $79 each. Using AI, it takes Callaia less than a minute to write its own coverage, which includes a synopsis, a list of comparable films, grades for areas like dialogue and originality, and actor recommendations. It also makes a recommendation on whether or not the film should be financed, giving it a rating of “pass,” “consider,” “recommend,” or “strongly recommend.” Though the foundation of the tool is built with ChatGPT’s API, the team had to coach the model on script-specific tasks like evaluating genres and writing a movie’s logline, which summarize the story in a sentence. 

“It helps people understand the script very quickly,” says Tobias Queisser, Cinelytic’s cofounder and CEO, who also had a career as a film producer. “You can look at more stories and more scripts, and not eliminate them based on factors that are detrimental to the business of finding great content.”

The idea is that Callaia will give studios a more analytical way to predict how a script may perform on the screen before spending on marketing or production. But, the company says, it’s also meant to ease the bottleneck that script readers create in the filmmaking process. With such a deluge to sort through, many scripts can make it to decision-makers only if they have a recognizable name attached. An AI-driven tool would democratize the script selection process and allow better scripts and writers to be discovered, Queisser says.

The tool’s introduction may further fuel the ongoing Hollywood debate about whether AI will help or harm its creatives. Since the public launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, the technology has drawn concern everywhere from writers’ rooms to special effects departments, where people worry that it will cheapen, augment, or replace human talent.  

In this case, Callaia’s success will depend on whether it can provide critical feedback as well as a human script reader can. 

That’s a challenge because of what GPT and other AI models are built to do, according to Tuhin Chakrabarty, a researcher who studied how well AI can analyze creative works during his PhD in computer science at Columbia University. In one of his studies, Chakrabarty and his coauthors had various AI models and a group of human experts—including professors of creative writing and a screenwriter—analyze the quality of 48 stories, 12 that appeared in the New Yorker and the rest of which were AI-generated. His team found that the two groups virtually never agreed on the quality of the works. 

“Whenever you ask an AI model about the creativity of your work, it is never going to say bad things,” Chakrabarty says. “It is always going to say good things, because it’s trained to be a helpful, polite assistant.”

Cinelytic CTO Dev Sen says this trait did present a hurdle in the design of Callaia, and that the initial output of the model was overly positive. That improved with time and tweaking. “We don’t necessarily want to be overly critical, but aim for a more balanced analysis that points out both strengths and weaknesses in the script,” he says. 

Vir Srinivas, an independent filmmaker whose film Orders from Above won Best Historical Film at Cannes in 2021, agreed to look at an example of Callaia’s output to see how well the AI model can analyze a script. I showed him what the model made of a 100-page script about a jazz trumpeter on a journey of self-discovery in San Francisco, which Cinelytic provided. Srinivas says that the coverage generated by the model didn’t go deep enough to present genuinely helpful feedback to a screenwriter.

“It’s approaching the script in too literal a sense and not a metaphorical one—something which human audiences do intuitively and unconsciously,” he says. “It’s as if it’s being forced to be diplomatic and not make any waves.”

There were other flaws, too. For example, Callaia predicted that the film would need a budget of just $5 to $10 million but also suggested that expensive A-listers like Paul Rudd would have been well suited for the lead role.

Cinelytic says it’s currently at work improving the actor recommendation component, and though the company did not provide data on how well its model analyzes a given script, Sen says feedback from 100 script readers who beta-tested the model was overwhelmingly positive. “Most of them were pretty much blown away, because they said that the coverages were on the order of, if not better than, the coverages they’re used to,” he says. 

Overall, Cinelytic is pitching Callaia as a tool meant to quickly provide feedback on lots of scripts, not to replace human script readers, who will still read and adjust the tool’s findings. Queisser, who is cognizant that whether AI can effectively write or edit creatively is hotly contested in Hollywood, is hopeful the tool will allow script readers to more quickly identify standout scripts while also providing an efficient source of feedback for writers.

“Writers that embrace our tool will have something that can help them refine their scripts and find more opportunities,” he says. “It’s positive for both sides.”

# Learning to Invest in U.S. Stocks from Scratch: Is an S&P 500 ETF Worth Considering? An In-depth Look at Opportunities, Risks, and Long-term Investment Strategies

In the U.S. stock market, many beginners often hope to achieve quick gains by hunting for the "next hot stock." However, the true test in the investment world is not one's ability to make short-term predictions, but rather one's understanding of risk, valuation, and long-term growth.

For those just starting their journey in the U.S. stock market, an S&P 500 ETF—such as VOO—is an investment vehicle worth exploring.

## I. What is VOO, and Why Is It Worth Considering?

VOO is an S&P 500 ETF issued by Vanguard, designed to track the overall performance of large, publicly traded U.S. companies.

It spans a wide range of sectors, including technology, finance, healthcare, and consumer goods. By investing in this single ETF, you gain indirect exposure to a broad basket of major American corporations.

Compared to purchasing shares of individual companies, an index ETF helps mitigate the risks associated with any single stock and spares investors the challenge of selecting specific companies.

## II. Three Key Advantages of Investing in VOO

**1. Diversification of Risk**

VOO covers approximately 500 large U.S. companies. If one company faces operational difficulties, the impact on your overall portfolio is generally much smaller than it would be if you held that company’s stock alone.

However, it is important to note that while diversification reduces the risk of holding individual stocks, it does not protect against a broad market downturn.

**2. Participation in the Long-term Growth of the U.S. Economy**

The United States boasts a mature capital market and numerous companies with strong global competitiveness. Through index investing, you can share in the growth and success of these major enterprises.

**3. Well-Suited for Long-term Investment**

Compared to frequent trading of individual stocks, long-term index investing reduces transaction frequency and the likelihood of making emotionally driven decisions—making it an ideal approach for those looking to build a long-term investment plan.

## III. What Risks Should You Be Aware of When Investing in VOO?

No investment is entirely free of risk.

First, systemic market risk cannot be ignored. In the event of a U.S. economic recession, shifts in interest rates, or a deterioration in market sentiment, the S&P 500 index may experience a significant pullback.

Second, the index has a heavy weighting in the technology sector. If major tech stocks decline simultaneously, the index could be substantially affected.

Finally, valuation risk is also a critical factor to consider. If investors commit large sums of capital when market valuations are excessively high, future returns may be suppressed.

Therefore, one should not assume that VOO’s strong historical performance guarantees continued gains in the future.

## IV. What investment skills should beginners master?

In my view, beginners should focus on four key areas:

First, invest in stages (dollar-cost averaging). Avoid deploying all your capital at a single point in time to mitigate the impact of poor market timing.

Second, manage position sizes. Do not invest money needed for essential living expenses, and exercise caution when using leverage.

Third, take a long-term perspective. Focus on factors like corporate earnings, economic growth, interest rates, and market valuations, rather than obsessing over daily stock price fluctuations.

Fourth, conduct regular reviews. Check whether your portfolio is overly concentrated and ensure it remains aligned with your personal risk tolerance.

## V. Where do future investment opportunities lie?

With the ongoing evolution of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, medical technology, and automation, large U.S. corporations continue to have significant opportunities for innovation.

However, a promising industry outlook does not mean that every related stock is worth buying at a high price.

For investors, it is more important to assess whether a company’s earnings growth can justify its current valuation, and to adjust investment strategies in response to changing market conditions.

## Conclusion: The first step in investing is not making money, but learning to manage risk.

While VOO offers a way to participate in the overall growth of large U.S. companies, it cannot eliminate market risk.

For beginners, developing a sound investment philosophy, understanding asset allocation, managing risk, and maintaining independent judgment are far more important than chasing short-term, outsized gains.

**Truly mature investors do not spend their days hunting for the fastest-rising stocks; instead, they understand why they are investing, what risks they are taking, and how to navigate market volatility.**

Investing is a process of long-term accumulation. By remaining patient, respecting the market, and practicing effective risk management, you position yourself to travel further and more steadily on your long-term investment journey. Click here to get in touch with me:

text:
How do founders know when their company's website needs a redesign?

A friend recently asked me this during a conversation, and it took few minutes to wrap my head around it.

Creating a website in 2026 has become accessible to anyone, but premium work is limited.

For a business to know when to redesign their website, I think it boils down to two things:

- The scale of the brand
- Current design trends

When I audited a business’ website some time ago, I noticed they had outgrown their website.

The numbers they were doing, the offers they were pushing, and the kind of business they had become were no longer reflected in a website they built a few years earlier.

It was great when they started, but the business had evolved. It made sense to redesign everything from the ground up.

And there's also design trends. I remember when Apple used glassmorphism in one of their designs. It quickly became a popular design direction in many tech companies and was doing quite well.

A website that looks great today might look outdated in two or five years when another design direction becomes popular.

Your website should evolve as your business evolves.

text:
Jensen Huang’s exit proves one thing beyond a shadow of a doubt: the "Chinese spy" conspiracy theory is dead—and Washington’s anti-Huang, anti-Trump hawks just scored a massive win.

Several US AI experts have already warned that seeing an industry pioneer step down like this is a major loss for global tech. Yet this whole mess was never a real national security crisis. Like we noted two days ago, DC partisan infighting—weaponizing the "China" label—started this storm, and that battle is far from over. The newly leaked office romance simply became the final straw, handing his opponents the exact outcome they wanted.

With more details coming to light, a much clearer picture is taking shape.

First, the "Chinese spy" logic makes zero sense.
Even if Huang was completely in the dark, you don't steal a $3 trillion semiconductor ecosystem—built on tens of thousands of engineers and complex supply chains—through pillow talk. More importantly, Huang successfully lobbied the White House to allow H200 chip sales to China. Risking a total export freeze by running a "honey trap" on your single most valuable public advocate would be pure strategic malpractice for Beijing.

Second, the "spy" probe was still unresolved—an internal HR blowup was the final straw.
When the #AliceHuang story broke on Sunday, Nvidia's board actually stood by him, seeing no proof of leaked secrets. The national security probe was still up in the air. What sealed his fate on Wednesday night was The New York Times citing five former insiders over an affair with his direct subordinate, VP #KimberlyPowell. In Corporate America, a CEO dating a direct report is an instant governance death sentence—the exact same HR violation that cost the CEOs of Intel and McDonald's their jobs. This became the final straw that forced the board to cut ties—handing his Washington rivals the exact scalp they wanted.

Third, there’s still zero hard proof on the spy claims—and the timing raises serious questions.
The core "spy" claims all relied on anonymous officials leaking to the press. Attorney General Todd Blanche admitted on Thursday that neither the DOJ nor FBI has concluded Alice Huang is a spy, and Singapore’s Home Affairs Ministry also confirmed its probe into her had nothing to do with espionage. Yet intelligence agencies sat on this info for over a year, only to drop it right before the early November midterms and keep turning up the heat ahead of the U.S.-China summit. Rather than genuine counterintelligence, this looks much more like a calculated political play.

Even with Huang out—and CFO Colette Kress stepping in as interim CEO—the anti-Huang and anti-Trump crowd isn't slowing down. In fact, they’re moving in:

Aiming straight at Trump: Senate Dem Leader Chuck Schumer, alongside Warren and Coons, is turning the fire directly onto Trump and his Cabinet—giving Lutnick, Rubio, and Stephen Miller a Nov. 17 deadline to preserve White House records for upcoming hearings.

Forcing Nvidia to fall in line: With a caretaker CFO at the helm, Nvidia’s lobbying muscle in DC is dead. Under relentless Washington pressure, the company—and whoever takes over permanently—will have no choice but to cooperate with congressional probes and "politically correctly" comply with strict export controls, just as hawks rush to pass stalled AI bans.

Putting Silicon Valley on notice: Fresh off winning back both the House and Senate this November, Democrats are taking down Silicon Valley’s biggest pro-Trump flag-bearer to send a clear message to Big Tech: Congress is back in charge of setting the rules. Meanwhile, even inside the GOP, China hawks like Mast and Moolenaar deeply resent tech bosses lobbying Trump to ease chip bans just to make money in China—making an example of Huang warns every other US exec not to use the White House to bypass export controls.

Many are comparing Huang’s exit to Steve Jobs leaving Apple. At the height of the U.S.-China tech rivalry, one takeaway is crystal clear: what’s sabotaging America's tech edge isn't outside competition or foreign spies—it’s Washington itself. The "Chinese spy" narrative was just a convenient weapon.

Is the AI bubble actually deflating, or is the market simply becoming more realistic about AI valuations?

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO is an interesting case to watch.

A few weeks ago, reports suggested that Anthropic could be targeting a valuation of around $2 trillion. But following the recent tech market selloff, some investors reportedly reconsidered that valuation, with discussions falling toward the $1.1T–$1.3T range.

There was also an initial reported IPO price range of $70–$80, which was later retracted. Subsequent reports discussed an updated $70–$78 range.

These figures come from different stages of reporting, so they shouldn’t be treated as one confirmed set of final IPO terms.

So, is this the beginning of an AI bubble deflating?

I think it’s more interesting to look at this as a possible shift in market expectations.

AI is still developing, and companies like Anthropic have real products and growing demand. But having strong technology doesn’t automatically justify any valuation.

Investors may be starting to look beyond the AI hype and pay closer attention to actual business performance, revenue, competition, infrastructure costs, and how long it might take for these companies to become profitable.

For traders, this is a reminder that market sentiment can change quickly. A company can have strong long-term potential while its valuation still gets reassessed.

text:
A substantial share of H-1B LCAs are certified at entry-level or junior prevailing-wage levels well below local medians, and there is clear evidence of cost-driven replacement of Americans (especially via outsourcing), though the picture is not uniform across all employers and is contested by some studies.

LCA wages are frequently set at levels for entry/qualified roles, not highly skilled/senior ones

Employers file a Labor Condition Application (LCA) with the Department of Labor before an H-1B petition. The required wage is the higher of the employer’s actual wage for similar workers or the prevailing wage. DOL sets four prevailing-wage levels from Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) data for each occupation and area:

Level I (entry): ~17th percentile — basic understanding, routine tasks under close supervision.
Level II (qualified): ~34th percentile — moderately complex tasks, limited judgment.
Level III (experienced): ~50th percentile (median).
- Level IV (fully competent): ~67th percentile.

These are official DOL/OFLC constructs (see Congressional Research Service summaries of the system).[](<https://t.co/5BxrQzRojr>)

Analyses of certified LCA data consistently show heavy concentration in the lower levels:

- Economic Policy Institute (Costa & Hira, FY2019 data): 60% of H-1B positions at Level I (14%) or Level II (46%)—both below the local median. For the top 30 employers, the share was also ~60%. Level III was 19% and Level IV only 12% (plus some private surveys).[](<https://t.co/Q489CFGjkM>)
- More recent data (e.g., analyses of DOL disclosure files): FY2025 roughly Level I ~20%, Level II ~42%, Level III ~21%, Level IV ~17%. Combined Levels I+II remain around 60%. Historical trends show Level I declining from higher shares in earlier years but Levels I+II still dominant.[](<https://t.co/1WVRSE6tHe>)[](<https://t.co/CinjyP02Gi>)
- A 2026 Federal Register notice on proposed prevailing-wage updates noted that in FY2024 about 62.6% of H-1B LCAs were at Level I or II.[](<https://t.co/3E0FYnFIya>)

Median offered wages track these levels: Level I often in the $70–90k range and Level II around $100–110k for common occupations (higher in high-cost metros, but still not senior rates). For software developers and similar roles that dominate H-1B filings, Level I/II wages are those of junior or mid-level positions, not the higher end of the distribution for experienced or highly specialized workers.[](<https://t.co/sQoMBTk3yE>)

The level is chosen by the employer based on the job’s stated requirements (experience, judgment, supervision), not the individual’s résumé. Critics (including EPI) argue this system lets employers legally set floors well below local medians for many specialty-occupation roles, even when workers have advanced degrees or experience. DOL has authority to set higher floors; proposals have repeatedly sought to raise the percentiles (e.g., Level I from 17th to 34th).

Not every LCA is low-level—some employers (especially certain pure tech firms) file more at Level III/IV and offer higher wages—but the overall distribution shows that a large majority of the program is not operating at “highly skilled/senior” pay rates.

Evidence of replacement for cost savings rather than pure skill gaps

Documented cases show U.S. companies contracting with outsourcing firms that bring in H-1B workers at lower wages to replace existing American IT staff, often requiring the Americans to train their replacements as a condition of severance:

Southern California Edison: Hundreds of IT workers laid off and replaced via Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys. Domestic pay averaged substantially higher; H-1B wages were lower (reports cited savings allowing multiple foreign workers for the cost of one American). Workers trained replacements. LA Times and EPI covered this extensively.[](<https://t.co/54w4OcfrsL>)[](<https://t.co/ZvH8arAupf>)

text:
THE ELORIA TRILOGY
Lethal • The Return • Unbreakable
A story of courage, pride, judgement, sacrifice and the horrific cost of being selected.
Part I: Lethal
The Girl Who Slayed a Dragon
Eloria was 15 when the dragon came.
It was a lovely morning, the kind of morning that guaranteed absolutely nothing. The summer sun was out over the fields, the grass was warm and the wild flowers were in full flow with their normal perfume in the breeze. Eloria was out on her own on a hillside just outside the village, her thoughts occupied as always with the trivialities of a girl of that age.
Then she listened to the screaming.
At first she thought it might have been kids playing. It came again though, a bit more piercing this time with the distant ring of bells.
The village bells.
They were ringing in alarm.
Eloria straightened and looked up towards the hill which separated the fields from her own home.
A column of black smoke was rising into the clear blue sky.
Then another.
And another.
She dropped everything and just ran.
By the time she'd got to the top of the hill she could feel the heat.
Below her the village was burning.
People were running through the streets with their children and whatever possessions they could scrounge up. Roofs were coming down in a shower of sparks. The livestock had all gone mad and were running everywhere. The screams of the injured were intermingled with the crackle and roar of the fires.
And in the market square was a dragon.
It was enormous, almost the size of a house, all dark scales as wet stone. Enormous scaly wings projected from its shoulders and smoke was oozing from between its teeth. Its claws were digging furrows into the cobbles as it turned towards another group of villagers who were scrambling to get away.
Eloria remained motionless.
She'd heard the stories about dragons of course. Everybody had. They were the dragons of the far mountains and the long forgotten ages, the dragons of the old folk tales and the tunes of the wandering minstrels.
They didn't belong here.
The dragon opened its mouth.
A torrent of fire went down on a nearby house.
Something inside Eloria had finally broken free of her fear.
She ran downhill.
She pushed through the panicking villagers, their cries of warning all around her. She went past the well, past the market stalls, past the baker's shop (all its windows shattered). She saw a man trapped under a beam and got him out.
Then she ran towards her own house.
Her dad was up by the door, shirt all stained with blood. He'd gone out to help defend the village and had been badly wounded.
He grasped her wrist as she knelt down beside him.
"Get out," he told her. "Take your mother and go."
But Eloria was looking past him, through the open door.
Above the hearth hung his sword.
It was an old weapon, very simple and much worn, passed down through the generations. Her father had carried it when he was young, though Eloria had never seen him draw it in anger.
She had held it before. He had even taught her a little of its use.
But she had never fought anyone.
Certainly not a dragon.
"Eloria," her father said, tightening his grip. "Listen to me."
She looked down at him.
Then she listened to a child screaming somewhere in the square.
She gently pulled her hand free.
"I'm sorry, Father."
She went in, took the sword from above the hearth and went back out into the burning streets.
The weapon was heavier than she recalled.
Her hands quivered around its shaft.
She was terrified.
But the screams went on and she knew what would happen if the thing wasn't stopped.
The dragon turned while she approached.
For a moment, it simply stared at her.
A tiny girl, barely a child, standing all by herself in the street with a sword which was absolutely huge for her.
It lowered its huge head.
Eloria raised the blade.
"Leave them alone!"
The dragon roared.
The sound shook the windows and sent her staggering backwards. Its wings spread out and completely blocked out the sun, its jaws opening to reveal the terrible orange light building in its throat.
Eloria threw herself behind the stone cistern.
Fire spread over the square.
Her exposed skin was blistering in the heat. The stones against her back were actually quite hot to the touch.
When the flames passed, she climbed out and charged.
Her first strike glanced harmlessly from the creature's scales.
Its tail swept toward her.
She barely got away, rolling under a market cart as the tail blew the wooden posts behind her to bits.
The dragon lunged.
Eloria fell backwards, her sword catching one of the claws. The blade bit between two scales and drew a thin line of dark blood.
The beast shrieked.
It could be hurt.
That was all she needed to know.
The battle became a desperate struggle through the ruined square. Eloria was quicker, but the dragon was stronger beyond all reckoning. Each missed blow would crack stone or shatter timber. Every breath of fire was a threat to her life.
She was wounded. Exhausted. Barely able to lift her father's sword.
And still she fought.
Then she saw a little boy trapped beneath the remains of a collapsed cart.
The dragon saw him too.
Its head turned.
Eloria knew she couldn't get to the lad before the flames.
She screamed and ran anyway.
Something awakened inside her.
A warmth moved through her chest, down her arms and into the sword. For one utterly impossible instant the old steel shone with a pale, brilliant light.
Eloria leaped between the child and the dragon.
The creature released its fire.
She raised the sword.
The flames broke around her.
She didn't know what was going on. She didn't have the time to.
The dragon recoiled and Eloria moved.
She leapt onto a pile of fallen masonry and then onto the creature's lowered shoulder. Those scales were scorching under her feet. One of the massive wings came down across her side and nearly threw her off the thing.
But she held on.
With a final cry, she drove her father's sword into the vulnerable scales under its jaw.
The blade entered deep.
The light flashed.
The dragon convulsed, stumbled backwards and collapsed into the square with a crash which shook the ground.
Then it lay still.
Eloria fell beside it.
For a long time, she could do nothing but kneel there, trembling, the sword hanging loosely in her hands.
The dragon was dead.
The village was saved.
And somewhere behind her someone started to cheer.
Others joined.
Soon the square was filled with voices.
"Eloria!"
"Eloria!"
"Eloria!"
She turned to them, bewildered and terrified, not the slightest idea why they were all celebrating when everything had been destroyed.
She'd only ever wanted to save her own home.
She'd only wanted to save the people she loved.
But the people saw something more.
They saw a hero.
And heroes, as Eloria would find out, are never allowed to stay ordinary people.
The making of a legend
The story circulated right beyond the village.
Within weeks people were turning up to see the girl who had killed the dragon. Within months she was the subject of songs in far away towns. Kings and the nobility were sending over messengers with gifts, invitations and offers of reward.
The village was rebuilt.
A statue from Eloria was raised in the square where the dragon had fallen.
She was embarrassed when it was unveiled.
The sculptor had made her taller, stronger, more beautiful than she thought herself to be. He'd placed a crown of laurels on her head and had her holding her sword aloft above the beast which she had just defeated.
"That's not what happened," she protested.
But the locals laughed.
"That's what ought to have happened," one of them told her.
And the legend expanded.
As Eloria got older she was increasingly called upon for protection and guidance. When there were bandits on the roads she'd ride out and deal with them. When one of the neighbouring villages was under threat she'd come to their aid. When there was a dispute which might well have escalated into a war, the rulers would come to her for advice.
She had a most unusual natural strength, a real courage about her and a gift for battle which no teacher could ever really impart.
There were four remarkable companions around her.
Mara, a warrior of great strength whose shield had stood up to the very worst of the charges that would have shattered any other army.
Tovan, an archer of extraordinary accuracy, capable of hitting a moving target at ranges most men could barely see.
Serin, a healer and scholar whose knowledge of old languages and forgotten powers was just as valuable as any weapon.
And Dain, a brilliant strategist whose cool intelligence had saved whole towns out of the most desperate of situations.
They grew inseparable.
All five of them did absolutely brilliant things together.
They defeated armies, ended feuds, drove monsters from the wilderness, and brought peace to lands that had known generations of violence.
Eloria became their leader.
Then a leader of thousands.
Then something approaching a queen, though she never actually claimed the title.
The people loved her.
More statues were built.
Great halls were named after her. The children were taught her stories. Minstrels sang her praises, sometimes before she'd even come back from battle.
At first, she corrected their exaggerations.
Eventually, she stopped.
And at some point the girl who had gone into a burning village because people needed her started to think that she was extraordinary simply because she was entitled to be.
She wasn't any longer grateful for the plaudits.
She expected it.
She wasn't in the least surprised any more when people would defer to her judgement.
She demanded it.
Her companions all stuck by her, though even they could see that something had changed.
Once Mara raised a question about an increasingly reckless decision, Eloria just ignored her.
When Dain pointed out that the eastern settlements were becoming increasingly vulnerable, Eloria declared that no enemy would venture to attack lands which were under her protection.
When Serin suggested that the people had started to rely on her too much, Eloria just laughed.
"Isn't that why we're here?"
And when Tovan asked whether they should ride out themselves to investigate troubling rumors beyond the eastern mountains, Eloria waved him away.
"Let the local commanders handle it."
For eleven years, Eloria's legend has grown.
She was now twenty-six.
Her name was spoken with reverence.
Her victories were countless.
Her power was unquestioned.
She had almost completely forgotten the little frightened girl who'd once stood all by herself in a burning street, clutching her father's sword because someone had to do something.
Part II: The Return
The Fall of the Eloria
The initial reports were from the east.
Entire villages had disappeared.
Travelers spoke of mountains burning at night, rivers turning to steam and animals found dead under skies of black ash.
Afterwards came the survivors.
They got there absolutely spent and terrified, with tales so incredible that Eloria's advisers would simply not believe them at all.
A dragon had appeared.
Not simply a dragon.
A creature larger than any living thing they had ever envisioned.
Its wings darkened entire valleys. Its claws tore trenches through the land. Its fire could incinerate a walled town in a single breath.
And it was moving west.
Eloria was initially sceptical about the reports.
Dragons were dangerous of course, but she'd killed one as a child. In the eleven years since then she'd faced far more enemies and far more sophisticated armies.
She had never been defeated.
But then a messenger arrived from the eastern frontier.
His horse gave way under him at the gates. His clothes were all in a state of being burned. His face was grey with fatigue.
Eloria received him in her great hall.
"What news?" she asked.
The messenger fell to his knees.
"My lady, the eastern watch is gone. The fortress at Valen's Pass is fallen. We could do nothing."
Eloria stood.
"How many?"
"All of them."
The room grew silent.
The messenger swallowed.
"And there is something else."
"Speak."
"The creature talks."
Eloria frowned.
"What does it say?"
The messenger looked up at her.
"One word, my lady."
He delayed.
"Eloria."
A buzz passed through the hall.
The messenger continued.
"Over and over. It comes to a village, destroys everything in its path, and calls your name."
Eloria's expression stiffened.
Then she smiled.
"So it remembers me."
Her companions exchanged apprehensive glances.
Mara advanced forward.
"We should bring the armies in. Evacuate the settlements. Find out what we're up against."
"No," Eloria replied.
Dain spoke next.
We don't know its strength. A creature that can blow Valen's Pass to bits is something we have to be cautious about.
Eloria looked at him with irritation.
"Have you forgotten who we are?"
Nobody answered.
She turned towards the massive tapestry behind her throne which showed her first victory, a young girl standing over the dragon.
"11 years ago I slew one of them with a rusty old sword and no training whatsoever. Now I have the very best warriors in the kingdom at my side."
She looked back at her companions.
"Let it come."
Then she reconsidered.
"No. We shall go to it."
The dragon in the east
They rode east beneath banners bearing Eloria's crest.
The people lined the roads to cheer them.
They threw flowers before their horses and were shouting blessings. The kids had wooden swords and were all pretending to be their very own champion.
Eloria smiled and raised her hand.
She felt no fear.
Why should she?
She'd become the most celebrated warrior in the known world.
For days they tramped through the abandoned settlements and the scorched countryside.
The closer they came to the eastern mountains, the quieter the world became.
There were no birds.
No insects.
Even the wind was holding its breath.
At last they came to a wide valley underneath a ridge of broken stone.
There, they found the dragon.
And for the first time in eleven years, Eloria felt something she had almost forgotten.
Fear.
The thing was utterly enormous.
Its body was enormous, the ruined fortress beneath it looking tiny in comparison. Its wings rose like black mountains. Its plates were a deep crimson, as if some infernal furnace was burning under its skin.
The dragon she'd fought as a child would have fitted right in one of its claws.
Mara murmured an oath.
Tovan slowly lowered his bow.
Dain just stared in silence, working out the distances, the weaknesses, the possibilities.
Finding none.
Then the dragon rotated its head.
Two vast, burning eyes fixed upon the five figures standing on the ridge.
Its mouth opened.
"ELORIA."
The word rolled across the valley like a rolling thunder.
Even the horses recoiled.
Eloria dismounted.
Her heart was thudding, but she managed a smile.
"So," she said, drawing her father's sword, "you've come looking for me."
The dragon slowly rose.
The ground trembled beneath its weight.
"ELORIA."
She raised her blade.
"You found me."
And she charged.
The breaking of the five
The battle went wrong straight away.
Tovan loosed the first arrow, aimed dead at the dragon's eye.
The shaft hit its plates and sheared.
Mara raced forward, shield raised, as the dragon's enormous claw descended.
She caught the blow.
For a short while, she held.
Then the force threw her across the valley, her shield splintering beneath the impact.
Dain bellowed for them all to break up.
The dragon swept its wings.
A hurricane of ash and stone threw them to the ground.
Eloria lunged toward its foreleg, driving her father's sword between two scales.
The blade hardly penetrated.
The dragon looked down at her.
And struck.
Eloria flew backward, crashing through a wall of broken stone.
Her armor cracked.
Pain burst through her ribs.
She struggled to her feet, blood running from her mouth.
"Again!" she shouted.
Her companions rallied.
Dain tried to get the creature's attention. Tovan was looking for a weak spot under its wings. Serin was pulling every protective art she had. Mara was hurt but not broken and was moving to protect the others.
They fought magnificently.
Against almost any other enemy, they would have prevailed.
But the dragon was beyond them.
Its fire ripped straight through Serin's protective barrier.
Its tail smacked the ground beneath Dain and he was buried in the rubble.
Its claws struck Mara down a second time.
Tovan's arrows accomplished nothing.
And Eloria, the great champion, the undefeated hero, the woman whose name was practically synonymous with victory, was completely at sixes and sevens.
She attacked again.
The dragon struck her to the ground.
She rose.
It struck her again.
She screamed in defiance and dragged herself upright, leaning on her father's sword.
The dragon looked at her almost inquisitively.
For the first time, it seemed to understand something about its opponent.
She was weaker than it had expected.
Eloria reeled forward.
Her sight blurred.
Her sword trembled.
"I... am... Eloria."
The dragon replied with a terrible roar.
It raised one immense claw.
Eloria tried to move.
Her body failed her.
The claw descended.
The earth broke beneath the impact.
And Eloria was buried in the ground.
Her sword fell from her hand.
Her body lay motionless among the shattered stones.
For a moment no one moved.
Then Mara screamed her name.
Tovan dropped his bow.
Serin crept towards the crater, knowing full well she was too late.
And Dain, pulling himself free from the rubble, looked down at the woman who had directed them for eleven years.
Their leader.
Their champion.
Their friend.
Dead.
The surviving troops started to break and run.
The dragon lifted its head, triumphant.
The legend from Eloria had come to an end.
The place between
Eloria opened her eyes.
She was standing in darkness.
There was no pain.
No sound.
No wind.
She looked down at herself.
Her armour was gone. Her injuries were all gone. She was dressed in the plain clothes of the girl she'd once been.
"Am I dead?"
Nobody answered.
Then five figures emerged from the darkness.
They were tall, formless and rather strangely luminous, the light around them illuminating absolutely nothing else.
Their faces were utterly impossible to see.
Eloria detected neither kindness nor cruelty in them.
Only an authority of such absolute magnitude that every king she'd ever known was utterly insignificant.
The five stood before her in silence.
Eloria straightened.
'I am Eloria' she said.
"We know," said the first.
The voice was neither male nor female. It seemed to come from everywhere.
"I slew the dragon of the western valley. I defended the kingdoms of men. I have fought..."
"We know," the second interrupted.
Eloria fell silent.
The third stepped forward.
"And we are not impressed."
The words hit harder than any punch.
Eloria stared at them.
"What?"
"You were given a gift," said the first.
"A purpose," said the second.
"A responsibility," said the third.
The fourth spoke with quiet severity.
"And you mistook it for a reward."
Eloria's anger rose.
"I saved thousands of lives!"
"Yes," replied the first.
"I fought battles that no one else would fight!"
"Yes."
"I gave everything!"
The fifth figure (who'd been standing completely still up until this point) took a step forward.
"Did you?"
Eloria opened her mouth.
No words came.
The darkness around them shifted.
She suddenly saw her village.
The burning houses.
The terrified children.
Her wounded father.
And a fifteen-year-old girl running through the flames with an old sword in her hands.
"Look at her," commanded the first.
Eloria watched her younger self leap between the dragon and the trapped child.
"Why did she fight?"
Eloria whispered, "Because they needed help."
"Did she seek glory?"
"No."
"Did she seek power?"
"No."
"Did she expect a statue?"
Eloria lowered her eyes.
"No."
The vision changed.
She saw herself older, seated in her great hall.
She saw her companions bringing warnings that she had dismissed.
She saw the frightened villagers waiting for protection while their champion was being honoured in the distant cities.
She saw the faces of people whose names she had forgotten.
People who had believed in her.
People who had needed her.
"Your strength was given so that others might live," said the fourth.
"Your courage was given so that others might find their own," said the second.
"Your power was never intended to make you great," said the third.
"It was meant to make you useful," said the fifth.
Eloria began to weep.
Not because she had lost.
Not because she had died.
Because she finally understood.
She'd been given something extraordinary and over the years she came to believe it was her own gift.
She'd forgotten the people it was for.
She fell to her knees.
"I'm sorry."
The five just regarded her in silence.
At last, the first spoke.
"Your work is unfinished."
Eloria looked up.
"You will return."
Hope flashed across her face.
But the figure raised a hand.
'Understand us. You've already been given more than most could ever imagine. You've wasted a great deal of it. We're not simply going to put you back in the life you had.'
The fifth stepped toward her.
"There will be a price."
Eloria swallowed.
"What price?"
"A fire," it said.
"One that will live within you for the remainder of your days."
"It will grant you the strength to fulfill your purpose," said the second.
"But it will burn you," said the third.
"Every moment," said the fourth.
"Every day," said the fifth.
"Until your final breath."
Eloria stared at them.
"Will it kill me?"
"No," said the first.
"It will not consume you."
The five figures drew closer.
You'll feel it in the heat when you wake. You'll feel it in battle and in peace. You'll feel it when you're being lauded and you'll feel it when you're being forgotten. It will be there to remind you of what you've been given, what you've neglected and what's still yours to do.
Eloria bowed her head.
She thought of Mara.
Tovan.
Serin.
Dain.
She thought of her dad and the kid under the cart.
She thought of all those now at the dragon's mercy.
Then she looked up.
"I understand."
The first one leaned over to her.
"Do you?"
Eloria held its gaze.
"I don't know if I can take it."
For the first time the numbers were happy.
"Then you have learned something."
The dark was beginning to lighten.
The five stepped away.
Eloria reached toward them.
"Wait. Who are you?"
No answer came.
The light grew stronger.
And just before the darkness disappeared, the first figure spoke again.
"Now go."
A pause.
"And do your job."
Part III: Unbreakable
The Fire That Would Not Die
The battle was over.
Or so the survivors believed.
Smoke hung over the valley, the ground strewn with broken weapons and broken stone. There were fires all along the ridge where the armies had actually fought.
The dragon was standing over the battlefield, victorious.
Mara knelt beside the crater where Eloria had fallen.
She had found her friend's body half buried beneath the rubble, broken and still.
Serin was beside her.
The healer had tried everything she knew.
Nothing worked.
Eloria was gone.
Tovan was a short way off, staring up at the huge creature looming over them.
Dain struggled to rally the surviving soldiers, but his commands fell on deaf ears.
There was nothing left to rally them for.
Then, deep within the crater, something moved.
A finger.
Barely perceptible.
Eloria's right hand twitched.
Serin stopped speaking.
She stared.
Another movement.
The hand slowly closed.
The dragon noticed.
Its immense head turned toward the crater.
At first, the creature seemed merely curious.
Perhaps some last involuntary movement of a dying thing.
Then Eloria's arm shifted.
The dragon lowered its head.
Its burning eyes narrowed.
Beneath the rubble, Eloria drew a breath.
A terrible, ragged breath.
And opened her eyes.
The awakening
Pain.
That was the first thing she knew.
Not the pain of her broken body.
Something deeper.
Something inside her.
A burning so profound that it seemed to reach into every part of her existence.
She tried to scream.
No sound came.
Her fingers dug into the earth.
Then she remembered.
There will be a price.
Eloria gritted her teeth.
Slowly, impossibly, she moved.
Her broken body began to mend as a faint orange glow appeared beneath her skin.
She pushed against the ground.
The stones shifted.
Mara stumbled backward.
"Eloria?"
A trembling arm emerged from the crater.
Then a shoulder.
Then the figure of a woman struggling to rise.
Eloria pulled one knee beneath herself.
And the fire began.
At first, it was little more than a flicker.
A soft, golden light deep within her chest.
It pulsed once.
Then again.
Thin veins of light spread across her arms and throat. Her hair began to lift in an invisible wind. Heat shimmered in the air around her.
Serin raised a hand to shield her face.
"What's happening?"
Eloria tried to stand.
The pain intensified.

Rabban's brutality reflects the larger Harkonnen philosophy: rule through fear, intimidation and punishment rather than loyalty. But there's an important detail: the Baron deliberately placed Rabban in charge of squeezing Arrakis dry, intending to replace him with Feyd-Rautha, who would appear comparatively merciful.

As for the officers, military hierarchy still requires communication, and some probably believe their usefulness will protect them.
But your criticism is valid. Rabban's behaviour creates a military where officers are too terrified to offer criticism or report problems honestly. A commander who executes everyone who challenges him doesn't create a stronger army; he creates an army too afraid to tell him when he's making a mistake.

3 Kislev - Rav Yaakov Moshe Kulefsky - 2000

On this day in the year 2000, Rav Yaakov Moshe Kulefsky passed away, making this day his yartzeit. He was born in Chicago on the third day of Chanukah in 1925, the only son among four children. His parents ran a business there and moved to St. Louis for a better opportunity. St. Louis had little to offer him in Jewish education. At fifteen he was sent back to Chicago alone to learn at Beis Medrash L’Torah under Rav Dovid Lifshitz. Three years later he moved to Mesivta Torah Vodaath, where he became close to Rav Shlomo Heiman. Rav Shlomo Heiman’s way of learning shaped him for the rest of his life.

He was drafted into the United States Army in August 1944. Every effort to get him released failed. On the Shabbosos he was given off he walked the miles from his training base to Torah Vodaath to say over the original insights he had worked out that week in the army. After his discharge he learned under Rav Reuven Grozovsky at Bais Medrash Elyon in Monsey for eight years. In 1954 a cousin introduced him to Rav Yaakov Yitzchok Ruderman, who hired him at Ner Israel in Baltimore to talk in learning with the boys. He was giving the lectures himself before long. He also tested candidates for ordination, sat on the rabbinical court and was the yeshiva’s authority on mikva. When Rav Shmuel Yaakov Weinberg died in the summer of 1999, Rav Kulefsky became Rosh Yeshiva. He held the position for seventeen months.

In his later years his eyesight failed badly. He had the pages of his Gemara enlarged and read them word by word under a powerful lamp and a magnifying machine. Preparing a single lecture took him hours. When the yeshiva was able to take in boys who had gotten out of Iran, he opened his home to them and set up a fund for them. He was scheduled for heart surgery when one of those boys was getting married. He insisted on performing the wedding. His family objected. He told them it was the wedding of a son, and a man does not give up such a wedding. He gave his lecture on Wednesday, the second of Kislev. He became ill that night and died the following day.

The three-day festival, being held from 13–15 Nov 2026, brings together gallantry awardees, veterans, military leaders, strategic thinkers and scholars for insightful discussions on military history, national security and evolving warfare. Military heritage exhibitions, weapons displays and the Clarion Call Theatre offer visitors a glimpse into the courage, capabilities and traditions of the Armed Forces.

A key highlight, SAMVAAD, provides a unique opportunity to interact with Maha Vir Chakra and Vir Chakra awardees, bringing inspiring stories of battlefield valour and sacrifice to life. Military art, philately exhibitions, cultural performances and vintage car displays further enrich the experience.

The festival strengthens civil-military bonds, promotes strategic awareness and inspires future generations with the enduring values of courage, honour and service to the Nation.

text:
WHEN FAITH SEES WHAT THE NATURAL EYE CANNOT SEE

Faith does not deny what the eyes can see; it recognises what the eyes cannot yet comprehend.

There is a dimension of seeing that goes beyond physical sight. It is the ability to perceive possibilities where circumstances present impossibilities, to recognise a future where the present offers no evidence, and to hold on to God’s promises when everything around you seems to contradict them.

The natural eye sees the storm; faith sees the One who commands the wind and the waves.

The natural eye sees a wilderness; faith sees a pathway being prepared.

The natural eye sees a closed door; faith sees the possibility of another entrance.

The natural eye sees a giant; faith remembers the greatness of God.

This is the mystery of faith: faith does not require visible evidence before it believes in the possibility of what God has spoken.

Hebrews 11:1 declares:

“Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.”

Consider Elisha’s servant in 2 Kings 6:15–17. When he woke up and saw the Syrian army surrounding the city, fear became his immediate response. His natural eyes could only interpret the danger before him. But Elisha saw something different.

He prayed:

“Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see.”

And when his eyes were opened, he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire surrounding Elisha.

What a revelation!

The servant’s problem was not that God had abandoned them; his problem was that he could not see what God had already positioned around them.

Sometimes, our greatest limitation is not the size of the challenge before us but the narrowness of our perception.

We become overwhelmed by what is happening because we have not yet understood what God is doing.

Faith teaches us that the absence of visible evidence is not necessarily the absence of divine activity.

However, faith is not wishful thinking, denial of reality or an excuse for irresponsibility. It is confidence in God’s character, even when His purposes are not yet visible.

Abraham saw no child, yet believed the promise. Moses saw the Red Sea, yet moved forward. David saw Goliath, yet remembered the God who had delivered him before.

They understood something profound: what is visible is not always the full picture.

The challenge of faith

What are you seeing today?

Are you seeing only the size of your opposition, or are you considering the greatness of your God?

Are you allowing today’s circumstances to define tomorrow’s possibilities?

Do not allow what your natural eyes see to silence what faith has taught your heart to believe.

For there are things that will never make sense to the natural mind until faith gives you a different perspective.

Sometimes, God does not change what is before your eyes immediately; He first changes what you are able to see.

And perhaps that is where your next breakthrough begins: not with a change of circumstances, but with a transformation of vision.

Faith sees beyond the present, believes beyond the evidence and walks beyond the boundaries of fear.

Scripture for further reflection: 2 Corinthians 5:7; Hebrews 11:27; Romans 4:18–21; Ephesians 1:18.

𝐈𝐑𝐀𝐍’𝐒 𝐀𝐑𝐌𝐘 𝐋𝐀𝐖 𝐋𝐈𝐌𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐖𝐎𝐌𝐄𝐍 𝐓𝐎 𝐌𝐄𝐃𝐈𝐂 𝐃𝐔𝐓𝐘 — 𝟓𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐉𝐔𝐒𝐓 𝐒𝐈𝐆𝐍𝐄𝐃 𝐔𝐏 𝐓𝐎 𝐅𝐈𝐆𝐇𝐓

Under Iran’s own Army Law, women serving in the military are limited to exactly one role: medic. No combat, no command, no exceptions — that’s the regime’s rule, written into its own books. That rule didn’t survive contact with footage out of Tehran this month, showing hundreds of women rappelling off training walls, firing rifles and learning to operate shoulder-fired missile systems. Supporters of the program abroad told state media they’re ready to fight side by side with the Iranian people against the United States and Israel.

The campaign has a name: Janfada — Farsi for “self-sacrifice.” According to movement spokesperson Sasan Zare, more than 500,000 women registered within 100 minutes of sign-ups opening, filling the first 1,000 “National Resistance” battalions. Zare called it proof the program reflects the “national identity of Iranians.” Iran’s own state media hasn’t independently verified that number — it’s the regime’s own claim, released for maximum effect.

The irony is written into Iran’s own law books. Under Article 32 of the Army Law, women are barred from combat service entirely — medical and health duty only. The regime enforces that same control over nearly every other part of a woman’s life: mandatory hijab, segregated classrooms, state-approved professions. But under Article 151 of its own constitution, the Basij militia is required to offer women “basic military training” if they volunteer — and this year, the regime decided to use every inch of that loophole.

That desperation runs deeper than photo-ops. The same mobilization push comes amid reports that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard has been enlisting children as young as 12 for checkpoint duty — one of them, 11-year-old Alireza Jafari, was k!lled at a checkpoint earlier this year. A regime that won’t let its own women near a service rifle under normal law is now arming them by the hundreds of thousands, and sending children to guard checkpoints, because it’s running out of grown men willing to do it.

None of this is happening in a vacuum. It comes as Trump’s pressure campaign and Iran’s collapsing economy squeeze the regime from every direction, with renewed threats of American and Israeli military action still hanging over Tehran. The mullahs built a country that polices women’s hemlines and headscarves. Now they need those same women holding rifles to survive — and that’s not strength. It’s a regime that knows exactly how thin its bench has gotten.

text:
At 19, Napoleon was a young officer with very little money.

While other young men spent their money on comfort, he lived frugally, often limiting himself to one meal a day, carefully saving what he could.
He loved books. He spent money on them, devoured history and military strategy, and kept studying even when life offered him little comfort. He also cared deeply about his family and helped support his brothers as he struggled to build his own future.
he was an ambitious young artillery officer with little money and almost no reputation.
he took command of the French Army of Italy. His own generals doubted him, but he led his soldiers across the Alps, defeated larger Austrian and Sardinian armies, and conquered much of northern Italy.
he forced Austria to make peace with France. At 28, he sailed to Egypt, fought the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids, and won a stunning victory, even though his campaign eventually ran into disaster.
he returned to France, overthrew the government, and became First Consul.
he became First Consul for life. He reformed France's administration, founded the Bank of France, and introduced the Napoleonic Code, which reshaped French civil law.
he crowned himself Emperor of the French.
Then came Austerlitz in 1805, where he crushed the combined Austrian and Russian armies. At Jena and Auerstedt, he shattered Prussian resistance. He defeated coalition after coalition and built an empire stretching across much of continental Europe.
The boy from Corsica, once an outsider in France, had become the most feared and influential man in Europe.
He went from an obscure officer to the most powerful man in France in less than a decade.

Then he turned 36!
Europe had never witnessed the rise of a power quite like his.

Colombian authorities believe Nancy Gómez, wife of the mayor of Uribia in La Guajira, was taken into Venezuela after she was kidnapped on 11 Nov. An army officer was kidnapped in Saravena, Arauca, on 4 Nov.

Venezuela's foreign ministry offered information-sharing through existing bilateral channels. Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora said Bogotá had asked the US to work with Caracas on the search for the officer.

Colombia has previously accused Venezuela of harbouring FARC and ELN rebels; Caracas has repeatedly denied it.
