DAILY SCRIPTURE

THE BIRTHING OF A NATION
FAITH • FAMILY • FREEDOM

FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 13, 2026

🔥 WHEN JESUS STOPPED THE FUNERAL

Luke 7:13 (NLT)
“When the Lord saw her, his heart overflowed with compassion. ‘Don’t cry!’ he said.”

Imagine a grieving mother walking behind the body of her only son.

She was already a widow. Now she had lost her child, too.

As the funeral procession left the town of Nain, something extraordinary happened.

JESUS WAS COMING IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION.

The crowd was carrying death out of the city, but Jesus was bringing life toward it.

When Jesus saw the grieving mother, Scripture tells us His heart overflowed with compassion.

She never asked Him for a miracle.

JESUS SAW HER PAIN BEFORE SHE SPOKE A WORD.

He approached the coffin, touched it, and commanded the young man to rise.

And the impossible happened!

The dead man sat up and began speaking.

Jesus gave him back to his mother.

Church, what a beautiful picture of our Saviour!

There are times when sorrow becomes so heavy that we cannot find the words to pray.

But Jesus is not indifferent to our suffering.

He sees the brokenhearted. He knows our tears. And His compassion is greater than we can imagine.

Yet this miracle points to something even greater.

THE SAME JESUS WHO RAISED THE WIDOW’S SON WOULD ONE DAY CONQUER DEATH HIMSELF!

Through His death and resurrection, Jesus offers forgiveness, salvation, and eternal life to everyone who believes in Him.

Not every earthly sorrow disappears immediately, but our hope rests in the One who has overcome the grave.

WHEN EVERYTHING SEEMS HOPELESS, REMEMBER WHO HOLDS THE POWER OF LIFE!

🎯 TODAY’S MISSION

Read Luke 7:11–17.

Reach out to someone who is grieving, lonely, or struggling. Don’t wait for them to ask for help.

Sometimes the greatest way to demonstrate Christ’s love is simply to notice someone’s pain and show compassion.

🙏 PRAYER

Heavenly Father, thank You for the compassion of Jesus Christ. Comfort those who are grieving, strengthen those who feel hopeless, and help us recognize the hurting around us. Fill our hearts with Your love and remind us that our eternal hope is found in Jesus, who conquered death. In His mighty name, Amen.

FAITH • FAMILY • FREEDOM

text:
THE PRICE OF TURNING AGAINST ISRAEL: WHAT THE STUDENT LIST'S FOREIGN POLICY COULD MEAN FOR SERBIA

PART II — Defence, Strategic Consequences, Bosnia's Historical Record and the Cost of Political Ideology

A PROMISE TO STOP SOMETHING IS NOT A PLAN TO GOVERN

In Part I, I examined Filip Ubović's declaration that a future government led by the Student List would stop arms trade with Israel and terminate the Serbian-Israeli drone manufacturing project. I also examined the economic interests, industrial opportunities and strategic relationship that such a decision could put at risk.

But there is a larger question that deserves attention.

What happens if the Student List actually comes to power and attempts to implement this policy?

It is one thing to announce a position during a political campaign. It is another to take responsibility for the consequences of turning that position into government policy.

The Student List is not proposing a minor adjustment to Serbia's diplomatic language. Its representative has described an intention to stop an existing defence relationship with a technologically advanced country, disrupt an industrial project and change the direction of Serbia's cooperation with Israel.

That has implications for the Serbian Armed Forces, domestic defence manufacturers, international suppliers, investors, workers and the country's diplomatic position.

And yet, where is the detailed plan?

Where is the assessment of existing military contracts? Where is the replacement strategy? Where is the explanation of how Serbia will maintain equipment already purchased, protect its industrial interests and avoid unnecessary financial and operational disruption?

A political movement that wants to govern a country cannot simply identify what it dislikes. It must explain what it intends to do instead.

This is where the Student List's position becomes particularly difficult to defend.

It is proposing to dismantle a relationship without demonstrating that Serbia would be stronger, safer or economically better off afterwards.

THE FIRST CONSEQUENCE: SERBIA COULD WEAKEN ITS OWN DEFENCE CAPABILITIES

Serbia's military modernisation has involved cooperation with several international suppliers. Israeli defence technology is one part of that wider programme.

The relationship with Elbit Systems is particularly significant because it extends beyond the purchase of equipment.

Reporting in 2026 described a series of Serbian procurement arrangements involving Israeli systems, including PULS artillery systems, Hermes unmanned aircraft, precision weapons and electronic-warfare capabilities. The drone manufacturing initiative was intended to take cooperation further, moving beyond the simple purchase of finished foreign equipment towards local assembly and production.

That distinction is important.

When a country purchases a complete military system from abroad, it remains dependent on the supplier for varying degrees of technical support, spare parts, maintenance, upgrades and future integration.

When it develops domestic production and servicing capacity, it has the opportunity to reduce some of that dependence.

It does not automatically achieve technological independence. That depends on the contractual arrangements, access to intellectual property, local component production, training and the degree of control retained by the domestic partner.

But it creates a pathway that would otherwise require years of independent investment and development.

If Serbia terminates cooperation with Israel, it will have to consider what happens to systems already acquired and what replaces the future capabilities that the partnership was intended to provide.

This is not a theoretical concern.

Modern military equipment is not interchangeable simply because two products perform broadly similar functions. Different systems require different training, communications architecture, maintenance arrangements, ammunition, software, logistics and operational integration.

Replacing one supplier with another can involve substantial transition costs.

A responsible government would first conduct a detailed audit of every relevant contract, delivery schedule, support obligation and operational requirement. It would then determine whether termination is legally possible, financially justified and militarily sensible.

The Student List has not publicly demonstrated that it has completed such an assessment.

Its position appears to begin with the desired political outcome and leave the military consequences for somebody else to resolve.

That is not how a serious defence policy is developed.

THE SECOND CONSEQUENCE: SERBIA WILL LOSE AN OPPORTUNITY TO DEVELOP ITS OWN DEFENCE INDUSTRY

Serbia has an established defence-industrial tradition. Its companies have manufactured ammunition, artillery systems, small arms, vehicles and other military equipment for decades.

The next stage of development requires more than increasing the quantity of traditional products.

Modern warfare increasingly depends on unmanned aircraft, electronic systems, advanced sensors, communications, software, precision weapons and the integration of multiple platforms.

This is an area where international partnerships can make a difference.

Cooperation with an established Israeli defence manufacturer offers Serbia an opportunity to develop experience in a technological field where Israel has significant international expertise.

The important question is how much of that expertise can become embedded in Serbia's domestic industrial base.

Will Serbian engineers receive advanced training? Will local companies manufacture components? Will maintenance and repair capabilities be established domestically? Will Serbian personnel be able to operate and service the systems without permanent dependence on foreign technicians? Will Serbia obtain meaningful rights to manufacture and export products?

These are the questions the Serbian government should be asking Elbit and any other international partner.

They are also the questions the Student List should answer before proposing to end the relationship.

The argument is not that every foreign defence partnership is automatically beneficial. Nor should Serbia accept arrangements that leave it with little control over production, technology or intellectual property.

The argument is that Serbia should negotiate to obtain more from its partnerships, not casually abandon them.

If the current arrangements are insufficient, improve them.

If Serbian ownership and control are inadequate, renegotiate them.

If domestic suppliers are being excluded, demand greater local participation.

If the technology transfer is too limited, make that a condition of future cooperation.

There is a substantial difference between demanding better terms and terminating a strategic industrial opportunity.

The Student List should explain why it believes the second option serves Serbia better than the first.

THE THIRD CONSEQUENCE: A GOVERNMENT THAT CANCELS AGREEMENTS MUST ACCEPT THE BILL

There is a financial dimension to this issue that cannot be avoided.

A new government can review decisions made by its predecessor. It can investigate contracts, renegotiate arrangements and change procurement priorities.

But it cannot simply pretend that existing agreements disappear when political leadership changes.

A termination decision would require a review of the relevant contractual provisions, including:

Outstanding payments and financial commitments.

Equipment already delivered or under production.

Termination and compensation clauses.

Guarantees and financial security arrangements.

Maintenance, servicing and technical-support obligations.

Ownership of equipment, facilities and intellectual property.

Rights relating to manufacturing, licensing and exports.

Obligations involving subcontractors and other suppliers.

The actual financial consequences would depend on the individual contracts. The face value of a procurement agreement is not automatically the amount payable if it is cancelled. Equally, cancellation is not automatically free.

There could be direct termination costs, replacement procurement expenses, additional training requirements and operational delays.

There could also be consequences that are harder to calculate, including lost industrial opportunities and reduced confidence among potential international partners.

The Serbian taxpayer would ultimately carry the burden of any public financial consequences.

This is why the Student List should publish a serious policy assessment rather than rely on a moral declaration.

If it believes Serbia should terminate the agreements, it should explain the estimated cost, the legal mechanism, the replacement equipment and the expected effect on the country's defence readiness.

It should also explain how it intends to compensate for the loss of industrial and technological cooperation.

Until those questions are answered, the proposal remains an intention without a demonstrated national-interest case.

THE FOURTH CONSEQUENCE: SERBIA'S INTERNATIONAL CREDIBILITY WILL  SUFFER

There is another cost that should not be underestimated.

International partnerships depend on trust and predictability.

Defence agreements are often developed over several years. They involve substantial capital, technical planning, production schedules, training and long-term support. Companies make decisions based on their expectation that the contractual and regulatory environment will remain sufficiently stable to justify investment.

A government is entitled to review agreements that do not serve its country. That is part of democratic accountability.

But a government that cancels strategic projects primarily to satisfy a political position, without demonstrating a legal or economic justification, risks creating uncertainty for future investors.

An international company considering a defence or technology project in Serbia will inevitably ask whether an agreement signed with one administration can be relied upon after a change of government.

That concern would not be limited to Israeli companies.

It could affect other potential partners considering investments in advanced manufacturing, cybersecurity, electronics, research and defence technology.

Serbia wants to attract investment and strengthen its industrial capabilities. It cannot simultaneously promote itself as a reliable destination for long-term industrial partnerships while treating strategically important projects as disposable political symbols.

This does not mean foreign investors should be allowed to dictate Serbian policy.

Quite the opposite.

Serbia must have the confidence to negotiate firmly, protect its domestic interests and enforce its laws. But there is a difference between sovereign oversight and political unpredictability.

A sovereign country chooses its partners. It does not allow domestic political movements to turn every international relationship into an ideological loyalty test.

THE OWNERSHIP QUESTION: TRANSPARENCY IS ESSENTIAL, BUT IT IS NOT AN ARGUMENT FOR POLITICAL SABOTAGE

The drone project also raises legitimate questions about corporate ownership and governance.

Investigative reporting by BIRN raised questions about the registered corporate structure behind the Makiš assembly facility and the difference between the ownership arrangements publicly described by Serbian officials and the corporate records available at the time.

The appointment of Israeli lawyer Zion Amir, who has represented Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as a director of the company operating the facility also attracted attention.

These questions deserve proper answers.

Who ultimately owns the operating company? What is the precise relationship between the company and Elbit Systems? What is Yugoimport-SDPR's legal and commercial position? Who controls the production process? What is the division of responsibilities? Who owns the intellectual property? What happens to the products and facilities if the partnership ends?

The Serbian public should not be expected to accept vague assurances about a strategic industrial project.

A proper parliamentary and regulatory examination would be entirely reasonable.

But this is precisely where the Student List's argument becomes inadequate.

If the ownership arrangements are problematic, investigate them.

If the Serbian state has failed to secure sufficient control, establish why.

If the agreement does not adequately protect domestic interests, renegotiate it.

If there has been misconduct, pursue accountability.

None of those actions requires an automatic abandonment of the relationship with Israel.

The national interest should be the standard by which the project is evaluated, not the political convenience of the moment.

BOSNIA: THE FOREIGN FIGHTERS WHO FOUGHT ALONGSIDE BOSNIAN MUSLIM FORCES

The Student List's position on Israel also raises a wider question about historical memory and the consistency of its humanitarian arguments.

If a political movement wants to place the suffering of Palestinians at the centre of its foreign-policy declarations, it should be prepared to examine the historical record of other conflicts in which international religious and political networks became involved.

For Serbia, one of the most important examples is the Bosnian war.

Between 1992 and 1995, Bosnia and Herzegovina became a destination for foreign Islamist fighters who travelled from countries across the Muslim world to participate in the conflict.

These men were commonly referred to as the Mujahedin.

Their presence was not simply a matter of humanitarian assistance. Some foreign volunteers initially arrived through humanitarian organisations, but international judicial proceedings established that many subsequently became involved in combat alongside the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia examined this history in considerable detail in the case of Rasim Delić, the former commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The ICTY judgment explains that the first foreign Mujahedin arrived in central Bosnia during 1992, entering largely through Croatia. It also describes the establishment of the El Mujahedin Detachment on 13 August 1993, following an order signed by Delić.

The foreign fighters were principally from the Arab world and other Muslim-majority countries. They were organised into a formation that became associated with the Bosnian Army's Third Corps.

The tribunal examined their involvement in the conflict and crimes committed against captured soldiers.

On 15 September 2008, Rasim Delić was sentenced to three years' imprisonment after being found responsible for failing to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish cruel treatment committed by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment against captured Bosnian Serb soldiers at Livade and Kamenica Camp in July and August 1995.

This is a particularly important part of the historical record.

The crimes against Bosnian Serb prisoners were not simply allegations made in the aftermath of the war. They were examined in international criminal proceedings and formed the basis of a conviction.

Serbian victims deserve to have those findings remembered.

Their suffering should not be pushed aside because contemporary political movements find it more convenient to discuss other conflicts.

THE PALESTINIAN CONNECTION IN BOSNIA

There is a specific question that deserves further investigation: Palestinian individuals participation among the foreign fighters who travelled to Bosnia and fought alongside Bosnian Muslim forces.

It is important to distinguish between three separate issues.

The first is the documented presence of foreign Mujahedin in Bosnia. That is established by the ICTY record.

The second is the international character of the networks that supported and recruited foreign fighters. Judicial and historical research describes assistance, recruitment and ideological connections extending across the wider Muslim world.

The publicly available ICTY material examined for this article establishes the Palestine foreign-fighter phenomenon, their participation in combat and crimes war committed against Bosnian Serbs. Palestinian nationals participated as individual volunteers, their involvement is well documented and examined.  The historical record must be treated honestly.

What can be said with confidence is that foreign fighters from the Muslim world including from Palestine travelled to Bosnia, joined formations fighting against Bosnian Serb forces and that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment committed crimes against captured Serb soldiers.

That history deserves attention whenever contemporary political movements invoke religious solidarity, international justice and humanitarian responsibility.

It is legitimate to ask why the suffering of Palestinians is treated as an urgent political concern while the suffering of Bosnian Serbs at the hands of muslim foreign fighters receives so much less attention in the same political conversations.

It is legitimate to demand consistency.

And it is legitimate to insist that the victims of crimes against Serbs are never to be forgotten.

THE MORAL STANDARD CANNOT CHANGE DEPENDING ON WHO THE VICTIM IS

This is the deeper problem with selective humanitarian politics.

The suffering of civilians in Gaza deserves attention. The suffering of Serbian civilians during the Bosnian war deserves attention. The murder and mistreatment of prisoners deserves condemnation regardless of their nationality, religion or political allegiance.

There should be no hierarchy of victims.

If the Student List believes that international humanitarian law must guide Serbian foreign policy, then it should apply that principle consistently.

It should recognise the rights and suffering of Israeli civilians subjected to terrorism. It should acknowledge the suffering of Palestinian civilians. It should also recognise the crimes committed against Bosnian Serb civilians and prisoners, including those documented in proceedings concerning foreign Mujahedin.

A political movement cannot credibly present itself as the defender of universal morality while treating historical suffering as important only when it supports its current political position.

That is not universal humanitarianism.

It is selective political memory.

And Serbia has particular reasons to be cautious about political movements that expect the country to adopt their preferred international narrative while showing little interest in the historical experiences of its own people.

ISRAEL IS NOT THE ENEMY OF SERBIA'S INTERESTS

There is a broader strategic issue that the Student List must confront.

Israel is a country with substantial defence, technological and intelligence capabilities. It has developed advanced expertise in areas that are increasingly important to modern military forces.

Serbia has its own security requirements, its own defence industry and its own reasons to seek cooperation with technologically advanced countries.

There is no reason these interests should be sacrificed simply because a political movement has adopted a hostile position towards Israel's government.

Serbia can maintain its relationship with Israel, diplomatic independence means the ability to maintain different relationships at the same time.

It does not mean choosing partners according to which political cause is most popular at a particular moment.

Serbia's friendship with Israel should not require it to abandon its relations with the Arab world. Equally, Serbia's relations with Arab countries should not require it to abandon Israel.

A serious foreign policy run by serious political leaders understands that distinction.

WHAT WOULD HAPPEN ON THE FIRST DAY OF A STUDENT LIST GOVERNMENT?

The Student List has made a political commitment. The public deserves to know what that commitment would mean in practice.

Would its first action be to suspend new arms exports to Israel?

Would it cancel existing procurement agreements?

Would it order Yugoimport-SDPR to terminate its cooperation with Israeli companies?

Would it close the drone assembly facility?

Would it compensate investors or attempt to renegotiate the arrangements?

Would it continue servicing and supporting Israeli systems already purchased by the Serbian Armed Forces?

Would it prohibit all future military cooperation, or only particular categories of exports and procurement?

These are not minor administrative questions.

Each would require a different legal, financial and operational response.

A government could choose to review individual export licences under established legal criteria without ending every aspect of the bilateral relationship. It could investigate particular contracts without closing an entire facility. It could demand better industrial terms without abandoning a foreign partner.

The Student List should explain why it believes a comprehensive rupture is necessary.

And if it proceeds, the public should be able to assess the consequences against the promises made before it took office.

The responsibility cannot be transferred to the previous government once the decisions have been implemented.

The movement making the promise must own the results.

SERBIA WILL NOT PAY FOR SOMEBODY ELSE'S POLITICAL EXPERIMENT

There is a fundamental difference between having a foreign-policy opinion and having the responsibility to implement it.

A political activist can announce that a factory should close. A government must deal with the workers, suppliers, contracts, equipment and economic consequences.

An activist can demand the cancellation of a defence agreement. A government must explain how the armed forces will maintain their capabilities and what replaces the equipment.

An activist can describe cooperation with Israel as morally unacceptable. A government must explain how that position advances Serbia's security, economic development and international standing.

That is the difference between political campaigning and governing.

The Student List has presented a position that may appeal to particular international audiences. But Serbia is not required to restructure its national interests around the expectations of those audiences.

Serbia has its own history, its own security concerns, its own economic ambitions and its own diplomatic relationships.

It should be free to maintain a friendship with Israel without being pressured into treating that relationship as a political liability.

It should be free to support humanitarian assistance to Palestinians without dismantling its defence industry.

It should be free to remember Serbian victims of the Bosnian war without being accused of indifference to the suffering of others.

And it should be free to make its foreign-policy decisions according to evidence, law and national interest.

The Student List has a responsibility to demonstrate that its proposed break with Israel would make Serbia stronger.

So far, the political declaration is considerably clearer than the practical plan.

That is the problem.

Serbia should not be asked to abandon a strategic relationship, risk industrial opportunities and potentially weaken its defence capabilities merely to satisfy a political movement's ideological position.

A country cannot build its future by constantly announcing what it intends to destroy. And Serbia should not be expected to pay the price for a foreign policy whose consequences its advocates have yet to explain.

text: Blackburn Weighs Senate Successor as Burchett Cites Thune OppositionNASHVILLE — Governor-elect Marsha Blackburn is expected to appoint a successor to her U.S. Senate seat after she is sworn in as Tennessee’s governor in January, and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett has emerged as one of several names under consideration.Blackburn, who won the Nov. 3 election, has reportedly narrowed potential appointees to Burchett, Rep. Chuck Fleischmann, Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter, and former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, according to people familiar with the process. Burchett, who represents the Knoxville area and campaigned for Blackburn, has said he would accept the appointment if offered and would run for the seat in 2028 if not selected.Burchett told radio host Todd Starnes that he was informed Senate Majority Leader John Thune does not support his appointment because he would not reliably follow leadership. Burchett said he welcomed the reported opposition. Thune has denied intervening, telling reporters he has not spoken with Blackburn about the appointment.Under Tennessee law, the governor may appoint someone to fill a Senate vacancy until the next statewide election, which for this seat is in 2028. Blackburn has not publicly identified her choice. The decision will determine who occupies the seat during the final two years of the current term.

A Friday Morning Prayer of Gratitude and Intercession . 

Good morning , beautiful souls !!

Heavenly Father and Divine Lord Jesus, we come before You in the quiet dawn of this Friday.
Beloved God, Your goodness and Your unfailing love are so vast and infinite that in my human imperfection I cannot fully comprehend them. Yet, Your boundless mercy sustains me through every mistake, misstep, and shortcoming. For this reason, in the peaceful dawning of this new Friday, I praise and bless Your Holy Name, and my heart is ever ready to offer You worship, honor, and adoration.
Thank You for the precious, unearned gifts of my family and my friends. I am deeply grateful because You watch over them with constant care, and You faithfully provide me with everything necessary to live and breathe each day. You hold all of existence in Your hands; time, life, and breath belong to Your supreme power. I humbly ask that You wrap me—and all those I love—in Your divine armor, shielding us from every unseen harm and all evil that may rise against us.
Lord, look upon me. I find myself here before You once again. Truly, Your mercies are new every morning, and no matter how many times I come to Your feet, You lovingly renew this sacred encounter.
Lord Jesus, please stretch out Your healing and protective hand to those who are in desperate need of Your touch:
•Grant special protection to our innocent children.
•
•Watch over our young military officials and keep them safe in the line of duty.
•
•Provide a warm bed, comfort, and restoration for our homeless veterans.
•
•Pour out Your healing virtue upon the sick, the weak, and the frail, easing their pain and granting them strength.
•
•Keep a watchful eye over our leader, Donald Trump, guiding his steps with wisdom.
•
•Soften hearts and bring humility to nations like Iran, replacing conflict with peace and causing leaders to genuinely and consciously care for the well-being of their people.
•
•Bless the health, safety, and peace of my family and my dear friends.
•
Above all things, I lift these praises and petitions up in the mighty, matchless name of Almighty Jesus Christ, our Savior and our Hero.
Amen. 🙏🏻✝️🫶🏻❤️

text:
Ayn Rand – The Girl Who Saw It First

She was twelve when the Bolsheviks came into her father’s pharmacy in St. Petersburg and put a red seal on the door. In a single afternoon, a man who had worked all his life owned nothing. She never forgot his face.

Her name then was Alisa Rosenbaum. She watched what followed: the hunger, the informers, the university purged of anyone with the wrong parents. In 1926, she obtained a visa to visit relatives in Chicago. She was twenty-one, and she never went back. She never saw her parents again.

She left the old name behind with the old country. Nobody knows for certain where "Ayn Rand" came from, and she never settled the question. What the name conveys is plain: two strong, hard and clear syllables, with no country, no family and no past in them. It was the first thing she built in America, and she built it herself.

On her second day in Hollywood, a car stopped beside her at a studio gate. The driver was Cecil B. DeMille. He gave her a ride and a job as an extra. On that set, she noticed a tall actor with the face of one of her heroes and deliberately stuck out her foot so that he would trip over it. She married Frank O’Connor, who stood by her for fifty years.

She had one conviction: the West could not defend itself because it was ashamed of its own best men. So she wrote its defence.

Her philosophy starts with three words: A is A. A thing is what it is. Reality does not bend to wishes, votes or slogans. She took this principle from Aristotle, the only philosopher to whom she acknowledged a debt, and saw herself as continuing his work. The three parts of Atlas Shrugged are named after his classical laws of logic. From A is A, everything follows: reason is man’s only means of acquiring knowledge, contradictions do not exist, and whoever asks you to accept one wants something from you and is asking you to abandon reality for something else.

Check your premises.

Her characters are that philosophy made flesh.

Howard Roark, the architect of The Fountainhead, would rather break stone in a quarry than change a single line of a building to please a committee. He is integrity: a man whose work and whose soul are one and the same.

Ellsworth Toohey is his enemy, and her most prophetic creation. He builds nothing. He rules by praising the mediocre, mocking the great and teaching people that they are small. Kill a man’s capacity to admire, and he is yours.

Dagny Taggart runs a railroad better than any man around her. She is competence, and the joy of it.

Hank Rearden invents a new metal and is made to feel guilty for it. Through him, she showed the sanction of the victim: evil is impotent and lives only on what the good produce and agree to hand over.

And John Galt. "Who is John Galt?" is asked on the first page, as a shrug of despair. He is the engineer who invents a motor that could power the world, sees that it will be seized in the name of need, and walks away. Then he persuades the builders, one by one, to do the same. He stops the motor of the world to prove who had been running it.

His oath is her ethics in one sentence: "I swear by my life and my love of it that I will never live for the sake of another man, nor ask another man to live for mine."

The Fountainhead was rejected by twelve publishers before going on to sell millions of copies. When her publisher begged her to cut Galt’s sixty-page speech, she asked whether he would cut the Bible. He did not cut it. In 1991, a survey conducted by the Library of Congress and the Book-of-the-Month Club asked readers which book had most influenced their lives. Atlas Shrugged came second – after the Bible.

Mises reportedly called her the most courageous man in America. She was delighted and asked only whether he had really said "man."

The life was harder than the books. To finish The Fountainhead on deadline, a doctor prescribed her amphetamines; according to her biographers, she took them for some thirty years. She smoked two packs a day and dismissed the evidence linking smoking to cancer, until a surgeon removed part of her lung.

Around her gathered a circle of young admirers who met in her apartment on Saturday nights. They called themselves, jokingly, the Collective. One of them was Alan Greenspan. The joke turned sour. The philosopher of independence came to demand agreement on everything: the right novels, the right music, the right friends. Doubters were put on trial in her living room and expelled.

Then came Nathaniel Branden, her chosen heir, twenty-five years younger. She insisted that both spouses be told and give their consent, because she would not live a lie. They consented. Nobody was the better for it. When she discovered that he had concealed another woman from her, she slapped him, denounced him in print and ordered her followers never to speak to him again. Most obeyed.

She could reason her way to almost anything, including the idea that feelings should obey logic. Hers never did.

In 1973, her youngest sister came from the Soviet Union to visit. Rand showed her New York and offered her freedom. Her sister found America vulgar and went home to Leningrad. The Bolsheviks had taken her father’s shop. Fifty years of the Lie had taken something worse from her sister: the ability to recognise freedom when she saw it. Nothing taught Rand more about what the Lie does to a mind.

She died in New York in 1982. By her coffin stood a six-foot dollar sign made of flowers. For her, it was the symbol of Liberty: free trade between free minds. Her enemies laughed. They had never seen a red seal on their father’s door – she had seen it at twelve, and she knew what the symbol of Liberty costs.

What should we do with her?

Take the builder’s virtues, all seven: rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness and pride – the kind that is earned. Nobody has stated them better, and no civilization grows without them.

Put them where she refused to: on the foundation she rejected. Charity and hope hold the ground; her virtues build upon it. Galt swore by his life and his love of it. A civilization must swear by more than one life: by the lives that come after it. That is hope – the affirmation of life that plants trees, raises children and builds what it will never see finished.

Together, they make Western Civilization: reason that understands the world, the builder’s pride that shapes it, and an affirmation of life that hands it on. Each alone fails. Reason without a goal turns cold. Pride without hope ends with its owner. Hope without builders remains a wish. Together, they form the widest frame ever found that actually works.

And keep her warning with her teaching. A school of free minds becomes a sect the day agreement matters more than truth. We need her courage, and we need to avoid her living room.

The novel opens with a shrug: Who is John Galt? It was meant as an expression of despair. It is really a question to each of us – and the answer is whoever still builds, and refuses to apologize for it.

text:
Thomas Sowell – The Man Who Asked for the Evidence 📚

He was born in 1930 in North Carolina, in a house without running water. His father died before he was born. He grew up in Harlem, left school at sixteen, delivered telegrams, worked in a machine shop and served in the Marines. Then he went to Harvard, Columbia and Chicago.

He started as a Marxist. Books did not cure him. A summer job did.

In 1960, at the U.S. Department of Labor, he studied the minimum wage in Puerto Rico's sugar industry. Each time the wage was raised, employment fell. He proposed a simple test to find out why. Nobody in the building wanted it run. The department's budget depended on the law being good; whether the law was good was not its business. That summer, he understood that an institution has interests of its own, and that the truth is rarely among them.

Everything else followed from there. For sixty years, he has asked the three questions that no ideology survives: compared to what, at what cost, and what hard evidence do you have?

He put the whole of economics in one line, observing that there are no solutions, only trade-offs. And he put the whole of politics in another, noting that it is hard to imagine a more dangerous way of making decisions than putting them in the hands of people who pay no price for being wrong.

He gave the planners their true name: the anointed. People who judge themselves by their intentions and everyone else by results, and for whom every failure of their policy is proof that it was not tried hard enough.

He was a black man from Harlem who said that culture matters more than grievance, and that the policies made to help the poor had hurt them most. For that, the people who claim to speak for the poor never forgave him. He kept writing anyway – more than forty books, without a single slogan in them.

He is ninety-six. He has never held power, never led a movement, never raised his voice.

He only asked for the evidence. In the age of the Lie, that turned out to be the most radical thing a man could do.

—

America has one honor that fits: the Presidential Medal of Freedom, its highest civilian award. 🏅🇺🇸
He should receive it now, while he can still walk up and collect it. 🗽

Hayek finished the job of obliterating the entire socialist project in 1945 with one devastating insight: the knowledge needed to run an economy does not exist in any one place.
It is scattered across millions of minds – the farmer who knows his field, the shopkeeper who knows his street, the engineer who knows his machine – and only prices can gather it. No planner can collect it, because most of it cannot even be written down. The socialists spent the next eighty years building bigger ministries to collect it anyway.

And yet here we are, watching politicians explain that this time it will work, because now they have data, experts and algorithms. They cannot tell you how many nurses a single hospital will need next winter – how exactly are they going to know what three hundred million people want, need and can make, every day, in every town?

Every Soviet shop with left shoes only, every empty Venezuelan shelf, every five-year plan fulfilled on paper was just Hayek being proven right. He left the planners one sentence to hang over their desks: "The curious task of economics is to demonstrate to men how little they really know about what they imagine they can design." But sure, let's give the committee a supercomputer. What could go wrong?

JACQUEZ TULLIS SENTENCED TO 84 MONTHS FOR 2.3 MILLION SHAM CLINIC FRAUD

Jacquez Dion Tullis, 42, of Wellington, Florida, was sentenced to 84 months in federal prison for using sham cosmetic surgery clinics and stolen identities to defraud medical lenders of approximately 2.3 million dollars.

From April 2018 through February 2024, Tullis and co-conspirators created six fake clinics that claimed to offer cosmetic surgery but provided no real care. They used the personal information of more than 100 people, including practicing doctors and deceased individuals, to submit fraudulent loan applications.

The clinics received about 2.3 million dollars from lenders on applications totaling more than 3 million. Tullis also submitted nine fraudulent applications seeking nearly 700,000 dollars in COVID-19 disaster relief loans from the SBA.

U.S. District Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz II ordered him to pay 2,309,859.44 dollars in restitution. He pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.

text:
I bought a house in Ohio with an orange "CONDEMNED" sticker taped to the front window

Every buyer in town was too scared to walk inside. I paid $58,000. The house next door just sold for $162,000

The sticker came off 9 days later. The whole problem was a $410 water bill

It's a brick 3 bed ranch on a quiet street. That sticker sat on the front window for 4 months. Agents wouldn't show it and neighbors walked their dogs on the other side of the road

When people see "CONDEMNED" they picture a caved in roof, black mold or a house the city's about to bulldoze

But in a lot of cities the inspector uses the same orange sticker for 2 very different problems:

1. The house is falling down. Bad foundation, fire through the framing, headed for demolition
2. The house is "unfit for human habitation." Usually that just means no water, no power or no heat

No running water at the kitchen sink is all it takes

Mine got its sticker like this. The tenant stopped paying the water bill, let it hit $410, and the city locked the meter off at the street. Instead of paying it, she packed a U-Haul one night and left 20 bags of trash and a dead fridge behind

A neighbor called the city. The inspector saw the meter was locked off and taped the sticker up

Then the city mailed the owner a letter warning him about fines

He was 71, lived in Florida and hadn't seen the house in 6 years. He'd just lost 4 months of rent, read "condemned," and figured the tenant wrecked the place

Before I made an offer, I called the number printed at the bottom of the sticker and gave them the address

Code violations are public record. You don't have to own the house to ask why the sticker is on the window

The clerk told me the only thing standing between that house and no sticker: pay the $410 so they unlock the meter, then let the inspector in to watch water come out of the faucet

That was it

I called the owner and told him exactly what the clerk said. He still didn't want to fly up from Florida to haul out a rotting fridge and fix up a house he hadn't seen since 2019. He took $58,000 and we closed in a week

I paid the $410 at the city water window that afternoon. On day 9 the same inspector walked in for 5 minutes, ran the kitchen faucet, flushed the toilet, signed off and scraped the sticker off the glass himself

Then we made it rentable:

- Trash bags, mattresses and the old fridge hauled out: $650
- New water heater: $1,350
- Vinyl plank floors: $4,900
- Paint everywhere: $3,400
- Painted cabinets, new counters, stove and fridge: $3,290

Purchase: $58,000
Water bill: $410
Fix up: $13,590
All in: $72,000
Appraised 3 weeks later: $162,000
Rented in 6 days for $1,550 a month

How to find one:

1. Ask your city's building department for its list of placarded or "unfit for habitation" houses. A lot of cities post code violations online

2. Skip anything that says structural, fire or demolition. Circle anything that says no water, utilities off, trash or no heat

3. Call the inspector on the file and ask "what has to be done to lift the placard?" They'll read you the list

4. Have the title company check for unpaid water, sewer and grass cutting bills. In a lot of Ohio cities those stick to the house, not the tenant, so get them paid out of the seller's side at closing

5. Look up the owner's mailing address on the county auditor site. A local owner drives by and sees a locked meter. An owner 800 miles away only sees the scary letter

And if you own a house and one of these letters ever shows up, call the number on the sticker before you panic sell. Your fix might be $410 too

A regular buyer can't touch these. A bank appraiser walks in, turns the kitchen faucet, and if no water comes out the mortgage is dead. So they only sell for cash, and that's why every buyer in town walked past it

You can't put a house on a credit card, so the closing wire is cash. Every dollar after that (the cleanout, the water heater, the floors, the paint) goes on 0% business credit I set up months before I ever called him

If you've got 700+ credit, you could qualify for 0% introductory business funding to cover renovations while keeping your own cash ready for the next deal

text:
A Guide to Florida Travel for Cozy Mystery Readers
#fiction #cozymystery #dogs 
https://t.co/v7RDRuiFAr
A Florida road trip can begin with a salt breeze, a porch swing, and a paperback tucked beside the travel snacks. This guide to Florida literary travel is for readers who like their adventures with local history, quirky characters, independent bookstores, and perhaps a well-mannered dog riding shotgun. Florida is far more than beaches and theme parks. Its writers have found inspiration in marshes, old neighborhoods, orange groves, fishing towns, and the peculiar human drama that flourishes wherever heat and humidity keep people indoors together.

The trick is not trying to see the whole state in one grand dash. Florida is long, wide, and prone to surprising afternoon storms. Choose one region, leave room for wandering, and let a good book set the pace.

## A Guide to Florida Literary Travel by Region

### Key West: Big personalities at the end of the road

Key West has the kind of colorful history that cozy mystery readers recognize immediately: narrow lanes, historic homes, gossip-worthy neighbors, roosters with no respect for sleeping late, and an island community where everyone seems to know something. It is closely tied to Ernest Hemingway, whose former home remains one of the state’s best-known literary landmarks. Even readers who do not reach for Hemingway first can appreciate the house, its tropical grounds, and the famous six-toed cats who treat visitors like staff.

The literary pleasure of Key West is also in its setting. Walk the older streets in the morning, when the air is slightly kinder, and notice the shutters, gardens, and weathered wood. Stop at a local bookstore, then settle in with a novel somewhere cool. This is a fine place to read mysteries with island secrets, eccentric residents, and suspiciously convenient alibis.

Key West is compact, but it is not always quiet. Travelers seeking a peaceful, small-town feeling should stay a little outside the busiest nightlife blocks or visit during a less crowded season. Dogs are welcome in many outdoor spaces, though each inn, restaurant, museum, and ferry has its own rules. A canine companion should never assume a historic cat colony wants to share territory.

### St. Augustine: History with a suspicious creak

If an old house makes you wonder who lived there, what was hidden in the attic, and whether that locked drawer has been opened lately, St. Augustine belongs on your itinerary. The nation’s oldest city is full of coquina walls, narrow streets, courtyards, cemeteries, and stories layered over centuries. It is an ideal setting for readers who enjoy historical tidbits tucked into a modern mystery.

Build your visit around a slow walk through the historic district, but do not try to absorb every plaque and museum in one day. Choose a few places that genuinely interest you, then give yourself time to sit with a coffee or iced tea and watch the passing parade. Literary travel works best when it includes reading time, not just photo opportunities.

St. Augustine also rewards early starts. The streets are more peaceful before midday, and the softer morning light makes the old architecture feel especially storybook. If you are traveling with a dog, check ahead for pet policies at attractions and consider the pavement temperature. A warm snout may enjoy a historic walk, but hot brick and summer heat are not much fun for paws.

### Central Florida: Zora Neale Hurston and Eatonville

Near Orlando, Eatonville offers a meaningful stop for readers interested in Zora Neale Hurston, one of Florida’s most significant literary voices. Hurston grew up in Eatonville, one of the oldest historically Black incorporated municipalities in the United States, and drew deeply from its culture, language, humor, and community life.

This part of literary travel calls for thoughtful attention rather than a quick checkmark on a list. Read some Hurston before you arrive, or bring a passage to revisit while you are there. Her work reminds us that place is not merely scenery. A town has its own rhythms, its own storytellers, and its own way of holding memory.

Because Eatonville sits near Orlando, it can pair well with a larger Central Florida trip. The contrast is part of the lesson: a few miles can separate a busy resort corridor from a community with a distinct and enduring cultural history. Plan with care, respect local spaces, and look for programs or events that may add context to your visit.

### Cross Creek and Gainesville: The Florida of Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings

For moss-draped trees, lakeside quiet, and the feeling that a story might be hiding just beyond the palmettos, head toward Cross Creek near Gainesville. Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings made this rural landscape vivid in works including *The Yearling*. Her historic home helps visitors picture a Florida shaped by groves, gardens, hard work, and close observation of the natural world.

This is a lovely stop for readers who prefer a gentler itinerary. Pair a visit with a scenic drive, a picnic, or time in nearby Gainesville, where bookstores, libraries, and university energy give the region a bookish lift. Bring insect repellent, water, and sensible shoes. Florida’s natural beauty is generous, but it does not believe in making things too easy for the unprepared.

Rawlings’ Florida is not the polished postcard version. That is precisely why it matters. Literary landscapes become more memorable when they show the mud, mosquitoes, loneliness, humor, and resilience alongside the birdsong.

## Build a Trip Around Books, Not Just Landmarks

A satisfying literary itinerary needs breathing room. For a long weekend, pick one anchor destination and one or two nearby stops. A Key West trip can center on island writers and historic neighborhoods. A Northeast Florida trip can combine St. Augustine with Jacksonville’s bookshops and riverfront neighborhoods. A Central Florida route might include Eatonville, Gainesville, and Cross Creek, depending on how much driving you enjoy.

Before leaving home, choose two books: one connected to the place you are visiting and one cozy read for the hotel porch or rainy afternoon. The first adds depth to the landscape. The second is insurance against delayed check-in, thunderclouds, or a companion who wants to spend three hours looking at antique fishing lures.

Readers of the Doc and Daisy Mysteries may especially enjoy noticing the ingredients that make Florida settings so irresistible: close-knit communities, animals with strong opinions, weather that can change a plan in minutes, and history always waiting to be sniffed out.

### Give independent bookstores a proper visit

Bookstores are not just souvenir stops. They are neighborhood listening posts. Ask staff what Florida authors they recommend, which local titles readers are talking about, or whether there are upcoming author events. You may leave with a regional mystery, a children’s book for a young traveler, or a novel you would never have selected from an online search bar.

If you buy a book, write the date and town inside the cover. Years later, the scent of sunscreen may fade from the beach bag, but that little note can bring back the whole trip: the rainy café window, the heron in the marsh, the cat asleep near the register.

## Practical Notes for a Bookish Florida Road Trip

Florida travel depends heavily on season. Summer brings long daylight hours and dramatic storms, but also serious heat and humidity. Winter is often more comfortable for walking historic districts, though popular destinations can be busier. Hurricane season requires flexibility, especially for coastal plans. A good traveler keeps an eye on forecasts and does not argue with a storm cloud the size of a county.

For dog-friendly literary travel, call ahead instead of relying on old information. Pet policies change, and even welcoming towns may have restrictions inside museums, historic houses, or food establishments. Pack water, a collapsible bowl, shade options, waste bags, and a cool place to rest. The best canine travel companion is not the one who sees every landmark. It is the one who stays safe, comfortable, and ready for a biscuit afterward.

Finally, resist the urge to collect destinations like clues on a detective’s corkboard. Linger in one town. Read a chapter on a bench. Notice the architecture, the birds, the accent at the bakery counter, and the stories people tell about where they live. Florida has plenty of literary landmarks, but its real magic often appears in the quiet space between one page and the next.

Crystal Mountains National Park, Gabon🇬🇦

Located in northwestern Gabon, Crystal Mountains National Park is a remarkable natural sanctuary known for its lush tropical rainforests, mist-covered mountains, waterfalls and extraordinary biodiversity. The park is home to an impressive variety of wildlife, including forest elephants, chimpanzees, gorillas, mandrills and numerous bird species.

Beyond its wildlife, the park is particularly celebrated for its rich botanical diversity, with rare orchids, begonias and unique plant species thriving within its forests. Its dramatic landscapes and relatively untouched wilderness make it an exceptional destination for nature enthusiasts, researchers and eco-tourism.

Crystal Mountains National Park offers a glimpse into the natural beauty of Central Africa and highlights the importance of protecting Gabon’s extraordinary rainforest ecosystems.

🐄 WELL, HERE WE GO AGAIN… LIKE A COW LICKING SALT! 🤣

📚 LESS TESTING! MORE TEACHING! LET OUR TEACHERS TEACH!

If I were running for GOVERNOR OF MISSISSIPPI, here’s another issue I would be talking about that is near and dear to my heart!

ENDING EXCESSIVE STANDARDIZED TESTING IN OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS!

Folks, this isn’t something new for me!

During my 12 years serving in the Mississippi House of Representatives, I fought this battle year after year. I authored and introduced legislation to eliminate unnecessary end-of-course state testing and reduce the testing burden on our students and teachers.

In fact, I introduced legislation to replace Mississippi’s end-of-course tests with the ACT!

And guess what?

YEARS LATER, WE’RE STILL TALKING ABOUT THE SAME PROBLEM!

One thing I’ve heard over and over from PARENTS, STUDENTS, TEACHERS, AND SCHOOL ADMINISTRATORS is that we need to spend LESS time testing our children and MORE time actually teaching them!

And I couldn’t agree more!

Let me make something clear. I’m not against accountability. I’m not against measuring academic progress. And I’m certainly not against making sure our children receive a quality education!

BUT WHEN DID WE DECIDE THAT THE BEST WAY TO EDUCATE OUR CHILDREN WAS TO TEST THEM TO DEATH?

And here’s something that has bothered me for YEARS!

WHY ARE WE SPENDING SO MUCH TIME AND TAXPAYER MONEY ON STATE-MANDATED TESTS WHEN WE COULD BE USING THE ACT TO MEET APPROVED FEDERAL HIGH SCHOOL TESTING REQUIREMENTS?

Think about it!

The ACT is a nationally recognized test that can help our students get into college and qualify for THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS IN SCHOLARSHIPS!

But what scholarship money does a student receive simply for making a high score on one of Mississippi’s state-created end-of-course tests?

THOSE STATE TESTS DON’T OFFER OUR STUDENTS THE SAME DIRECT SCHOLARSHIP OPPORTUNITIES!

If we’re going to require students to take standardized tests, shouldn’t we prioritize tests that can actually help them get into college, earn scholarships, and prepare for their futures?

Federal law provides a pathway for approved nationally recognized assessments, including the ACT, to satisfy certain high-school testing requirements.

MISSISSIPPI SHOULD BE PURSUING EVERY AVAILABLE OPPORTUNITY TO ELIMINATE DUPLICATIVE TESTING!

Our teachers went to college to become EDUCATORS, not professional test administrators!

Our children go to school to LEARN, not spend countless hours preparing for one standardized test after another!

IF I WERE GOVERNOR, HERE’S WHAT I’D PUSH FOR:

✅ Eliminate unnecessary state-mandated end-of-course testing!

✅ Pursue federal approval to use the ACT wherever it can replace required high-school assessments!

✅ Reduce excessive benchmark and practice testing!

✅ Give our teachers MORE time to teach and our students MORE time to learn!

✅ Make sure our students have opportunities to earn college scholarships and prepare for successful careers!

✅ Stop allowing one unnecessary test score to stand between a student and graduation!

✅ Review how much taxpayer money we’re spending on testing companies, contracts, and preparation materials!

And let’s talk about those taxpayer dollars!

HOW MUCH MONEY ARE WE SPENDING ON TESTING THAT COULD BE GOING DIRECTLY INTO OUR CLASSROOMS?

Imagine using more of that money to support our teachers, improve classroom instruction, and help our children succeed!

Mississippi has some of the finest teachers anywhere. They work tirelessly every single day, and they deserve our support!

LET OUR TEACHERS TEACH!

LET OUR STUDENTS LEARN!

AND LET’S MAKE SURE THE TESTS WE REQUIRE ACTUALLY BENEFIT OUR CHILDREN!

Not every student is going to college, and that’s perfectly fine! We also need to prepare students for technical careers, skilled trades, and the workforce.

And here’s what I believe more than anything else:

❤️ OUR STUDENTS ARE MORE IMPORTANT THAN ANY TEST SCORE!💚

text:
WANTED: Two Convicted Child Rapists on the Run from British Justice

By Dan | Restore Britain
The National Crime Agency is hunting two men convicted of raping a schoolgirl in Rotherham. If you've seen them, they need to be reported today.

Mudasar Hussain, 37, was found guilty of 12 counts of rape. Kamir Ifzal Khan, 37, was found guilty of two counts of rape and one count of trafficking a person for sexual exploitation. A jury at Sheffield Crown Court reached unanimous verdicts on Thursday 12 November 2026.

Neither man was there to hear it. Both absconded before their trial, and they're being sentenced today in their absence.

What they did

Between 2008 and 2010, the pair separately groomed a vulnerable girl aged 13 and 14, plying her with cannabis, alcohol and gifts.

Hussain, known to her as "Muddy", raped her "countless times over the course of around 18 months", according to the NCA, in a house in Rotherham, in public places and in his car. She told officers he threatened her with a baseball bat.

Khan abused her over seven months and offered her up to other men as a "favour".

How they got away

Hussain was on bail awaiting trial and had handed his passport to the NCA as a condition. Even so, the NCA says he may have left the country illegally, and at least one of the two men is believed to have fled abroad.

A third man, Hussain's brother Ghazanfar Hussain, 42, was convicted of one count of rape and is in custody.

Have you seen them?

Philip Marshall, head of Operation Stovewood at the NCA, said: "My officers are determined to find the men, to ensure that both of them serve the sentences handed down to them in due course." He has asked for any information, "no matter how insignificant".

Do not approach them. If you see either man or know where they are, call 999 or contact the National Crime Agency. You can also report anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Share this. Someone, somewhere, knows where they are.

Sources: National Crime Agency, CPS, BBC News, The Independent, The Star (12 and 13 Nov 2026). Photos: CPS / NCA.

text:
The History of Bogner Amplifiers, 1987-2026

Reinhold Bogner’s journey from German amplifier modification to American boutique manufacturing helped establish modern multichannel, high-gain tube amplification. His designs combined sophisticated gain staging, extensive voicing controls and flexible switching architectures.

1987 - German beginnings

Raised in Ulm, Germany, Bogner developed an early interest in vacuum-tube electronics through his father’s radio equipment. As a teenager, he studied Marshall, Hiwatt, Orange, Vox and Mesa/Boogie circuits. By 1987, he was demonstrating modified amplifiers to professional musicians in Germany.

1989 - Los Angeles

Bogner relocated to Los Angeles with a heavily modified Marshall JCM800. Connections with professional guitarists and equipment-rental operations helped establish his reputation for custom amplifier modifications.

1989-1990 - Triple Giant

His early commercial three-channel tube rack preamplifier offered separate gain structures for professional rack systems. Approximately 25 original Bogner-built units preceded production under license by Hafler.

1990-1993 - Fish

The Fish featured four independently voiced channels: Country, Strato, Shark and Brown. Approximately 250 original units were manufactured. The preamplifier became closely associated with Jerry Cantrell.

1992 - Ecstasy

The three-channel Ecstasy established Bogner’s flagship amplifier architecture. Early 100A and 100B configurations used 6L6 and EL34 output tubes, respectively. Independent channel controls, pre-EQ switching and power-section adjustments provided extensive flexibility.

1990s - Caveman

A limited-production, two-channel tube amplifier, with approximately 60 examples reported, demonstrated Bogner’s interest in vintage-inspired circuitry alongside increasingly sophisticated multichannel designs.

1999 - Shiva

The two-channel Shiva combined clean and overdrive circuits, with EL34 and 6L6 versions offered across its production history. Later variants expanded switching and boost capabilities.

2001 - Überschall

Designed for extreme gain and substantial low-frequency response, the original Überschall used four EL34 output tubes. Subsequent revisions expanded its gain structure, controls and channel flexibility.

2007 - Spider Valve

Bogner collaborated with Line 6 on an amplifier combining digital modeling technology with Bogner-designed tube amplification circuitry.

2008 - Alchemist

A two-channel amplifier incorporating onboard effects and selectable power operation, expanding Bogner-designed equipment into a more accessible market.

2009 - Goldfinger and Anniversary Ecstasy

The Goldfinger emphasized vintage-oriented clean and overdriven circuitry. The 20th Anniversary Ecstasy introduced additional refinements to the established platform.

2010s - Atma

The compact Atma offered selectable output power and multiple gain configurations for lower-volume applications.

2014 - Helios

The Helios revisited Bogner’s early Marshall modification experience through British-inspired gain circuitry and expanded voicing options.

2020s-2026 - Continuing evolution

The Ecstasy 3534, Ecstasy Pandora and Überschall Ultra extended Bogner’s established amplifier families through compact formats, revised gain structures and additional switching capabilities.

Technical legacy

Bogner’s principal contribution was the integration of sophisticated preamplifier gain staging, frequency shaping, multichannel switching and adjustable power-amplifier response. These developments helped establish the modern boutique amplifier as a flexible, self-contained performance system.

text:
Today is Feast of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini. At Mother Cabrini Shrine in Golden, United States, the date has a place, a community, and a story behind it. Here, the annual observance belongs to the living prayer of the destination. If you hope to join the celebration, check today’s Masses, processions, access, and public veneration directly with the shrine, parish, diocese, or custodian.

West of Denver, the road climbs toward the eastern slope of Lookout Mountain. The city begins to fall away, the air thins, and the landscape opens toward the plains. Mother Cabrini Shrine stands here not because Frances Xavier Cabrini went looking for a scenic monument to herself, but because she saw a practical need. Girls from Denver’s Queen of Heaven Orphanage needed a summer place outside the city. What began as a camp with barns, farm work, mountain air, and a serious shortage of water became one of the most distinctive Catholic pilgrimage places in the American West.

Frances Cabrini was born in 1850 at Sant’Angelo Lodigiano in northern Italy. She wanted to become a missionary and took Xavier as part of her religious name in honor of St. Francis Xavier. With seven companions she founded the community that became the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Her imagination initially reached toward China, but Pope Leo XIII redirected her attention toward the immense pastoral needs of Italian emigrants crossing the Atlantic. The phrase remembered from that encounter—“not to the East, but to the West”—became the direction of a life.

In the United States, Cabrini encountered immigrants who had traveled far but had not necessarily found security. Many lacked money, social standing, English, education, medical care, and the protection of familiar institutions. She and her sisters opened schools, hospitals, and orphanages, visited the sick, and defended the dignity of people who could easily be ignored or exploited. Her missionary map expanded across North, Central, and South America. The Vatican’s account of her life names journeys from New York and New Jersey to Pennsylvania, Illinois, California, Louisiana, and Colorado. Distance did not distract her from particular people; it enlarged the field in which she served them.

Cabrini first encountered the foothills west of Denver while visiting Italian workers and their families in Colorado mining districts in 1902. The property that attracted her belonged to the town of Golden and lay on the east slope of Lookout Mountain. Around 1909–1910 she negotiated its purchase as a summer camp for girls from the orphanage. Three sisters established a farm there, living in the loft of a barn and tending poultry, livestock, and dairy cows. Groups of girls came during the summer, sharing outdoor recreation with the ordinary chores that sustained the place.

The difficulty was water. The shrine’s history says that no reliable source was known on the property. Drinking and cooking water had to be carried uphill from a stream in Mt. Vernon Canyon. In September 1912, when the sisters complained that the camp could not continue this way, Cabrini directed them to lift a particular rock and dig. They found water. The spring was later enclosed in an 8,000-gallon tank, and the shrine says it has continued to flow. Pilgrims still drink or collect the water, and many associate it with prayers for healing and peace.

That story deserves both reverence and precision. Mother Cabrini Shrine is not a Marian-apparition site, and the spring should not be presented as though the Church had issued a scientific or canonical declaration about every healing attributed to it. What can be visited is clear: a spring identified by the shrine with Cabrini’s 1912 direction, preserved within an active Catholic shrine where generations of people have prayed. The careful language does not drain the story of wonder. It lets the pilgrim distinguish the documented history of the place from personal testimonies of grace.

Cabrini’s last Colorado visit also left other marks on the mountain. She planned a native-stone dormitory for the girls with builder Thomas Eckrom. Construction began in 1912 and ended in 1914. The Stone House served the orphanage camp and later became a retreat facility. The shrine also preserves the Heart of Stones. Its account says Cabrini, several sisters, and children climbed the highest hill, gathered white stones, and arranged them as a heart surmounted by a cross, with smaller stones forming a crown of thorns. She dedicated the hill to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

The pilgrimage landscape continued to develop after her death. A Lourdes-style grotto was erected over the spring in 1929; the present sandstone grotto replaced it in 1959. In 1954, a twenty-two-foot statue of the Sacred Heart of Jesus was placed on an eleven-foot base above the Heart of Stones. That same year work began on the Stairway of Prayer. Its 373 steps were completed in sixty-seven days and follow the path associated with Cabrini, the sisters, and the children. Stations of the Cross lead the ascent, followed by mysteries of the Rosary that direct prayer toward the life of Christ.

A good visit therefore has a spiritual order. Begin below at the spring and grotto, where the original problem of thirst becomes an invitation to prayer. Visit the historic Stone House and the museum if they are open. Then make the ascent slowly. The stairs are not merely transportation to a viewpoint. The mosaics, Stations, and Rosary mysteries turn physical effort into a devotional path. At the summit, the Sacred Heart statue and preserved stone heart interpret the whole mountain through the spirituality that animated Cabrini’s congregation.

This is demanding terrain. The shrine publishes daily grounds hours and a regular schedule of Mass and confession, but pilgrims should verify both before traveling because liturgies, events, weather, and mountain conditions can alter a visit. The campus includes steep grades and the 373-step route; anyone with limited mobility should contact the shrine about accessible approaches rather than assuming the stairs are the only way to pray there. The shrine also offers retreat spaces and overnight accommodations, making it possible to stay rather than treating the mountain as a hurried stop from Denver.

Cabrini died in Chicago in 1917. She was canonized by Pope Pius XII in 1946 and proclaimed patroness of immigrants in 1950. Those honors make the Colorado shrine more than a record of one resourceful religious sister finding water. The place belongs to a much larger Catholic story about migration: people uprooted from home, communities trying to preserve faith and dignity, and a woman who crossed oceans and continents to build institutions for those the prosperous world often overlooked. Her prayer before the tabernacle and her formidable administrative energy were not competing parts of her life. The first gave direction to the second.

From the summit, a pilgrim can look back toward Denver and remember the orphan girls for whom this property was purchased, the miners’ families Cabrini traveled to meet, and the sisters carrying water up a dry mountain. The shrine’s beauty came through service before it became a destination. That may be its sharpest lesson. Catholic pilgrimage is not only about finding places where something extraordinary is remembered. It is also about seeing how holiness responds to ordinary human need—with prayer, courage, intelligence, persistence, and a willingness to lift the rock and begin digging.

Explore the story and plan a visit:
https://t.co/qnJ4pv4PLz

St. Frances Xavier Cabrini, pray for us.

X-Energy $XE The Nuclear Fuel Play Behind the Next Generation of Reactors

Most investors looking at the nuclear energy trade are focused on reactor developers. 

But X-Energy offers a different angle: it isn't just building the technology that generates power. It's positioning itself to supply the fuel that keeps those reactors running.

That distinction matters as the nuclear industry moves toward small modular reactors and advanced high-temperature gas-cooled designs.

Q3 revenue and grant income reached $66.3M, up 118% year over year, consisting of $51.5M in services revenue and $14.8M in grants.

The biggest development was regulatory. The NRC issued the construction permit for the Dow Seadrift project more than a month ahead of schedule. 

It's the first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in nearly 60 years. Importantly, this authorizes construction but does not mean Dow has made a final commitment to build.

The commercial pipeline is also expanding. 
Projects include the proposed 960 MW, 12-reactor development involving AEP and Amazon in Indiana, alongside Energy Northwest. Meanwhile, TX-1, X-Energy's first commercial-scale nuclear fuel facility, has reached vertical construction on schedule.

There is a significant financial caveat. 
Operating expenses increased 139% to $169.9M, operating cash use reached $51.2M and capital expenditures were $71.8M. 

This remains a capital-intensive development story. However, X-Energy ended the quarter with $1.8B in cash and investments, no debt, and $618M in DOE reimbursements received to date.

Friday, November 13, 2026

The global commodity board enters Friday session digesting post WASDE supply adjustments alongside active late week export and cash positioning. 

December corn futures hold steady near $4.46/bu following Tuesday's USDA yield reduction to 179.6 bpa, while January soybeans trade near $12.33 1/2/bu as tighter ending stocks and steady Chinese buying balance harvest completion.
