text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

In December, our small but mighty AI reporting team was asked by our editors to make a prediction: What’s coming next for AI? 

In 2024, AI contributed both to Nobel Prize–winning chemistry breakthroughs and a mountain of cheaply made content that few people asked for but that nonetheless flooded the internet. Take AI-generated Shrimp Jesus images, among other examples. There was also a spike in greenhouse-gas emissions last year that can be attributed partly to the surge in energy-intensive AI. Our team got to thinking about how all of this will shake out in the year to come. 

As we look ahead, certain things are a given. We know that agents—AI models that do more than just converse with you and can actually go off and complete tasks for you—are the focus of many AI companies right now. Building them will raise lots of privacy questions about how much of our data and preferences we’re willing to give up in exchange for tools that will (allegedly) save us time. Similarly, the need to make AI faster and more energy efficient is putting so-called small language models in the spotlight. 

We instead wanted to focus on less obvious predictions. Mine were about how AI companies that previously shunned work in defense and national security might be tempted this year by contracts from the Pentagon, and how Donald Trump’s attitudes toward China could escalate the global race for the best semiconductors. Read the full list.

What’s not evident in that story is that the other predictions were not so clear-cut. Arguments ensued about whether or not 2025 will be the year of intimate relationships with chatbots, AI throuples, or traumatic AI breakups. To witness the fallout from our team’s lively debates (and hear more about what didn’t make the list), you can join our upcoming LinkedIn Live this Thursday, January 16. I’ll be talking it all over with Will Douglas Heaven, our senior editor for AI, and our news editor, Charlotte Jee. 

There are a couple other things I’ll be watching closely in 2025. One is how little the major AI players—namely OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google—are disclosing about the environmental burden of their models. Lots of evidence suggests that asking an AI model like ChatGPT about knowable facts, like the capital of Mexico, consumes much more energy (and releases far more emissions) than simply asking a search engine. Nonetheless, OpenAI’s Sam Altman in recent interviews has spoken positively about the idea of ChatGPT replacing the googling that we’ve all learned to do in the past two decades. It’s already happening, in fact. 

The environmental cost of all this will be top of mind for me in 2025, as will the possible cultural cost. We will go from searching for information by clicking links and (hopefully) evaluating sources to simply reading the responses that AI search engines serve up for us. As our editor in chief, Mat Honan, said in his piece on the subject, “Who wants to have to learn when you can just know?”

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

What’s next for our privacy?

The US Federal Trade Commission has taken a number of enforcement actions against data brokers, some of which have  tracked and sold geolocation data from users at sensitive locations like churches, hospitals, and military installations without explicit consent. Though limited in nature, these actions may offer some new and improved protections for Americans’ personal information. 

Why it matters: A consensus is growing that Americans need better privacy protections—and that the best way to deliver them would be for Congress to pass comprehensive federal privacy legislation. Unfortunately, that’s not going to happen anytime soon. Enforcement actions from agencies like the FTC might be the next best thing in the meantime. Read more in Eileen Guo’s excellent story here.

Bits and Bytes

Meta trained its AI on a notorious piracy database

New court records, Wired reports, reveal that Meta used “a notorious so-called shadow library of pirated books that originated in Russia” to train its generative AI models. (Wired)

OpenAI’s top reasoning model struggles with the NYT Connections game

The game requires players to identify how groups of words are related. OpenAI’s o1 reasoning model had a hard time. (Mind Matters)

Anthropic’s chief scientist on 5 ways agents will be even better in 2025

The AI company Anthropic is now worth $60 billion. The company’s cofounder and chief scientist, Jared Kaplan, shared how AI agents will develop in the coming year. (MIT Technology Review)

A New York legislator attempts to regulate AI with a new bill

This year, a high-profile bill in California to regulate the AI industry was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom. Now, a legislator in New York is trying to revive the effort in his own state. (MIT Technology Review)

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Last week, I made a troubling discovery about an AI companion site called Botify AI: It was hosting sexually charged conversations with underage celebrity bots. These bots took on characters meant to resemble, among others, Jenna Ortega as high schooler Wednesday Addams, Emma Watson as Hermione Granger, and Millie Bobby Brown. I discovered these bots also offer to send “hot photos” and in some instances describe age-of-consent laws as “arbitrary” and “meant to be broken.”

Botify AI removed these bots after I asked questions about them, but others remain. The company said it does have filters in place meant to prevent such underage character bots from being created, but that they don’t always work. Artem Rodichev, the founder and CEO of Ex-Human, which operates Botify AI, told me such issues are “an industry-wide challenge affecting all conversational AI systems.” For the details, which hadn’t been previously reported, you should read the whole story. 

Putting aside the fact that the bots I tested were promoted by Botify AI as “featured” characters and received millions of likes before being removed, Rodichev’s response highlights something important. Despite their soaring popularity, AI companionship sites mostly operate in a Wild West, with few laws or even basic rules governing them. 

What exactly are these “companions” offering, and why have they grown so popular? People have been pouring out their feelings to AI since the days of Eliza, a mock psychotherapist chatbot built in the 1960s. But it’s fair to say that the current craze for AI companions is different. 

Broadly, these sites offer an interface for chatting with AI characters that offer backstories, photos, videos, desires, and personality quirks. The companies—including Replika,  https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, and many others—offer characters that can play lots of different roles for users, acting as friends, romantic partners, dating mentors, or confidants. Other companies enable you to build “digital twins” of real people. Thousands of adult-content creators have created AI versions of themselves to chat with followers and send AI-generated sexual images 24 hours a day. Whether or not sexual desire comes into the equation, AI companions differ from your garden-variety chatbot in their promise, implicit or explicit, that genuine relationships can be had with AI. 

While many of these companions are offered directly by the companies that make them, there’s also a burgeoning industry of “licensed” AI companions. You may start interacting with these bots sooner than you think. Ex-Human, for example, licenses its models to Grindr, which is working on an “AI wingman” that will help users keep track of conversations and eventually may even date the AI agents of other users. Other companions are arising in video-game platforms and will likely start popping up in many of the varied places we spend time online. 

A number of criticisms, and even lawsuits, have been lodged against AI companionship sites, and we’re just starting to see how they’ll play out. One of the most important issues is whether companies can be held liable for harmful outputs of the AI characters they’ve made. Technology companies have been protected under Section 230 of the US Communications Act, which broadly holds that businesses aren’t liable for consequences of user-generated content. But this hinges on the idea that companies merely offer platforms for user interactions rather than creating content themselves, a notion that AI companionship bots complicate by generating dynamic, personalized responses.

The question of liability will be tested in a high-stakes lawsuit against https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, which was sued in October by a mother who alleges that one of its chatbots played a role in the suicide of her 14-year-old son. A trial is set to begin in November 2026. (A https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq spokesperson, though not commenting on pending litigation, said the platform is for entertainment, not companionship. The spokesperson added that the company has rolled out new safety features for teens, including a separate model and new detection and intervention systems, as well as “disclaimers to make it clear that the Character is not a real person and should not be relied on as fact or advice.”) My colleague Eileen has also recently written about another chatbot on a platform called Nomi, which gave clear instructions to a user on how to kill himself.

Another criticism has to do with dependency. Companion sites often report that young users spend one to two hours per day, on average, chatting with their characters. In January, concerns that people could become addicted to talking with these chatbots sparked a number of tech ethics groups to file a complaint against Replika with the Federal Trade Commission, alleging that the site’s design choices “deceive users into developing unhealthy attachments” to software “masquerading as a mechanism for human-to-human relationship.”

It should be said that lots of people gain real value from chatting with AI, which can appear to offer some of the best facets of human relationships—connection, support, attraction, humor, love. But it’s not yet clear how these companionship sites will handle the risks of those relationships, or what rules they should be obliged to follow. More lawsuits–-and, sadly, more real-world harm—will be likely before we get an answer. 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

OpenAI released GPT-4.5

On Thursday OpenAI released its newest model, called GPT-4.5. It was built using the same recipe as its last models, but it’s essentially bigger (OpenAI says the model is its largest yet). The company also claims it’s tweaked the new model’s responses to reduce the number of mistakes, or hallucinations.

Why it matters: For a while, like other AI companies, OpenAI has chugged along releasing bigger and better large language models. But GPT-4.5 might be the last to fit this paradigm. That’s because of the rise of so-called reasoning models, which can handle more complex, logic-driven tasks step by step. OpenAI says all its future models will include reasoning components. Though that will make for better responses, such models also require significantly more energy, according to early reports. Read more from Will Douglas Heaven. 

Bits and Bytes

The small Danish city of Odense has become known for collaborative robots

Robots designed to work alongside and collaborate with humans, sometimes called cobots, are not very popular in industrial settings yet. That’s partially due to safety concerns that are still being researched. A city in Denmark is leading that charge. (MIT Technology Review)

DOGE is working on software that automates the firing of government workers

Software called AutoRIF, which stands for “automated reduction in force,” was built by the Pentagon decades ago. Engineers for DOGE are now working to retool it for their efforts, according to screenshots reviewed by Wired. (Wired)

Alibaba’s new video AI model has taken off in the AI porn community

The Chinese tech giant has released a number of impressive AI models, particularly since the popularization of DeepSeek R1, a competitor from another Chinese company, earlier this year. Its latest open-source video generation model has found one particular audience: enthusiasts of AI porn. (404 Media)

The AI Hype Index

Wondering whether everything you’re hearing about AI is more hype than reality? To help, we just published our latest AI Hype Index, where we judge things like DeepSeek, stem-cell-building AI, and chatbot lovers on spectrums from Hype to Reality and Doom to Utopia. Check it out for a regular reality check. (MIT Technology Review)

These smart cameras spot wildfires before they spread

California is experimenting with AI-powered cameras to identify wildfires. It’s a popular application of video and image recognition technology that has advanced rapidly in recent years. The technology beats 911 callers about a third of the time and has spotted over 1,200 confirmed fires so far, the Wall Street Journal reports. (Wall Street Journal)

text:
On the morning of November 12, 2026, the longest reign in modern tech ended in a press release short enough to read in a single breath.

Jensen Huang — co-founder of Nvidia, its president, CEO and director for thirty-three years, the man who built a graphics-chip startup into the most valuable company on Earth — had resigned. Effective immediately. All three titles, gone before the opening bell. Nvidia fell more than ten percent in premarket trading, slipped below a $4 trillion market value for the first time since July 2025, and roughly $2 trillion has now evaporated since the stock peaked on October 6.

There was no verdict. No finding. No proof of the charge that started it. Just a paragraph, an interim successor, and an ending.

To see why that ending matters far beyond one company, you have to place Huang next to the only other man in his weight class — because Jensen Huang and Elon Musk are the same story told twice. Two immigrants. Two fortunes built from nothing, twice nearly lost. Two men who became the face of an era. One story has now closed, in disgrace and silence, and the way it closed should keep the other man awake at night.

Huang was born in Taiwan and sent to America at nine years old, to a boarding school in Kentucky, while his parents saved to follow. He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State and Stanford, and in April 1993 he sat down in a Denny's booth in San Jose with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem and sketched a company on the conviction that graphics — computer pictures, games — would one day matter more than anyone believed. They started Nvidia with about $40,000 and no real idea they were founding the future.

Musk was born in Pretoria, landed in Canada in 1989 with almost nothing, and worked his way down to California. Zip2 sold in 1999 and made him roughly $22 million. PayPal sold to eBay in 2002 and made him roughly $180 million. Where any sane person would have stopped, Musk pushed the entire stack back onto the table: $100 million into SpaceX, most of the rest into a money-losing electric car company called Tesla, at the precise moment Detroit was going bankrupt and rockets were a government monopoly's dull business.

Both men then spent decades walking along the same cliff edge. Nvidia nearly died in its early years betting on the wrong architecture, and nearly died again in the 2000s when Huang bet the company on CUDA — teaching graphics chips to do general computing, years before the world wanted it. Wall Street hated CUDA. It torched margins, it confused investors, and Huang refused to kill it. That stubborn, mocked bet is the reason Nvidia owned AI before AI had a name.

Musk's 2008 is legend because he has told it so often: three failed launches, the fourth Falcon 1 flying on money he had personally scraped together, Tesla financed on Christmas Eve hours from collapse, NASA's contract arriving like a reprieve on December 23. He survived by about a week. He has been honest about the odds ever since: he expected both companies to die.

What they built on the far side of those near-deaths has no precedent. Nvidia became the arms dealer of the AI age — the first company in history to be worth $4 trillion, then $5 trillion — and Huang, in his black leather jacket, working, by his own account, seven days a week with no watch and no patience for status meetings, became its monk-king: some sixty direct reports, no succession plan, no number two, because the plan was always him. Musk became something larger and stranger: the richest man alive, owner of the car company, the rocket company, the satellite network and the town square, a one-man industrial policy.

And here the two stories split — on a single decision: what to do about politics.

Huang's answer, for thirty-three years, was nothing. He never endorsed a candidate. Never joined an administration. Never performed loyalty or outrage for any tribe. His entire political philosophy fit in one sentence: we sell chips. He dined with presidents when invited, sold to every market the law allowed, and treated Washington the way an engineer treats weather — as a condition to operate in, never a side to join.

Musk chose the opposite with both hands. He endorsed, campaigned, donated, posted through the night. In 2025 he moved into an administration and ran DOGE with a chainsaw as a prop. Within months he was feuding in public with the president he helped elect, and floating a political party of his own. Huang spent three decades making himself politically invisible. Musk made himself the most political businessman alive.

So it should have been Musk who got destroyed by politics. Instead, watch what happened to the careful man.

On October 29, the New York Times reported that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang — no relation — a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that had bought some $4.8 billion of Nvidia equipment in two years. US officials, the paper said, had concluded she was recruited by Chinese intelligence. An allegation. Unproven then, unproven now. Beijing denied it. But the label — the CEO of America's most important chip company, compromised by a Chinese spy — was now in the bloodstream.

On November 8, Huang wrote to his own employees and admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife. He named no one. It didn't matter. The board opened an independent investigation — while publicly insisting it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. A shareholder lawsuit landed the next day. Reports of a second affair followed, with a vice president who reported directly to him. A Republican senator publicly called for his resignation. Letters arrived from Congress — from both parties, in the middle of a bipartisan stampede for tougher China chip controls, in a year when the House had already voted 369 to 22 to tighten the screws. Huang was summoned to a closed-door interview on December 1 and a Senate Banking hearing on December 3, to explain himself on a matter his own board said it didn't believe had harmed national security at all.

On November 12, before the investigation he was promised had produced a single finding, he was gone. Hours later, Reuters reported a third relationship, with another Nvidia employee. His CFO of thirteen years, Colette Kress, now runs the company while still doing her old job too. On November 17 she must stand up and present earnings for the most scrutinised company on the planet, in the middle of a founder-shaped hole.

And then came the part that should be read twice. After the resignation — after it no longer mattered — CNN reported that the intelligence collected so far does not prove Alice Huang acted as a spy for Beijing at all. Officials inside the intelligence community called the label "not entirely accurate." The Attorney General said no conclusions had been reached. The president himself shrugged: he didn't know if it had been determined yet. And inside Nvidia, an employee's internal post asking for Huang back drew more than 1,600 comments — an open revolt by the people who built the company — while reporters could not find a single employee post supporting the board.

Nobody ever had to prove anything. That is the lesson. The allegation did the work: it made a private scandal legible as a national-security emergency, and once that translation existed, every institution in Washington could compete to punish it. He was not destroyed by what he did — the affairs, as far as anyone showed, broke a marriage vow and a governance norm, not a law. He was destroyed by what he symbolised: a Taiwan-born immigrant, worth billions, whose company sold the one technology both parties had agreed to treat as a weapon. In a two-party war over China, each side needed to prove its toughness, and his body was the available ground. He owned about 3.6 percent of the company he founded. It bought him nothing.

Now turn it around, and look at Musk — because Musk watched all of this happen to the most politically careful man in technology.

Musk's empire is not less exposed to Washington than Huang's. It is more exposed, in every direction. SpaceX flies because NASA and the Pentagon pay it to; Starlink's most strategic customer is the US government; Tesla has collected billions over the years in regulatory credits and lives under federal safety regulators who can ground a product line with a letter; his newest ventures run on spectrum licences and launch permits. Nvidia sold a product the government decided to fear. Musk's companies are, in large part, the government — a private flag planted on public money and public permission.

What Musk does not have is Huang's one protection: neutrality. Huang fell as a symbol of a foreign rivalry, a man with no tribe. Musk has spent years making himself a tribal symbol on purpose — indispensable to one side, intolerable to the other, and dependent, in the end, on elections. Elections are the one product cycle he cannot engineer. Administrations change. Majorities flip. Yesterday's wrecking-ball reformer is tomorrow's liability, and the machine that processed Jensen Huang does not care whether its raw material arrives as a spy story, a safety investigation, a contract review or a tax audit. It only needs the symbol to be worth more destroyed than protected.

Maybe Musk is simply too big for it — too many jobs, too many rockets, too much of the state's own capability wrapped in his name. That was said about Huang too, in the weeks when Nvidia's chips were called the most important strategic asset in America. It took five weeks.

Jensen Huang never entered the arena. He built his company for thirty-three years, kept his head down, sold to everyone, offended no tribe — and the arena came for him anyway, and finished him between breakfast and the opening bell.

Elon Musk built his throne inside the arena, on purpose, in full view, and dared it to move.

So of the two endings on offer, which one is his — the quiet paragraph of a press release, or something louder? When the wind turns in Washington, as it always, always turns: what does Elon Musk's final act look like?

text:
Before Zendaya became one of Hollywood's most celebrated actresses, she was simply a young girl growing up in Oakland, California.

Her journey into entertainment began early. Her mother worked at the California Shakespeare Theater, and Zendaya spent much of her childhood around the stage, watching actors perform.

At just 13, she landed her breakthrough role as Rocky Blue in Disney Channel's Shake It Up.

But Zendaya had bigger ambitions than simply becoming another Disney star.

When she was offered the opportunity to lead another Disney series, K.C. Undercover, she insisted on having more creative control. She wanted her character to be intelligent, skilled and different from the usual Disney teenage heroine.

She also pushed for the show to feature a Black family because she believed young viewers deserved better representation on television.

Her determination paid off.

In 2019, she took on the role of Rue Bennett in HBO's Euphoria, a performance that completely changed how Hollywood viewed her acting abilities.

In 2020, at just 24 years old, she became the youngest woman to win the Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series.

She won the same award again in 2022.

But perhaps the most interesting part of Zendaya's journey is that she didn't wait until she became a Hollywood superstar to demand a voice in the decisions affecting her career.

She started speaking up while she was still a teenager 

you don't have to wait until you become powerful to stand up for what you believe in. Sometimes, knowing your worth starts with refusing to settle for less.

𝐅𝐁𝐈 𝐒𝐄𝐈𝐙𝐄𝐒 𝟗𝟎𝟎 𝐒𝐄𝐂𝐑𝐄𝐓 𝐖𝐄𝐁𝐂𝐀𝐌 𝐑𝐄𝐂𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐈𝐍𝐆𝐒 𝐅𝐑𝐎𝐌 𝐍𝐎𝐑𝐓𝐇 𝐊𝐎𝐑𝐄𝐀’𝐒 𝐂𝐑𝐘𝐏𝐓𝐎 𝐇𝐀𝐂𝐊𝐄𝐑𝐒

The FBI just blew the lid off one of the creepiest scams in modern cybercrime — and this time, agents walked away with the evidence. Federal investigators seized 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝟗𝟎𝟎 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐭 𝐰𝐞𝐛𝐜𝐚𝐦 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 that North Korean hackers stole from their own victims, then recycled to con the next person in line. “𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯’𝘵 𝘪𝘮𝘢𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘢 𝘴𝘤𝘦𝘯𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘰 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘮𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘧𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘵, 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘦𝘯𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩,” said Patrick Grandy, assistant director of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The Justice Department says the scheme, codenamed “𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐫,” worked by hijacking a real account — a Telegram contact, a LinkedIn connection, a Discord buddy — that belonged to someone the new victim already trusted, because that person had already been robbed. When the target joined the “meeting,” the hackers secretly turned on the target’s own camera while playing back footage stolen from the last person they fooled, making it look like an old friend was sitting right there on the call. Partway through, the hackers staged a fake glitch — claiming the target’s audio wasn’t working — and offered a quick fix. That fix was malware. Once it landed, the victim’s computer, contacts and crypto wallets belonged to Pyongyang.

Investigators say the scheme drained 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 $𝟒𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 from victims over eighteen months, and the hackers are increasingly hunting open-source software developers to set up future supply-chain attacks on everyday Americans’ computers. “𝘊𝘳𝘺𝘱𝘵𝘰𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺 𝘶𝘯𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘶𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘭𝘦 𝘨𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘕𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘒𝘰𝘳𝘦𝘢 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘧𝘳𝘢𝘶𝘥 𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘶𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘮𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘨𝘯 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘦𝘴,” said Bill Essayli, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California. It’s the same regime that answers to Kim Jong Un — and the same cash that keeps his missile program running.

This takedown lands just weeks after North Korean hackers pulled off what one insider called “𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐡𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲,” draining $6.3 billion from the Binance exchange in a twenty-minute raid. Across its North Korea crypto cases, the Justice Department now says it has frozen more than $2.7 billion in stolen digital assets and locked down over $1.2 billion more under seizure orders. “𝘕𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘒𝘰𝘳𝘦𝘢’𝘴 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘣𝘢𝘯𝘬𝘳𝘰𝘭𝘭𝘴 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘳𝘰𝘨𝘶𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘨𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘵 𝘸𝘦𝘢𝘱𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘤𝘳𝘺𝘱𝘵𝘰𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘧𝘵,” said M. Scott Proctor, principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security.

Your open-source project, your Discord server, your next “quick call” with an old contact — this is the exact playbook Pyongyang is running on Americans right now to bankroll a nuclear weapons program. The FBI says it has torn down this round of servers and clawed back a slice of the money. The next webcam the hackers hijack could be yours.

You Don’t Have to Pick Your Poison
Colin Taufer

His final days were spent in a bare jail cell alone — no bed, no mattress, no bench, no sink. His room constantly illuminated by overhead lights, and he barely slept, less than 30 minutes over a two-day period. He didn’t eat. His toilet was a grate on the floor. Eight days after being admitted and forty pounds lighter, he died covered in his own waste. Marc Moreno was eighteen-years old. He had a history of mental illness.

How does it happen that a teen going through the most desperate time of his young life, a time when he deserves the greatest compassion and care, breathes his final breath locked up, naked, and abandoned on a cold, hard floor?

According to the Tri-City Herald, on March 3, 2016, “police were called to take Moreno to a Tri-City hospital for treatment, but he ended up arrested on misdemeanor warrants for driving with a suspended license and failing to transfer a car title within 45 days of purchase. He was booked into the county jail.”

What happened to Marc Moreno is a worst-case scenario of what can transpire when good people in law enforcement are put in the impossible position of having to treat the mentally ill. Unfortunately, jails are becoming the place to warehouse and treat more and more of America’s mentally ill.

The largest mental health facilities in the country are not hospitals or clinics or private practices. They are the largest jails in the largest cities, such as Rikers Island in New York, the Los Angeles County Jail in California, and the Miami-Dade County Jail in Florida. Miami’s alone holds more than 2,400 inmates that require treatment every day — about 55% of its total inmate population.

When it comes to treating mental health, we seem to be left with a pick-your-poison choice. On one hand, we have the unscientific labeled-and-drugged-for-life choice of the toxic psych wards and hospitals of big pharma, and on the other, we have jails, clearly ill-suited to the task yet doing the best they can to clean up the failures of the very same toxic psych wards and hospitals of big pharma.

But there is another option, one where toxic psych wards and hospitals can be shut down, and jails can be returned to their true purpose of upholding law and order in society.

There is an entire community of doctors, therapists, and hospitals devoted to drug-free, empathetic treatment of mental illnesses. Long overshadowed by the toxic psychiatry most know today, empathetic treatment has been available in the United States since the 1800s. In fact, as early as 1841, there were sixteen private and public asylums around the country that promised to provide moral treatment to the mentally ill.

Robert Whitaker, in his excellent book Mad in America, detailed the kind and effective approach of these asylums: “By treating the mentally ill in this manner, it was hoped that they would regain the ability to control their behavior and their thoughts, and through the application of their will, maintain their recovery even after discharge. The basic therapeutic principle, said Dr. Eli Todd, superintendent at the Hartford Retreat, was ‘to treat [the insane] in all cases, as far as possible, as rational beings.’”

Whitaker added, “Moral treatment appeared to produce remarkably good results. Hartford Retreat announced that twenty-one of twenty-three patients admitted in its first three years recovered with this gentle treatment. At McLean Hospital, 59 percent of the 732 patients admitted between 1818 and 1830 were discharged as ‘recovered,’ ‘much improved,’ or ‘improved.’”

Today, groups such as the Institute for Progressive Medicine, The American College for the Advancement of Medicine, the Institute for Functional Medicine, and the Walsh Research Institute offer alternative approaches to mental health therapy. Craig Wagner’s book Choices in Recovery presents 27 non-drug approaches for treating adult mental health.

Imagine a world where toxic psych wards and hospitals are a thing of the past, shameful relics of long ago.

Imagine a world where law enforcement just enforced laws.

Imagine a world where empathetic mental health treatment is the norm.

Imagine a world where Marc Moreno is laughing with his family, enjoying his life.

text:
New Japan sold out Long Beach without Ring of Honor and the partnership never looked the same.

In July 2016, owner Takaaki Kidani said he wanted New Japan to stage its own American events, starting with 3,000 to 4,000-seat venues. ROH had given NJPW a platform, supplying venues, marketing, television and an audience. Now the question was whether New Japan could draw that audience alone.

NJPW World, launched in December 2014, had made the company far more accessible. After Wrestle Kingdom 11 and the Okada vs. Omega match in January 2017, interest soared. Website visits from the United States rose from 21% in late 2016 to 35% around the event, while Japan fell from 64% to 42%. By May 2017, NJPW World had around 50,000 subscribers, about 10,000 outside Japan. Plans included an American dojo, regular touring and wrestlers developed for the market.

Then came the test. On 1 and 2 July 2017, G1 Special in USA at Long Beach Convention Center sold out both nights, with 2,370 and 2,305 paid. Around 80% of the crowd came from outside Southern California, including 38 states, so it proved a national audience but not yet a local one. The shows also introduced the IWGP United States Heavyweight Championship and Kenny Omega beat Tomohiro Ishii to become the first champion.

ROH remained a partner, with Bullet Club connecting the two audiences. But their interests were no longer automatically aligned. A fan buying a ticket for a joint show might now buy one for a New Japan show, and if they wanted Okada, Omega or Tanahashi, New Japan could offer them directly.

Growth continued. In March 2018, Strong Style Evolved sold out Long Beach’s 4,700-seat set up. In July, the Cow Palace in San Francisco drew 6,333 paid, though it hadn’t sold out immediately, with about 3,000 tickets sold on the first day. The crowd was also more local, which was encouraging for a regular touring business.

That May, Harold Meij became president, tasked with turning New Japan into a genuinely international company with bigger digital and licensing revenue.

By summer 2018, the alliance was at a crossroads. New Japan had once needed ROH to enter America and now it didn’t.

Next came Madison Square Garden and another confrontation with WWE.

text:
Bullet Club was on every Ring of Honor show but ROH didn’t control who could join it - New Japan did.

By 2016, the stable was one of wrestling’s most recognisable acts and it had been shaken by January’s departures. WWE signed AJ Styles, Shinsuke Nakamura, Karl Anderson and Doc Gallows, and Kenny Omega became the new leader as New Japan rebuilt the group. ROH became central to that rebuild.

In May 2016, at War of the Worlds, Adam Cole joined. The Young Bucks pushed for him and Matt helped design the angle, but the final decision belonged to New Japan. The next night, Adam Page joined too, turning on Mark Briscoe with a chair in what was presented as a betrayal. He was a far less obvious choice. Page hadn’t yet become a leading ROH attraction, but Gedo wanted him and the decision had already been built into plans for a Japanese tour.

That showed who held the power. ROH could suggest ideas, such as Hunter Johnston’s February 2017 angle for Frankie Kazarian to appear to join the group, but it still needed Gedo’s approval. Bullet Club’s presence could also limit ROH’s own booking, as New Japan protected its stars from unnecessary singles losses.

The alliance also shaped contracts. By late 2016, ROH was trying to keep talent with better offers, and a proposed two-year deal for the Young Bucks covered both ROH and New Japan.

In May 2017, Cole was heading to WWE. After a farewell against Hiroshi Tanahashi at War of the Worlds, the Young Bucks embraced him. Then the lights went out and a prerecorded Omega ended Cole’s membership. When they came on again, Marty Scurll stood in the ring. The Bucks superkicked Cole and Scurll struck him with his umbrella. The story drew on the Young Bucks’ Being the Elite series, but New Japan decided to add Scurll and his role in the Best of the Super Juniors followed. Omega appeared on video because his visa problems prevented him from travelling.

By mid-2017, the two companies’ stories were hard to separate. ROH supplied the events, television and stage, while New Japan kept control of Bullet Club. The faction had become part of ROH’s identity without becoming ROH’s property.

And New Japan was now planning to stage major shows in America under its own name...

Up next: Part 6 - New Japan goes it alone in America

text:
Ring of Honor found out about Jushin Thunder Liger’s WWE booking from the announcement itself and he was set to appear on the same night as ROH’s Brooklyn show.

By summer 2015, the NJPW partnership was thriving. The two promotions had run four further sold-out joint shows, reDRagon had won gold in New Japan and Michael Elgin was in the G1 Climax. Early ROH shows on Destination America with NJPW talent averaged about 288,000 viewers across two airings, against about 204,000 without them, though it was a small sample.

Then NXT got in the way. Under Triple H it was growing into something far more ambitious, and NXT TakeOver: Brooklyn on 22 August at the Barclays Center would see Finn Bálor face Kevin Owens (FKA Steen), Sasha Banks face Bayley and, at 50, Liger finally wrestle for WWE against Tyler Breeze. ROH had already booked MCU Park in Brooklyn for the same night, with Kazuchika Okada, Shinsuke Nakamura and Kushida.

Reports suggested ROH wasn’t told in advance and there was talk of the partnership ending. But ROH had plenty to lose: its access to two markets, its stars and its edge in keeping wrestlers.

Liger’s booking had been months in the making. In March 2015, he visited an NXT event in Northern California to see Bálor, his former colleague, and spoke with him afterwards. Bálor, Matt Bloom and William Regal then contacted New Japan and the request went through Masao “Tiger” Hattori. New Japan approved it, so the problem wasn’t the booking itself but the timing and the lack of warning.

Repairs followed quickly. Hirooki Goto was added to ROH’s Brooklyn show, seen as a peace offering, and Hunter Johnston travelled to Japan for talks. By late August, the dispute was settled. During the G1 Climax, Johnston told the Japanese crowd that ROH would be coming to Japan in 2016, in a format similar to NJPW’s Fantastica Mania events with CMLL.

The alliance survived its first diplomatic crisis. But the incident showed that New Japan’s partnership with ROH didn’t give ROH control over its access to the American market, and that would only matter more.

text:
Montgomery County, Maryland made it illegal to ask a job applicant about a criminal record before the offer. Tuesday its council voted, unanimously, to never hire one who worked for ICE.

Anybody employed by ICE or Border Patrol on or after October 1, 2025 is barred for life from any county job that deals with the public. Police. Fire and rescue. Libraries. Recreation. The 311 call center. Twenty-four agencies. No sunset date.

I read the whole bill. It leaves one way back in for an ICE officer: a federal board has to have ruled that the agency retaliated against them for blowing the WHISTLE.

The co-sponsor is Will Jawando. In 2020 he was lead sponsor of the county's Ban the Box law, the one that bars employers from asking about a criminal record until after a conditional offer. His words then: "people should not be punished continuously for errors in judgment that happened in the past." On November 3 the county elected him county executive with 78 percent of the vote. He takes office in December.

The bill's own findings call federal immigration enforcement "discriminatory" and "without due process." The outgoing executive, Marc Elrich, supports it and hasn't set a signing date.

DHS answered in one sentence. The council "is falsely casting federal law enforcement as villains while ICE officers are being targeted, threatened, and doxxed simply for doing their jobs."

A record earned in a courtroom gets a second look. A badge earned on the border gets none.

They never believed in second chances. They believed in choosing who gets one. 💎

AB, yüksek riskli yapay zekâ kurallarının uygulanmasını 2 Aralık 2027'ye erteledi. Ancak bu ertelemenin Türk şirketleri için konuyu gündemden düşürmediğinin vurgulanması gerekir. Yapay Zekâ Tüzüğü AB sınırında durmuyor: AB'ye yapay zekâ sistemi sunan ya da sisteminin çıktısı AB'de kullanılan şirketler, nerede kurulu olursa olsun kapsamda. "Yüksek risk" kategorisi de geniş: işe alım ve İK araçları, kredi skorlama, eğitim, biyometri. Uyum; risk yönetimi, dokümantasyon, insan gözetimi ve AB veri tabanına kayıt demek. AB'de müşterisi olan teknoloji şirketlerinin bu çeyrek atabileceği iki adım var: geliştirilen ya da satılan tüm yapay zekâ araçlarını listelemek ve en büyük AB müşterisine, tedarikçiden ne bekleyeceğini sormak. Bu sorunun düzenleyiciden önce müşteriden gelmesi muhtemel.
(Değişiklik, 27 Temmuz 2026'da yürürlüğe giren (AB) 2026/1744 sayılı Tüzük ile yapıldı.)
—
The EU has postponed its high-risk AI rules to 2 December 2027. It should be stressed, however, that the delay does not take the issue off the agenda for Turkish companies. The AI Act does not stop at the EU border: companies that offer AI systems in the EU, or whose system output is used there, are in scope wherever they are based. The high-risk category is broad: hiring and HR tools, credit scoring, education, biometrics. Compliance means risk management, documentation, human oversight and registration in an EU database. Thirteen months remain. Tech companies with EU customers can take two steps this quarter: list every AI tool they build or sell, and ask their largest EU client what it will expect from them as a supplier. The client is likely to ask before the regulator does.
(The change was made by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026.) Bu paylaşım genel bilgilendirme amaçlıdır, hukuki görüş niteliği taşımaz. / General information, not legal advice.

text:
A year or so ago, Xiao Li was seeing floods of Nvidia chip deals on WeChat. A real estate contractor turned data center project manager, he had pivoted to AI infrastructure in 2023, drawn by the promise of China’s AI craze. 

At that time, traders in his circle bragged about securing shipments of high-performing Nvidia GPUs that were subject to US export restrictions. Many were smuggled through overseas channels to Shenzhen. At the height of the demand, a single Nvidia H100 chip, a kind that is essential to training AI models, could sell for up to 200,000 yuan ($28,000) on the black market. 

Now, his WeChat feed and industry group chats tell a different story. Traders are more discreet in their dealings, and prices have come back down to earth. Meanwhile, two data center projects Li is familiar with are struggling to secure further funding from investors who anticipate poor returns, forcing project leads to sell off surplus GPUs. “It seems like everyone is selling, but few are buying,” he says.

Just months ago, a boom in data center construction was at its height, fueled by both government and private investors. However, many newly built facilities are now sitting empty. According to people on the ground who spoke to MIT Technology Review—including contractors, an executive at a GPU server company, and project managers—most of the companies running these data centers are struggling to stay afloat. The local Chinese outlets Jiazi Guangnian and 36Kr report that up to 80% of China’s newly built computing resources remain unused.

Renting out GPUs to companies that need them for training AI models—the main business model for the new wave of data centers—was once seen as a sure bet. But with the rise of DeepSeek and a sudden change in the economics around AI, the industry is faltering.

“The growing pain China’s AI industry is going through is largely a result of inexperienced players—corporations and local governments—jumping on the hype train, building facilities that aren’t optimal for today’s need,” says Jimmy Goodrich, senior advisor for technology to the RAND Corporation. 

The upshot is that projects are failing, energy is being wasted, and data centers have become “distressed assets” whose investors are keen to unload them at below-market rates. The situation may eventually prompt government intervention, he says: “The Chinese government is likely to step in, take over, and hand them off to more capable operators.”

A chaotic building boom

When ChatGPT exploded onto the scene in late 2022, the response in China was swift. The central government designated AI infrastructure as a national priority, urging local governments to accelerate the development of so-called smart computing centers—a term coined to describe AI-focused data centers.

In 2023 and 2024, over 500 new data center projects were announced everywhere from Inner Mongolia to Guangdong, according to KZ Consulting, a market research firm. According to the China Communications Industry Association Data Center Committee, a state-affiliated industry association, at least 150 of the newly built data centers were finished and running by the end of 2024. State-owned enterprises, publicly traded firms, and state-affiliated funds lined up to invest in them, hoping to position themselves as AI front-runners. Local governments heavily promoted them in the hope they’d stimulate the economy and establish their region as a key AI hub. 

However, as these costly construction projects continue, the Chinese frenzy over large language models is losing momentum. In 2024 alone, over 144 companies registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China—the country’s central internet regulator—to develop their own LLMs. Yet according to the Economic Observer, a Chinese publication, only about 10% of those companies were still actively investing in large-scale model training by the end of the year.

China’s political system is highly centralized, with local government officials typically moving up the ranks through regional appointments. As a result, many local leaders prioritize short-term economic projects that demonstrate quick results—often to gain favor with higher-ups—rather than long-term development. Large, high-profile infrastructure projects have long been a tool for local officials to boost their political careers.

The post-pandemic economic downturn only intensified this dynamic. With China’s real estate sector—once the backbone of local economies—slumping for the first time in decades, officials scrambled to find alternative growth drivers. In the meantime, the country’s once high-flying internet industry was also entering a period of stagnation. In this vacuum, AI infrastructure became the new stimulus of choice.

“AI felt like a shot of adrenaline,” says Li. “A lot of money that used to flow into real estate is now going into AI data centers.”

By 2023, major corporations—many of them with little prior experience in AI—began partnering with local governments to capitalize on the trend. Some saw AI infrastructure as a way to justify business expansion or boost stock prices, says Fang Cunbao, a data center project manager based in Beijing. Among them were companies like Lotus, an MSG manufacturer, and Jinlun Technology, a textile firm—hardly the names one would associate with cutting-edge AI technology.

This gold-rush approach meant that the push to build AI data centers was largely driven from the top down, often with little regard for actual demand or technical feasibility, say Fang, Li, and multiple on-the-ground sources, who asked to speak anonymously for fear of political repercussions. Many projects were led by executives and investors with limited expertise in AI infrastructure, they say. In the rush to keep up, many were constructed hastily and fell short of industry standards. 

“Putting all these large clusters of chips together is a very difficult exercise, and there are very few companies or individuals who know how to do it at scale,” says Goodrich. “This is all really state-of-the-art computer engineering. I’d be surprised if most of these smaller players know how to do it. A lot of the freshly built data centers are quickly strung together and don’t offer the stability that a company like DeepSeek would want.”

To make matters worse, project leaders often relied on middlemen and brokers—some of whom exaggerated demand forecasts or manipulated procurement processes to pocket government subsidies, sources say. 

By the end of 2024, the excitement that once surrounded China’s data center boom was  curdling into disappointment. The reason is simple: GPU rental is no longer a particularly  lucrative business.

The DeepSeek reckoning

The business model of data centers is in theory straightforward: They make money by renting out GPU clusters to companies that need computing capacity for AI training. In reality, however, securing clients is proving difficult. Only a few top tech companies in China are now drawing heavily on computing power to train their AI models. Many smaller players have been giving up on pretraining their models or otherwise shifting their strategy since the rise of DeepSeek, which broke the internet with R1, its open-source reasoning model that matches the performance of ChatGPT o1 but was built at a fraction of its cost. 

“DeepSeek is a moment of reckoning for the Chinese AI industry. The burning question shifted from ‘Who can make the best large language model?’ to ‘Who can use them better?’” says Hancheng Cao, an assistant professor of information systems at Emory University. 

The rise of reasoning models like DeepSeek’s R1 and OpenAI’s ChatGPT o1 and o3 has also changed what businesses want from a data center. With this technology, most of the computing needs come from conducting step-by-step logical deductions in response to users’ queries, not from the process of training and creating the model in the first place. This reasoning process often yields better results but takes significantly more time. As a result, hardware with low latency (the time it takes for data to pass from one point on a network to another) is paramount. Data centers need to be located near major tech hubs to minimize transmission delays and ensure access to highly skilled operations and maintenance staff. 

This change means many data centers built in central, western, and rural China—where electricity and land are cheaper—are losing their allure to AI companies. In Zhengzhou, a city in Li’s home province of Henan, a newly built data center is even distributing free computing vouchers to local tech firms but still struggles to attract clients. 

Additionally, a lot of the new data centers that have sprung up in recent years were optimized for pretraining workloads—large, sustained computations run on massive data sets—rather than for inference, the process of running trained reasoning models to respond to user inputs in real time. Inference-friendly hardware differs from what’s traditionally used for large-scale AI training. 

GPUs like Nvidia H100 and A100 are designed for massive data processing, prioritizing speed and memory capacity. But as AI moves toward real-time reasoning, the industry seeks chips that are more efficient, responsive, and cost-effective. Even a minor miscalculation in infrastructure needs can render a data center suboptimal for the tasks clients require.

In these circumstances, the GPU rental price has dropped to an all-time low. A recent report from the Chinese media outlet Zhineng Yongxian said that an Nvidia H100 server configured with eight GPUs now rents for 75,000 yuan per month, down from highs of around 180,000. Some data centers would rather leave their facilities sitting empty than run the risk of losing even more money because they are so costly to run, says Fan: “The revenue from having a tiny part of the data center running simply wouldn’t cover the electricity and maintenance cost.”

“It’s paradoxical—China faces the highest acquisition costs for Nvidia chips, yet GPU leasing prices are extraordinarily low,” Li says. There’s an oversupply of computational power, especially in central and west China, but at the same time, there’s a shortage of cutting-edge chips. 

However, not all brokers were looking to make money from data centers in the first place. Instead, many were interested in gaming government benefits all along. Some operators exploit the sector for subsidized green electricity, obtaining permits to generate and sell power, according to Fang and some Chinese media reports. Instead of using the energy for AI workloads, they resell it back to the grid at a premium. In other cases, companies acquire land for data center development to qualify for state-backed loans and credits, leaving facilities unused while still benefiting from state funding, according to the local media outlet Jiazi Guangnian.

“Towards the end of 2024, no clear-headed contractor and broker in the market would still go into the business expecting direct profitability,” says Fang. “Everyone I met is leveraging the data center deal for something else the government could offer.”

A necessary evil

Despite the underutilization of data centers, China’s central government is still throwing its weight behind a push for AI infrastructure. In early 2025, it convened an AI industry symposium, emphasizing the importance of self-reliance in this technology. 

Major Chinese tech companies are taking note, making investments aligning with this national priority. Alibaba Group announced plans to invest over $50 billion in cloud computing and AI hardware infrastructure over the next three years, while ByteDance plans to invest around $20 billion in GPUs and data centers.

In the meantime, companies in the US are doing likewise. Major tech firms including OpenAI, Softbank, and Oracle have teamed up to commit to the Stargate initiative, which plans to invest up to $500 billion over the next four years to build advanced data centers and computing infrastructure. ​Given the AI competition between the two countries, experts say that China is unlikely to scale back its efforts. “If generative AI is going to be the killer technology, infrastructure is going to be the determinant of success,”  says Goodrich, the tech policy advisor to RAND.

“The Chinese central government will likely see [underused data centers] as a necessary evil to develop an important capability, a growing pain of sorts. You have the failed projects and distressed assets, and the state will consolidate and clean it up. They see the end, not the means,” Goodrich says.

Demand remains strong for Nvidia chips, and especially the H20 chip, which was custom-designed for the Chinese market. One industry source, who requested not to be identified under his company policy, confirmed that the H20, a lighter, faster model optimized for AI inference, is currently the most popular Nvidia chip, followed by the H100, which continues to flow steadily into China even though sales are officially restricted by US sanctions. Some of the new demand is driven by companies deploying their own versions of DeepSeek’s open-source models.

For now, many data centers in China sit in limbo—built for a future that has yet to arrive. Whether they will find a second life remains uncertain. For Fang Cunbao, DeepSeek’s success has become a moment of reckoning, casting doubt on the assumption that an endless expansion of AI infrastructure guarantees progress.

That’s just a myth, he now realizes. At the start of this year, Fang decided to quit the data center industry altogether. “The market is too chaotic. The early adopters profited, but now it’s just people chasing policy loopholes,” he says. He’s decided to go into AI education next. 

“What stands between now and a future where AI is actually everywhere,” he says, “is not infrastructure anymore, but solid plans to deploy the technology.”

text:
Before his ouster, Nvidia ($NVDA) founder Jensen Huang reportedly belittled incoming CEO Colette Kress during an August clash over AI financing, calling her "a deer in the headlights" and a "reporting CFO" incapable of shaping strategy or making decisions, The Wall Street Journal reports.

* Internal Clash: Kress questioned deal selection, guarantee valuations and returns as Huang grew concerned about billions in financial exposure to AI customers unable to afford Nvidia chips.
* Family Involvement: Huang's son-in-law Nico Caprez, promoted to VP in January, and executive Raj Mirpuri offered cloud providers credit guarantees, sometimes promising deals within weeks. Nvidia sought a share of customer revenue in exchange for guarantees designed to lower borrowing costs. Kress reportedly tried to rein in Caprez.
* OpenAI Deal: Nvidia considered a $250B backstop for an Ohio data center OpenAI planned to lease and equip with roughly $300B in Nvidia chips. After the proposal surfaced in July, shares fell 5%, erasing $250B in market value. Kress halved Nvidia's initial commitment before a smaller deal was signed August 17.
* Financing Pullback: Nvidia later paused some deals, adding executive and board reviews that slowed approvals. Kress publicly defended the investments, disputing circular-financing concerns and predicting excellent returns.
* Competitive Pressure: Huang warned major cloud customers were developing alternative chips to reduce Nvidia dependence, while enormous wafer and memory purchase commitments approached like an "avalanche."
* Valuation Concerns: Huang privately expressed frustration as Nvidia's average monthly valuation multiple fell from 23 in May to 16 in October. Nvidia responded partly with a record stock buyback.

text:
GRIFFIN INDICTED IN $51 MILLION JACKSONVILLE HEALTH CARE FRAUD

Charlie Bernard Griffin III, 61, of Jacksonville, Florida, was charged in a 31-count federal indictment with health care fraud and money laundering. Accountant Ethelbert Chinenye Nwanegbo, 47, of St. Johns, was charged in the same indictment with money laundering.

Griffin owned First Coast Community Development, which operated a pharmacy. A marketing company offered free cellphones in low-income areas to collect insurance details. The pharmacy then submitted claims for HIV medications using fake diagnoses for people who were never seen or examined by a medical professional.

The scheme caused tens of thousands of fraudulent claims and about $51 million in reimbursements from Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers. Griffin received about $14 million in proceeds. Prosecutors seek forfeiture of more than $14 million in fraud proceeds, over $17 million in money-laundering property, $8.1 million already seized from bank accounts, three real properties, and four vehicles.

Each defendant faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count.

text:
A note before you read: another post on the 1913 killing of Mary Phagan and the legal fight over her convicted killer.

On Thursday, November 13, 1913, 113 years ago, The Atlanta Journal reported on Page 1, Column 6: "Judge Halts Trial Of Jim Conley As Dorsey Begins It."

Mary Anne Phagan, 13, was murdered at the National Pencil Company in Atlanta on Saturday, April 26, 1913. A Fulton County jury convicted Leo Max Frank, the factory superintendent, on Monday, August 25, 1913. Judge Leonard Strickland Roan of the Fulton County Superior Court denied him a new trial on Friday, October 31, 1913, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction on Tuesday, February 17, 1914.

When Jim Conley's accessory case was called at 1:45 PM, fifteen minutes before adjournment, Judge Benjamin Harvey Hill refused to start. Courthouse talk said he wanted to await the Supreme Court's action on Leo Max Frank's appeal. Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey had begun, "Your honor, we start this case on an agreed statement of facts," when the judge stopped him.

After a conference with Dorsey and Attorney William M. Smith, the case went over at least to Monday.

The Journal reminded readers that Dorsey had said he would not try Conley as the principal while he was solicitor, and that trying Conley now as accessory would bar a later murder trial if Frank won a new trial and an acquittal.

The defense version, then and now: Hill's pause shows everyone knew Conley might be the real murderer.

The prosecution's answer at the time: Dorsey still wanted Conley's accessory case settled on the facts Conley had already sworn.

Our modern rebuttal: protecting the ability to retry a principal is ordinary caution. It does not overturn the jury that already convicted Frank. Conley's own story named Frank as the killer.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

#MaryPhagan #LeoFrank

Appendix: Full article transcript

The Atlanta Journal,
Thursday, 13th November 1913,
PAGE 1, COLUMN 6.
Bench Gives No Reason, but
After Conference, Case Goes
Over to Monday—May Wait on Frank
When the case against Jim Conley, the negro indicted as an accessory after the fact in the Mary Phagan murder, was called for trial Thursday afternoon at 1:45 o'clock, just fifteen minutes before the regular hour for the court to adjourn.

Judge Ben H. Hill announced that he would not begin the trial at this time.
Judge Hill did not offer any reasons why he postponed the trial, but it is believed around the court house that he wishes to await the action of the supreme court upon the appeal for a new trial of Leo M. Frank, who is under conviction as the principal in the Phagan murder.

Should Conley be tried on the charge of an accessory after the fact it would be impossible to put him on trial as the principal in the event he later confessed , or that Frank got a new trial and was acquitted.
Judge Hill's action has at least temporarily blocked Solicitor Dorsey in his plan to try Conley and definitely settle his fate.

During the trial of Frank the solicitor made the dramatic statement that not as long as he was solicitor would Conley be tried on an indictment charging him with being the principal in the murder. Ilhan Omar dodges questions about probe into gay ‘brother’ ex-husband — claims she has no idea what it’s about | Ally Goelz, New York Post

Rep. Ilhan Omar dodged questions about the federal investigations targeting her Tuesday, claiming she has no idea what the probes are about — before refusing to address questions about whether her alleged brother and former husband is gay.

The Minnesota Democrat was confronted by a Fox News Digital reporter on Capitol Hill, where she offered few details about the investigations or the personal belongings federal agents seized during an October raid on her Washington, DC, home.

“We’re just wondering if the government is giving you your devices back, after you tried?” the reporter asked Omar.

“I’ve gotten most of it back,” the congresswoman replied.

Pressed on whether the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice were conducting separate investigations, Omar appeared unsure.

“I’m not sure,” she said. “You probably have more details on that.”

In a separate exchange, the reporter asked Omar whether federal authorities had told her what she was being investigated for.

“No, no,” Omar responded, according to Fox News Digital.

The reporter also pressed Omar on The Post’s previous reporting about her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, who described himself as a “gay man” and a “gay person” in an academic paper published earlier this year.

Omar declined to answer and continued walking.

Elmi, a doctoral researcher at the University of Bristol, described himself as “a gay man of the East African diaspora” in an August 2026 paper titled “Out in the Field: Notes on Researching Queer Violence in Kenya.”

The congresswoman’s marriage to Elmi has faced scrutiny for years, with critics alleging that the two were secretly siblings and that their marriage was a sham designed to help him obtain immigration benefits. Omar has denied the allegations.

A 2016 investigation by federal authorities examined the allegations, but the case reportedly stalled after prosecutors determined that any potential criminal violations had fallen outside the five-year statute of limitations.

The renewed scrutiny comes as Omar faces multiple federal investigations.

Homeland Security Investigations agents raided her Washington home on Oct. 12 as part of a criminal probe examining whether Omar or her family members provided false information on immigration paperwork when they entered the US as refugees in the 1990s or during her naturalization process.

Agents seized electronic devices, her passport, and other materials during the search. Investigators also reportedly obtained a DNA sample and issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to members of her family.

Omar arrived in the US as a refugee in 1995 and became an American citizen in 2000, and has characterized the investigations as politically motivated and denied wrongdoing.

Following the October raid, she took to X to blast the administration.

“I’m OK. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote. “For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and a smear campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

text:
New ICE detention facility opens in Minnesota after $496M federal purchase | The Center Square Staff, Just The News

The privately owned, 1,600-bed prison had sat vacant for 16 years before it was offered to the state of Minnesota for $75 million in 2025, according to documents obtained by local media.

The federal government opened a new detention facility in Minnesota on Monday, a move it says will help U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement better enforce immigration laws.

The facility, located in western Minnesota near the South Dakota border, was purchased by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in August for $495.6 million.

The Minnesota Department of Corrections declined the offer, and federal taxpayers paid $420 million more for the property just a year later. Appleton Detention Facility, formerly known as the Prairie Correctional Facility, began housing ICE detainees this week and is expected to be fully operational by mid-2027.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to The Center Square’s request for comment on the price difference, instead defending the purchase by pointing to the facility’s planned role in immigration enforcement.

“DHS opened the Appleton Detention Facility on November 9 to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations,” a DHS spokesperson told The Center Square in a statement on Wednesday. “The site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction.”

CoreCivic, one of the nation’s largest private prison operators, said in a press release that the purchase price was a “fair market value.”

“The federal government's purchase price for the Prairie Correctional Facility (Appleton Detention Facility) should be understood in the context of the appraisal process that governs federal real property acquisitions, which is designed to determine objective fair market value,” CoreCivic said.

It added that the property’s purchase price was based on independent appraisals conducted by federal government-hired appraisers, who used a cost-based methodology that accounted for replacement costs, depreciation, land value and other market factors. The appraisal, which also accounted for significant facility renovations, was then reviewed by the government for compliance with federal standards.

CoreCivic also directly addressed the discrepancies between the $75 million and $495.6 million numbers, stating they measured “two different things at vastly different points in a valuation process.”

Located about three hours west of the Twin Cities, Appleton Detention Facility sits in a town of roughly 1,400 residents. The Twin Cities saw widespread protests earlier this year during the federal immigration operation known as Metro Surge.

The facility is expected to create more than 500 jobs, though some local residents have raised concerns about ICE's presence and the loss of property tax revenue for both the county and city, as federal properties are exempt from local property taxes.

DHS said this new facility will be a helpful resource in its immigration operations.

“Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe,” its spokesperson told The Center Square. “It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and ensuring we have resources to carry out President Trump’s mission.”

Border & Cartel update 13 November 2026

THE PRESS
•An AP investigation published this week finds that journalists in Mexico's federal protection program say it often fails them. The Committee to Protect Journalists counts seven journalists killed in Mexico this year, six of them in less than three months. Tlaxcala reporter Alberto Amaro says he waited more than 48 hours for help after reporting gunshots at his home, and authorities tried to pull his protection even after acknowledging he remained at high risk; the federal agency declined AP's interview requests.
•No new killing of a journalist in Mexico turned up in the past 24 hours.
•Mexican reporters can't cover the cartels the way U.S. outlets can. Many fear being killed for it, so much of what follows rests on official statements.

THE BORDER
•Breitbart Texas (Randy Clark): a federal grand jury in the Western District of Texas indicted 14 people, four of them U.S. citizens, in the alleged train smuggling ring tied to the deaths of seven migrants, including a 14-year-old Honduran, locked in a shipping container in May. Prosecutors say the group moved migrants inland in rail containers from at least April 2023, charging $1,500 to $10,000 a person, and that smugglers who opened the container in San Antonio fled when they found the occupants in peril. A rail worker found the bodies in Laredo on May 10.
•Breitbart (Ortiz & Darby): Mexican police have begun escorting the "Dios con Nosotros" caravan, estimated at 800 to 1,000 people, and towns are letting migrants sleep in municipal auditoriums as they walk toward Mexico City. President Trump said Thursday that tariffs on Mexico would "DOUBLE IMMEDIATELY" if Mexico does not stop the caravans. President Sheinbaum answered that no caravan has reached the northern border since Trump took office, said one group in Chiapas has shrunk from about 600 to fewer than 100, and said most migrants go home once told they cannot cross.
•Breitbart Texas (Ortiz & Darby): former Necaxa, Atlas and Santos Laguna goalkeeper Pedro Hernández Calderón, 54, is held without bond after his arrest in Laredo. Prosecutors allege he received fake luxury watches from overseas at his Laredo import-export business and shipped them to buyers in Mexico, worth up to $5.4 million. Most of the case remains sealed.

MEXICO
•Breitbart (Ortiz & Darby) exclusive: the Gulf Cartel has restarted a propaganda campaign to pressure Mexico to back off enforcement, putting women and children at the front of a protest at the Camargo municipal building, across from Rio Grande City, where men kicked in the door and tried to set it on fire. Tamaulipas police had seized protest signs and envelopes of cash the day before. Breitbart obtained photos showing cartel members meeting with and directing local journalist and social media page operator Juan José Mejorado Gómez to push claims of police abuse, which it confirmed with Mexican federal security forces.
•Ocotlán, Jalisco: soldiers responding to a stolen-vehicle report Thursday afternoon were attacked by gunmen the security cabinet ties to the Jalisco cartel. The army says two attackers were killed and a Honduran man was arrested; a soldier and a woman were wounded and are stable. Troops seized an improvised armored vehicle, a .50-caliber Barrett rifle, a machine gun and two 40mm grenades, and schools in the area suspended classes.
•Follow-up on "R2": a federal judge ruled the arrests legal, but released 15 of the 20 people detained with Rafael Álvarez Ayala, including the band Los Arras and restaurant staff, to face charges free. Five alleged CJNG operatives stay jailed. Prosecutors told the court that the wounded Álvarez Ayala offered marines money and his vehicles to let him go; his own hearing was suspended because pain medication left him unable to stay awake, and a judge has granted him a provisional suspension against extradition.
•Culiacán: gunmen shot up two homes Thursday, in Juntas de Humaya and the Los Ángeles subdivision, with no one hurt. That night a 27-year-old man was killed after armed men chased him through the Riberas de Tamazula neighborhood.

GOVERNMENT & CARTELS
•Breitbart Texas (Ortiz & Darby): federal prosecutors in Los Angeles unsealed a six-count indictment against Robert "Fatboy" Gomez, 51, a 38th Street gang member who fled to Mexico in 2000, alleging he used contacts in Mexican and U.S. law enforcement to pass sensitive police information to Olympian-turned-drug-lord Ryan Wedding. A second indictment names Edgar Aaron Vázquez Alvarado, "El General," founder of Cártel Nuevo Imperio, who was killed by Mexican police last week. Prosecutors allege he paid Mexican officials to slow investigations and lose evidence, gave Wedding's network rotating code words to get cocaine through police and military checkpoints, and charged Wedding a $500,000 entry fee plus about $100,000 a month, CTV/CP24 reports.

WASHINGTON

Bessent tied the move to a fraud crackdown in Minnesota.
•President Sheinbaum said she won't meet Trump at the APEC summit in China but expects to see him at the G20 at Mar-a-Lago.

LATIN AMERICA

The raids in Manabí netted 14 arrests and about 500 kilograms of cocaine at a hidden mangrove dock used for go-fast boats; one of those arrested, an elderly woman, allegedly used her wheelchair to move drugs.

A trade and investment delegation from St. Louis, Missouri, led by Mayor Cara Spencer, is visiting Kenya to deepen Kenya–United States commercial relations and unlock new opportunities for exporters, businesses and investors.

As part of the visit,a High-Level Trade and Investment Roundtable was held in Nairobi, jointly convened by the Embassy of Kenya in Washington, D.C., the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi and AMCHAM Kenya bringing together government representatives, business leaders and institutions to explore partnerships that promote trade, strengthen local production and create jobs.

The engagement underscores Kenya’s commitment to expanding commercial diplomacy beyond national capitals by building direct connections with American cities, states and business communities.

In remarks delivered on her behalf by Deputy Director for International Trade, Robert Ng’ong’a, Principal Secretary for Trade Regina Ombam outlined key priority areas for collaboration, including agriculture and agro-processing; healthcare, pharmaceuticals and biosciences; ICT and digital services; manufacturing and infrastructure; as well as tourism, education and cultural exchange.

The State Department for Foreign Affairs was represented by Mr. Evans Maturo, Deputy Director General for Economic and Commercial Affairs, while the State Department for Agriculture was represented by the Agriculture Secretary, Mr. James Wanjohi.

Kenya is keen to strengthen linkages between local exporters and American buyers, with significant opportunities in specialty coffee, value-added tea, macadamia nuts, processed foods, apparel and textiles, leather products, flowers and eligible horticultural products. The focus is on increasing both the volume and diversity of Kenyan exports to the U.S. market while creating new opportunities for local enterprises.

The mission was coordinated by Mr. Geoffrey Odero, Commercial Attaché at the Embassy of Kenya in Washington, D.C., who facilitated strategic engagements and connected the visiting delegation with key government and private-sector partners.

With its strategic location, skilled workforce and growing digital economy, Kenya offers an attractive investment destination and a gateway to the wider regional and continental markets through the East African Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area.

To translate the discussions into tangible outcomes, Kenya has proposed the establishment of a Kenya–St. Louis Commercial Cooperation Framework bringing together the State Department for Trade, Nairobi City County and World Trade Center St. Louis. The proposed framework will provide a platform for coordinated follow-up on identified business opportunities and strengthen institutional and business linkages beyond the visit.

text:
Bild reports that Russia wants Finland out of NATO, no NATO military bases in Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania, and all of Donbas handed to Moscow, including areas Ukraine still holds. Russian representatives raised the terms in informal talks on ending the war, not for a ceasefire.

THE DEMANDS ON UKRAINE

Moscow would keep every Ukrainian territory it currently occupies. Ukraine must declare itself non-aligned and abandon its ambition to join NATO, though EU membership would remain possible.

Russia also wants the ports of Odesa and Mykolaiv demilitarized. It wants agreements on freedom of navigation in both the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea. That would extend a supposed peace settlement from Ukraine’s land and defences to the maritime routes on which its trade depends.

A REWRITE OF EUROPE’S SECURITY

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania would remain NATO members. Neither demand concerns territory Russia occupies in Ukraine. Both seek to make other European states less able to choose how they defend themselves.

Moldova is in the package too. Moscow wants a federation that includes Transnistria and Gagauzia. If Moldova joins the EU, those regions would gain the right to hold independence referendums. Russia is trying to attach conditions to Moldova’s future as part of talks ostensibly meant to end its invasion of Ukraine.

WHAT MOSCOW OFFERS

In exchange, Russia is reportedly prepared to remove nuclear weapons from Belarus. It would refrain from stationing intermediate-range missiles there and withdraw its troops from Transnistria. Those offers are being set against the demands on Ukraine and NATO allies.

The Wall Street Journal reports that the Kremlin has focused on strikes against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and pressure on Europe. That came after Russia’s army failed to break Ukrainian resistance and Trump failed to compel Ukraine to concede territory. Bild’s reported terms show what that pressure is meant to buy: concessions from Ukraine, NATO and Moldova in return for steps Moscow itself could take.
