text:
A scientific demolition of climate-change denial

How a collection of genuine geological facts is manipulated to produce a profoundly misleading conclusion.

The passage is an unusually sophisticated example of climate-change misinformation. Unlike crude assertions that global warming is a hoax, it deploys genuine scientific findings, impressive geological timescales and apparently authoritative statistics. Much of its descriptive material is broadly correct.

But its central argument is scientifically indefensible. It confuses the conditions under which life evolved over hundreds of millions of years with the conditions under which human civilisation developed over a few thousand. It confuses the oceans' enormous capacity to absorb heat with an ability to make excess heat disappear. And it invokes natural processes operating over tens of thousands or millions of years to explain away a dramatic change occurring within a single human lifetime.

Above all, it commits one enormous intellectual fraud: because the Earth has been much warmer in the distant past, it concludes that rapid warming today cannot be dangerous.

That is about as sensible as arguing that because human beings can survive temperatures of 40°C, a sudden rise in someone's body temperature from 37°C to 40°C is nothing to worry about.

1. The 542-million-year deception

The author cites Judd and colleagues' important 2024 Science paper reconstructing global temperatures over the Phanerozoic Eon.

The research is genuine. Its use here is misleading.

Earth has indeed experienced much warmer climates, sometimes without permanent polar ice sheets. But these climates existed under radically different conditions of continental geography, ocean circulation, atmospheric composition and biological evolution.

Modern civilisation, agriculture, cities, infrastructure and coastal settlements developed during the comparatively stable climate of the Holocene, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago.

The relevant question is not whether dinosaurs inhabited a warmer planet. It is whether eight billion people, their agricultural systems, water supplies and coastal cities can accommodate extraordinarily rapid climatic change without immense disruption.

Furthermore, the geological evidence is not a refutation of carbon dioxide's warming influence. It helps demonstrate that influence: atmospheric CO₂ has been an important contributor to the great temperature changes in Earth's history.

2. The claim that 1,000 ppm of CO₂ would be 'ideal'

This is an assertion masquerading as science.

Carbon dioxide is essential to photosynthesis. Nobody disputes that. But the fact that a substance is necessary for life does not mean that increasing its concentration indefinitely is beneficial.

Water is essential to life too. That does not make flooding desirable.

The author offers no scientifically defensible basis for declaring 1,000 parts per million an ideal atmospheric concentration.

Pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ was approximately 280 ppm. It has now risen above 420 ppm, an increase of more than 50%, principally because of human activities.

The increase has been extraordinarily rapid by geological standards.

The scientific issue is not whether CO₂ is poisonous at current concentrations. It is whether adding it to the atmosphere changes Earth's energy balance.

It does. That is elementary, experimentally established atmospheric physics.

CO₂ absorbs and emits infrared radiation. Increasing its concentration reduces the rate at which heat escapes to space until the climate warms sufficiently to restore the energy balance.

The suggestion that because CO₂ was higher millions of years ago it cannot cause dangerous warming today turns the geological evidence on its head.

3. The oceans: the most revealing distortion

Here the author presents some largely correct information and then draws precisely the wrong conclusion.

Yes, the oceans store vastly more heat than the atmosphere.

Yes, they absorb approximately 90% of the excess heat accumulating in the climate system.

But consider what that means.

The oceans are absorbing the overwhelming majority of the additional heat trapped by greenhouse gases. They are not disproving global warming. They are recording it.

Ocean heat content has risen dramatically, and measurements show continuing accumulation of energy.

The oceans' enormous heat capacity delays atmospheric warming, but it does not prevent it. Nor does the energy simply disappear.

Warming oceans expand, contributing to rising sea levels. They intensify marine heatwaves, damage coral ecosystems and influence atmospheric weather patterns.

The author describes the oceans as the Earth's air conditioners. That analogy is deeply misleading. An air conditioner transfers heat out of a room. The oceans largely store and redistribute heat within the Earth system.

The distinction is fundamental.

4. Water vapour: the familiar greenhouse-gas trick

The author correctly observes that water vapour makes a larger contribution to Earth's natural greenhouse effect than CO₂.

But this is not an argument against human-caused warming.

Water vapour acts predominantly as a feedback, whereas the human addition of long-lived CO₂ is an important forcing.

As CO₂ warms the atmosphere, warmer air can contain more water vapour. That additional water vapour amplifies the original warming.

In other words, the very importance of water vapour makes CO₂-driven warming more consequential, not less.

The passage also confuses the relative contributions of different greenhouse gases to the existing greenhouse effect with their roles in causing the present increase in temperature.

These are two different questions.

5. Milankovitch cycles cannot explain the present warming

The author invokes changes in Earth's orbit and axial orientation.

These are real and important. Milankovitch cycles help explain the pacing of glacial and interglacial periods.

But their principal cycles operate over approximately 23,000, 41,000 and 100,000 years.

They cannot account for the extraordinary warming observed since industrialisation, especially during the last half-century.

Nor can tectonic movements, which generally operate over millions of years.

The passage effectively argues that because very slow natural processes can change the climate, a much faster human-induced process cannot do so.

There is no logical or scientific connection between those propositions.

The existence of natural causes does not exclude additional human causes.

6. 'We are still in an ice age'

Technically, yes.

In geological terminology, Earth remains within an icehouse state because substantial permanent ice sheets survive, particularly in Antarctica and Greenland.

But the author exploits a specialised definition to create a false impression.

Being in a long geological ice age does not mean that rapid warming within an interglacial is harmless.

Indeed, the great continental ice sheets are among the reasons global warming presents a long-term threat.

Their melting contributes to sea-level rise, potentially continuing for centuries or millennia.

The survival of polar ice is not evidence that additional warming is desirable.

7. The most demonstrably false claim: nobody would notice rising seas

The assertion that warming would raise sea levels by only a few millimetres, imperceptibly over a lifetime, is contradicted by direct observation.

Global mean sea level has risen by roughly 20–25 centimetres since 1900, with the rate increasing in recent decades.

That rise is measured using tide gauges and satellites.

It is already affecting coastal communities through more frequent tidal flooding, erosion and saltwater intrusion.

A few millimetres of additional sea level each year may sound trivial. Accumulated over decades, it is anything but.

And sea-level rise is not simply a matter of thermal expansion. Melting land-based glaciers and ice sheets also add water to the oceans.

The author has mistaken the small annual increment for the cumulative effect, and ignored the acceleration.

8. 'There is no global warming crisis'

This is not a scientific conclusion supported by the preceding evidence. It is a political declaration.

It does not follow from anything established about ancient temperatures, tectonic plates, ocean currents or orbital cycles.

Nor does it follow that wind turbines and solar panels are a 'terrible dead end'.

Renewable-energy technologies have environmental costs, including mining, land use, waste and ecological impacts. These deserve serious scrutiny.

But the relevant comparison is with the environmental and climatic consequences of continuing to burn fossil fuels, not with an imaginary energy system that has no adverse effects.

The author never undertakes that comparison.

The result is not a scientific argument but a polemic dressed in the language of science.

9. The most damning evidence is the paper the author cites

There is a particularly revealing irony in the reference to Judd et al. (2024).

The paper is entitled A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature. Notice, incidentally, that the actual reconstruction covers 485 million years, not the entire 542-million-year Phanerozoic invoked in the passage.

Its authors found a strong relationship between atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperatures, identifying CO₂ as a dominant control on long-term climate variations.

That is virtually the opposite of what this polemic invites readers to believe.

Squarespace+1

The same reversal occurs with the oceans. The author cites their absorption of more than 90% of excess heat as though this makes global warming insignificant. In reality, measurements of increasing ocean heat content are among the strongest independent confirmations that the planet is accumulating energy.

Global Sea Level Change

And the sea-level claim is especially indefensible. The European Environment Agency reports approximately 23 centimetres of global sea-level rise since 1900, while NASA's satellite measurements show that the rise is continuing.

European Environment Agency (EEA)+1

10. What climate science actually says

There is an important distinction between the claim that warming is human-caused and the suggestion that uncontrollable, unlimited 'runaway warming' is inevitable.

The latter is not the mainstream scientific position. Climate scientists do not generally predict a Venus-like runaway greenhouse effect on Earth.

They do establish that human activities have unequivocally caused global warming, that additional greenhouse-gas emissions will produce further warming, and that the risks increase with its magnitude and rate.

IPCC

Recognising this distinction strengthens the scientific argument rather than weakening it.

A concise rebuttal suitable for publication

This is a masterclass in how to misrepresent science without necessarily inventing the facts.

Yes, Earth was warmer millions of years ago. Yes, CO₂ is essential to life. Yes, oceans regulate climate, water vapour is a powerful greenhouse gas, and orbital cycles influence ice ages.

But NONE of these facts refutes human-caused global warming.

Indeed, the 2024 Science paper cited by the author identifies atmospheric CO₂ as a dominant influence on Earth's climate over geological time. The oceans' absorption of 90% of excess heat is evidence of warming, not evidence against it. Water vapour amplifies CO₂-driven warming. Milankovitch cycles operate over tens of thousands of years, not decades.

And the claim that rising seas are imperceptible is demonstrably false: global sea level has risen approximately 23 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is accelerating.

The fundamental deception is to confuse the fact that Earth has survived radically different climates with the proposition that human civilisation can safely endure rapid climatic disruption.

Dinosaurs survived on a warmer planet. That tells us remarkably little about the vulnerability of modern agriculture, freshwater supplies, coastal cities or eight billion human beings.

This is not a refutation of climate science. It is a collection of scientific facts arranged to conceal the conclusions that follow from them.

The most revealing feature is that the author's own principal scientific source contradicts the argument being made.

Principal scientific references

Judd et al., Science (2024): 485 million years of Earth's temperatures

IPCC Sixth Assessment: Observed warming and its causes

IPCC: Greenhouse gases, water vapour and climate feedbacks

European Environment Agency: Measured sea-level rise

NASA: Ocean heat accumulation
The strongest way to challenge the original author is to ask one question: Why cite a major scientific paper about 485 million years of climate history while omitting its central finding that CO₂ is a dominant control on global temperature?
That omission goes to the heart of the argument.

text:
A Palestinian child has died from exposure to the cold in the Gaza Strip, raising the number of children reported to have died from extreme cold since last winter to 13, as Israel continues to block the entry of humanitarian aid and new tents, according to medical sources and humanitarian organizations.

The death of Kinan Ahmed Raqiq was confirmed by Nasser Hospital. According to medical sources, the child died inside his displaced family’s tent in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. His death came shortly after an Israeli airstrike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six Palestinians and wounded more than 20, including patients and medical staff.

Across the enclave, infrastructure devastated by months of massive bombardment has left thousands of families unable to return to their homes. They continue to face shortages of adequate shelter, blankets, heating equipment, and other basic necessities while living in makeshift tents. Israel, meanwhile, continues to violate the ceasefire through attacks, killings, and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance, including trucks carrying thousands of urgently needed new tents.

The alert arrives as winter rains and cold begin to close in on the coastal enclave, where nearly the entire population has been uprooted. Around 1.9 million people, close to 90% of Gaza’s residents, have lost their homes since the war erupted in October 2023. Children make up roughly 40% of the territory’s population, and they have shouldered much of the suffering.

The scale of exposure is staggering. More than half a million children now brace for another season without adequate protection, their fourth consecutive winter since the fighting began. Many are packed into torn tents and improvised shelters that offer little protection from rain and wind.

🙏 A Humble Request on Behalf of the People of Coastal Karnataka!

🚆 Heartfelt Thanks for Introducing the Madgaon–Yeshwantpur Vande Bharat Express!

Hon'ble Prime Minister @narendramodi, Railway Minister @AshwiniVaishnaw, Karnataka Chief Minister @DKShivakumar and all concerned public representatives,

The introduction of the new Vande Bharat Express connecting Madgaon with Yeshwantpur (Bengaluru) is a very welcome development for the people of Coastal Karnataka.

This train will greatly benefit passengers from Karwar, Ankola, Kumta, Honnavar, Bhatkal, Kundapura, Udupi, Mangaluru and surrounding regions.

It will provide better connectivity for students, employees, business people, tourists and senior citizens travelling to Bengaluru.

However, I would like to bring a few important concerns to your attention.

1️⃣ Please Reduce the Ticket Fare

The reported full-route fares are:

• AC Chair Car (CC) – ₹2,015
• Executive Chair Car (EC) – ₹3,580

These fares are quite expensive for middle-class and ordinary families.

Vande Bharat should not become a premium service accessible only to financially well-off passengers. It should also be affordable for common people.

I sincerely request the Railway Ministry to consider reducing the ticket fares.

2️⃣ Reduce the Journey Duration

The current journey takes approximately 13 hours.

The main purpose of introducing Vande Bharat is to provide faster and more comfortable transportation.

I request Indian Railways to explore all technically feasible options to reduce the journey time to around 7–8 hours, if operationally possible.

3️⃣ Consider the Needs of Senior Citizens

Many senior citizens from Coastal Karnataka travel to Bengaluru for medical treatment, family visits and other important purposes.

For elderly passengers, train travel is often more comfortable than long-distance bus journeys.

However, this Vande Bharat service offers only Chair Car seating.

text:
@LilianaHebe A scientific demolition of climate-change denial

How a collection of genuine geological facts is manipulated to produce a profoundly misleading conclusion.

The passage is an unusually sophisticated example of climate-change misinformation. Unlike crude assertions that global warming is a hoax, it deploys genuine scientific findings, impressive geological timescales and apparently authoritative statistics. Much of its descriptive material is broadly correct.

But its central argument is scientifically indefensible. It confuses the conditions under which life evolved over hundreds of millions of years with the conditions under which human civilisation developed over a few thousand. It confuses the oceans' enormous capacity to absorb heat with an ability to make excess heat disappear. And it invokes natural processes operating over tens of thousands or millions of years to explain away a dramatic change occurring within a single human lifetime.

Above all, it commits one enormous intellectual fraud: because the Earth has been much warmer in the distant past, it concludes that rapid warming today cannot be dangerous.

That is about as sensible as arguing that because human beings can survive temperatures of 40°C, a sudden rise in someone's body temperature from 37°C to 40°C is nothing to worry about.

1. The 542-million-year deception

The author cites Judd and colleagues' important 2024 Science paper reconstructing global temperatures over the Phanerozoic Eon.

The research is genuine. Its use here is misleading.

Earth has indeed experienced much warmer climates, sometimes without permanent polar ice sheets. But these climates existed under radically different conditions of continental geography, ocean circulation, atmospheric composition and biological evolution.

Modern civilisation, agriculture, cities, infrastructure and coastal settlements developed during the comparatively stable climate of the Holocene, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago.

The relevant question is not whether dinosaurs inhabited a warmer planet. It is whether eight billion people, their agricultural systems, water supplies and coastal cities can accommodate extraordinarily rapid climatic change without immense disruption.

Furthermore, the geological evidence is not a refutation of carbon dioxide's warming influence. It helps demonstrate that influence: atmospheric CO₂ has been an important contributor to the great temperature changes in Earth's history.

2. The claim that 1,000 ppm of CO₂ would be 'ideal'

This is an assertion masquerading as science.

Carbon dioxide is essential to photosynthesis. Nobody disputes that. But the fact that a substance is necessary for life does not mean that increasing its concentration indefinitely is beneficial.

Water is essential to life too. That does not make flooding desirable.

The author offers no scientifically defensible basis for declaring 1,000 parts per million an ideal atmospheric concentration.

Pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ was approximately 280 ppm. It has now risen above 420 ppm, an increase of more than 50%, principally because of human activities.

The increase has been extraordinarily rapid by geological standards.

The scientific issue is not whether CO₂ is poisonous at current concentrations. It is whether adding it to the atmosphere changes Earth's energy balance.

It does. That is elementary, experimentally established atmospheric physics.

CO₂ absorbs and emits infrared radiation. Increasing its concentration reduces the rate at which heat escapes to space until the climate warms sufficiently to restore the energy balance.

The suggestion that because CO₂ was higher millions of years ago it cannot cause dangerous warming today turns the geological evidence on its head.

3. The oceans: the most revealing distortion

Here the author presents some largely correct information and then draws precisely the wrong conclusion.

Yes, the oceans store vastly more heat than the atmosphere.

Yes, they absorb approximately 90% of the excess heat accumulating in the climate system.

But consider what that means.

The oceans are absorbing the overwhelming majority of the additional heat trapped by greenhouse gases. They are not disproving global warming. They are recording it.

Ocean heat content has risen dramatically, and measurements show continuing accumulation of energy.

The oceans' enormous heat capacity delays atmospheric warming, but it does not prevent it. Nor does the energy simply disappear.

Warming oceans expand, contributing to rising sea levels. They intensify marine heatwaves, damage coral ecosystems and influence atmospheric weather patterns.

The author describes the oceans as the Earth's air conditioners. That analogy is deeply misleading. An air conditioner transfers heat out of a room. The oceans largely store and redistribute heat within the Earth system.

The distinction is fundamental.

4. Water vapour: the familiar greenhouse-gas trick

The author correctly observes that water vapour makes a larger contribution to Earth's natural greenhouse effect than CO₂.

But this is not an argument against human-caused warming.

Water vapour acts predominantly as a feedback, whereas the human addition of long-lived CO₂ is an important forcing.

As CO₂ warms the atmosphere, warmer air can contain more water vapour. That additional water vapour amplifies the original warming.

In other words, the very importance of water vapour makes CO₂-driven warming more consequential, not less.

The passage also confuses the relative contributions of different greenhouse gases to the existing greenhouse effect with their roles in causing the present increase in temperature.

These are two different questions.

5. Milankovitch cycles cannot explain the present warming

The author invokes changes in Earth's orbit and axial orientation.

These are real and important. Milankovitch cycles help explain the pacing of glacial and interglacial periods.

But their principal cycles operate over approximately 23,000, 41,000 and 100,000 years.

They cannot account for the extraordinary warming observed since industrialisation, especially during the last half-century.

Nor can tectonic movements, which generally operate over millions of years.

The passage effectively argues that because very slow natural processes can change the climate, a much faster human-induced process cannot do so.

There is no logical or scientific connection between those propositions.

The existence of natural causes does not exclude additional human causes.

6. 'We are still in an ice age'

Technically, yes.

In geological terminology, Earth remains within an icehouse state because substantial permanent ice sheets survive, particularly in Antarctica and Greenland.

But the author exploits a specialised definition to create a false impression.

Being in a long geological ice age does not mean that rapid warming within an interglacial is harmless.

Indeed, the great continental ice sheets are among the reasons global warming presents a long-term threat.

Their melting contributes to sea-level rise, potentially continuing for centuries or millennia.

The survival of polar ice is not evidence that additional warming is desirable.

7. The most demonstrably false claim: nobody would notice rising seas

The assertion that warming would raise sea levels by only a few millimetres, imperceptibly over a lifetime, is contradicted by direct observation.

Global mean sea level has risen by roughly 20–25 centimetres since 1900, with the rate increasing in recent decades.

That rise is measured using tide gauges and satellites.

It is already affecting coastal communities through more frequent tidal flooding, erosion and saltwater intrusion.

A few millimetres of additional sea level each year may sound trivial. Accumulated over decades, it is anything but.

And sea-level rise is not simply a matter of thermal expansion. Melting land-based glaciers and ice sheets also add water to the oceans.

The author has mistaken the small annual increment for the cumulative effect, and ignored the acceleration.

8. 'There is no global warming crisis'

This is not a scientific conclusion supported by the preceding evidence. It is a political declaration.

It does not follow from anything established about ancient temperatures, tectonic plates, ocean currents or orbital cycles.

Nor does it follow that wind turbines and solar panels are a 'terrible dead end'.

Renewable-energy technologies have environmental costs, including mining, land use, waste and ecological impacts. These deserve serious scrutiny.

But the relevant comparison is with the environmental and climatic consequences of continuing to burn fossil fuels, not with an imaginary energy system that has no adverse effects.

The author never undertakes that comparison.

The result is not a scientific argument but a polemic dressed in the language of science.

9. The most damning evidence is the paper the author cites

There is a particularly revealing irony in the reference to Judd et al. (2024).

The paper is entitled A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature. Notice, incidentally, that the actual reconstruction covers 485 million years, not the entire 542-million-year Phanerozoic invoked in the passage.

Its authors found a strong relationship between atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperatures, identifying CO₂ as a dominant control on long-term climate variations.

That is virtually the opposite of what this polemic invites readers to believe.

Squarespace+1

The same reversal occurs with the oceans. The author cites their absorption of more than 90% of excess heat as though this makes global warming insignificant. In reality, measurements of increasing ocean heat content are among the strongest independent confirmations that the planet is accumulating energy.

Global Sea Level Change

And the sea-level claim is especially indefensible. The European Environment Agency reports approximately 23 centimetres of global sea-level rise since 1900, while NASA's satellite measurements show that the rise is continuing.

European Environment Agency (EEA)+1

10. What climate science actually says

There is an important distinction between the claim that warming is human-caused and the suggestion that uncontrollable, unlimited 'runaway warming' is inevitable.

The latter is not the mainstream scientific position. Climate scientists do not generally predict a Venus-like runaway greenhouse effect on Earth.

They do establish that human activities have unequivocally caused global warming, that additional greenhouse-gas emissions will produce further warming, and that the risks increase with its magnitude and rate.

IPCC

Recognising this distinction strengthens the scientific argument rather than weakening it.

A concise rebuttal suitable for publication

This is a masterclass in how to misrepresent science without necessarily inventing the facts.

Yes, Earth was warmer millions of years ago. Yes, CO₂ is essential to life. Yes, oceans regulate climate, water vapour is a powerful greenhouse gas, and orbital cycles influence ice ages.

But NONE of these facts refutes human-caused global warming.

Indeed, the 2024 Science paper cited by the author identifies atmospheric CO₂ as a dominant influence on Earth's climate over geological time. The oceans' absorption of 90% of excess heat is evidence of warming, not evidence against it. Water vapour amplifies CO₂-driven warming. Milankovitch cycles operate over tens of thousands of years, not decades.

And the claim that rising seas are imperceptible is demonstrably false: global sea level has risen approximately 23 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is accelerating.

The fundamental deception is to confuse the fact that Earth has survived radically different climates with the proposition that human civilisation can safely endure rapid climatic disruption.

Dinosaurs survived on a warmer planet. That tells us remarkably little about the vulnerability of modern agriculture, freshwater supplies, coastal cities or eight billion human beings.

This is not a refutation of climate science. It is a collection of scientific facts arranged to conceal the conclusions that follow from them.

The most revealing feature is that the author's own principal scientific source contradicts the argument being made.

Principal scientific references

Judd et al., Science (2024): 485 million years of Earth's temperatures

IPCC Sixth Assessment: Observed warming and its causes

IPCC: Greenhouse gases, water vapour and climate feedbacks

European Environment Agency: Measured sea-level rise

NASA: Ocean heat accumulation
The strongest way to challenge the original author is to ask one question: Why cite a major scientific paper about 485 million years of climate history while omitting its central finding that CO₂ is a dominant control on global temperature?
That omission goes to the heart of the argument.

It confuses the oceans' enormous capacity to absorb heat with an ability to make excess heat disappear. Above all, it commits one enormous intellectual fraud: because the Earth has been much warmer in the distant past, it concludes that rapid warming today cannot be dangerous.

1. The 542-million-year deception

The author cites Judd and colleagues' important 2024 Science paper reconstructing global temperatures over the Phanerozoic Eon.

The research is genuine. Its use here is misleading.

The relevant question is not whether dinosaurs inhabited a warmer planet. It is whether eight billion people, their agricultural systems, water supplies and coastal cities can accommodate extraordinarily rapid climatic change without immense disruption.

Furthermore, the geological evidence is not a refutation of carbon dioxide's warming influence. It helps demonstrate that influence: atmospheric CO₂ has been an important contributor to the great temperature changes in Earth's history.

2. The claim that 1,000 ppm of CO₂ would be 'ideal'

This is an assertion masquerading as science.

Carbon dioxide is essential to photosynthesis. Nobody disputes that. But the fact that a substance is necessary for life does not mean that increasing its concentration indefinitely is beneficial.

Water is essential to life too. That does not make flooding desirable.

The author offers no scientifically defensible basis for declaring 1,000 parts per million an ideal atmospheric concentration.

Pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ was approximately 280 ppm. It has now risen above 420 ppm, an increase of more than 50%, principally because of human activities.

The increase has been extraordinarily rapid by geological standards.

The scientific issue is not whether CO₂ is poisonous at current concentrations. It is whether adding it to the atmosphere changes Earth's energy balance.

It does. That is elementary, experimentally established atmospheric physics.

CO₂ absorbs and emits infrared radiation. Increasing its concentration reduces the rate at which heat escapes to space until the climate warms sufficiently to restore the energy balance.

The suggestion that because CO₂ was higher millions of years ago it cannot cause dangerous warming today turns the geological evidence on its head.

3. The oceans: the most revealing distortion

Here the author presents some largely correct information and then draws precisely the wrong conclusion.

Yes, the oceans store vastly more heat than the atmosphere.

Yes, they absorb approximately 90% of the excess heat accumulating in the climate system.

But consider what that means.

The oceans are absorbing the overwhelming majority of the additional heat trapped by greenhouse gases. They are not disproving global warming. They are recording it.

Ocean heat content has risen dramatically, and measurements show continuing accumulation of energy.

The oceans' enormous heat capacity delays atmospheric warming, but it does not prevent it. Nor does the energy simply disappear.

Warming oceans expand, contributing to rising sea levels. They intensify marine heatwaves, damage coral ecosystems and influence atmospheric weather patterns.

The author describes the oceans as the Earth's air conditioners. That analogy is deeply misleading. An air conditioner transfers heat out of a room. The oceans largely store and redistribute heat within the Earth system.

The distinction is fundamental.

4. Water vapour: the familiar greenhouse-gas trick

The author correctly observes that water vapour makes a larger contribution to Earth's natural greenhouse effect than CO₂.

But this is not an argument against human-caused warming.

Water vapour acts predominantly as a feedback, whereas the human addition of long-lived CO₂ is an important forcing.

As CO₂ warms the atmosphere, warmer air can contain more water vapour. That additional water vapour amplifies the original warming.

In other words, the very importance of water vapour makes CO₂-driven warming more consequential, not less.

The passage also confuses the relative contributions of different greenhouse gases to the existing greenhouse effect with their roles in causing the present increase in temperature.

These are two different questions.

5. Milankovitch cycles cannot explain the present warming

The author invokes changes in Earth's orbit and axial orientation.

These are real and important. Milankovitch cycles help explain the pacing of glacial and interglacial periods.

But their principal cycles operate over approximately 23,000, 41,000 and 100,000 years.

They cannot account for the extraordinary warming observed since industrialisation, especially during the last half-century.

Nor can tectonic movements, which generally operate over millions of years.

The passage effectively argues that because very slow natural processes can change the climate, a much faster human-induced process cannot do so.

There is no logical or scientific connection between those propositions.

The existence of natural causes does not exclude additional human causes.

6. 'We are still in an ice age'

Technically, yes.

In geological terminology, Earth remains within an icehouse state because substantial permanent ice sheets survive, particularly in Antarctica and Greenland.

But the author exploits a specialised definition to create a false impression.

Being in a long geological ice age does not mean that rapid warming within an interglacial is harmless.

Indeed, the great continental ice sheets are among the reasons global warming presents a long-term threat.

Their melting contributes to sea-level rise, potentially continuing for centuries or millennia.

The survival of polar ice is not evidence that additional warming is desirable.

7. The most demonstrably false claim: nobody would notice rising seas

The assertion that warming would raise sea levels by only a few millimetres, imperceptibly over a lifetime, is contradicted by direct observation.

Global mean sea level has risen by roughly 20–25 centimetres since 1900, with the rate increasing in recent decades.

That rise is measured using tide gauges and satellites.

It is already affecting coastal communities through more frequent tidal flooding, erosion and saltwater intrusion.

A few millimetres of additional sea level each year may sound trivial. Accumulated over decades, it is anything but.

And sea-level rise is not simply a matter of thermal expansion. Melting land-based glaciers and ice sheets also add water to the oceans.

The author has mistaken the small annual increment for the cumulative effect, and ignored the acceleration.

It does not follow from anything established about ancient temperatures, tectonic plates, ocean currents or orbital cycles.

text:
Peace talks to end the war in Ukraine could take a major turn as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy demands European nations directly join the negotiating team.

Here is the detailed, easy-to-understand breakdown of Zelenskyy's strategic gamble and the continued intense fighting on the ground:

1. "Europe is no bystander" (Zelenskyy’s big demand)

What happened: On November 13, at the European Political Community (EPC) summit in Dublin, Ireland, President Zelenskyy held high-stakes talks with U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

He made a critical demand: "In the next round of peace talks, Europe must join as an active member of the negotiating team, not just as observers or mediators."

His reasoning: The war is being fought on European soil, so European security is directly on the line. Bringing Europe into the negotiation room gives Ukraine crucial backing, helping to ensure they aren't pressured into a bad deal or forced to give up territory without major security guarantees.

2. "Will Putin agree to European involvement?" (The U.S. envoy's take and Russia's view)

The U.S. Envoys' View: Following the meetings, U.S. Envoy Kushner shared a notable insight: when he asked Russian President Vladimir Putin if he would be open to "attempting" to include Europe in the negotiations, Putin seemed to show some agreement or willingness to consider it.

The Kremlin's Caution: However, the Kremlin has yet to formally confirm any acceptance. In fact, Putin threw skepticism at the U.S. envoys, saying, "The U.S. needs to figure out whether Europe actually wants peace for Ukraine, or if they are just looking to extend this war for their own interests." This highlights Putin's deep mistrust toward European nations that verbally call for peace while supplying weapons.

3. "Massive prisoner swap on the table, but evacuation routes contested"

A glimmer of hope: On a positive note, Zelenskyy expressed strong hope for an upcoming prisoner swap agreed upon during talks in Abu Dhabi, predicting it would be the "largest of its kind to date."

Disagreements over evacs: However, the two sides remain deeply split over Putin's proposal to evacuate trapped civilians from areas like Kostiantynivka in Donetsk.

Zelenskyy has stayed quiet on the offer, with experts warning that Putin might be using "humanitarian" routes as a PR stunt to demonstrate full Russian military control over these hotly contested territories.

4. Grim reality on the ground: "1,200 drones intercepted and civilian casualties"

While leaders debate peace, the battlefields remain brutal.

The Russian Ministry of Defense claimed it intercepted a staggering 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, in one of the largest coordinated drone assaults of the war.

The attacks reportedly hit oil and industrial facilities in southern Russian regions like Volgograd, killing four civilians. In retaliation, Russian forces launched heavy strikes on coastal areas near Ukraine's port city of Odesa, underscoring that a peaceful resolution remains far off on the ground.

To sum it all up!While Zelenskyy’s push to bring European nations directly into the negotiation room has been met with skepticism from Putin—who questions Europe's motives—peace efforts like a massive prisoner swap are being completely overshadowed by relentless warfare, including a massive 1,200-drone offensive, highlighting the immense gap between diplomatic talks and the brutal reality on the ground.

"No," I cut in, even. "You told this congregation you labored over the hearth. When I returned four days after having my abdomen cut open, the sink was filled with days of grease. And twenty-seven minutes after I crossed our threshold, you demanded I stand over a hot stove to cook for you. So which meals did you cook?"

Gasps.

"How DARE you! I spent thousands of my own—"

"You spent thirty-two hundred dollars of OUR emergency savings," Owen's voice boomed from the back.

He walked forward and dropped a stack of bank statements on the table beside the parish register.

"You told me it was for doula care. Then you wired it to Desert Horizon Furnishings in Phoenix to pay off a leather sectional."

Whispers rippled. Two deaconesses exchanged looks.

"You would humiliate me in front of the church?" Harriet choked. "You are my son!"

"You orchestrated this to humiliate my wife," Owen said, now beside me, arm around my shoulders. "You wanted an audience, Mom. Look around. You have one."

A chair scraped. Rosemary Vance stood, straightening her cardigan.

"Two weeks ago, Harriet told the neighborhood committee that Vivien was ashamed of her home and found our charity intrusive. Eight families cancelled based on that lie. We believed you, Harriet. You didn't want privacy. You wanted isolation."

Harriet stood frozen, her story exposed, gaze darting from Glenda — who stared at the tablecloth — to the neighbors holding the food she turned away, to Owen, who was no longer bending to please her.

She grabbed her bag and escaped through the kitchen service doors. They shuddered closed behind her.

It took four months and three registered letters from Dad's attorney to get the $3,200 back. We spent it on eighty hours of postpartum physical therapy and a college bond for Clover.

Harriet flew back to Phoenix forty-eight hours later. She didn't ask for a ride. Owen didn't offer. When Glenda called to guilt-trip us, Owen read her the transaction numbers and told her the state-line boundary would remain until his mother apologized without conditions. She never called again.

Every evening at 5:15 for two weeks after I returned to Cedar Falls, someone knocked softly. Rosemary, Mrs. Henderson, the young couple down the street. Pot roast. Wild-rice casserole. Handwritten notes for Clover.

I accepted every meal. Accepting real help is strength, not weakness.

Owen started counseling in Waterloo. No miracle. Some nights his shoulders still tightened when conflict came. But he stayed. He didn't withdraw.

Eight months later, October. Clover in her highchair in a sunflower bib, investigating gravity by dropping banana slices.

The back screen door squeaked. Dad walked in with a cast-iron Dutch oven wrapped in a blue towel.

"Afternoon, crew. Beef stew. Six hours. Enough to carry you through Thursday."

"Dad, you drove ninety miles on a Sunday just to drop off stew?"

"Had to check the plumbing," he said, though our pipes were immaculate. He let Clover grab his thick index finger with her sticky fist.

Owen came up from the basement, primer on his forearms, toolbox in hand. He extended a steady hand.

"Afternoon, Dale."

Dad took it in a firm grip. "Get that baseboard sealed?"

"Finished the second coat."

By the kitchen window, I watched the two men I loved set the table. Outside, wind swept leaves from our silver maples.

Only eight months before, I'd been on that sofa, twenty-seven minutes home from surgery, holding a newborn against an open wound, being told to cook.

I thought I needed an army that day.

I didn't.

I needed to know that loving someone doesn't mean demanding they bleed to prove their worth. That home isn't about who has authority to order dinner, but who stands at the doorway to make sure everyone inside can heal safely.

"Dinner's ready, Viv," Owen called softly, pulling out my chair.

Smiling, I lifted Clover and went toward the light.

END.

text:
As a Nigerian, I want to make this declaration: I will never allow anyone to buy my conscience with money, gifts or temporary benefits.

We must stop selling our future for what cannot sustain us beyond a few days. That ₦5,000, ₦10,000 or bag of rice offered in exchange for your vote is not generosity; it is an investment in your silence.

Think about it: if a politician can spend millions buying votes, how much do you think they intend to recover once they get into power?

When you collect money to vote against your conscience, you surrender your right to complain about bad leadership. You cannot sell the power to choose your leaders and then expect those leaders to respect your future.

Your vote is not merchandise. Your conscience is not for sale. Your future is not a bargaining chip.

Don't vote because someone paid you. Don't participate in electoral malpractice because someone promised you a reward. Vote based on competence, character, track record and the ability to deliver.

Nigeria will not change if we keep rewarding the very behaviour that keeps us trapped.

Let us stop exchanging tomorrow for the little we can collect today.

text:
Independent insurance agencies...
 
If a "prospect" asks for a quote and then insists you join THEIR Zoom link.... do not click it.
 
Two of my clients brought this up on calls this week.
 
One is in South Carolina and the other is in Texas.
 
They've never met each other.
 
This is a cybersecurity problem, and it's showing up in your inbox dressed as a lead.
 
An email comes in asking for a quote.
 
It reads like AI wrote it, which isn't a red flag by itself anymore because real buyers are sending AI bots out to shop for insurance right now.
 
Your team replies and asks when they can talk.
 
The "prospect" says they're out of the country and can't take a phone call.
 
Or they want their spouse on the call, so it has to be Zoom.
 
So your team offers to send over a Zoom link.
 
And they say no, we're going to use ours.
 
That link is the entire attack.
 
From what I've read on these, it opens a page that looks like Zoom and asks you to install an update before you can join.
 
The "update" is remote access software, and whoever sent it now has control of that computer.
 
Think about what's sitting on a CSR's computer.
 
Your AMS is on there, along with the carrier portals, the saved passwords, and every client's personal information.
 
My South Carolina client told me how his team handles it.
 
They host the call on their own link or they get on the phone, and if the "prospect" won't do either, there's no meeting.
 
My Texas client told me a lot of what came into his agency over the last two weeks was AI and fraud, with people trying to set up a Zoom.
 
I asked him if a carrier had sent out any kind of warning.
 
He hadn't seen one.
 
So I'm telling you guys.
 
Send this to your CSRs and producers TODAY, because the newest person on your team is the one who's going to click.
 
Quick rule of thumb....
 
A real buyer will take a phone call.
 
Has this one hit your inbox yet?

text:
I remember when my mom put my public school.

I was halfway thru third grade and had been homeschooled/co op schooled in Colorado up to that point.

When we moved to Texas, there was a raging legal battle going on. Truancy officers were taking kids out of homes. Lots of bad stuff, and my mom was afraid of all of it. So I was enrolled in the local school.

I went from going to a co up with six total students ages 6-9 to being number 32 in my third grade classroom. 

It was the most stressful thing that ever happened to me. It’s still one of the worst. I cried and screamed every single morning. I had a pit in my stomach basically all day. I pulled my it chunks of my hair almost constantly.

The biggest issue for me was being away from my family. I’d been away in my co op, but it was a natural environment. A big elementary school was so unnatural to me and I just wanted to be with my mom.

That feeling never left. I got a pit in my stomach every day through ninth grade. I didn’t want to be homeschooled when my mom offered in 8th and 9th grades, maybe because of my friends? I don’t remember why.

When I was finally homeschooled again in tenth grade, I lost that pit in my stomach. I took control of my little life and I absolutely thrived. I didn’t need much direction, I was just ready to launch.

When I became a mom, I kept that feeling in mind. When my kids wanted to stay with me in church, I let them. When they wanted to come sleep with me, I let them. And I never sent them to school, obviously. Any time they felt like they needed my comfort, I gave it to them.

As they’ve gotten older, they are all very independent. They rarely need my comfort anymore (although it’s sometimes needed).

School with strangers isn’t natural. Sending your kids away from you at 5 years old and earlier is definitely not.

The St. Joe Company $JOE owns more than 150,000 acres of land, mostly in the Florida Panhandle.

The $4.1 billion developer builds and runs residential communities, commercial buildings, hotels and golf courses on that land.

After last week's election, the stock broke out of a long sideways consolidation and into fresh new highs.

The logic is migration. Business owners and investors worry about higher taxes and heavier regulation in states like New York, California and Illinois.

Florida offers the opposite: no state income tax and a business-friendly reputation.

People have already voted with their feet. According to the U.S. Census, Florida's population has grown by at least 1.87 million since 2020.

$JOE also has a demographics kicker. Millions of baby boomers want to retire somewhere warm, and the Panhandle is one of the places they are choosing.

The election added fuel by raising questions about whether traditional red-state strongholds like Texas could shift. That makes Florida look even more like the destination of choice.

We published a favorable note on $JOE back in January on exactly this thesis. The breakout to new highs says the trend is accelerating, not fading.

For investors who expect more Americans to keep moving toward lower taxes and lighter regulation, $JOE is a direct way to own that land.

Is $JOE the best stock market play on Florida's growth?

text:
But a party can be repudiated without every political philosophy it claims to represent being repudiated along with it.

It matters because Republicans have spent the better part of a decade calling nearly everything President Donald Trump supports “conservative,” even when those policies directly contradict ideas conservatives have defended for generations.

A decade ago, my book Still Right made the case that this distinction matters.

By then, “conservative” had increasingly come to mean support for Trump administration policies. Free trade had become suspect. Tariffs had become patriotic. Immigration itself had become a problem. NATO had become questionable. Deficit spending had become someone else's concern. Easy money had become acceptable when the stock market liked it.

The argument was not that conservatives must oppose everything Trump supports. It was that conservatism has to mean something independent of Donald Trump, the Republican Party, or any other politician. Otherwise, it is not a philosophy.

It is a fan club.

Last week gave Republicans a painful opportunity to rediscover the distinction.

What Counts as Conservative?

The American conservative tradition has never been a perfectly uniform ideology.

It combines Edmund Burke's ordered liberty, Adam Smith's and Friedrich Hayek's classical liberalism, the Founders' constitutionalism, William F. Buckley's and Barry Goldwater's anti-communism, and Ronald Reagan's belief in free markets, limited government, strong alliances, and peace through strength.

Conservatives disagree about plenty.

But certain principles used to be recognizable.

Government should be limited because concentrated political power threatens liberty.

Markets generally allocate resources better than politicians.

Private property means very little if the government can decide how, where, and with whom someone may exchange it.

Taxes and spending should be restrained because the government is spending other people's money.

Immigration should be lawful, but immigration itself strengthens a free and prosperous nation.

Military strength exists principally to deter war, not start it.

Alliances magnify American power.

Conservatism is not anti-government. It is about ordered liberty: order requires a functioning government, and liberty requires limiting that government to its proper functions, recognizing that freedom does not work without a responsible citizenry.

Now compare those principles with the policies Republicans actually defended.

Start with the easiest one.

Tariffs Are Taxes

If there was one issue in this election where conservative philosophy and voter dissatisfaction collided almost perfectly, it was tariffs.

Free trade fits the conservative philosophy precisely because it puts individual liberty above government power.

If a person produces a product or service, that person should generally be free to voluntarily exchange it with another willing person. A tariff interferes with that transaction, makes purchasing decisions instead of consumers transferring economic power from private hands to government.

Hayek understood this.

Thatcher understood it.

Reagan understood it.

Adam Smith figured it out before there was a Republican Party.

Free trade is about individual liberty, whereas tariffs are about governmental power.

The Republican Party chose the wrong side.

Its 2024 platform explicitly called for “baseline Tariffs on Foreign-made goods.” The Trump administration subsequently imposed tariffs on a wide range of imports. Even after the Supreme Court invalidated tariffs imposed under one emergency authority earlier this year, the administration imposed a temporary 10 percent import surcharge, while other tariffs remained in place.

Call that economic nationalism.

Call it protectionism.

Call it America First industrial policy.

Just do not pretend Adam Smith came up with it.

More importantly for campaign professionals, voters hated the results.

The AP Voter Poll surveyed more than 100,000 midterm voters (that’s a lot). Nearly nine in ten said the cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their congressional vote. About two-thirds said Trump's policies contributed to inflation. Voters across the country broadly said the administration's tariffs had done more economic harm than good.

That is where the philosophical argument meets the electoral reality.

Republicans promised to lower prices while raising them by taxing imports.

Then they discovered something economists have understood for centuries: A government can call it a tariff, a duty, a surcharge, or economic patriotism.

The cash register does not care.

It’s a tax, and consumers eventually pay it.

Uncle Sam, Venture Capitalist

The drift from free-market conservatism went further.

Last year, the federal government acquired roughly a 10 percent stake in Intel, converting billions of dollars in government commitments into hundreds of millions of shares of a private corporation. The administration defended the arrangement as necessary to strengthen domestic semiconductor production and national security.

There is a serious national-security argument for maintaining domestic semiconductor capacity.

There is also a serious conservative question.

When did Uncle Sam become a venture capitalist?

Still Right harshly criticized bank bailouts, corporatism, and policies that allow politicians to use government power to favor particular companies or industries for the purposes of staying in power.

That is not a free market.

Markets require rules. They require the government to punish fraud, enforce contracts, protect property, and police bad actors.

But a referee is different from a shareholder.

The government cannot simultaneously regulate the game and own stock in one of the teams without creating an obvious conflict between political and market incentives.

There is a name for an economy in which politicians own the commanding heights of the economy. It’s called socialism.

“Limited government” it is not.

Fiscal Conservatism Without the Fiscal Part

Then there is spending.

The government spends too damn much money.

The Congressional Budget Office reported this week that the federal government ran a $2 trillion deficit in fiscal year 2026, up $217 billion from the previous year. The deficit equaled 6.2 percent of gross domestic product, compared with the 50-year average of 3.8 percent. Federal debt held by the public reached 100 percent of GDP.

But ho hum.

CBO estimated earlier this year that the 2025 reconciliation law increased projected deficits from 2026 to 2035 by $4.7 trillion, including economic and debt-service effects. Higher tariffs partially offset that increase by a massive wealth transfer from consumers to the government.

Think about the philosophical gymnastics required here.

The government spends trillions more than it collects.

Then it imposes taxes on trade to collect more money.

And then it uses that money to grow an even bigger government.

Then Republicans describe both policies as conservative.

It is like watching a person chew on raw meat while claiming to be a vegan.

The deficit wasn’t a dominant issue among voters last week. Voters didn’t bring CBO tables into the voting booth.

But campaign professionals should understand what it reveals.

A party cannot spend years abandoning fiscal restraint and then interpret its election defeat as evidence that voters rejected fiscal conservatism.

Limited Government Means Limiting Your Government

The same rule applies to executive power.

Conservatives spent decades warning of an imperial presidency.

Then a Republican President arrived, and constitutional restraint suddenly became considerably less fashionable.

The principle ought to be simple.

Government power does not become less dangerous because your guy or gal wields it.

Limited government rests on precisely that understanding political power must be restrained because human beings cannot safely be trusted with unlimited authority. Liberty requires institutions strong enough to restrain the state.

The AP Voter Poll found that democracy and constitutional government mattered especially to higher-income voters. The administration had used executive authority to alter spending, reduce the federal workforce, and impose enormous tariffs, among other actions, without new congressional approval. The Supreme Court ultimately invalidated some of those tariffs.

Individual executive actions can be defensible.

Presidents can possess substantial authority under existing statutes.

But conservatives should apply the same test regardless of who is in the White House:

If a governing philosophy suddenly changes depending on who is President, it is not a philosophy.

It is season tickets.

Immigration Is Not the Same Thing as Illegal Immigration

Immigration may expose the philosophical divide even more clearly.

Conservatives should distinguish between immigration and illegal immigration. A government has the right and responsibility to control its borders and to enforce its laws. Ordered liberty requires order.

But liberty matters, too.

America has been extraordinarily successful at absorbing people who come here seeking work, opportunity, safety, and freedom. Free people moving voluntarily to participate in a free economy should not be instinctively viewed as an economic threat.

Anti-immigration, indeed, anti-immigrant, rhetoric had increasingly replaced serious debate on legal immigration, assimilation, labor markets, and border enforcement.

The Republican Party instead promised the “largest deportation operation in American history” and a legal immigration system explicitly designed to protect American workers from foreign competition. The administration went beyond illegal immigration. Its H-1B policy now requires a $100,000 payment for many new petitions from skilled foreign workers entering the country.

There are legitimate arguments about H-1B abuse.

There are legitimate arguments about wage suppression.

There is nothing unconservative about enforcing immigration law.

But there is a substantial difference between enforcing the border and adopting the populist assumption that foreign workers, goods, companies, and competition are inherently suspect.

Voters appeared capable of making their own distinctions.

Hispanic voters shifted substantially away from Republicans this year after moving toward Trump in 2024, notably in Texas, where Hispanics have lived since before Texas was an American state. AP found that economic concerns, corruption, and concerns about the immigration crackdown were key drivers of that shift. After the election, Trump himself said the enforcement effort may have become “too tough.”

Republicans should pay attention to that without drawing the equally foolish conclusion that voters want an open border.

Politics does not exist in a binary world, and those are not the only two options.

Peace Through Strength Is Supposed to Produce Peace

Foreign policy offers another useful comparison.

The military that defends freedom must be strong.

But the first purpose of military strength is not fighting wars.

It is preventing them from happening in the first place.

That was Reagan's point in “peace through strength.” Military capability gives diplomacy credibility and deters enemies from testing American resolve. America also needs alliances, especially NATO, because they multiply American strength and make aggression more costly.

The Republican platform promised to “PREVENT WORLD WAR THREE” and “RESTORE PEACE” in Europe and the Middle East.

By Election Day, the United States had been at war with Iran for eight months.

About six in ten midterm voters told the AP Voter Poll that military action against Iran was the wrong decision. The war was not the top issue for most voters -- affordability and corruption mattered more -- but it also pushed energy prices higher and turned a foreign-policy issue into a kitchen-table issue.

That’s why it matters and should matter.

Iran alone did not cost Republicans the election.

Tariffs alone did not cost Republicans the election.

Immigration did not.

Executive power did not.

Candidate quality, the traditional midterm penalty against the President's party, redistricting, local issues, Democratic recruitment, turnout, and dozens of other variables all mattered.

Politics is multivariate.

Anyone who explains a national election with a single variable should not be allowed near a regression model or a campaign budget.

But the voter evidence tells an important story.

The policies for which Republicans were punished most heavily were hardly a referendum on conservatism.

The Party Is Not the Philosophy

This is the campaign lesson.

Never confuse political marketing with the actual product they were trying to sell.

Republicans carried the conservative brand into this election.

That does not mean everything they sold was conservative.

The administration pursued policies recognizable to traditional conservatives: lower taxes, deregulation, greater domestic energy production, stronger defense spending, and conservative judicial appointments.

But some of the governing program's most distinctive features stemmed from a different political tradition.

Protectionism.

Economic nationalism.

Government-directed industrial policy.

Restrictions on legal as well as illegal immigration.

Large deficits.

An expansive presidency.

A willingness to use government power aggressively to advance favored economic and political objectives.

That tradition has a perfectly serviceable name.

Populism.

And populism is not conservatism or even a distant cousin.

The two philosophies begin from different instincts.

Classical liberalism asks how government can preserve the space in which free people make their own economic and personal choices.

Populism asks how political power can be mobilized on behalf of the people its leaders believe deserve protection and favored status.

One distrusts concentrations of government power.

The other is willing to use that power aggressively if the right people are in control.

One says government should referee the market.

The other is comfortable picking the lineup.

That difference existed before Donald Trump and will exist after him.

Read the Election Before Writing the Obituary

Democrats should be careful, too.

They had an extraordinary election.

That does not mean voters endorsed every progressive idea.

Despite Republican losses, a slight majority of voters still held a favorable view of capitalism, compared with roughly one-third who viewed socialism favorably.

So, Democrats should not interpret the election as proof that America suddenly embraced democratic socialism.

Republicans should not interpret it as proof that America rejected conservatism.

Both conclusions ask the election results to say more than voters actually said.

What voters clearly did say was that they were angry about prices. They disliked the tariffs. Most thought Trump's policies contributed to inflation. Many opposed the war in Iran. Significant numbers objected to how presidential power was being exercised. Hispanic voters moved sharply away from Republicans amid concerns, including the immigration crackdown. And roughly three-quarters of voters said they were angry or dissatisfied with the country's direction.

That is enough information to conduct a serious autopsy.

Just don’t bury the wrong body.

Over the last fifty years, conservatives went from the kids’ table to the head of the table under Reagan, then to a chair in the corner under Bush, and finally to no longer even being invited to dinner.

Today, the conservative name has been appropriated to advance populism.

But it was not conservatism that lost Congress, at least five governorships, legislative chambers, nearly all of Texas, and races up and down the ballot.

It was a Republican Party governing under the conservative label while pursuing many policies fundamentally at odds with classical liberal conservatism.

If Republicans want to determine whether classical liberal conservatism can still appeal to American voters, there is a wonderfully straightforward way to find out.

Try it.

Conservatism is still right.

Rick Tyler is director of the Advanced School of Politics and author of Still Right.

text:
At 16, Brian Banks was one of the best high school linebackers in America. USC had offered him a full scholarship. Pete Carroll personally called him.

One afternoon at school he made out with a classmate. Consensual. By the end of the day he was in jail, charged with kidnapping and rape.

She said he dragged her into a stairwell. It never happened.

The DNA came back negative. His mother sold her house and her car to pay for a lawyer.

He couldn’t make bail. He spent a year behind bars waiting for trial.

His lawyer told him: plead no contest, or risk 41 years in prison. He was 17. He took the deal.

He did 5 years in prison. Then 5 more on parole. Registered sex offender. GPS monitor on his ankle. Couldn’t go near schools or parks. No one would hire him.

Meanwhile, the girl and her mother sued the school district for not keeping her safe. They won $1.5 million.

In 2011, a Facebook friend request popped up on his screen.

It was her.

She wanted to “let bygones be bygones.”

Brian went to a private investigator. They hid cameras in the office and invited her to talk. She came by bus.

On tape, she admitted it. He never raped her. He never kidnapped her.

Then she said she still wouldn’t tell prosecutors the truth. Because she’d have to give back the money.

In May 2012, a judge cleared his name. The hearing took less than a minute.

10 years of his life. Gone in one lie. Erased in 60 seconds.

A few days later his phone rang. “I’m looking for a linebacker. You know where I can find one?”

It was Pete Carroll. The same coach who recruited him 10 years earlier.

He finally signed with the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons. At 27. The dream he had at 16.

She was ordered to pay $2.6 million back.

What should happen to someone who steals 10 years of your life with one lie

Yes. People born in the United States have defected from the country, especially during the Cold War and Vietnam War era, though these cases were far less common and less celebrated than the reverse (people defecting to the US from communist countries).⁠Reddit

“Defection” usually means abandoning one’s country for political, ideological, or military reasons and seeking refuge with an adversary, often involving renunciation of citizenship or formal asylum. Here are well-documented examples of US-born people who did so:

Lee Harvey Oswald (born New Orleans, 1939): In 1959 he traveled to the Soviet Union, announced his intent to renounce US citizenship, and lived in Minsk for about three years before becoming disillusioned and returning in 1962. He later assassinated President Kennedy.⁠Foreignpolicy
US soldiers who crossed into North Korea (all US-born):

Charles Robert Jenkins (born North Carolina, 1940): In 1965, while stationed at the DMZ, he walked across after drinking, largely to avoid possible deployment to Vietnam. He spent nearly 40 years in North Korea (often under harsh conditions), later left for Japan, and was court-martialed.⁠Wikipedia
James Joseph Dresnok (1962), Larry Abshier (1962), Jerry Parrish (1963), and Joseph White (1982) also defected. Most lived out their lives there and appeared in North Korean propaganda.⁠Newsweek
NSA cryptologists William Martin and Bernon Mitchell (1960): They defected to the Soviet Union and provided information on US signals intelligence.⁠Foreignpolicy
Vietnam War period: Tens of thousands of US-born draft resisters and military deserters went to Canada (Canadian estimates often cited in the 30,000–40,000 range for draft-related moves, with higher figures sometimes used); roughly 1,000 went to Sweden, many receiving political asylum. Smaller numbers went elsewhere.⁠Reddit
Other cases include various leftists who went to Cuba, spies or collaborators who fled to the USSR or Eastern Bloc, and earlier examples like Benedict Arnold (Revolutionary War).

Defections from the US were real but relatively rare compared with the reverse flow during the Cold War, when the West offered more freedom and higher living standards. Many American defectors later expressed regret.

Beyond strict “defection,” large numbers of US-born people have permanently left or renounced citizenship for taxes, lifestyle, family, or political reasons. The US publishes lists of renunciations (thousands per year in recent decades), and estimates put several million Americans living abroad. US citizens have also filed roughly 14,000 asylum claims abroad since 2000.⁠Papers.ssrn

In short: yes, it has happened, including clear cases of political or military defection by people born in the United States. The numbers and public attention were simply much smaller than for people arriving in the US.

text:
Imagine sitting down with an AI model for a spoken two-hour interview. A friendly voice guides you through a conversation that ranges from your childhood, your formative memories, and your career to your thoughts on immigration policy. Not long after, a virtual replica of you is able to embody your values and preferences with stunning accuracy.

That’s now possible, according to a new paper from a team including researchers from Stanford and Google DeepMind, which has been published on arXiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. 

Led by Joon Sung Park, a Stanford PhD student in computer science, the team recruited 1,000 people who varied by age, gender, race, region, education, and political ideology. They were paid up to $100 for their participation. From interviews with them, the team created agent replicas of those individuals. As a test of how well the agents mimicked their human counterparts, participants did a series of personality tests, social surveys, and logic games, twice each, two weeks apart; then the agents completed the same exercises. The results were 85% similar. 

“If you can have a bunch of small ‘yous’ running around and actually making the decisions that you would have made—that, I think, is ultimately the future,” Park says. 

In the paper the replicas are called simulation agents, and the impetus for creating them is to make it easier for researchers in social sciences and other fields to conduct studies that would be expensive, impractical, or unethical to do with real human subjects. If you can create AI models that behave like real people, the thinking goes, you can use them to test everything from how well interventions on social media combat misinformation to what behaviors cause traffic jams. 

Such simulation agents are slightly different from the agents that are dominating the work of leading AI companies today. Called tool-based agents, those are models built to do things for you, not converse with you. For example, they might enter data, retrieve information you have stored somewhere, or—someday—book travel for you and schedule appointments. Salesforce announced its own tool-based agents in September, followed by Anthropic in October, and OpenAI is planning to release some in January, according to Bloomberg. 

The two types of agents are different but share common ground. Research on simulation agents, like the ones in this paper, is likely to lead to stronger AI agents overall, says John Horton, an associate professor of information technologies at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who founded a company to conduct research using AI-simulated participants. 

“This paper is showing how you can do a kind of hybrid: use real humans to generate personas which can then be used programmatically/in-simulation in ways you could not with real humans,” he told MIT Technology Review in an email. 

The research comes with caveats, not the least of which is the danger that it points to. Just as image generation technology has made it easy to create harmful deepfakes of people without their consent, any agent generation technology raises questions about the ease with which people can build tools to personify others online, saying or authorizing things they didn’t intend to say. 

The evaluation methods the team used to test how well the AI agents replicated their corresponding humans were also fairly basic. These included the General Social Survey—which collects information on one’s demographics, happiness, behaviors, and more—and assessments of the Big Five personality traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extroversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. Such tests are commonly used in social science research but don’t pretend to capture all the unique details that make us ourselves. The AI agents were also worse at replicating the humans in behavioral tests like the “dictator game,” which is meant to illuminate how participants consider values such as fairness. 

To build an AI agent that replicates people well, the researchers needed ways to distill our uniqueness into language AI models can understand. They chose qualitative interviews to do just that, Park says. He says he was convinced that interviews are the most efficient way to learn about someone after he appeared on countless podcasts following a 2023 paper that he wrote on generative agents, which sparked a huge amount of interest in the field. “I would go on maybe a two-hour podcast podcast interview, and after the interview, I felt like, wow, people know a lot about me now,” he says. “Two hours can be very powerful.”

These interviews can also reveal idiosyncrasies that are less likely to show up on a survey. “Imagine somebody just had cancer but was finally cured last year. That’s very unique information about you that says a lot about how you might behave and think about things,” he says. It would be difficult to craft survey questions that elicit these sorts of memories and responses. 

Interviews aren’t the only option, though. Companies that offer to make “digital twins” of users, like Tavus, can have their AI models ingest customer emails or other data. It tends to take a pretty large data set to replicate someone’s personality that way, Tavus CEO Hassaan Raza told me, but this new paper suggests a more efficient route. 

“What was really cool here is that they show you might not need that much information,” Raza says, adding that his company will experiment with the approach. “How about you just talk to an AI interviewer for 30 minutes today, 30 minutes tomorrow? And then we use that to construct this digital twin of you.”
