text:
Torus uses spare grid connections to bring modular data centers online in 12–16 weeks | Neetika Walter, Interesting Engineering

Torus has launched a modular computing system designed to bring inference capacity online at existing commercial and industrial sites, using available grid connections instead of waiting for new data center infrastructure.

The Salt Lake City-based energy and infrastructure company unveiled Foundry on November 11, alongside a $500 million funding announcement led by Magnetar. The funding will support manufacturing expansion and deployments of its energy storage and computing systems across the US.

Kinsey projects that data center demand for inference will grow at a compound annual rate of 35 percent through 2030, compared with 22 percent for training.

Bringing compute to power

Foundry combines computing hardware, power systems, energy storage, cooling and networking in a prefabricated modular unit. Torus says each site can support between 1 and 20 megawatts of computing capacity and can move from contract to operational workloads in 12 to 16 weeks.

The system is designed to operate at existing commercial and industrial sites with available electrical capacity. Rather than waiting for new grid connections or large-scale infrastructure upgrades, Torus aims to use existing interconnections and manage electricity demand through its Torus Reserve energy storage system.

Reserve combines battery storage and inertial-based technology to manage peak demand, provide backup power, and adjust electricity consumption. The company says its load-management controls can help accommodate the fluctuating power requirements of computing hardware while supporting grid stability.

Foundry is also designed for distributed deployment, placing computing resources closer to businesses and the workloads they serve. Torus argues this could appeal to enterprises seeking greater control over where their data is processed, alongside security and intellectual property protections.

Scaling modular capacity

Torus is offering Foundry through three deployment models. The Strategic option provides a powered enclosure without GPUs, while the Partner configuration includes computing hardware. Its Direct model offers dedicated, single-tenant inference capacity for enterprise customers.

The company named AI infrastructure provider Hydra Host among Foundry’s first customers, alongside another unnamed cloud provider. Torus says thousands of GPUs are already deployed in Foundry units and plans to increase that number to more than 47,000 by the end of 2027.

One, Torus’s 545,000-square-foot facility in Salt Lake City, Utah. The company says its Foundry production line is designed to support 500 megawatts of IT load, with plans to expand capacity to 1 gigawatt.

Torus also says Foundry uses a closed-loop, waterless cooling system that consumes 95 percent less water than evaporative cooling systems. These environmental and performance figures are company-reported claims.

The $500 million financing round was led by Magnetar, with participation from ICONIQ, Origin Ventures, Ridgeline Partners and Trinity Capital.

The launch reflects a growing effort to address data center power constraints by distributing computing capacity across existing sites. However, Foundry’s deployment timelines, available grid capacity, and planned GPU expansion remain dependent on individual site conditions and future execution.

🧭 A DAY OF COURAGE, CONNECTION & CONSEQUENCE

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

ANNALS OF THE DAY 🪔

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A HISTORICAL CHRONICLE • NOVEMBER 13TH EDITION

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⏱️ READING TIME: APPROXIMATELY 13–16 MINUTES

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🪔 EPIGRAPH

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to light the road behind us, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” — Hodgepodgery, 2026

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📑 TABLE OF CONTENTS

🪔 Epigraph — A thought to frame the day.

🔎 Intro — The stories and contradictions behind November 13.

🧭 Calendar Overview — The date, its place in the year, and its observances.

🏛️ Major Historical Events — Five consequential moments that changed the course of events.

🔬 Scientific, Technological & Cultural Milestones — Discoveries and innovations that changed how we see and experience the world.

🎂 Famous Birthdays — Notable people born on this date.

🥀 Memoriam — Remembering those whose lives ended on November 13.

🏟️ Sports Highlights — Records, milestones, and extraordinary sporting moments.

📣 There's More History Waiting! — Today's publication schedule.

🦉 The Stoic Mind — One thought from the Stoic tradition.

✅ Quiz Answer — The answer and its historical explanation.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🔎 INTRO

November 13 juxtaposes human achievement and consequence: a tunnel joined two cities, a Supreme Court ruling struck at segregation, a London protest was met with force, a volcano overwhelmed a Colombian town, and terrorist attacks devastated Paris.

Yet this date also brought a cinematic experiment, extraordinary views of Saturn, and a referendum that shaped Europe's political future.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🧭 CALENDAR OVERVIEW ♏️

November 13 is the 317th day of 2026 (≈86.85% completed), with 48 days remaining (≈13.15%). Today is Friday, in ISO week 46. It is World Kindness Day, established by the World Kindness Movement in 1998, and Sadie Hawkins Day. 🌍

🐶 SPOT: Sadie Hawkins Day wasn't an ancient folk custom. Cartoonist Al Capp invented it for his Li’l Abner comic strip in 1937. The fictional event became so popular that colleges and communities began holding real-life celebrations, where women took the initiative in asking men for dates.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

—— ❦ ——

1887 — BLOODY SUNDAY ERUPTS IN LONDON'S TRAFALGAR SQUARE 🇬🇧

On November 13, 1887, thousands of demonstrators gathered in central London to protest mass unemployment, poverty, and British policy in Ireland. The authorities had banned public meetings in Trafalgar Square, turning a demonstration into a confrontation over the right to assemble and speak.

Police, cavalry, and soldiers charged crowds. Three people died, more than 200 were injured, and 75 were arrested. Among those caught up in the violence were prominent reformers and socialists, including John Burns and Robert Cunninghame Graham. The day became known as Bloody Sunday.

🧩 TRIVIA: Socialists, Irish nationalists, labor activists, and reformers joined forces; supporters included William Morris, Annie Besant, and Eleanor Marx.

🐶 SPOT: The police commissioner had issued a notice banning meetings in the square only days earlier. A surviving copy of that notice is now preserved by the London Museum—a small piece of paper documenting the official order that helped turn a public square into a flashpoint over civil liberties.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The right to protest is most severely tested when those in power find the message inconvenient.

—— ❦ ——

1927 — THE HOLLAND TUNNEL OPENS BENEATH THE HUDSON RIVER 🚗

On November 13, 1927, the Holland Tunnel opened to traffic, connecting Manhattan, New York, with Jersey City, New Jersey. It was an engineering landmark.

Named for chief engineer Clifford Milburn Holland, who died in 1924, the tunnel was ceremonially opened on November 12 by President Calvin Coolidge, who activated the opening signal remotely from Washington. Regular vehicular traffic began at 12:01 a.m. on November 13.

🧩 TRIVIA: The tunnel was the first mechanically ventilated underwater vehicular tunnel. Its four ventilation buildings housed 84 fans—42 blowers and 42 exhaust fans.

🐶 SPOT: At full speed, the ventilation system could completely change the tunnel's air every 90 seconds. The breakthrough was keeping the air breathable beneath a river.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most important breakthroughs are not always visible. Sometimes the technology that makes progress possible is the system quietly keeping people alive.

—— ❦ ——

1956 — THE SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN BUS SEGREGATION IN MONTGOMERY ⚖️

On November 13, 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the federal court ruling in Browder v. Gayle, holding that racial segregation on public buses in Montgomery, Alabama, violated the Constitution. The decision dealt a decisive legal blow to the system of segregated city transportation challenged by the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

The case was brought by four Black women—Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith. The decision came while Martin Luther King Jr. was in court defending himself against a charge connected with the boycott's carpool system. The boycott continued until December 20.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rosa Parks was not a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle. The lawsuit was brought by four other women whose experiences helped establish the constitutional challenge to bus segregation.

🐶 SPOT: Claudette Colvin was only 15 when she refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus in March 1955—nine months before Parks's arrest. Her role was central to the legal case, even though her name became far less familiar to the public.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Historic change is rarely the work of one famous individual. It is built by many people whose courage may receive unequal recognition.

—— ❦ ——

1985 — NEVADO DEL RUIZ DESTROYS ARMERO, COLOMBIA 🌋

On November 13, 1985, the Nevado del Ruiz volcano erupted in Colombia. Heat from the eruption melted part of the mountain's glacier, sending volcanic mudflows—known as lahars—racing down river valleys. The flows overwhelmed Armero and other communities, killing more than 23,000 people in Armero alone and approximately 25,000 across the affected region.

Armero was almost completely buried. Scientists had identified the danger, but conflicting information, poor communication, and no effective evacuation system prevented an adequate response. The tragedy became one of the deadliest volcanic disasters of the 20th century.

🧩 TRIVIA: Lahars are fast-moving mixtures of water, ash, rock, and debris, made especially dangerous when an eruption melts a volcano's snow and ice.

🐶 SPOT: The catastrophe unfolded over hours, not in one instantaneous blast. Ash began falling in Armero around 4 p.m.; the major explosive phase began at 9:09 p.m., generating the flows that swept down the mountain's river valleys.

💡 INSIGHT: Armero was not destroyed by an eruption alone. The scale of the loss exposed the deadly distance that can separate scientific knowledge from public action.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A warning that does not reach people—or cannot be acted upon—is not enough. Preparedness must connect evidence to evacuation, communication, and protection.

—— ❦ ——

2015 — TERRORIST ATTACKS SHATTER PARIS 🕯️

On November 13, 2015, coordinated terrorist attacks struck Paris and the nearby suburb of Saint-Denis. Three ISIS suicide bombers targeted the area around the Stade de France during a football match, while gunmen attacked café and restaurant terraces and stormed the Bataclan concert hall during a performance by the American band Eagles of Death Metal.

The attacks are now officially commemorated as having claimed 132 lives, including 90 at the Bataclan. Hundreds were injured. France declared a state of emergency. The attacks became one of the deadliest episodes of peacetime violence in modern French history.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first explosions occurred outside the Stade de France during a friendly football match between France and Germany. French President François Hollande was in attendance and was evacuated from the stadium.

🐶 SPOT: The Bataclan's security chief, known publicly as Didi, repeatedly entered the concert hall to open emergency exits and help spectators escape. He later explained that he had returned inside to open additional routes, putting himself in danger. He requested anonymity because he feared retaliation.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Terror seeks to turn public life into a place of fear. Remembering the victims—and the courage of those who helped them—is one way to refuse that purpose.

The pages of history turn. The lessons remain. 📜

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🔬 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL & CULTURAL MILESTONES

—— ❦ ——

1940 — DISNEY'S FANTASIA PREMIERES IN NEW YORK 🎼

On November 13, 1940, Walt Disney's Fantasia held its world premiere at the Broadway Theatre in New York City. The film paired animated sequences with classical compositions performed by the Philadelphia Orchestra under conductor Leopold Stokowski, with music commentary by Deems Taylor.

The film made animation an interpretation of music. Its early stereo system, Fantasound, required specially equipped theaters, limiting its initial release.

🧩 TRIVIA: Fantasia originally contained eight animated sequences, including interpretations of Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D Minor, Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker Suite, Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, and Dukas's The Sorcerer's Apprentice.

🐶 SPOT: Fantasound required Disney to install specialized playback equipment in theaters. The system was so expensive and complicated that the film initially opened in only 14 specially equipped theaters—an artistic gamble whose technology was years ahead of what most cinemas could support.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Innovation often arrives before the world is ready to accommodate it. Visionaries sometimes have to build the tools as well as the work.

—— ❦ ——

1980 — VOYAGER 1 COMPLETES ITS SATURN ENCOUNTER 🪐

On November 13, 1980, NASA's Voyager 1 completed its near-encounter phase at Saturn, following its historic close approach the previous day. Its cameras and scientific instruments had revealed extraordinary details about the planet's rings, atmosphere, and moons, giving scientists views impossible from Earth.

Voyager revealed that Saturn's broad rings consisted of many narrower ringlets and that its atmosphere was more dynamic than expected.

🧩 TRIVIA: Voyager 1 photographed Saturn's moon Titan, whose dense atmosphere obscured the surface from the spacecraft's cameras. The atmosphere was found to consist primarily of nitrogen, with methane and other compounds.

🐶 SPOT: Voyager 1's path was deliberately chosen to make a close pass by Titan. The gravity assist sent the spacecraft out of the plane of the planets, ending its opportunity to visit Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 followed the route that preserved those later planetary encounters.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Every great exploration involves choices. A path toward one extraordinary discovery can close the door to another.

—— ❦ ——

1994 — SWEDEN VOTES TO JOIN THE EUROPEAN UNION 🇸🇪

On November 13, 1994, Swedish voters approved joining the European Union in a national referendum. The result was 52.3 percent in favor and 46.8 percent opposed, with turnout reaching approximately 83 percent.

The advisory vote settled Sweden's place in post-Cold War Europe; political parties had agreed to respect the result. Sweden joined the EU on January 1, 1995.

🧩 TRIVIA: Sweden's referendum was not a landslide. The margin between the yes and no votes was only 5.5 percentage points, revealing a country divided over the political and economic implications of membership.

🐶 SPOT: The result did not itself make Sweden an EU member. Parliament completed the formal decision in December 1994, and membership began the following January—an important distinction between a public mandate and the legal act that implements it.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Democratic decisions can be decisive without being unanimous. A close vote still carries a responsibility to govern the whole community.

Here's to curious minds, bold ideas, and discoveries that move humanity forward. 🚀

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎂 FAMOUS BIRTHDAYS

Today we celebrate a theologian, a master storyteller, a pioneering jurist, and celebrated performers.

—— ❦ ——

354 — AUGUSTINE OF HIPPO 📜

Augustine of Hippo, North African Christian theologian and philosopher, became one of the most influential Christian thinkers in Western history. His Confessions and The City of God shaped centuries of thought. Born in Thagaste, in what is now Algeria.

🧩 TRIVIA: Augustine’s mother, Monica, was a major influence on his spiritual life. He later wrote about her persistence and devotion in Confessions, one of the most influential autobiographical works of late antiquity.

1312 — EDWARD III OF ENGLAND 👑

Edward III, King of England (1327–77), is noted for his military success, for restoring royal authority during the opening phase of the Hundred Years’ War, for parliamentary development, and for ruling through the Black Death. Born in Windsor Castle, Berkshire, England.

🧩 TRIVIA: Edward founded the Order of the Garter, traditionally dated to 1348. It became England’s highest order of chivalry and remains one of the oldest surviving orders of knighthood.

1850 — ROBERT LOUIS STEVENSON ✒️

Robert Louis Stevenson, Scottish novelist and poet. His works include Treasure Island, Kidnapped, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, and A Child’s Garden of Verses. He was born in Edinburgh, Scotland.

🧩 TRIVIA: Stevenson trained as a lawyer and passed the Scottish bar in 1875, but he never practiced law. His father’s family had a distinguished history of lighthouse engineering, a profession he chose not to follow.

1856 — LOUIS D. BRANDEIS ⚖️

Louis D. Brandeis, American lawyer and associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States (1916–39). He became the first Jewish U.S. Supreme Court justice when appointed by Woodrow Wilson in 1916. He championed civil liberties, privacy, and the public interest. He was born in Louisville.

🧩 TRIVIA: Brandeis became famous for the “Brandeis brief,” which used social-science research and factual evidence to support a legal argument.

1934 — GARRY MARSHALL 🎬

Garry Marshall, American TV writer (The Dick Van Dyke Show), TV producer (The Odd Couple, Happy Days, Laverne & Shirley), and film director (Pretty Woman, Runaway Bride, The Princess Diaries). Born in New York City.

🧩 TRIVIA: Marshall’s television success created an interconnected comedy universe. Happy Days generated several successful spin-offs, including Laverne & Shirley and Mork & Mindy.

1955 — WHOOPI GOLDBERG (age 71) 🎭

Whoopi Goldberg (born Caryn Elaine Johnson) is an American comedian, actress (The Color Purple, Sister Act), singer, and TV host (The View). Her celebrated work includes The Color Purple, Ghost. Born in New York City.

🧩 TRIVIA: Goldberg won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Ghost (1990), becoming the first Black woman to win that category since Hattie McDaniel in 1940.

Happy birthday! 🎉

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🥀 MEMORIAM

We remember those who died on November 13 and the legacies they left in art, music, public life, and sport.

—— ❦ ——

1868 — GIOACHINO ROSSINI (aged 76) 🎼

Rossini transformed opera with The Barber of Seville, La Cenerentola, and William Tell. His theatrical music made him one of the 19th century's most celebrated composers. He died at his villa in Passy after a long illness and complications following surgery for rectal cancer.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rossini largely stopped composing major operas after William Tell premiered in 1829, when he was only 37. He lived for nearly four more decades, producing occasional later works, including his Petite Messe solennelle.

—— ❦ ——

1903 — CAMILLE PISSARRO (aged 73) 🎨

Pissarro was a central Impressionist and mentor to artists including Cézanne and Gauguin. The only artist to exhibit in all eight Impressionist exhibitions, he died in Paris from sepsis.

🧩 TRIVIA: Pissarro was the only painter to participate in every one of the eight Impressionist exhibitions, making him a unique constant in a movement whose membership and style continually evolved.

—— ❦ ——

1974 — KAREN SILKWOOD (aged 28) ☢️

Silkwood was a chemical technician and union activist who raised safety and contamination concerns at a Kerr-McGee plutonium plant. She was traveling to meet a union representative and a New York Times reporter. The circumstances of her death remain controversial; allegations of foul play were never substantiated. She died in a car crash near Crescent, Oklahoma.

🧩 TRIVIA: A federal investigation established that two biological samples submitted by Silkwood contained plutonium that had not been present when the samples were originally collected. Investigators never established who had introduced the material.

🧬 HUMAN: Beyond the headlines and controversy, Karen Silkwood was a 28-year-old mother of three who loved music, road trips, and auto racing. Friends remembered a spirited young woman whose life included ordinary pleasures and personal connections. Her story deserves to be remembered not only for how it ended, but for the person she was before the world knew her name.

🐶 SPOT: The documents Silkwood was reportedly carrying to the meeting were never recovered from the wrecked car. Their disappearance became one of the enduring unanswered questions surrounding her death, but it does not establish that she was murdered.

—— ❦ ——

2005 — EDDIE GUERRERO (aged 38) 🤼

Mexican-American wrestler Eddie "Latino Heat" Guerrero, a member of the celebrated Guerrero family, became a major WWE star. He won the WWE Championship in 2004 and was admired for his technical skill and charisma. He died in Minneapolis from arteriosclerotic heart disease.

🧩 TRIVIA: Guerrero's famous motto, “Lie, Cheat, and Steal,” became a defining part of his wrestling character. His ability to combine rule-breaking comedy with elite in-ring skill made him a fan favorite.

In remembrance. 🕯️

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🏟️ SPORTS HIGHLIGHTS

—— ❦ ——

1934 — THE NHL RECORDS ITS FIRST PENALTY-SHOT GOAL 🏒

On November 13, 1934, Ralph "Scotty" Bowman of the St. Louis Eagles scored the first penalty-shot goal in NHL history. His successful attempt came against the Montreal Maroons, although the Eagles still lost the game 2–1.

Bowman scored on only the second penalty-shot attempt in NHL history.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first penalty shot in NHL history had been awarded only days earlier, on November 10, 1934. Montreal's Armand Mondou failed to score against Toronto goaltender George "Hainsy" Hainsworth.

🏆 FIRST: Bowman is credited with the first successful penalty-shot goal in NHL history.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A first does not always come with a victory. Sometimes its place in history is secured by the moment itself.

—— ❦ ——

1964 — BOB PETTIT BECOMES THE NBA'S FIRST 20,000-POINT SCORER 🏀

On November 13, 1964, St. Louis Hawks forward Bob "The Bombardier from Baton Rouge" Pettit became the first player in NBA history to score 20,000 career points. He reached the milestone with a 29-point performance against the Cincinnati Royals, although the Hawks lost 123–106.

He won two NBA Most Valuable Player awards and led the Hawks to the 1958 championship.

🧩 TRIVIA: Pettit retired in 1965 with 20,880 career points and was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1971.

🏆 FIRST: Pettit was the first NBA player to reach 20,000 regular-season career points.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Milestones are often built quietly, one game at a time, until the numbers finally reveal the scale of an extraordinary career.

—— ❦ ——

1979 — DARRYL DAWKINS SHATTERS A BACKBOARD WITH A DUNK 💥

On November 13, 1979, Philadelphia 76ers center Darryl "Chocolate Thunder" Dawkins shattered the glass backboard with a powerful dunk during a game against the Kansas City Kings. Dawkins leaped over defender Bill Robinzine and brought the basket down in a spectacular moment that stunned the crowd.

The league subsequently moved toward safer breakaway rims and shatter-resistant backboards.

🧩 TRIVIA: Dawkins gave the dunk an extravagant name: “The Chocolate-Thunder-Flying, Robinzine-Crying, Teeth-Shaking, Glass-Breaking, Rump-Roasting, Bun-Toasting, Wham-Bam Glass-Breaker-I-Am Jam.”

🐶 SPOT: The shattered glass did not simply fall harmlessly to the floor. Pieces reportedly nicked players and became lodged in Julius Erving's Afro. The danger helped make clear that spectacular dunks needed safer equipment.

🏆 FIRST: Dawkins became the first NBA player widely credited with shattering a backboard during a regular-season game.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A moment of spectacle can change the rules of a sport when it exposes a danger that can no longer be ignored.

And that is November 13 on the sporting calendar: a day when a single payment helped change a sport, an arena became a shrine to hockey, and one player owned the boards. 🏆

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On November 13, 1956, which U.S. Supreme Court case affirmed that racial segregation on Montgomery's public buses was unconstitutional?

[A] Plessy v. Ferguson

[B] Brown v. Board of Education

[C] Browder v. Gayle

[D] Loving v. Virginia

Think it over before scrolling to the answer. 👀

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🌎 CLOSING

November 13 asks what happens when human decisions meet human consequences. London protesters demanding dignity were met with violence; a Supreme Court ruling advanced the struggle against segregation; the Holland Tunnel joined communities; and Armero exposed the terrible cost of failed warnings.

The Paris attacks reveal the human cost of hatred, while the courage of survivors and rescuers shows what people can do in darkness. Fantasia expanded cinema, Voyager widened our view of Saturn, and Sweden made a consequential democratic choice.

World Kindness Day offers a fitting challenge: history records the damage people inflict, but also the compassion and courage that resist it. Remember those behind the milestones, give overlooked voices their place, and never mistake progress for a guarantee.

History has had its turn. Now make yours. ✨

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [C] — BROWDER v. GAYLE.

On November 13, 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the federal court's ruling that segregation on Montgomery's public buses violated the Fourteenth Amendment. The case was brought by Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith, four Black women whose experiences challenged the city's discriminatory bus laws.

The ruling was a crucial victory for the boycott, which continued until December 20, 1956, when the buses were integrated. The case reminds us that the struggle for civil rights was advanced not only by famous leaders, but also by people whose names deserve to be remembered.

text:
Curiosity – Part 2 of 2: Curiosity learns. Control yearns.

Scripture

“You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to the heavens; I will raise my throne above the stars of God; I will sit enthroned on the mount of assembly, on the utmost heights of Mount Zaphon. I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.’” – Isaiah 14:13-14 (NIV)

Reflection 

Yesterday we looked at George Washington Carver, who prayed to the Creator, studied the peanut with humble curiosity and gave Him the credit for the nearly 300 uses for it that he promoted.

Today, the opposite.

Joseph Stalin studied to be a priest at a seminary in Tiflis, in the country of Georgia, until the seminary expelled him in 1899. Thirty years later he ruled the Soviet Union and forced its farmers to give up their farms, animals and harvests to collective farms run by the government. When farms came up short of the grain quotas set in Moscow, Soviet officials took the grain anyway. In Ukraine alone at least 3.9 million people starved to death in 1932 and 1933.

Nikolai Vavilov, a world-famous Soviet plant scientist, traveled the world collecting seeds to breed crops that would end famine. He publicly disagreed with the farm science Stalin backed. Stalin’s secret police arrested Vavilov in 1940 and he starved to death in a Soviet prison on Jan. 26, 1943 – three weeks after Carver died in Alabama.

Curiosity learns. Control yearns.

Today’s verses describe Satan’s fall. That is how I read them and how many Christians have read them for centuries. The prophet Isaiah placed them in a message addressed to the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), a man who ruled nations by force, and the pride in that king’s heart came from the same enemy. Count the times “I will” shows up in those two verses: five. Not one of the five asks God a question. The fifth is the goal: “I will make myself like the Most High.” The serpent made Eve the same offer in the garden – eat the fruit and she would be like God (Genesis 3:5).

I believe the desire to control without consulting God comes from the enemy. We may not see it in ourselves, but when we use whatever means necessary – power and money – to impose our will, and our will is not God’s will, we are trying to be higher than God, more powerful than God and praised instead of God. We glorify “I” instead of the “I AM” – the name God gave Moses for Himself (Exodus 3:14) – and our true identity is in Him. That is a dangerous and foolish way to think and live.

None of us runs a country. We do have power and money at our level – the final say with our kids, a paycheck we write, a following online – and the temptation is the same: decide what we want, then push until we get it, without asking God whether He wants it.

Isaiah wrote that the one who made those five claims is brought down to the grave (Isaiah 14:15). Stalin died in 1953, and in 1961 the Soviet government took his name off the city of Stalingrad.

Are we asking God where He is working and how to join Him? Or do we pray only after we’ve already made up our minds?

Two points to ponder:

1. Check what you want against what God wants. Power and money are tools. Before you spend the money, pull rank or push harder to get your way, ask God whether it is His will.

2. Ask who gets the praise. Carver gave the Creator the credit. Stalin’s government named cities after him. When we get our way, who do we want people to thank?

Application

Pray and ask God to show you one situation you are trying to control today – a decision your grown kid is making, an argument with your spouse you intend to win, a coworker you’ve been working around, an outcome you’ve been throwing money at. Or something altogether different. Then ask God two questions: “God, is what I want here what You want?” and “Where are You already working in this and how do I join You?” If He tells you to let go, let go.

Prayer

Father, we confess that we often decide what we want and then ask You to bless it. We have used money, position and pressure to get our way without asking whether it was Your way. Forgive us for trying to take Your place. You are the I AM. Give us – and our children – a humble curiosity to see where You are working and the courage to join You there. We give You the credit and the praise. Amen.

🔟 So what can the US actually control? Two things.

First, it can control that China doesn't buy ASML's EUV machines. That's easy.

Second, it can try and control where banned chips end up. For instance, Nvidia can sell Blackwell chips to a data center in Singapore or Malaysia. US rules then require that those chips stay there and don't get resold to Chinese firms. In practice, however, that's hard to check from Washington.

That is why Megaspeed, the Alice Huang-led Singapore firm, is at the center of the Jensen affair. It bought more than $4bn of Nvidia chips, more than half of them Blackwell. It is suspected of passing them to Chinese firms.

What does this mean for chip founders, especially in Europe? Export rules now shape the market as much as technology does. A US rule can reach a European product if it contains enough American technology, so founders need to know where their parts and tools come from. ASML shows that one European company can hold a position no one else can fill. And with the US and China each trying to stop depending on the other, there's room for chips, software, and tools that offer a third option. 

Meanwhile, whatever comes next for him, Jensen built one of the great companies of our time, starting from that booth at Denny's. He spent his last year as CEO persuading Washington to finally let Nvidia sell to China. For now, Beijing is the one saying no./.

text:
Behind the Scenes from London Through Jordanian Eyes

Washington's Political Earthquake, Israel's Uncertainty and Britain's Strategic Recalibration

The Middle East is entering a decisive political phase. Washington's shifting balance of power and Israel's political uncertainty are creating new diplomatic calculations, raising an important question: how will Britain respond?

The Democrats' victory in both chambers of the US Congress has altered Washington's political landscape. Meanwhile, Israeli President Isaac Herzog's decision to task Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government signals a potential change in Israel's political direction, although the outcome remains uncertain.

For London, these developments present an opportunity to reassess Britain's approach to the Middle East, balancing its traditional alliance with Washington against its strategic interests and international responsibilities.

From a Jordanian perspective, this changing landscape reinforces the importance of His Majesty King Abdullah II's longstanding diplomatic vision: regional stability cannot be secured through military power alone, but through dialogue, international law and recognition of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.

Jordan's strategic position, established international partnerships and historic Hashemite Custodianship of Jerusalem's Islamic and Christian holy sites give the Kingdom a central role in efforts to restore regional stability.

For Britain, strengthening cooperation with Amman offers an opportunity to advance de-escalation, humanitarian access to Gaza and renewed momentum towards a just and lasting two-state solution.

Yet political change in Washington or Israel does not automatically guarantee diplomatic progress. Real transformation requires political courage, consistency and a willingness to turn opportunities into meaningful action.

Britain possesses the diplomatic experience and international relationships to contribute to a more balanced regional future. Its credibility will depend on its commitment to international law, constructive partnerships and a just political settlement.

The Middle East needs more than changing governments and shifting alliances. It needs a lasting political vision built on justice, stability and mutual respect.

The question remains: Will London seize this historic moment to help shape a more balanced Middle East, or allow yesterday's political assumptions to determine tomorrow's future?

Helmi Al-Harahsheh
Political Writer & Analyst | London

WASHINGTON - Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren attended the Business 20 (B20) USA 2026 Summit, hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce November 9–11 in Washington, D.C. The gathering brought together business leaders, governors and international representatives for discussions on economic growth, investment and business development. 

The B20 serves as the business engagement forum of the Group of Twenty (G20). This year marked the first B20 Summit held in the United States, providing an opportunity to bring Navajo perspectives into conversations with business and government leaders from around the world.

President Nygren attended sessions hosted by program leaders like UPS Chief Executive Officer Carol B. Tomé, Maryland Governor Wes Moore, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt and other leaders from manufacturing, energy, technology and sports. 

Discussions addressed how businesses reach customers, attract investment, strengthen supply chains and respond to changes in the economy. 

President Nygren also spoke with fellow participants and received a challenge coin during the gathering.

For Navajo communities, these discussions connect to practical priorities including:

• Supporting Navajo-owned businesses through access to financing, new customers and opportunities to supply larger companies.

• Strengthening roads, broadband and reliable utilities so local businesses have the services they need to operate and grow.

• Connecting Navajo workers and students with education, apprenticeships and employers while supporting more employment opportunities close to home.

National workforce trends also show the importance of connecting people with available opportunities. In September 2026, the United States had approximately 7.5 million job openings and 7.1 million unemployed people, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. For Navajo communities, access to employment requires attention to training, transportation, childcare and where jobs are located. 

President Nygren also spoke with Isiah Thomas, chairman and chief executive officer of Isiah Enterprises, about making sports accessible to children of every skill level. Their conversation focused on safe places to play and the role adults and community partners have in helping cover participation costs.

For Navajo youth, the message is straightforward: every child deserves opportunities to participate, learn and enjoy sports, regardless of athletic ability or family income. Supporting recreation means investing in places and programs where children feel welcome, stay active and build friendships.

President Nygren’s participation offered an opportunity to build relationships and explore ideas relevant to the Nation’s work. Pursuing those opportunities means keeping Navajo sovereignty and community priorities at the center, with a focus on supporting local businesses, employment and young people.

text:
If your ex is a police officer, he may be able to look up where cameras have spotted your car. No warrant needed. And many departments do little to check who's searching.

A Washington Post investigation found more than two dozen cases of officers accused of using plate readers to keep tabs on wives, girlfriends, exes and their new partners, or women they wanted to meet. Most of those cases ran on one company's cameras. That company offers an alert that flags suspicious searches to supervisors. Agencies have to switch it on. Want to guess how many have?

The rest of this week's issue is about other settings somebody else chose:

Kenya uses AI to guess what families earn from their floors, toilets and radios, then sets their health insurance payments from that guess. When it guesses wrong, an adviser to the health ministry says, it was set up to lean one particular way. His explanation for why is hard to forget.

A disaster nonprofit in India says its AI can pick out the family under the hottest roof in a heat wave. Another counts a farm's trees with drones and AI, and says it can now show a farmer how a payment was figured. Nice claims, mostly from the nonprofits themselves.

And a newspaper chain fed a reporter's story about a man and his golden retriever into an AI tool. What came out the other side, and what happened to the writer's name, is a good look at why unions want AI rules in writing.

Issue 45 of Smarter Society AI is called "Somebody Has to Set the AI Thermostat." Every office has a thermostat fight. The people stuck under the vent rarely get to pick the number.

Link is in the comments.

Demand for .si has spread from Slovenia to the rest of the world in a matter of weeks. AI companies want the name that matches their .ai, brand owners want to secure theirs before someone else does, and investors are buying short names in bulk.

Many go to their hosting provider, MSP or agency first, with two questions: should we register .si, and who can set it up? In this article, we look at:

What the SI order changed
Why .si demand can turn into years of renewals
Three .si services you can sell
How to protect your margin and your clients
The SI order gives you a new reason to talk domains with every client
On 29 September 2026, the US government made “super intelligence”, or SI, its official term for AI in federal communications. Slovenia’s country code uses the same two letters, in the same way Anguilla’s .ai matched “AI”, and new .si registrations rose from 3,515 in August to 46,066 in September.

The executive order “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence” tells US federal agencies to use “SI” and “super intelligence” in official communications. It covers only the US federal government, so companies can keep using “AI”. Even so, news of the order put the letters SI in front of business owners, and many now want a matching domain. Slovenia’s registry felt that demand first.

Slovenia’s ccTLD has gone global, and global ccTLDs bring years of renewal revenue
A ccTLD is a country-code top-level domain, such as .de for Germany or .si for Slovenia. Slovenia’s Academic and Research Network runs https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG, and for most of its history the domain served Slovenian entrepreneurs and organizations.

That changed after the executive order in Washington DC. https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG’s domain count grew by more than a fifth in just over a week, and the registry could accept buyers from any country because .si has an open registration policy: anyone, anywhere can register a .si name without a Slovenian address or company. Many ccTLDs ask for a local presence, so this open policy is what turns a national domain into a global product your customers can buy.

Anguilla’s .ai followed the same path. It began as the country code of a small Caribbean territory, and AI companies turned it into a global address. Domain fees now bring in almost half of Anguilla’s government revenue, according to Premier Cora Richardson Hodge.

Slovenia’s position is different. https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG charges registrars a flat fee per name, each registrar sets its own end price, and Slovenia has a far larger economy, so .si plays a much smaller role in its budget. For resellers, the more useful lesson from .ai is renewals: about 90% of .ai names renew after two years, according to the IMF. Those renewals start with the questions your clients ask today.

Your clients will ask you about Superintelligence .si domain .si, so have a clear recommendation ready
https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG, the registry that runs .si, has advised businesses to register their brand and company names as Superintelligence .si domains as soon as possible. Many of your clients will read this in the news, and because you manage their domains, they will ask you whether they need a .si too.

Two groups are likely to ask first. Clients with registered trademarks want to secure their names before someone else holds them. AI and SaaS companies with a .ai or .com address want the matching .si, so their brand looks the same across extensions. Netcraft already counts more than 44,000 names that exist in both .si and .ai, and our recent .si and .ai comparison covers how the two extensions differ.

Each of these requests is a chance to sell a service that renews every year, and three services fit .si well.

Three .si services that add recurring revenue to every client account
You can package .si into three services that renew every year: defensive .si registration for client brands, .si bundled with .ai and .com for AI launches, and lookalike monitoring as part of a .si brand protection retainer.

Each one fits the domain portfolio management work you already do:

Defensive .si for client brands: start with each client’s core brands and company name, which keeps costs low.
.si with .ai and .com for AI launches: offer the .si alongside the .ai and .com in one package, so no one else can claim the matching name.
Lookalike monitoring: watch for new domains that copy a client’s brand with a small spelling change, and act early.
More .si names in your clients’ portfolios also mean more work for your abuse desk and your renewal process, so plan for both from the start.

Protect client trust and renewal revenue by planning for .si abuse now
In research from 24 September to 1 October 2026, Netcraft found a low level of fraud on .si and no rise in phishing linked to the rename. It expects criminals to take more interest if “SI” becomes a more trusted term. One risk stands out: “s” sits next to “a”, so a .si name is one typo away from its .ai version. Criminals can register these lookalikes, a tactic called typosquatting, to copy legitimate AI sites.

Speculation also affects renewals. Netcraft found that buyers put about 52% of the Superintelligence .si domain  names they bought at one registrar between 19 and 22 September up for resale. Some investors will let unsold names expire, so build a lower year-two renewal rate into your forecasts and set up renewal reminders early.

If someone else holds a client’s .si name, the dispute goes through https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG’s own process, so point them to the registry’s rules first. Clear processes protect your margin, and so does the price you pay for every name you sell.

Keep your .si margin intact with cost-plus Membership pricing
When a domain trends, more registrars add it and compete on price. Providers that pay full price for each name lose margin on every sale.

Openprovider Membership gives you cost-plus access to every TLD we are accredited for, including .si, with plans from $4.99 a year, so you can set your own margin on top.

Until 30 November 2026, new resellers can register up to 5 .si for €8.39 each in the first year, after verification. After that, every .si renews at €10.29 a year (€10 for Members), so year two stays predictable.

With the economics in place, getting started takes three steps.

Start earning from .si in three steps
First, compare each client’s brands and company names against .si, and list the core names still free. Next, run that list through our bulk check, which searches up to 500 .si names at once, and register the names your clients approve in a single order. Finally, add .si to the storefront your customers already use, through our WHMCS module or the Openprovider API, which you can test first in a free sandbox, a test environment that never touches live domains.

The providers who answer client questions about .si first become the ones they trust with the rest of their portfolio. Compare Membership plans to get .si at registry cost prices, or register your .si domains while our first-year offer runs until 30 November 2026.

Frequently asked questions (FAQ)
What does SI stand for?
SI stands for “super intelligence”. On 29 September 2026, a US executive order told federal agencies to use “SI” and “super intelligence” in place of “AI” in official communications. SI is also Slovenia’s country code, which is why demand for .si grew so quickly.

Who runs the Superintelligence .si domain ?
Slovenia’s Academic and Research Network runs https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG, the registry behind .si. Anyone, anywhere can register a .si name without a Slovenian address or company. https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG charges registrars a flat fee per name, and each registrar sets its own end price.

Should agencies register .si for clients?
For clients with registered brands, yes. https://t.co/ZLlbZEemBG advises brand owners to secure their .si as soon as possible. Start with each client’s core brands, and add .si to new AI launches alongside .ai and .com, so no one else can claim the matching name.

Is .si safe from abuse?
Netcraft reports low fraud on .si so far. Because “s” sits next to “a” on the keyboard, criminals could register .si lookalikes of .ai sites, a tactic called typosquatting. Brand owners with a .ai domain can register the matching .si, and providers can monitor client brands for new lookalikes.

text:
The next few months could be the darkest period in Bitcoin and crypto history.

And I don’t think most investors are prepared for what’s coming.

Two dangerous forces are converging: a political reckoning in Washington and an AI-powered cybersecurity threat that could wipe out billions in crypto wealth.

First, Trump losing the midterm elections marks the beginning of the end of his political power.

As his influence weakens, his political opponents have an opportunity to investigate the financial empire built around his presidency.

And crypto is an obvious target.

Follow the money.

Justin Sun invested $75 million in the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial.

Abu Dhabi-backed MGX used USD1, the Trump-linked stablecoin, for a $2 billion investment in Binance.

Trump subsequently pardoned Binance founder CZ.

Then there’s the $TRUMP memecoin, whose largest holders were offered exclusive access to presidential events.

These relationships don’t establish corruption. But they raise questions about conflicts of interest that Democrats have already begun investigating.

Imagine months of congressional hearings, subpoenas, investigations, and damaging headlines involving some of the biggest names in crypto.

The consequences could spread far beyond Trump.

And that’s only the political threat.

The second threat is AI. And this one worries me even more.

We’ve already witnessed multibillion-dollar hacks in crypto.

Binance says it replenished the assets lost in its latest major security breach. But how many other companies could survive losing billions?

What happens when the next victim is a custodian holding billions in customer funds?

Or an exchange that doesn’t have Binance’s financial resources?

For many companies, that would be the end. Their customers could lose everything.

And artificial intelligence is making this threat increasingly serious.

Every major AI breakthrough potentially gives attackers better tools for discovering vulnerabilities, developing malware, impersonating employees, and executing sophisticated attacks.

AI doesn’t need to break Bitcoin’s cryptography to cause catastrophic damage.

It only needs to compromise the systems and people protecting our coins.

We’ve seen Tether and Circle freeze stolen stablecoins in certain incidents.

But Bitcoin has no central issuer capable of freezing stolen BTC.

If your private keys are compromised, your coins can disappear permanently.

No bailout. No reversal. No second chance.

Now here’s the part I want every Bitcoin investor to understand.

Bitcoin WILL reach $1 million. That’s my conviction.

But the road there will be brutal.

There will be crashes, scandals, hacks, bankruptcies, and moments when the entire industry appears to be collapsing.

And many investors who correctly predicted Bitcoin’s future will still lose everything.

Because being right about the future doesn’t guarantee you’ll survive long enough to experience it.

This brings me to Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s philosophy, which I would summarize in one sentence:

“To get rich, you first need to survive.”

Avoid the risk of ruin.

Protect your private keys. Diversify custody. Avoid excessive leverage. Never allow one exchange, one investment, or one security failure to wipe you out.

You can recover from a 70% market crash if you still own your coins.

You cannot recover from losing everything if you have no capital left.

I am not bearish on Bitcoin.

I am bearish on how many investors will survive the journey.

Bitcoin WILL reach $1 million.

But the question is whether you’ll still own any when it does.

text:
The following summary from Grok does not include any of your statements : **The statement is incorrect on both counts.**

### 1. “It was substantially correct and very damning”

This is not supported by the major investigations.

- **Mueller Report (2019)**: Did not establish that the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government. Many of the dossier’s specific conspiracy claims were not corroborated.
- **DOJ Inspector General Horowitz Report (2019)**: Found that much of the material in the Steele reports “could not be corroborated,” certain allegations were “inaccurate or inconsistent” with other FBI findings, and the primary sub-source (Igor Danchenko) told the FBI that Steele had misstated or exaggerated information. Steele was not the originating source of the factual information.
- **Special Counsel Durham Report (2023)**: Explicitly stated that the FBI “did not and could not corroborate any of the substantive allegations” in the Steele reports. The FBI even offered Steele $1 million to corroborate them; he could not.
- Specific high-profile claims (e.g., Michael Cohen’s alleged Prague meeting, Carter Page’s meetings with Igor Sechin and Igor Divyekin, the existence of a “well-developed conspiracy,” the “pee tape”) were never verified and in several cases contradicted by evidence or denials.
- Steele himself described the memos as unverified “raw intelligence.”

Broader, separately established facts (Russian election interference, Putin’s preference for Trump over Clinton, contacts between some Trump associates and Russians) do not make the dossier’s specific, central claims “substantially correct.” Official reviews treated most of its substantive allegations as unverified or false.

### 2. “That’s why the Republicans who commissioned it stopped paying for it”

This misstates the timeline and who paid for what.

- In late 2015, the conservative *Washington Free Beacon* (backed by Republican donor Paul Singer) hired Fusion GPS for general opposition research on Trump and other GOP primary candidates. This work focused mainly on domestic and business issues.
- The Free Beacon ended its contract in spring 2016 (around May) once Trump became the presumptive nominee—standard practice for primary opposition research.
- Christopher Steele was hired by Fusion GPS only *after* this, in June 2016, when the Democratic National Committee and Clinton campaign (via the law firm Perkins Coie) took over funding.
- The Free Beacon stated it had “no knowledge of or connection to the Steele dossier, did not pay for the dossier, and never had contact with, knowledge of, or provided payment for any work performed by Christopher Steele.”

Republicans funded earlier, non-Steele Fusion GPS research. They did not commission the Steele dossier/report itself, and they stopped paying because the primary was over, not because of damning Steele findings (which had not yet been produced under their funding).

### Outcomes
- The dossier was used by the FBI in FISA warrant applications on Carter Page (Horowitz identified 17 significant errors/omissions in those applications).
- It heavily shaped media coverage and political narratives in 2016–2017.
- Subsequent official reviews (Horowitz, Durham, Mueller) found the core collusion claims unsubstantiated.
- The DNC and Clinton campaign were later fined by the FEC for misreporting the payments to Perkins Coie as legal services rather than opposition research.

In short: the dossier was not substantially verified as correct, and Republicans did not commission or then abandon it because of its content. The Democratic funding chain and the failure of official investigations to corroborate its key allegations are the documented record.[](<https://t.co/QdEvSy6JTL>)[](<https://t.co/fYpUYvFl2c>)[](<https://t.co/nX3LHqfT4J>)[](<https://t.co/sO4ukiAzqd>)

text:
Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” 

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” 

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. 

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. 

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. 

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. 

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.  

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

text:
I think people are blowing ears of control for a prospect out of proportion when it comes to MLB and the new CBA discussions.

For example, the Tampa Bay Rays are not going to wake up post-CBA and start operating differently because they can't. Today, you would offer prospect A, B, and C for a Tampa Bay Ray player, and those players come with six years of control. If Tampa Bay still likes prospect A, B, and C, they're not going to not make that trade anymore because the control is five years now instead of six. They're not going to start spending a ton of money because a prospect comes with one less year of control.

Fundamentally, one thing it may alter is in regards to how teams like Tampa Bay operate. They may choose to trade that player one year sooner in order for that player to still have retained value due to years of control. But as far as acquiring players, teams like Tampa Bay and other small market teams aren't going to just stop being a prospect-churning machine. It's how they operate, it's how they have to operate regardless if a cap exists or not, regardless if a floor exists or not. Teams like Tampa Bay will spend up to the floor and then they will continue to trade key players with a few years left of control, in their prime, for a shit ton of prospects, and they will still rely on their player talent evaluation and everything that has made Tampa Bay successful. That will not change, and one less year of control will not alter how they run their organization

I say this because, in regards to transactions happening before December 1st, I've listened to a lot of podcasts and radio shows that rely on this year of control debate on whether deals should be done or not since teams don't know what they're buying. And they do know what they're buying: they're buying a prospect that they have long-term control of, because that's how they operate their baseball team, and one year isn't going to alter how they run their team, period. So deals should and likely will, I think, be possible before the end of the month. #STLCards

text:
Love is Kept by Being Shared

A Course in Miracles offers this thought: “All gifts I give my brothers are my own.”

I find myself returning to that simple truth this morning.

There is something deeply meaningful about genuine presence, for it remains the most honest offering.

One of the wake-up calls in life is discovering how differently we each move through the world.

Among those who have experienced awakening, the paths are different, as are the ways that deeper realization finds expression.

There is no judgment in that. We each unfold in our own way.

Still, I sometimes find myself wondering why the simple, open sharing of Love can seem so elusive.

I had imagined that, in recognizing our Oneness, something would naturally begin to coalesce between us. 
That what is realized within would find its way into how we meet one another in presence.

Perhaps that gathering into the One is already happening, just beneath the surface, in a timing entirely its own.🪶
